11119.title: Landscape Architecture Studio 1
11119.description: This subject is an introduction to landscape architecture, equipping you with an understanding of the practice's core themes and its design techniques. You'll develop skills in recognising, describing and shaping landforms to create contextually sensitive topographic designs. Through hands-on site analysis and technical exercises, you'll learn to articulate the physical attributes of landscapes, using both analogue and digital methods, in combination, to express landform characteristics functionally and artistically. You'll also explore various scales of landscape interpretation and representation, integrating these skills into a cohesive design process for site-specific proposals. Complementing the subject's practical work, lectures provide insight into design theory and its application in landscape architecture, drawing on historical and contemporary sources to illustrate key design concepts such as site, context, change and criticality
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a growing awareness and appreciation for landform: its expressive qualities, cultural meanings, physical properties, and functions.
Establish a critical engagement with varied source materials through primary and secondary research.
Use an iterate design process to generate, test and evaluate a design proposal.
Make effective use of fundamental representational forms, techniques and conventions.
Present work, visually and verbally, in a logical, precise and engaging manner.

11128.title: Communications 1
11128.description: This subject prepares you to effectively communicate landscape architectural ideas using both digital and analogue tools, developing fundamental technical abilities and an aptitude for critical thinking. You'll engage with a variety of techniques such as CAD for 2D and 3D drawings, collage, hand-sketching for analysis, and multimedia strategies to create a unified presentation of your design concepts. Additionally, you'll refine your verbal presentation skills to articulate your ideas to diverse audiences. Through lectures, digital labs, and studio sessions, you'll perform iterative exercises that foster a comprehensive understanding of design communication.
learningOutcomes: Use digital drawing softwares as tools for representing the medium of landscape.
Practice hand drawing as a tool for exploration and communication.
Create and present a coherent set of visuals documents using an effective communication strategy.

11129.title: Communications 2
11129.description:
A landscape’s capacity for change is considered indeterminate: variable and unpredictable. Whilst convention in landscape architecture views this as a problem, experimental practice understands indeterminacy to be an unavoidable and productive function of designed landscapes and their processes of creation. This subject argues that this shift necessitates a re-imaging of representation and communication as functions of designing. In the interests of surpassing existing constraints and dogmas, this subject thinks critically and expansively about the visual outputs associated with designed landscapes from the perspective of the increasing prominence of disruptive technologies, including, but not limited to: generative AI and social media.

Built on exposure to theories and philosophies of change, indeterminacy and technological disruption students are challenged to critically consider how indeterminate landscapes might be known, valued, generated, constructed, managed and documented with the aid of artificial intelligence and networked communications. Investigations are structured across a series of visual experiments, using contemporary built precedents as case studies for examining the relationship between different indeterminate registers and new technologies. On the basis of these experiments, students consider how indeterminacy, in the affirmative, prompts us to re-imagine design and designing, and the form and function of representations and communication therein.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish between different approaches to change in landscape architecture using the concept of indeterminacy and its various registers
Identify how the concept of indeterminacy impacts the ways designed landscapes are created, managed and valued.
Critically evaluate the impacts of emerging technologies on design outcomes and their attendant processes of design
Carry out case study research in a manner that draws critically on a variety of different source materials

11130.title: Landscape Architecture Studio 3
11130.description:
This subject is centred on the transformation of large scale territorial environments, focusing on hydrological systems which intersect agricultural, urban, wetland and coastal spaces. 

Through fieldwork and territorial data analysis, you will explore the accumulation, erosion, and deposition of materials from air and water currents, as well as anthropogenic activities. Design proposals produced in this studio will be informed by a diverse range of community voices, each offering a window into the challenges of working across both social and ecological spaces.

Digital programs will be used to enhance student’s digital cartographic visualisation skills, with a focus on learning QGIS and its adjacent softwares. Alongside QGIS, students will also learn photogrammetry, and digital modelling with Rhino and Grasshopper. Combined, these technologies will be utilised to analyse and represent systems such as estuaries, dunes and wetlands across a variety of scales and perspectives.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of material processes and flows with respect to natural landscape systems.
Effectively deploy digital strategies and tools for diagnostic and generative purposes.
Critically reflect on an intervention’s impacts across scales of time and space.
Use appropriate representational forms and techniques to effectively communicate material processes and flows, and ecological relationships.
Collaborate in a manner that is equitable, respectful and constructive.

11148.title: Landscape Architecture Global Studio B
11148.description: This subject takes you beyond Australian borders to explore international landscape and architectural practices, encouraging you to critically reassess the discipline's identity and your own preconceptions. Through direct engagement with a foreign locale, you'll gain valuable insights into new design methodologies, sociocultural dynamics, and ways of living. This experience not only broadens your knowledge but also hones your skills in navigating and appreciating the unfamiliar with cultural sensitivity. Additionally, it offers opportunities for international networking and developing a global design mindset. Your immersive learning will include site visits, discussions, and collaborative workshops, enriching your professional growth and perspective.
learningOutcomes: Identify and describe the characteristics of Landscape Architectural practices particular to a prescribed international location.
Critically reflect on alternative cultural experiences in a manner that is both inquisitive and respectful of difference.
Critically employ visual media to apprehend and document exemplars: built works, urban environments and regional landscapes.
Execute work to a high standard of rigor and craft.

11172.title: Landscape History and Theory 1
11172.description:
History and Theory 01: Climatic Histories of Architecture and Landscape 

“Think about it: a geological time (vast, almost unthinkable), juxtaposed in one word with very specific, immediate things – 1784, soot, 1945, Nagasaki, plutonium. This is not a historical age but a geological one. Or better: we are no longer able to think history as exclusively human, for the very reason that we are in the Anthropocene.”

  • Timothy Morton, Hyperobjects: Philosophy and Ecology After the End of the World, p.5.

This subject introduces students to landscape/architectural thinking, and the socio-political forces that have produced our contemporary climatic attitudes. Our encounters with climate are always mediated, whether it be via bodily sensation, data collection, news, or scientific reporting. Therefore, this subject seeks to engage with the history of climate through a variety of media, focusing on how climate manifests in material, epistemological, and landscape histories. The subject traces key moments from our current critical moment of the Anthropocene to the beginning of the Industrial Revolution, examining the entanglements that connect concepts such as climate change, decolonisation, and environmental and social justice to landscape architectural projects, practices, technologies and techniques.

Through studying a range of critical theory texts, historical events, and case studies, students will explore connections between climate histories, ecological transformations, and design proposals. This subject takes a non-chronological approach to studying the history of climate, choosing instead to focus on four typologies and scales of human-nature interactions throughout time. The subject encourages critical reflection on the socio-political dimensions of design and the evolving definitions of community, environment, and justice, equipping students with a deeper understanding of environmental attitudes, landscape stories, and histories.
learningOutcomes: Describe the historical, cultural, and theoretical aspects of climate change, colonisation, and social justice with respect to landscape architecture.
Identify methodologies involved in the study and production of climate history and theory.
Demonstrate how climate data is generated and interpreted by different actors
Explain the material links between climate change and the historic production of objects, rituals, places, and landscapes.
Engage critically with scholarly work, academic texts, visual evidence, and cultural products and construct and deliver rigorous and persuasive arguments using relevant sources.

11174.title: Landscape History and Theory 2
11174.description: This subject critically assesses key concepts in landscape architecture, such as landscape, nature, wilderness, and notions of the picturesque, sublime, and pastoral. It investigates the historical and cultural evolution of these ideas across various domains, including architecture, art, literature, and science. You'll also explore the significance of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander traditional knowledge and land connections, considering their impact on the future of Australian landscape architecture. This comprehensive examination aims to deepen your understanding and respect for the diverse influences shaping the field.
learningOutcomes: Exhibit a critical understanding of both modern and historical perspectives on landscape culture and design.
Show proficiency in formulating formal written arguments and in the selective use or production of images.
Apply fundamental academic research techniques for information retrieval, evaluation, and proper academic referencing and writing.

11177.title: Botany
11177.description: This subject equips you with foundational knowledge in botany, horticulture, and plant aesthetics, essential components of landscape architecture. You'll learn to observe, research, identify, and document various plant species, understanding their horticultural needs. This forms the basis for planting design and fosters an appreciation for vegetation. Your learning experience combines lectures, tutorials, and discussions, complemented by potential site visits and workshops.
learningOutcomes: Independently research and learn about plant species and communities using observation, identification and research skills.
Develop ways of observing, drawing and documenting plants individually and in natural associations (i.e. plant communities) through a range of media.
Build skills and knowledge in the cultivation of plants, including propagation, plant selection, soil types, care and plant tolerances.
Develop drawing techniques for plant documentation and design. Curate and communicate phenomena through writing, drawing and photography.

You'll study landscape construction fundamentals, material properties, assembly processes, and the intricacies of construction detailing and documentation. Additionally, you'll learn about the management and maintenance of landscapes. The subject highlights the importance of integrating technology with landscape and design objectives, enhancing your understanding of the design process from concept to completion.

Apply technology in a landscape context to achieve design intent.
Prepare detailed representations of constructions in two and three dimensions.

11182.title: Urbanisms
11182.description: This subject provides a comprehensive understanding of urban development, examining cities within their regional contexts and across various times, locations, and cultures. You'll explore architectural and urban planning theories, the impact of new technologies on urban growth, and the urban challenges posed by climate change. The course aims to equip you with skills to research, discuss, and design urban environments, leveraging your architectural or landscape architectural expertise. You'll delve into the interplay between cities, regions, and their supporting systems, addressing future urban issues. Emphasising the unique perspectives of architecture and landscape architecture, you'll investigate urbanism through diverse projects and debates, building upon prior knowledge and fostering a deeper grasp of the dynamics shaping cities and their urbanisms. This will enable you to situate your studio work within broader urban discourses.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a critical understanding of the range of forces and processes that have shaped a range of cities, and the development of different forms of urbanism.
Demonstrate an understanding of key architectural, landscape architectural and other thinkers on the city, and of influential design projects, both built and unbuilt.
Synthesise complex ideas and evidence about the array of social, technical and environmental practices that constitute cities and urbanism.
Carry out research and analysis that meets the subject’s objectives.
Work individually, and as part of a team, to produce high quality architectural research, analysis and communication.

11183.title: Ecology
11183.description: This subject immerses landscape architecture, interior architecture, and architecture students in ecological thinking, teaching them to observe and comprehend nature and its systems. You'll explore Sydney's geology, soil, and vegetation through lectures and field trips. The course presents ecology as a scientific discipline, alongside geology and botany, and may include indigenous perspectives on nature. You'll learn about threats to natural systems and landscape architecture's role in environmental stewardship. The blend of on-campus learning and field excursions allows you to directly engage with and analyse ecological communities, understanding the interactions within nature.
learningOutcomes: Use text and visual media to describe and analyse ecological phenomena.
Utilise appropriate field methods to assess, identify and document biophysical field conditions.

Demonstrate knowledge of the interrelated ecological and human systems of the Sydney region, identifying ecological patterns, processes and interrelationships through engagement with class readings, field trips, discussions and assessment tasks.
Be capable of utilising ecological knowledge to produce well-informed, interesting, responsible and site-appropriate work.

11186.title: Grading and Site Works
11186.description: This subject explores the fundamentals of landscape grading, introducing you to the tools and methods used to alter the world around us. You will learn how to read common landform typologies, regrade with contour plans and sections, work with typography and hydrology, and adjust landscapes for both human and non-human activities. It also examines soil as a core material, exploring its composition, applications and essential role for terrestrial ecology. This comprehensive analysis will prepare you for one of the most fundamental activities practiced in Landscape Architecture.
learningOutcomes: Accurately manipulate landform using a range of conventional grading methods.
Effectively employ standard graphic conventions and symbols used in landform grading.
Meaningfully incorporate material considerations, spatial qualities and topographic functions into landform designs.
Use grading methods in a creative manner to overcome site and design challenges.
Practice design in a gradual and progressive manner using effective time management skills.

11188.title: Landscape Architecture Studio 5
11188.description: In Studio 5, you will delve into urban landscapes, complementing the year-long focus established by Studio 6. You'll investigate the complexities of highly modified urban systems and their adverse effects on life, aiming to innovate constructed ecologies across connected scales. Your study will centre on Sydney's urban landscape, examining its form, open space typologies, density, connectivity, and micro-climates. Through immersive observation and interaction, both in the field and at your desk, you will develop a detailed understanding of the area's social relations and built environment. You will then create physical and programmatic proposals that cater to the needs of specific stakeholders, enhancing the collective experience of the urban landscape.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of urban landscape form and experience, in drawn, written and verbal forms.
Recognise and describe in precise terms the lived experience of an urban landscape's stakeholders.
Acquire physical and programmatic strategies for improving the lived experience of urban landscapes.
Communicate landscape architectural ideas through an integrated and compelling set of representations, that engage a professional and non-professional audiences.
Adopt strategies for engaging communities and fellow designers that are respectful of cultural differences and diverse lived experiences.

11189.title: Practice: Research Cultures
11189.description:
In this subject, you'll adopt a new perspective on design practice, grounded in an understanding of 'good' and 'rigorous' research to enhance your design propositions. You're encouraged to hone your research skills, discover personal interests, and shape your research agenda. By the end, you'll be equipped to use these skills to forge a direction for your future practice.

You'll explore various research methods, with a focus on design research practices. The curriculum includes design and research techniques, key texts, thesis writing, and research conventions. You'll engage with diverse research viewpoints, actively participate in design reviews, present exemplary projects, and engage in critical discussions, all aimed at deepening your research acumen.
learningOutcomes: Articulate the distinctiveness of design research and describe its value
Construct design research questions that are scalable, connecting the specific and general
Source and synthesise information of relevance your research topic
Use scholarly written and visual forms and conventions as a means of inquiry and communication
Frame a design research project based on an understanding of good and rigorous research

The knowledge and skills gained are designed to aid you in adopting a critically informed approach to design and intellectual inquiry, appreciating the interplay between theory, critique, and practice.

11197.description:
Studio options in this subject are centred on strategies for engaging with and transforming our environment, each underpinned by a conceptual framework and specific representational methods. You'll join a community of projects, practitioners, and scholars, learning to critically position your work within this context. Design becomes an intellectual and material exploration.

You'll approach design from diverse perspectives and scales, experimenting with spatial, material, and systemic ideas through various outputs, including drawings, models, and discussions in presentations, tutorials, and workshops.

The outcomes reflect the diversity of landscape architectural design, each aiming to drive positive change. Themes include small to system-scale landscape thinking, ecologies, geologies, and hydrology.

You'll grasp the essentials of landscape architecture design, focusing on site-specific influences like topography and hydrology. Working across scales, you'll investigate grading techniques, design interventions, and representation methods, aiming to create landscapes that are expressive and dynamic.

Develop a scheme through topographic design.

You'll learn how landscape architecture can guide urbanisation to create better urban spaces. The approach involves a thorough analysis of local ecology, built environment, and human activity, developing multi-scalar strategies for urban growth, and employing speculative design for form-making and landscape processes, all while considering contemporary political, economic, social, and environmental issues. You'll engage with integrating urban and landscape design principles, designing streets, parks, housing, and transport systems, and delve into the ethics of urban planning, legislative frameworks, land management in New South Wales, and landscape-led urban design.

11212.title: Architectural History and Theory: Orientations
11212.description:
History and Theory 01: Climatic Histories of Architecture and Landscape introduces students to architecture, landscape, and the forces that have shaped their social and material histories. The subject traces key moments from the Anthropocene to the Ancient World, examining the entalgements  that connect Climate Change (Decarbonisation and Biodiversity), Inclusivity (Designing with Country and Decolonisation) and Equity (Urban Transformation and Housing Affordability) to landscape and architecture, projects, practices, technologies and techniques. 

Through case studies, students will explore connections between climate histories, ecological transformations, and design proposals. The course encourages critical reflection on the socio-political dimensions of design and the evolving definitions of community, environment, and justice, equipping students with a deeper understanding of architecture and landscape stories and histories.
learningOutcomes: Acquire a knowledge base of different chronologies of architectural history
Be more effective verbal and visual communicators, both technically and conceptually
Display a basic repertoire of the language and themes underpinning architecture and be able to draw connections between architecture and expanded fields.
Demonstrate basic competency in using drawn analysis of buildings and landscapes, formal written arguments, interpretation of texts and visuals for meaning, academic referencing, and research.

11301.title: Architectural Special Project (Global B)
11301.description:
This elective provides students with an immersive international learning experience centred on a host location outside Australia. Through a combination of field-based investigation, cultural engagement, design research, and project development, students critically examine the social, cultural, environmental, and spatial conditions that shape the built environment in diverse global contexts.

Working across architecture, interior architecture, and landscape architecture, students undertake site observation, documentation, mapping, precedent analysis, and engagement with local communities, practitioners, institutions, and stakeholders. These activities inform the development of a situated design proposition that responds to opportunities and challenges identified through research.

The subject fosters intercultural understanding, global citizenship, and critical design thinking by exposing students to different cultural perspectives, design practices, and approaches to the built environment. Through direct engagement with place, students develop the ability to interpret context, translate research into design outcomes, and reflect on the role of design within diverse social and environmental settings.
learningOutcomes:
Contextual Understanding
Analyse and interpret local cultural, social, environmental, and spatial conditions, and articulate how these factors inform design decisions across different global contexts.

Cross-Cultural Engagement
Demonstrate culturally responsive and ethical design thinking through direct engagement with local practices, stakeholders, and ways of inhabiting space.

Design Research & Translation
Employ appropriate design research methods (e.g. observation, mapping, documentation, prototyping) and translate findings into discipline-specific design propositions.

Critical Reflection & Comparison
Critically reflect on differences and similarities between local and Australian contexts, evaluating how global perspectives challenge or expand existing design assumptions.

Communication & Collaboration
Communicate design ideas clearly and professionally through visual, verbal, and written formats, and collaborate effectively within multidisciplinary and cross-cultural teams.

11328.title: Australian Modernism
11328.description:
This PG seminar is an introduction to the story of modern architecture in Australia. Students explore the origins of modernism firstly through the lens of European and North American key texts and modernist practitioners, while closely analyzing significant case studies from the post WW2 era to the 1990’s. Studentsl track their influence on architects and architecture more broadly in Australia through reference sources from magazines and newspapers to current TV documentaries and beyond.

The modernist Australian story however remains only half told. The modern century saw an exceptional number of non-western influences start to significantly impact our Architecture, shaping Australian modernism differently to that developed in other parts of the world. The seminar ends in the final weeks with an exploration of these other cultural influences on architecture from the 1950’s on, taking us to precedents in Indonesia, Japan, India and more, as generally unrecognized influences on some of our most prominent architectural works. Arguably, students open the door on this, the untold history of modern architecture in Australia.

The seminar involves reading and a short lecture and discussion each week, as well as a number of guest appearances from home owners to academics and a number of site visits which are being explored for modernist projects in the Sydney Area (like the Alexander House in the image above), ...so some local travel may be involved. The program will be confirmed in Week 1. There are no costs for this subject.

11333.title: Constructing Architectural Space
11333.description:
Wareama, Wareamah, Warrayama, Cockatoo Island, holds deep cultural significance for the local Aboriginal Peoples of Sydney. The island has a rich and complex history reflecting both ancient Indigenous heritage and the more recent colonial and industrial periods. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage-listed site; however, the listing only acknowledges the colonial heritage of the island. Wareama, Wareamah, Warrayama has borne witness to the devastating and traumatic effects of colonisation, affecting Country, and both Indigenous and non-Indignenous Peoples.

Students interrogate the island and the colonial retelling of her histories. A self-directed brief forms, and students site their projects most aligned with the direction of their project. A diverse range of (Aboriginal) perspectives in the studio ensures a prioritising of truth-telling, balancing of narratives and a (re)centring Country.
learningOutcomes: Set up design processes that engage with Indigenous methodology.
Demonstrate design thinking preceding with Indigenous Knowledges with ongoing respect to Country.
Collaborate in a cross-disciplinary learning environment with a focus on engagement with Indigenous People and Practice.

11340.title: Expanded Architecture in the Urban Environment
11340.description: This subject challenges you to integrate architecture, ecology, and aesthetics, contemplating how a 'thickened ground' can transform urban spaces. Inspired by Bruno Latour's concept of Critical Zones, you'll view climate change as an intrinsic part of our environment, prompting a search for diverse knowledge to inform and visualise new urban forms that acknowledge more-than-human interactions. You'll alternate between theoretical study and practical application, developing a unique ecological perspective through text analysis and creative urban space experimentation.

11344.title: Computational Design for Decarbonisation
11344.description:
The most urgent task design professionals face is reimagining the construction and operation of our built environment to respect planetary boundaries. The ability to negotiate many complex constraints and desires and to evaluate populations of possible outcomes both qualitatively and quantitatively offered by computational design processes make them invaluable tools in the transition towards a decarbonised built environment.

Students learn and apply computational design and evolutionary optimisation tools to negotiate solar and structural analysis and for a spatial design task emerging from a precedent case study. This subject is aimed at students from Architecture, Landscape Architecture and Interior Architecture.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an ability to interpret a precedent project’s performance and develop a parametric model to evaluate design variations.
Demonstrate an ability to implement and interpret performance simulations appropriate to the design context.
Demonstrate an ability to design and implement a multi-criteria optimisation process to explore and select high-performing design outcomes.
Demonstrate an ability to interpret analysis results and refine design through an iterative feedback process.
Demonstrate an ability to communicate design processes and outcomes visually and verbally.

11345.title: Starting with Country
11345.description:
Starting with Country, students begin to decolonise the unique remnant ecologies of what we now know as central Sydney. Throughout the ongoing destructive process of Colonisation, these spaces have been given associations such as diseased, death, plagued and gendered, binary categorisations. An example of these denigrations can be found in the casuarina labelled as “she oak” by settlers due to it being ‘deemed’ useless, frail and difficult. However, Country here holds Millenia old knowledges, cultural practices and Ceremony, all in a complex, interconnected and interrelated with lifeworlds.

How can we reclaim and decolonise these spaces of stigma?

How can the urban park support practices of care for Country, her Peoples, her ecologies?

11361.title: Before and After Air Conditioning
11361.description:
Much of the global building industry’s carbon emissions comes from operational energy: HVAC systems reliant on fossil fuels. Our comfort within a building depends on this carbon-intensive infrastructure; it also depends on specific cultural expectations. Comfort has a history, one in which architects played an essential role.

This elective examines design methods before HVAC, as a way to prepare for the design of buildings after HVAC. It explores how modern architectural experiments were also devices for climatic adaptability; this history informs speculations on how cultural and technological transformation can produce zero carbon thermal environments in the near future.

11364.title: Building Anatomies
11364.description: We can transform Sydney to run on resources that will never run out - and benefit both socially and economically from the transition. A New Normal facilitates the modelling and prototyping of an actionable strategy to transform our cities energy, water, waste and food production systems to function self sufficiently within a 10 year period. Following on from the launch at Design Week Melbourne in 2021 - A New Normal is set to transform Sydney in 2024. In this elective, groups of 3 students work together with the team at finding infinity (www.findinginfini-ty.com) to help write a book to accelerate Greater Sydney’s transition. This book will be launched at Vivid Festival 2024 with an art installation / architectural exhibition involving some of Sydney’s best architects. Each group collaboratively works on 1 of the 12 chapters including: researching global case studies, writing, creating infographics, and more. Collectively students help transform Sydney into a city that never runs out!

11366.title: Elective Heritage
11366.description:
This elective unpacks the definition of an architectural ‘atmosphere’, not as a generalised ‘tone’ or ‘feeling’, but as an intentional and choreographed spatial and visual experience.

We will look to the aesthetic infrastructure, material culture, and mechanical operation of the ‘Magic Show’, and its role in constructing a narrative of illusion.

‘Magic’ implies a special relationship to space and time. Magicians, in a tradition of devising and performing their tricks and illusions, are experts in understanding and exploiting human attention and awareness.

The magician, the stage, and its props generate an experience for onlookers, which unfolds, in a controlled sequence of causes and effects, to bemuse and engage the magical subject. This is no different from the approach that architects must use when creating sensorial spaces within a spatial, formal and material environment.

As a magic trick to its audience, Architecture can be transformative, by reconditioning its environment to disrupt, defamiliarise and redirect behaviours.

11368.title: Introduction to Parametric Modelling
11368.description: Grasshopper 3D has revolutionised architectural design, enabling architects of all skill levels to engage with parametric modelling without traditional coding. This tool, along with its open-source plugins, facilitates a blend of analytic and generative design, offering rapid data analysis and diverse design variations. As a result, computational design literacy has become essential, with firms globally integrating these tools into practice, often through specialised research groups. This elective covers Grasshopper 3D from beginner to intermediate levels, potentially including advanced topics, and explores its application in design processes, including the use of various plugins, with students invited to suggest their own interests.

11379.title: Spatial Discontinuities: Visualizing Hidden Geographies of Consumption
11379.description:
Improvements in transport and communication or ‘the annihilation of space through time’, as Karl Marx puts it, would lead inevitably to globalisation. Undoubtedly, especially in the Western cities, the shift from production to consumption-based economy has transformed our cities and the nature of everyday life. As much as we have (seemingly) become hyper-connected, we are just as obscure (if not lost) of our place within the complex web of consumption. By supplying us with plentiful consumables (be it energy, food, fashion, the leftovers) most efficiently, this annihilation of space through time has satisfied our most basic needs, while making those needs appear inconsequential. We rarely stop to wonder how they reach us nor their afterlife.

To see the world through consumption is to see it with lateral vision: to understand how apparently disparate phenomena are in fact connected. Using various visual techniques such as mapping, photography and cinematography, the course aims to analyse and illuminate the crucial relationship between our cities and practices of consumption to better understand the invisible impact it has on our lives.

11391.title: Research Methods, Information Retrieval and Project Proposal
11391.description:
This subject introduces students to the fundamental skills underpinning sound academic research. The subject provides an overview of disciplinary-specific research methods and approaches to the collection and organisation of information. With this overview, students learn to support their thesis proposal by undertaking a literature review and defining an appropriate research method.

This subject supports 11392 Honours Thesis: Preparatory. Its focus is on enabling students to define and develop the academic structures required for a sound thesis proposal. Therefore, the final project proposal is demonstrative; it should show a student's capacity both to define and enact a relevant research method and complete a comprehensive literature review. The overall objective is to develop an advanced awareness of the research structures and skills required in postgraduate study.

The honours program is an individually defined project, typically taught on a one-on-one basis between student and supervisor. The negotiation of this learning contract may result in a range of different study programs, but contact typically occurs on a weekly basis.

requisite.text: Admission into C09048 Bachelor of Design (Honours) in Architecture

11392.title: Honours Thesis: Preparatory
11392.description:
This subject supports students to undertake the preparatory work required to develop an honours thesis topic. Students develop the skills required to analyse and organise references in order to produce a final literature review. The overall aim of the subject is to ensure students gain the basic academic skills to organise the direction of a research project and use this knowledge to establish the scope of a research project.

The work completed in this subject enables students to fulfil the learning requirements of 11391 Research Methods, Information Retrieval and Project Proposal. The technical and academic knowledge and skills developed in this subject structures and positions the work necessary to assemble the research proposal in 11391.

11502.title: Practice: Finance and Project Management
11502.description:
This subject introduces you to the financial, legal, and project management aspects integral to architecture and landscape architecture practice. The course outlines the professional skills, responsibilities and practice of the Architect and Landscape Architect, with particular focus on the National Standard of Competency for Architects, and the Assessment Criteria for AILA Registration.

Through a series of weekly lectures and tutorial discussion, this subject addresses the regulatory and technical aspects of professional practice as well as the social and ethical context of the profession. Topics include the design, documentation, project delivery and practice management aspects of the profession. Areas such as fee proposals, service agreements, documentation standards, procurement methods, construction contracts, site inspections are addressed.
learningOutcomes: Exhibit knowledge of project and financial management within the context of local and international architectural practice.
Implement design intentions effectively through contractual agreements and the construction process.
Understand and navigate the multifaceted social, ethical, environmental, political, and regulatory frameworks of architectural practice.
Acquire professional practice skills necessary for registration, including contractual and legal obligations.

11503.title: Practice: The Profession
11503.description: This core subject, part of the Master of Architecture, is essential for degree completion and prepares you for the multifaceted roles in architecture amidst new media, business practices, and global economies within complex social and environmental frameworks. It equips you with leadership, advocacy, and research skills for a significant impact on the built environment. You'll explore the architect's historical and current roles, future challenges, professional formation, and regulatory processes like registration and insurances. The subject also covers individual career trajectories, examining both traditional and emerging practice models and their influence on your future in the industry. Additionally, it addresses office management, interdisciplinary team leadership, communication, and organisational dynamics, preparing you for contemporary and prospective practice models.
learningOutcomes: Understand the multifaceted contexts of architectural practice including social, ethical, environmental, political, and regulatory factors.
Recognise the interplay between architectural discipline and profession, particularly in contemporary practice settings.
Acknowledge the variety of applications for architectural knowledge and understand the implications of different practice models.
Acquire a comprehensive understanding of office structures, management processes, and human resource strategies, with an exploration of these elements through case studies.
Develop a critical perspective on the establishment, management, and advancement of innovative architectural practices.

11526.description:
The Masters Special Project series engages Industry Professionals/Advocates/Affiliates in discourse across the topics of Decarbonisation, Decolonisation + Urban Equity, relative to the Practice of Architecture. Drawing on varied methods, which can include speculative design / technological prototyping / theory / writing / exhibition + encounters, students collaborate and formalise their own positions in response to the specific briefs set by the curated Elective Leads. The Masters Special Project electives are announced in the Master of Architecture Prospectus prior to the commencement of each session and introduced at the Ballot Day, when self-enrolment opens.

Sustainable Sydney 2050

With the global urban population projected to increase by 75 percent by 2050, the need for sustainable liveability in cities, including Sydney, is crucial. This course leverages the City of Sydney Council's ‘Sustainable Sydney 2050’ strategy to explore the critical intersection of city making and policymaking.

Led by an elected City Councillor, this immersive course places future architects in the heart of real-world urban challenges and opportunities. Students engage in strategic design interventions to examine Sydney’s transformative drivers for 2050, such as housing for all, creating a swimmable harbour, greening the city, advancing a circular economy, and delivering First Nations ‘Walking on Country’ (Yananurala).

Emphasis is placed on understanding urban governance, strategy, complex systems change, and the political dynamics that shape sustainable city transformation. Students develop a comprehensive understanding on how to design in the public interest, equipping them with the skills to contribute meaningfully to support the realisation of Sydney’s vision for 2050 and beyond.
learningOutcomes: Critically analyse and articulate the key components of a long-term city strategy and their implications for urban design and policymaking.
Develop and apply strategic design interventions that address relevant urban challenges
Demonstrate an understanding of the principles and practices of designing in the public interest, with a focus on sustainable liveability and resilience
Understand the needs and roles of diverse stakeholders, including policymakers and community representatives
Create innovative design solutions that contribute to urban spaces and the enhancement of public life

In this technically focused professional practice subject, you'll explore how performance criteria and constraints inform design. You'll learn to align the technical and material aspects of architecture with the design strategies you utilise in your studio subject.

Throughout the process of creating a professional drawing package that adheres to industry standards, you will be asked to produce a drawing index across multiple stages and detailed drawings.

A focus on quality and performance standards, the impact on the Country and the environment, and the whole-life carbon impact of the selected material systems will be undertaken.

12515.description: This subject teaches you to manage property assets strategically, considering economic and social influences across the asset lifecycle, from raw land to disposal. You'll learn asset management concepts and techniques, including industry frameworks and life cycle costing. Applying these, you'll develop a property life cycle cost model and document your findings in a professional report, honing both technical and communication skills. 12535.title: Property Investment and Development Feasibility
12535.description:
This core subject in the Master of Real Estate Investment and Master of Property Development programs demystifies modeling and feasibility analysis in real estate. You'll grasp the logic, terminology, and formulas essential for real estate modeling, forming the basis of your first assignment. The course prioritises first principles over proprietary models, using Excel to build analytical models and understand model sensitivities, preparing you for future use of advanced software.

You'll develop feasibility models for income-producing properties like Retail, Office, and Industrial, focusing on discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis for valuing land, investments, and development projects under varying conditions. The course covers financial analysis basics, including the time value of money and capital expenditure (CAPEX), and explores sensitivity factors in property investment and development feasibility.

Engagement through class discussions, DCF modeling exercises, online activities, and group work enhances your learning experience. The skills acquired will aid in making informed decisions in real-life investment and development scenarios, with assessments designed to test your understanding of DCF principles and feasibility analysis.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the rationale of conducting feasibility analysis and modelling.
Identify and source relevant cash flows that related to investment and development projects.
Demonstrate an understanding of DCF analysis and develop DCF models using excel modelling skills.
Analyse DCF modelling results affected by changed project conditions.

12537.title: Construction Management
12537.description:
You will explore the organisation and management of construction projects, focusing on professional practice, ethics, and sustainability. You'll examine stakeholder roles, the project lifecycle, and master communication and human resource management. Legislation on industrial relations, work health and safety (WH&S), and dispute resolution methods such as mediation and litigation will be key components of your study. Through in-class workshops using case studies, you'll develop your ethical reasoning within professional contexts.

Additionally, you'll delve into managing construction work and site operations, learning about site establishment, construction methodology, and site planning. You'll also become proficient in using Building Information Modelling (BIM) and digital tools for project management.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of construction project management and site operations.
Demonstrate an understanding of the project life cycle.
Demonstrate an understanding of critical legislation and lawful dispute resolution processes in the construction industry.
Demonstrate knowledge of Building Information Modelling (BIM) in the construction industry.

15146.title: Sustainable Urban Development
15146.description:
This subject introduces sustainable development, focusing on the triple bottom line of environmental, economic, and social sustainability, alongside the ESG framework of environment, social, and governance. You'll engage with sustainable practices through case studies, guest lectures, group discussions, exercises, and field visits, with compulsory attendance for block sessions to participate in group work and earn marks.

Initially, you'll explore urban resilience, examining sustainability challenges in global cities and Sydney's local strategies. Topics include climate change impacts, greenhouse gas reduction, alternative energy strategies, air quality, population growth, economic resilience planning, and social sustainability issues like housing affordability and the night-time economy.

The second block delves into sustainable urban development at the precinct and building scale, discussing eco-footprints, sustainable building assessment methods, and physical development constraints. You'll evaluate sustainability performance, consider rating tools' effectiveness, and discuss sustainable transport, energy use, new builds versus retrofitting, green roofs, and urban vegetation. The feasibility of alternative sustainability evaluation methods is also covered.
learningOutcomes: Develop teamwork and communication strategies.
Demonstrate understanding of the relationships among urban structure, resource consumption, and sustainability.
Apply the principles of environmental, economic, and social sustainability to urban development.
Critique policies and plans using evidence-based analysis.
Understand environmental risks and mitigation strategies in urban development.

15327.title: Lean and Agile Project Management.
15327.description:
Lean thinking provides a foundational approach to understanding how value is defined, created, and delivered in project environments. By emphasising value from the stakeholder perspective, reducing waste, improving flow, and supporting continuous improvement, Lean introduces a systems-oriented view of project work that is essential in complex and dynamic settings.

Building on these foundations, Agile project management has been widely adopted across industries to enhance responsiveness, collaboration, and adaptability. While originating in software development, Agile principles are now applied across diverse sectors including engineering, consulting, marketing, education, and government.

This subject introduces the core values, principles, and mindsets of Lean and Agile approaches, alongside key frameworks such as Scrum and Kanban. Students will develop practical skills through hands-on exercises using agile software and simulations that reflect real-world project environments. The subject content aligns with the Scrum Master Certified (SMC) qualification by Scrum Study, preparing students for the optional online certification exam. Students who wish to pursue the certification may be supported in undertaking the exam, including financial support where available.

Beyond tools and techniques, the subject critically examines when and how Lean and Agile approaches are appropriate in different organisational and project contexts. It explores hybrid models that combine Agile and traditional project management practices, and considers the organisational, team, and decision-making dynamics that influence successful implementation.

By the end of the subject, students will be equipped to evaluate, adapt, and apply Lean and Agile approaches to deliver value in diverse and uncertain project environments.
learningOutcomes: Critically explain the principles of Lean and Agile approaches, including concepts of value, waste, flow, and continuous improvement, and their relevance to project environments.
Apply Lean and Agile tools and frameworks, such as value stream mapping, Scrum, and Kanban, to design appropriate approaches for different project contexts.
Evaluate the suitability of Lean, Agile, and hybrid project management approaches in diverse and complex environments, considering organisational, stakeholder, and governance factors.
Reflect on and justify project management decisions in Lean–Agile settings, demonstrating awareness of team dynamics, collaboration, and continuous improvement.

15608.school: Institute for Public Policy and Governance
15608.description: This subject equips local government professionals with the knowledge and skills to deliver public services effectively while embracing democratic processes. 15640.title: Public Engagement in Decision-Making
15640.school: Institute for Public Policy and Governance
15640.description:
In advanced democracies, there is a common assumption that citizens have a role to play in shaping decisions that impact their lives.

Governments at all levels, public authorities, private sector and not-for-profile service providers all tend to facilitate some form of community involvement in their work, motivated either by regulatory requirements, good corporate practice, and/or a genuine desire to be open and accountable to the people. While this involvement is hoped to lead to better policies, strategies, programs or services, there is a wide variety of practices in existence, not all of them evidence based and outcome-orientated.  Further, there are many engagement tools and techniques in use that are not fit-for-purpose in terms of the participants, the agency, or the program or policies that matter most to one or more of the parties.

This subject looks at good practice public engagement and participation in decision making, reflective of the contemporary requirements, circumstances, resourcing, complexity of needs, time constraints and other risks. The premise is that there is no single engagement model, set of tools or techniques that will guarantee positive outcomes, as each participation process needs to be carefully project managed with a clear and transparent purpose and outcomes.

The subject introduces students to key theories, concepts and approaches to community engagement and stakeholder consultations. It considers the historical context as it relates to involving citizens in public decision-making. It also explores different concepts of participatory and deliberative democratic theory; social justice principles of inclusion and participation; plus different legislative, regulatory and policy settings that underpin contemporary practice.

Students have the opportunity to gain knowledge of key consultation techniques and develop practical skills in the design, delivery and evaluation of engagement processes.

Learners will be encouraged to think critically about different forms of engagement practice and consider the risks and benefits for the engagement sponsor, the participants, and the engagement facilitators. They will also be encouraged to think about the adequacy and representativeness of specific engagement used in decision making and additional steps that may need to be taken to ensure a diversity of voices and views are being heard. Finally the course will assist students to challenges and risks associated with public engagement in decision making and to consider what mitigations or practical measures could be deployed to lessen their negative impacts.
learningOutcomes: Identify, examine and evaluate literature, concepts and arguments which are informing contemporary public engagement practice

Critically reflect and develop new ideas in relation on the challenges and opportunities in delivering public engagement, considering a wide variety of contextual factors such as communities, public institutions, legislative environments.
Apply advanced understanding of theories and debates to the identification and evaluation of an innovative public engagement process.
Acquire knowledge, understanding and skills in the design, planning and execution of public engagement programs and techniques relevant to specific public policy or decision-making environments
Effectively communicate understanding of key concepts and their complexities.

16006.title: Introduction to Resilient Development
16006.description: In this subject you will investigate urban resilience and the sustainability challenges faced by global cities, and more specifically by the City of Sydney and the Greater Sydney area as a demonstration of how these challenges are considered and addressed locally. You are introduced to the concept of sustainable development and will explore the business concepts of the triple bottom line (environmental, economic, and social sustainability) and ESG (environment, social, and governance), with particular focus on how these are applied in sustainable urban planning and property development. The causes and urban effects of global warming are discussed, as are issues relating to population growth, greenhouse gas emissions (and reduction), carbon footprint & decarbonisation strategies, energy consumption (and alternative energy development strategies), air quality and waste challenges, water sensitive urban design, economic planning for resilience, and the built environment industries' responsibility to create safe places. Sustainable solutions and practices are discussed and demonstrated using national and international case studies, guest lectures, in-class/online group discussions and exercises, and, if possible, field trips. To gain maximum benefit from this class, students should attend each class session. Attendance is taken via a weekly quiz/in-class exercises which is only available to students attending in-person.

16014.title: Artificial Intelligence for AEC Industry
16014.description:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) engineering and related technologies have emerged as the powerful technological forces, revolutionising various sectors of the economy. The use of AI for the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry has escalated dramatically in recent years. With the recent advancement in AI engineering and related technologies, they have the potential to revolutionise the construction industry by improving efficiency, safety, and sustainability. Recent advancements in AI, including machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), offer transformative potential for the AEC industry, enhancing efficiency, safety, and sustainability.

The subject explores different types and methods of AI engineering and related technologies, and how the construction sector has applied these technologies successfully. Students are guided to develop a critical point of view of the technologies, feasibility, effort and impacts. The subject also focuses on the ethics and risks of AI engineering and related technologies in the AEC industry. By the end of this subject, participants develop a foundational understanding of AI in construction towards innovation in their careers.

16016.title: Construction Futures
16016.description: This subject addresses the potential for change and improvement in the construction and property industry, exploring why change is necessary, emerging technological options, and enablers for change. You will need to understand global social, environmental, political, and economic trends affecting the industry, identify a transformative technology, and articulate its relevance to Australia's industry future. You are also encouraged to envision an alternative future for the sector. The course, taught online, uses a guided learning approach with curated resources, aiming to set you on a path of lifelong intellectual development.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the global trends that will shape the future of the construction industry
Analyse and evaluate emerging digital technologies in the particular context of the Australian construction industry
Reflect on the barriers and opportunities for alternative construction industry futures
Appreciate and value organisational innovation as an agent of change in the construction industry

16017.title: Property Futures
16017.description:
This subject introduces emerging technologies and applications transforming the property industry, including artificial intelligence (AI), Generative AI (GenAI), smart and sustainable building technologies, intelligent property development and management platforms, the Internet of Things (IoT), digital twins, and blockchain.

Delivered through four on-campus block-mode classes, the subject is supported by extensive online learning resources, site visits, and practical, hands-on learning activities conducted during block classes. The subject is designed to develop industry-relevant practical skills through applied learning and assessments, including on-campus individual class tests conducted during each block class, a group assignment, and an individual showcase assignment, with formative feedback provided through staged reviews of student work.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate understanding of global technology trends shaping the future of the property industry through active participation in in-class discussions and applied learning activities.
Analyse and evaluate how transformative smart technologies can address key challenges in the Australian property industry.
Reflect on the barriers and opportunities for delivering smart and sustainable built environments through the adoption of emerging  technologies at building, precinct, and city scales.
Apply emerging technologies to enhance occupant comfort and support evidence-based property performance decisions.
Apply smart building approaches to optimise building management systems to improve operational efficiency and long-term property value.

16018.title: Property Technology and Innovation
16018.description: This subject prepares you to lead and innovate in the property industry, covering roles from advisory and investment to design, construction, and management. You will learn how technology and innovation are revolutionising commercial real estate, making work more engaging and buildings more efficient and sustainable. The interactive course teaches human-centred design and agile techniques, enabling you to actualise ideas and gain valuable insights. Through lectures, tech showcases, expert discussions, and practical exercises, you will explore technology's potential and challenges, equipping you with innovative problem-solving skills to propel your career.
learningOutcomes: Effectively identify, assess and select the right technology to meet customer and commercial needs and practice human-centred design techniques to identify and design new innovations.
Articulate a compelling case for investing in innovation and technology.
Recognise the challenges, pitfalls and risks in realising the benefits of innovation and develop effective strategies to mitigate against them.
Understand the history of innovation and technology in commercial real estate and analyse emerging trends and opportunities.
Effectively evaluate the legal and ethical boundaries and opportunities in the use of data and emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence.

16021.title: Performance-based Building Design
16021.description: In Australia, building design is governed by state and territory legislation, transitioning from prescriptive to performance-based regulations. Performance-based design (PBD) offers design flexibility, encourages innovation, and can enhance constructability, potentially reducing costs and giving practitioners a competitive advantage. The National Construction Code (NCC) underpins PBD as a mandatory standard for new buildings. This subject teaches you to develop 'Performance Solutions' as outlined in the NCC, a critical skill for collaboration and success in the competitive, global building industry.
learningOutcomes: Develop an ability to propose and prepare innovative and cost-efficient performance-based building designs.
Develop an ability to work effectively in multi-discipline groups of associated practitioners (relating to Performance Solutions).
Develop an ability to effectively engage in critical and insightful thinking in the context of building design (relating to Performance Solutions)
Develop an ability to effectively engage in objective discussion of NCC requirements and practical applications (relating to Performance Solutions).
Develop an ability to evaluate data and assess its relevance to innovative thinking and problem-solving processes (relating to Performance Solutions).

16022.title: Construction Law & Ethics
16022.description:
In this foundational subject, you’ll be introduced to the basic principles of construction law, gaining the knowledge needed to manage legal risks with commercial awareness as a future construction professional.

You will develop a solid understanding of the Australian legal system, with a focus on key causes of action relevant to construction projects. Additionally, the subject covers the fundamentals of contract administration, emphasising the legal, ethical and commercial aspects of project delivery.

This course aims to enhance your commercial and legal awareness while refining your communication skills.
learningOutcomes: Understand an overview of the legal frameworks and related commercial principles relevant to construction projects.
Differentiate between legal, commercial and ethical considerations in the construction sector.
Exhibit proficiency in contract management and apply legal principles to the commercial management of construction projects.
Understand the legal risks in the construction sector. Demonstrate proficiency in written and oral communication of legal and commercial issues to various stakeholders.
Demonstrate knowledge of the role of key industry bodies, including an overview of the history and current industrial relations legislation

16105.description: In this subject, you'll delve into the measurement of construction quantities, understanding its significance and application. Through detailed exercises, you'll practice calculating, measuring, and describing construction quantities, harnessing electronic CAD/BIM technology. Apply electronic CAD /Building Information Modelling (BIM) and other technologies in measuring quantities.

16109.title: Construction Technology 1
16109.description: This subject delves into the construction technology of residential buildings, focusing on single detached houses (Class 1a). Key stages of the residential construction life cycle, including site considerations, foundations, structure, internal linings, cladding, services, and finishes, are explored in depth. Demonstrate an understanding of conventional construction methods, materials, terminology and details for Class 1A buildings.
Demonstrate an understanding of the purpose (attributes and intent of application) of standard building elements and make informed decisions of the appropriateness of alternate solutions.
Apply the statutory regulations governing construction in Australia to the management of residential construction projects.

16137.description: This subject introduces you to the information technologies shaping the planning, design, construction, and operations of the built environment, with a special emphasis on building information modelling (BIM). You'll learn about the features, limitations, and advantages of these tools, and how they contrast with traditional practices. 16138.title: Site Establishment and Management
16138.description:
This subject explores construction site establishment, operation, and surveying, addressing the dynamic nature of sites as projects progress. You'll delve into excavation issues, including shoring and piling, and the design and erection of temporary structures. You'll also develop advanced site surveying skills, using theodolites and mastering building marking out techniques, with a continuous focus on safety and legal liabilities.

Through individual and group work, you'll create operational plans for site efficiency and safety, select temporary facilities, determine excavation stabilisation methods, optimise earthmoving productivity, manage site traffic, and conduct precise surveying and setting out.

As a construction manager, you're expected to master these principles and practices, combining theoretical knowledge with practical application of manual and technological tools.
learningOutcomes: Methodically examine a project site environment and conditions in order to effectively establish a site.
Investigate and describe the sub-strata conditions of a site.
Survey and set out buildings.
Develop site and environmental plans.

16203.title: Cost Management 2: Estimating
16203.description: This subject focuses on estimating practices and techniques used by contractors, with a core emphasis on construction pricing. You'll dissect costs into labour, materials, plant, subcontract, and indirect costs, and differentiate between quantity-related, time-related, and fixed costs. Through tutorials and exercises, you'll quantify and price construction work items and activities. Strategic estimating topics, such as tender preparation, builder's bills of quantities, sub-contractor quotations, pricing preliminaries, and calculating profit and overhead margins, are also covered. You'll use estimating software and explore advanced practices integrating cost estimating with building information modelling (BIM) systems.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a knowledge of the PMBOK Competency Unit for Project Cost Management
Understand the process of estimating and the techniques used by construction contractors in preparing a tender with the use of current estimating software available in Australia
Determine costs of construction for bill of quantities items by calculating unit rates based on labour, materials, plant and sub-contract components
Understand the use of published and historical cost data and the methods for calculation of profit and overheads
Obtain and analyse the accuracy of sub-contract quotes and estimate the cost of facilities and supervision supplied by the head contractor

16206.title: Structures
16206.description: This subject delves into the role of structural engineers and the essential structural knowledge project managers need for effective project management and supervision, including collaboration with structural engineers within the design team. You'll grasp structural principles by examining loads on various structures and how they're supported and transferred to footings. You'll gain insight into the behaviour of common and temporary structural systems by calculating internal forces and moments. Additionally, you'll learn to interpret structural design documentation, focusing on structural drawings and specifications.
learningOutcomes: Understand the fundamental roles, principles and systems of structural engineering within construction projects.
Apply knowledge of structural loads and analysis to ensure building stability.
Interpret and use structural design documentation.
Demonstrate an understanding of possible mechanisms of failure of structures.
Determine deflections in simply supported and continuous beams.
16206.recommended: Students need to meet relevant prerequisites as advertised in the handbook

16207.title: Cost Management 3: Cost Planning
16207.description: This subject introduces you to construction economics, focusing on project scope management, budget establishment, preliminary estimating, cost planning, cost modelling, and elemental cost analysis. You'll explore the cost planner's role and the concept of 'designing to a cost' rather than 'costing a design', distinguishing between project price, cost, and value. Emphasis is placed on the importance of scope management, including identification, management, and control. You'll also engage with historical cost data, price indices, and advanced cost planning software to deepen your understanding.
learningOutcomes: Understand and apply the processes involved in the PMBOK Competency Unit for Project Cost Management through applications in tutorials.
Establish project budget, preliminary estimating and elemental cost plan.
Discuss various cost planning methods and their accuracy.
Adjust estimates for time, location and market condition.
Use of cost planning software and Building Information Modelling.

16212.title: Digital Design and Construction 1
16212.description: This subject equips you with the skills to create 3D models and 2D plans vital for construction, focusing on Building Information Modelling (BIM) to enhance contractor coordination, reduce errors, and streamline design. You'll learn to produce and scrutinise detailed residential designs using 3D modelling, preparing you for pre-construction roles. Your learning involves hands-on workshops and computing labs, applying your knowledge to real-world projects, fostering proficiency in virtual design, construction and other emerging technologies.
learningOutcomes: Apply knowledge of 3D modelling and auditing processes and the use of 3D software for interrogating and verifying the quality of design and construction data.
Develop model-based documentation to effectively describe fabrication and construction assemblies.
Use information standards and protocols for organising and exchanging model content.
Evaluate residential construction elements, materials and building components based on functional requirements, technical performance and building standards.
Communicate effectively in various formats.

16216.title: Introduction to Property and the Built Environment
16216.description: This is a core first-year subject in the Bachelor of Property Economics. Typical professional career paths and opportunities are examined, and the role and regulation of the various property professionals and professional organisations are explored. The subject introduces the range of professional property sectors, local and global property markets, and students learn to undertake a property market analysis. The nature and structure of the property and built environment industry, and contemporary issues and challenges facing the industry are investigated through a research project. Students are introduced to the main forms of professional communication and documentation used in the industry - with the fundamentals of report-writing, academic writing and professional communication incorporated into the subject, as well as examining the appropriate and ethical use of AI for academic and industry communication.
learningOutcomes: Analyze the structure of the property and built environment industries, identifying key issues and challenges, and describing the roles and responsibilities of main stakeholders and professionals within these industries, and demonstrating professional report writing proficiency.

Read, interpret, and discuss ethical issues in a groupwork context and apply informed ethical judgements related to industry challenges, managing conflict, and the use of AI in academic and professional work in your individual assessments.

Identify and describe Prop Tech, AI & sustainability solutions and their relevance for use in property and built environment contexts, and demonstrate your understanding of the ethical implications associated with their use.
Read, interpret, and discuss market analysis concepts, analyse market data, and communicate findings using written report and data visualisation strategies.
Take useful and shareable notes on class content, related to meeting/groupwork scenarios, and related to research, readings and other types of content.

16217.title: Built Environment Law & Professional Practice
16217.description: This is a core first year subject in the Bachelor of Property Economics.  In this subject you will gain an understanding of the legal and regulatory framework in place in Australia and how that applies to the Built Environment.  You will be introduced to the basic principles of land titling in Australia, and your rights and responsibilities in relation to the land.  Sale and ownership, including easement, covenants, mortgages, and leases will be covered with reference to both Strata Title and Torrens title.  The relevant areas of Contract Law, Torts Law, Consumer Law, and Australian Competition Law will also be covered, with real life examples drawn from the body of cases dealing with construction and property law.  You will also gain indigenous perspectives related to land management, heritage and biodiversity.
learningOutcomes: Communicate legal issues relating to the Built Environment in a professional and effective manner
Understand the major sources of legal liability for construction and property professionals in Australia
Understand the basic principles of Land titling in Australia
Apply legal principles covered in the course to relevant simple legal problems
Be able to articulate the Indigenous perspective on land management

16219.title: Quantitative Analysis for Property
16219.description: This subject equips students with the foundations to conduct advanced property investment analysis in professional practice. Students will develop essential quantitative skills for the property industry. Techniques will be explored, and skills will be built in the use of both financial calculators and Excel for financial analysis. In particular, the subject emphasises the analytical approach to property valuation, covering key topics such as capitalisation, time value of money, and discounted cash flows. Students will explore concepts, formulas, and calculations, as well as learn basic data visualisation using Excel tables, diagrams, and graphs.
learningOutcomes: Apply the analytical approach to capitalisation principles.
Explore time value of money concepts, formulas, and calculations to address a range of problems in property economics.
Develop skills in property data collection, statistical analysis, and data visualisation using Excel tables, charts, and graphs.
Apply discounted cash flow analysis using Excel to support the evaluation and discussion of property investment problems.

16231.title: Property Management
16231.description:
This is a core subject in the second year of the Bachelor of Property Economics. The subject is an in-depth study of management of commercial property, and the relationship between owner, managing agent and tenant. It encompasses various lease structures, the role of the property manager, and their statutory obligations and requirements, including the enforcement of lease conditions, budgeting and forecasting.

Among the facets of property management covered are facilities management, which underpin the operations of commercial, industrial and retail property. The increasing importance of workplace health and safety are addressed within statutory and operational frameworks. An introduction to the theories of negotiations for property managers.

Students are exposed to financial budgeting, forecasting, planning for operating and capital expenditure and strategic investment and asset planning using practical examples which demonstrate the application of these facets of the property management process. The theory underpinning each topic aligns with practical real-life examples in providing context for the concepts and theories addressed in this subject.
learningOutcomes: Define and apply commercial property management functions and responsibilities
Engage with Workplace Health and Safety WHS environment and sustainability standards
Read and negotiate commercial & retail leases & commercial management and FM agreements
Calculate net, gross & face rents, undertake rent reviews & participate in the resolution of rent disputes
Define, apply and collect property outgoings and prepare income & expense budgets
