Admission into MAJ03539 54cp Telecommunications and Electronics (MPE)
Admission into MAJ03534 54cp Electrical Energy Systems (MPE)
Admission into MAJ03512 Biomedical Engineering Major

48530.recommended: It is recommended that students enrolled in this subject have knowledge of basic electrical circuits and devices and basic circuit analysis skills.

48531.title: Electromechanical Automation
48531.description: This subject aims to solidify your understanding of (i) electromagnetic field and circuits as well as the interchange of electric, magnetic, and electromagnetic energy, (ii) modelling and control of electromechanical systems and their application in industrial automation. You will learn about the electromechanical energy conversion, and operation principles of typical electric motors. You will also learn to model electromechanical automation systems using electric motors, simulate their performance, design closed-loop controllers, and observe the integration of sensing, actuation and communication in a smart factory. You will be able to handle mains voltage equipment, power instrumentation, PLCs, measure motor characteristics, and improve your practical skills. You are expected to achieve levels of knowledge ranging from essential problem-solving and awareness of modern automation systems. A key component is the development of laboratory skills, including electrical safety, accurate measurements, design validation, and experimental verification.
learningOutcomes: Apply fundamentals of electric and magnetic fields to solve electric and magnetic circuit problems and to interpret electromechanical energy conversion. (D.1)
Model electromechanical automation systems using DC and AC motors, and design closed-loop control as well as simulate their performance. (C.1)
Carry out work on electric machines and equipment at normal mains supply voltage, and with programmable logic controllers used in automation systems. (D.1).
Demonstrate laboratory skills, ranging from electrical safety, measurements, design validation and experimental verification. (D.1)

args.text: Admission into MAJ03534 54cp Electrical Energy Systems (MPE)

48540.title: Signals and Systems
48540.description: This subject lays the theoretical groundwork for system analysis and equips you with skills for designing components within control and communication systems. You will learn to derive models from actual devices, compare predictions with experimental outcomes, and apply your knowledge through a group project focused on a real-world control or communication challenge. Core topics include signal representation, system modelling with equations and transforms, signal processing, the interplay between discrete and continuous data, feedback effects, system performance, stability, and control design principles. Through various learning activities, you will also improve your academic literacy and gain insight into engineering's diverse practice areas. The subject incorporates lectures, tutorials, lab work, and project assignments. Lab sessions, integrated with MATLAB simulations, reinforce theoretical concepts and allow you to engage with practical applications directly.
learningOutcomes: Apply the mathematical tools associated with transform theory to the analysis and design of continuous-time and discrete-time systems. (D.1)
Analyse, design, simulate and test parts of a communication system and a control system in both the time-domain and frequency-domain. (D.1)
Model real and complex systems using a hierarchical approach, and be able to simplify them with appropriate assumptions. (D.1)
Measure time and frequency characteristics of signals and systems using appropriate laboratory equipment. (D.1)
Communicate technical ideas, decisions, calculations and experimental results in a written document. (E.1)

args.text: Admission into MAJ03539 54cp Telecommunications and Electronics (MPE)
Admission into MAJ03512 Biomedical Engineering Major

48540.recommended: It is recommended that students enrolled in this subject have knowledge of circuit analysis in both the time and frequency domains, utilising mathematics involving solutions to differential equations using time-domain techniques as well as transform methods.

48550.title: Renewable and Power Systems Studio
48550.description: This studio introduces you to modern renewable energy technologies, encompassing sustainability, environmental impact, and various energy sources such as solar, wind, fuel cell, and hydro. You'll explore energy storage, system integration, and applications like microgrids. In-depth discussions on design techniques for renewable energy systems prepare you for a group project, where you'll engage in system specification, options analysis, and design implementation. The subject aims to equip you with the knowledge and skills to design a renewable energy system effectively.
learningOutcomes: Identify sustainability and environmental issues which impact the design of renewable energy and power systems. (B.1)
Apply contemporary renewable energy technologies to design generating and storage systems. (C.1)
Use appropriate tools to calculate, design and apply circuit, energy and project analysis techniques to practical problems and projects. (D.1)
Demonstrate communication and collaboration skills in the context of a design project. (E.1)
Reflect on challenges and achievements to identify future learning needs. (F.1)

args.text: Admission into MAJ03534 54cp Electrical Energy Systems (MPE)

48560.title: Automation Studio
48560.description:
This studio-based subject is a hands-on, project-based subject that introduces the principles and technologies of modern industrial automation. You will explore how industrial sensors, actuators, controllers, and communication systems work together to automate complex processes in fields such as manufacturing, energy, transport, and smart infrastructure. The subject focuses on practical design and implementation, using tools such as programmable logic controllers (PLCs), human-machine interfaces (HMIs), real-time monitoring, and control systems. You will learn how to program, integrate, and test automated process, while developing critical skills in system design, fault diagnosis, and process optimisation. Through workshops and studio activities, you will work collaboratively to build and validate complete automation solutions. These hands-on projects provide experience in translating engineering concepts into real-world applications, while also considering key challenges such as safety, scalability, and sustainability.

By the end of the subject, you will be able to design and deploy intelligent automation systems that respond dynamically to real-time inputs. You will understand how automation supports innovation in Industry 4.0 and prepares the foundation for advanced work in control, robotics, and cyber-physical systems. Therefore, Automation Studio equips you with practical skills and creative confidence to take on engineering challenges in a rapidly evolving technological landscape.
learningOutcomes: Model and analyse dynamic systems for control purposes (D.1)
Propose, design and validate suitable control strategies to create an autonomous control system that conforms to given specifications. (C.1)
Identify model uncertainties and/or disturbances that can affect the control system performance in order to enhance robustness. (D.1)
Translate theoretical control designs into control algorithms to achieve a practical implementation of the developed autonomous control system. (D.1)

48561.title: Electric Machines and Drives Studio
48561.description: Electrical machines are the fundamentals for electric power generation and electric drives, and power electronics is a crucial technology that enables the efficient management and conversion of electrical power in various applications, including motor drives, renewable energy systems, data centres, and HVDC networks. This studio provides an engaging learning experience, equipping you with the skills to understand and control electric motor drives. Throughout this subject, you will explore the details of circuitry and control challenges inherent in electrical machine and drive systems. You will gain practical experience using commercial software for thorough circuit analysis and development, allowing you to design circuits that meet industry standards and custom specifications. By the end of the studio, you will have the knowledge to create basic electric drive circuits tailored for transportation electrification and renewable energy applications, preparing you for a career in this dynamic and essential field.
learningOutcomes: Analyse the impact of power electronic and drive systems on utility supply and environment. (B.1)
Develop power electronic circuits according to customised specifications and industry standards. (C.1)
Analyse, design, implement and test power electronic devices, circuits and systems by using appropriate mathematical model, simulation and design tools and datasheets. (D.1)
Demonstrate design approach to problem solving using communication and collaboration between various people. (E.1)
Reflect on challenges and achievements to identify future learning needs. (F.1)

48572.title: Electrical Power Systems
48572.description: This subject equips you with methods for analysing and designing electric power networks, building on previous circuit analysis knowledge. You'll gain practical understanding of contemporary power system theory and its application to real-world problems.
learningOutcomes: Apply models in power system apparatus for the purpose of power system modelling and analysis. (D.1)
Analyse power systems under steady-state, transient and faulted conditions. (D.1)
Demonstrate proficient use of specialised laboratory equipment for testing power system parameters and behaviour (D.1).
Professionally communicate technical information following industry norms (E.1).

It is assumed that the students have prior knowledge in the following: Complex numbers and its application to the analysis of AC circuits. Circuit analysis. Fundamentals of electrical machines. MATLAB programming to solve simple problems.

48580.title: Intelligent Control Studio
48580.description: This studio subject focuses on aspects of advanced control engineering design for multivariable systems. This subject will provide you a rich and attractive practice-based learning environment to gain advanced control engineering skills, essential for managing complex, multivariable systems such as power grids and aircraft. You will become proficiency in sophisticated control techniques beyond classical methods, enhancing your ability to design and implement systems that handle nonlinear dynamics. Learning is hands-on, blending theory with practice as you progress from concept to product realisation. Through reflective design, teamwork, and deep learning, you will prepare for senior roles, mastering design, simulation, and practical validation of advanced control systems.
learningOutcomes: Mathematically model, simulate and analyse multivariable (not necessarily linear) systems for control purposes. (D.1)
Propose, design and validate advanced control strategies to create a multivariable autonomous control system conforming to given specifications. (C.1)
Identify model uncertainties and/or disturbances that can affect the control system performance in order to enhance robustness. (D.1)
Translate theoretical advanced control designs into control algorithms to achieve a practical implementation of the developed autonomous multivariable control system. (D.1)
48580.recommended: It is essential that students enrolled in this subject have completed previous study of simple control systems using transfer functions and state-variables is essential

48582.title: Power Systems Studio
48582.description: This studio equips you with practical skills in power systems modelling, analysis and design, essential for careers in electrical engineering. You'll learn to analyse synchronous machines, manage system stability, and control power flow, alongside understanding transmission line performance. Your learning combines self-study with collaborative projects, where you'll apply theory to a design product, guided by academic and industry experts. This blend of individual and teamwork ensures a comprehensive grasp of the subject matter.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and evaluate modern power system components and integration challenges. (D.1)
Design and apply advanced control strategies for power system operation. (D.1)
Assess power system stability and dynamic performance under high renewable penetration. (C.1)
Develop and evaluate protection schemes for modern and distributed power systems. (D.1)

48610.title: Introduction to Mechanical Engineering
48610.description: This subject introduces you to the fundamentals of engineering visualisation and design, from sketching and drawing to computer-aided design and solid modelling. You will learn to represent components graphically through sketching and computer methods, employing standard techniques like orthogonal projection. The subject also covers basic engineering mechanics, enabling you to analyse simple machines and structures, and introduces engineering management tools, which you will apply in the design and hands-on construction of a mechanical prototype.
learningOutcomes: Create technical drawings by hand to communicate details of mechanical components. (D.1)
Create computer models of mechanical components and devices using CAD solid modelling software. (D.1)
Solve introductory engineering mechanics problems to analyse mechanical components and systems. (D.1)
Analyse, solve and document engineering problems. (C.1)

48622.title: Embedded Mechatronics Systems
48622.description: Embedded Systems are essential for Physical Computing, which involves interactive, often distributed systems that sense and respond to their environment. You'll learn about digital and programmable electronic circuits, small computer systems' hardware architecture, and low-level programming for embedded software. Topics include digital sequential circuits, state diagrams, hardware-software interplay, CPU architecture, memory subsystems, computer system buses, and input/output devices. Additionally, you'll study micro-controller theory, hardware interfacing design, real-time programming basics, and connect MEMS microphones, accelerometers, and other sensors.
learningOutcomes: Explain and apply the fundamentals of digital and programmable electronic circuits and their engineering applications. (D.1)
Explain and apply the fundamentals of microcontrollers. (D.1)
Identify the principles of low-level programming and use ability to write simple embedded software. (C.1)
48622.recommended: It is recommended that students enrolled in this subject have a basic knowledge in electrical engineering and programming.

48641.title: Fluid Mechanics
48641.description: This subject provides a comprehensive introduction to fluid behaviour under static and dynamic conditions, including the underlying principles and assumptions crucial for the design and optimisation of pipelines, water treatment plants, air conditioning systems, and aircraft. The subject also encourages you to explore fluid mechanics in the real-world applications, fostering interest for further specialised study or research. Key topics include fluid properties, statics, kinematics, conservation laws, differential flow analysis, dimensional analysis, pipe flow, flow measurements, and external flow. You will acquire problem-solving and critical thinking skills and hands-on skills in experimentation and data analysis acquired through workshops, tutorials and laboratory practices.
learningOutcomes: Understand and apply the concepts of fluid behaviour to static and flowing conditions in a real world engineering problems. (D.1)
Design theoretical solutions using engineering systems and devices involving fluids and flow. (C.1)
Recognise possible applications and links to other disciplines, and engage in further specialised study or research. (C.1)
Develop collaborations through team building, team work and leadership skills. (E.1)
Reflect on the principles of fluid mechanics and apply this knowledge to current and future professional engineering practice. (F.1)
48641.recommended: It is recommended that students enrolled in this subject have a good background in physics, mechanics and applied mathematics

48730.title: Cybersecurity
48730.description: This subject equips you with vital cybersecurity skills, addressing the dual aspects of people management and technology to mitigate risks like legal repercussions, financial losses, and eroded trust. You'll develop a robust understanding of cyber-attacks, defense mechanisms, and security services—confidentiality, integrity, availability. You'll also gain hands-on experience with industry-standard technologies such as IPSec, SSL, PGP, and S/MIME. Through practical application, you'll be prepared to enhance the cybersecurity posture of contemporary organisations.
learningOutcomes: Recognise and compare major theories and principles that are used in the implementation of a secure network. (D.1)
Apply the underlying algorithms used to construct Security Protocols. (D.1)
Identify and recognise major security threats and their mitigation strategy. (D.1)
Explain major methodologies for secure networks and what threat they address. (D.1)

48821.title: Environmental Engineering Principles and Practice Studio
48821.description: This developing studio promotes a holistic approach to solving complex environmental challenges, with a strong emphasis on water quality and treatment. You will engage in multidisciplinary projects that integrate chemical, physical, and biological principles to analyse data and develop innovative design solutions. Through team-based, open-ended projects, you will explore the complexities of real-world engineering practice. Weekly studio workshops will support the development of both theoretical understanding and practical application. The focus on collaboration enhances your skills in design, teamwork, communication, and project management. By the end of the studio, you will be prepared to address environmental challenges with technical competence and professional responsibility.
learningOutcomes: Evaluate a design solution by considering its environmental, social, and economic impacts. (B.1)
Design an efficient process to a waste treatment system project to meet client expectations. (C.1)
Apply environmental engineering principles to assess integrative design options. (D.1)
Engage in professional dialogue to refine solutions and apply systematic approaches in managing the project. (E.1)
Reflect on feedback to improve professional practice and achieve project goals. (F.1)

48881.title: Water and Environmental Design Studio
48881.description: This pre-professional studio provides you with the opportunity to address complex engineering challenges in water and land management, considering cultural and environmental factors. You will develop skills in assessing cultural sensitivities, exploring engineering options, and understanding the uncertainties influencing project outcomes. The focus is on practical applications, mirroring industry practices throughout the project lifecycle, including planning, management, and stakeholder engagement. You will work collaboratively and receive continuous feedback to develop a comprehensive understanding of project development.
learningOutcomes: Evaluate stakeholder needs across a range of social, economic and cultural contexts relating to water and land management (B1).
Design a solution to meet client expectations through application of established engineering models including use of commercial design software to simulate system performances (C1).
Apply relevant civil and environmental theories to evaluate integrative design engineering options. (D.1)
Communicate project management roles and responsibilities through written formats using professional engineering conventions (E.1).
Reflect on ways of using feedback to address own professional development in relation to achieving project goals. (F.1)

49001.title: Judgment and Decision Making
49001.description: This subject explores key theories and concepts in judgment and decision making, including biases, heuristics, and decision analysis, particularly under uncertainty. You'll learn about decision-making models ranging from cognition-driven to model-driven and data-driven approaches, crucial for modern complex systems. The subject also covers organisational principles for group, strategic, and leadership decision makings, enabling you to understand and apply effective decision-making strategies in various contexts.
learningOutcomes: Identify cognitive biases and heuristics that influence decision-making processes and mitigate their impact in various scenarios. (B.1)
Apply decision analysis tools and frameworks to evaluate and resolve complex problems. (C.1)

Implement diverse decision-making models, including model-driven, cognition-driven, and data-driven approaches, grasping their strengths, weaknesses, and optimal applications in real-world contexts. (D.1)
Utilise group and strategic decision-making strategies to solve complex decision situations across varied scenarios and organisational levels. (E.1)

Construct project related documentation while working in a team environment. (E.1)
Reflect on the impact of personal and professional decisions on prepared plans. (F.1)

You will delve into systems theory and systems thinking, with a particular focus on complex adaptive systems that evolve and adapt over time. Engaging in a real-life sustainability-focused project, you will use diverse quantitative and qualitative methods to understand and address the complexity inherent in all natural and some human-made systems and their interactions,

Organise team work, manage interdisciplinary collaboration, and assess own and other team member’s contributions. (E.1)

49047.title: Finite Element Analysis
49047.description: This subject provides a foundational understanding of the finite element method (FEM), essential for civil and mechanical engineers to model structures accurately. You will learn to create different types of elements and structures and understand their applications within various contexts. Aimed at engineering students, the subject covers both theory and practical use of FEM, focusing on structural mechanics for stress analysis. You'll explore direct stiffness method, derivation of stiffness matrices for different elements in two and three dimensions, analysis of truss structure, and numerical integration. The subject also addresses the limitations and accuracy of FEM and includes practical lab sessions where you'll apply your knowledge using finite element software.
learningOutcomes: Apply the fundamental theory of the finite element method to design real world civil engineering structures involving various types of elements. (C.1)
Design and conduct a 2D and 3D static analysis of a building structure and its components. (D.1)
Perform analysis of engineering structures using commercial finite element analysis packages. (D.1)
Present the FEA results (stress, displacement, moment and forces) in a succinct and concise form for structural engineering projects. (E.1)

49069.title: Leadership and Responsibility
49069.description: This subject will develop your understanding of the role of engineering and technical managers as responsible leaders in organisations. It focuses on the need to work through other people, not only subordinates and supervisors, but also other managers and leaders. You'll explore leadership theories within a historical context, understanding its complexities and the inherent responsibilities that come with positions relying on trust. Because leadership is not just about theoretical knowledge, the subject emphasises practical experience through in-class activities and industry guest speakers that will challenge you to engage, find motivation and think critically. You will be developing your leadership skills working within groups to perform under pressure in settings emulating dynamic professional environments.
learningOutcomes: Apply critical thinking to analyse complex situations, problems and/or requirements to understand options and inform decision-making. (C.1)
Apply leadership theory and practice concepts to develop own leadership mindset and methods that adapt to situations and goals pursued. (B.1)
Organise teams, manage interdisciplinary and multicultural collaboration, and assess own and other team members' personal, leadership and managerial fit for specific situations. (E.1, F.1)
Apply professional written and verbal communication skills to persuasively present ideas and plans to different audiences. (E.1)

49106.title: Road Engineering Practice
49106.description: This subject equips you with the ability to design, construct and maintain roads in accordance with current professional practice in NSW, covering pavement design and geometric design. You will learn to design following the standards adopted by the Transport for NSW, AUSTROADS and the Australian Road Research Board with a special focus on the residential street network. You will also develop an understanding of current issues in road engineering, particularly quality assurance contracts, road safety needs of pedestrians and cyclists, and the use of innovative techniques in road construction and maintenance.
learningOutcomes: Explain legislative requirements and procedures governing road construction and maintenance. (D.1)
Design road infrastructure compliant with the relevant NSW road engineering standards. (C.1)
Calculate the performance indicators for road network management. (C.1)
Reflect on your own learning of the geometric and structural design of roads that examine solutions for prescriptive and performance-based requirements as per road engineering standards. (F.1)

49116.title: Contaminated Site and Waste Remediation
49116.description: This subject addresses the growing need to manage contaminated sites, focusing on predicting contaminant distribution, fate, and transport for remediation. Despite the complexities of waste, rock, water, and microbial interactions, you'll learn to navigate these challenges using ASTM 1527-21 and ASTM 1903-19 frameworks. You'll conduct site investigations, utilise GIS, and engage in contaminant transport modelling to develop remediation strategies. The subject hones your skills in designing soil and groundwater studies, interpreting data for modelling contaminant behaviour, and crafting remediation plans, culminating in professional presentation of your findings.
learningOutcomes: Identify stakeholders, key concepts, contaminants, subsurface site conditions, and uncertainties in site investigations in accordance with ASTM 1527-21. (B.1)
Apply contaminated site conceptual models including water/rock/waste interactions to site remediation projects in accordance with ASTM 1903-19. (C.1)
Develop and analyse predictive models for contaminant fate/ transport and/or site management plans (ASTM D447-04) (D.1)
Communicate to the hypothetical stakeholders via reports and an oral presentation, the outcomes, and recommendations for site remediation. (E.1)
Reflection of own and others' oral presentation performance to articulate strengths and areas for professional growth. (F.1)

49134.title: Structural Dynamics and Earthquake Engineering
49134.description:
In this subject, you will explore how civil structures respond to dynamic loads such as earthquakes, wind, and mechanical vibrations. You’ll learn to model and analyse structural behaviour using core principles of structural dynamics, aligned with Australian Standards. Key topics include vibration analysis of single- and multi-degree-of-freedom (SDoF and MDoF) systems, seismic response, and performance-based design. You’ll also engage in hands-on learning through live shake table testing and interpretation of experimental data to deepen your understanding of real-world applications.

You will also be introduced to Generative AI (GenAI) and Digital Engineering (DE)—tools that are reshaping modern engineering practice. Through interactive workshops and inquiry-based projects, you’ll gain experience using AI-assisted modelling and simulation tools that support creative problem-solving and informed decision-making. By the end of the subject, you’ll be equipped to assess structural responses, apply digital technologies in analysis and design, and contribute to the development of intelligent, resilient infrastructure.
learningOutcomes: Apply structural dynamics concepts in engineering design approaches in compliance with Australian Standards, employing appropriate tools and modelling techniques. (C.1)
Demonstrate an application of structural dynamics and earthquake engineering principles in civil engineering design. (D.1)
Evaluate the outcomes of computational and AI tools for the modelling, analysis, and communication of structural dynamic behaviour. (D.1)
Communicate structural dynamics and earthquake engineering design effectively in professional contexts, including peer discussion and evaluation. (E.1)
Critically reflect on the process of evaluating computational and AI tools and their outputs in structural dynamics modelling (F.1)

49150.title: Prestressed Concrete Design
49150.description: This subject equips you with advanced skills in prestressed concrete (PSC) design, enhancing your ability to make informed decisions in structural engineering. You'll develop a deep understanding of PSC behaviour and design techniques, including the analysis of continuous beams and flat slab systems, tension member design, loss estimation, and anchorage reinforcement, all aligned with AS3600 Concrete Structures standards. Learning is interactive, focusing on real-world applications and problem-solving to ensure practical competence in PSC design.
learningOutcomes: Design and construct prestressed concrete elements by utilising modelling and analysing skills to meet professional guidelines and codes of practice. (C.1)
Identify the problem definition and apply appropriate approaches and methods of problem solving in determining the viability of all types of prestressed concrete structures. (D.1)
Interpret and apply Australian Standards in design and construction of prestressed structures. (C.1)
Recognise, identify and make decisions on the different uses of conventional and prestressed concrete to optimize the required strength, serviceability and durability with appropriate budget. (D.1)

49151.title: Concrete Technology and Practice
49151.description: This subject deepens your understanding of concrete, the most widely used construction material in the world. You will learn to assess the fresh and hardened, serviceability, durability and sustainability properties and mechanistic behaviours of concrete. Design requirements, concrete properties, concrete mix formulations and concrete material factors will be integrated and utilised through practical examples and hands-on experiences to design a concrete materials specification to address specific project requirements, including the constructability, mechanical performance, volume stability, durability, and sustainability design stages of projects. You will also use Australian Standard test methods to obtain experimental data and determine concrete properties and related behaviours. This subject develops your systems engineering framework, integrated engineering design and reflective practice skills, enabling you to select and specify the most appropriate concrete for field applications.
learningOutcomes: Identify and analyse factors contributing to the properties of concrete in the design and construction of concrete structural members and apply Australian Standard test methods for the testing of concrete. (D.1)

Predict the behaviour of concrete and synthesise appropriate solutions for selecting concrete mixes that address the specification, sustainability, and service life requirements of a concrete infrastructure design and construction project brief. (C.1)
Reflect on the performance of an engineering team to design and develop alternative solutions for addressing changes for concrete materials specifications. (F.1)

49202.title: Communication Protocols
49202.description: This subject equips you with a robust grasp of communication protocol theory and practice, focusing on TCP/IP and associated protocols and applications. You will develop analytical skills and gain hands-on experience with widely used open-source networking tools such as Wireshark and iperf3, which you will apply to design, analyse and troubleshoot large scale IP networks. The learning process is highly interactive, with a strong emphasis on laboratory work to reinforce theoretical concepts.
learningOutcomes: Identify fundamental concepts of communication protocols such an encapsulation/decapsulation and overhead; switching, routing, fragmentation, IP addressing, transport layer, and IP/MPLS based services. (D.1)
Use the 'wireshark' packet sniffing program. (D.1)
Combine 1 and 2 above in the implementation, analysis, performance measurement and troubleshooting of networks. (C.1)
Recognise basic configuration and measurement procedures on an industry-standard service router platform. (D.1)

49227.description: This subject equips you with the expertise to harness the potential of the Internet of Things (IoT) through sensor technology, a rapidly expanding sector with significant economic impact. Troubleshoot a sensor network to conduct real environmental experiments and analyse sensor-produced data that can be aggregated that may feed into business applications. (D.1)
Apply knowledge in WSN theory and technology such as routing and security to stay up to date with the current R&D. (D.1)

49254.title: Advanced Soil Mechanics and Foundation Design
49254.description: This subject focuses on advanced soil mechanics and foundation design, exploring theoretical and experimental methods to address complex geotechnical challenges. You'll study stress-strain analysis, consolidation theory, and the design of foundations subjected to multi-directional forces. Topics include critical state soil mechanics, soil plasticity, unsaturated soil mechanics, and earthquake geotechnics. Practical learning encompasses footing deformation, pile group and piled raft design, and caisson construction. A major project enhances your ability to critically review engineering documents and develop research skills. Upon completion, you'll be adept at analysing soil and foundation behaviour, applying soil models, and using test data for designing infrastructure under various load conditions.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate fundamental knowledge to carry out laboratory and field work associated with various soil types. (D.1)
Evaluate performance of foundations of various structures subjected to complex loading. (D.1)
Analyse the behaviour of soil considering various failure criteria and stress and strain paths in both small and large scales, and design appropriate foundations. (C.1, D.1)
Recommend the most appropriate geotechnical solution and foundation option for both saturated and unsaturated soils. (C.1)

49256.title: Flood Estimation
49256.description: This subject equips you with knowledge of flood estimation techniques, from both theoretical and practical perspectives. You'll learn flood risk assessment methods and learn to calculate flood flows using statistical and deterministic methods. Key topics include point flood flow estimation techniques, such as at-site frequency analysis, regional techniques, and simulation-based approaches, as well as system flood flow estimation. You'll master statistical methods, regional strategies, and simulation techniques, all essential for accurate flood prediction and risk management.
learningOutcomes: Interpret design flood estimation predictions. (D.1)
Estimate and interpret the uncertainty in design flood prediction. (D.1)
Apply alternative approaches for estimating design floods. (D.1)
Design studies for estimation of design flood characteristics. (C.1)

Apply the basic principles and procedures associated with GIS to various scenarios from Civil and Environmental Engineering. (C.1)

49261.title: Biomedical Instrumentation
49261.description: This subject provides a practical understanding of the principles, design, and application of medical instruments commonly used in clinical settings. You will gain hands-on experience with specific devices, focusing on cardiovascular disease, neurological disorders, and physical disabilities. You will explore the physiological and electrophysiological aspects of these areas, learn about biopotential measurements and critical-care analytes for monitoring and diagnostics, and examine the design of therapeutic biomedical devices. Additionally, you'll be encouraged to adopt good design practices and consider new developments for improved treatments and assessments.
learningOutcomes: Explore the development status and trend of classical and modern biomedical instruments. (B.1)
Master the working principle and main components of common biomedical instruments. (D.1)
Familiar with the functional components commonly used biomedical instruments and apply general design steps for the development of typical biomedical instruments. (C.1)
Learn the ability to design and develop medical instruments using engineering knowledge by working in the laboratories in a team. (C.1)

Keep abreast of emerging technologies and trends in computer-aided design. (D.1)
Integrate numerical simulation and design optimization methods, as well as mechanical fundamentals, into design practice. (C.1)

49680.description: This subject equips you with the skills to optimise value chains, integrating engineering, IT, and management principles to enhance productivity, quality, and performance in various manufacturing industries. You'll learn to design value chain systems that comply with manufacturing practices and regulations, support growth, manage risks, and foster continuous learning. Use operational and supply chain management tools to analyse distribution centres, transport, procurement and other components in the value chain. (D.1)
Apply value chain tools to solve value chain problems and add value to an organisation. (C.1)

51913.title: Academic Research Practice
51913.school: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
51913.description: This subject supports your early development as a researcher, prompting reflection on your contributions to your project and guiding you to craft a tailored plan for your UTS thesis and ongoing research career. You'll define your project's values, aims, and potential impact, using these to understand its demands. Encouraged to think expansively, you'll explore the possibilities of your research and its broader significance. Learning from your own and peers' projects, as well as insights from Indigenous scholars, you'll engage with journaling to contemplate the interplay between your life, career, and research. As you progress, you'll enact your learning plan and critically evaluate it through journal entries, connecting with research training resources across the faculty and university.
learningOutcomes: Describe the necessary skills for academic research practice in an evolving context
Identify the strengths and weaknesses of their own current relevant skill set
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of a range of professional development resources and tools for academic research skills
Demonstrate their research capacity-building practices and reflect on outcomes

52600.title: Communication and Society
52600.description: In this subject you learn about the role of communication practices in promoting inclusion and social justice. You explore the social context of communication and why it is important for communication professionals to understand the social world and social change. You learn foundational communication theories, explore contemporary case studies drawn from public and popular culture, and develop academic skills to support your development as a communication professional.

Communicate effectively and appropriately in different contexts.
Organise and present information from scholarly and other information source.
Critically reflect on diverse values, beliefs, ethics and identities in relation to contemporary communication practices.

52601.title: Communication and Technology
52601.description: In this subject you learn about the impact of automated technologies and Artificial Intelligence (AI) on society and contemporary communication practices. The subject covers the social, ethical, and political implications of rapidly evolving and emerging digital technologies. As a case in point, there is a focus on the collection, development and governance of data and AI regarding Australian Indigenous communities. Through exploring the challenges and opportunities presented by AI in the communication industries and beyond, you develop an understanding of the ethical and responsible use of technology. This also includes the potential for communication practitioners to influence technology development, in collaboration with different specialists.
learningOutcomes: Analyse how evolving digital technologies influence and are influenced by people, cultures and social norms within communication practices.
Compare and contrast the ethical challenges and opportunities of automated technologies/AI.
Explore concepts of data sovereignty and data justice in relation to Indigenous Australians.
Collaborate in interdisciplinary teams (digital and in-person) to produce innovative projects on the use of automated technologies/AI.
Demonstrate good scholarly practice in writing and referencing.

52602.title: Communication and Work Futures
52602.school: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
52602.description: In this subject you explore contemporary debates about the past, present and future of work and employment, with a focus on communication industries. You develop critical insights into changes taking place in the labour market and have opportunities to reflect on your working future in light of these. The subject covers new forms of work including debates around digital labour, creative labour and affective labour; entrepreneurship and the demand to create your own work; free labour and the changing relations between work and remuneration; ethics at work; the gig economy; and flexible work and the erosion of boundaries between work and leisure. You are given opportunities to apply knowledge and insights through contemporary case studies, as well assessing your own transferable workplace skills via skills audits.
learningOutcomes: Examine debates about the past, present and future of work and employment.
Analyse changing characteristics in different workplaces and industries.
Reflect on the relationship between your university studies and your career aspirations.
Reflect critically on transferable professional skills.
Practice professional communication skills.

You produce and collectively workshop your own writing in a chosen genre, demonstrating an understanding of the conventions of genre/form, and a willingness to challenge and extend those conventions. Classes are grouped to enable you to write in your chosen genre/form.
learningOutcomes: Recognise creative writing genres and forms
Understand and apply the conventions of a chosen genre or form
Write specific creative pieces in a chosen genre or form in a sophisticated manner
Evaluate critically your own work and the work of other students

52604.description: This subject encourages an innovative and experimental approach to writing, and fosters an environment that enables you to link concepts relating to art and creativity to your creative practice.  You explore key questions and texts from cultural, critical and literary debates, and link these to contemporary experience. You are exposed to experimental writing by Indigenous authors, and explore the sophistication and ingenuity of Indigenous creative writing and the ways that Indigenous experience is represented through these creative works. You can create work in any medium or form you choose: fiction, non-fiction, screenwriting, graphic or multimedia, poetry, philosophical or fictocritical writing, or other innovative forms. You consider the design as well as the content of w demonstrate innovative and non-traditional ways of presenting or delivering creative work that is also of a professional standard.

Write in innovative, experimental, and/or imaginative forms
Apply appropriate formats for the design, construction, publication and exhibition of written works
Engage with Indigenous creative writing and develop knowledge of Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP)

52605.description:
This subject provides you with a contemporary understanding of podcasting as a core method of audio-driven storytelling, audience engagement, education and creativity. Underpinned by current scholarship and industry research, you will gain knowledge and skills in analysis, podcast production, editing skills, and awareness of best professional practice in both Australian and international contexts. In this subject, you will gain experience as a specialist listener/producer and explore a range of podcast genres and their influence.

Students will be expected to be active podcast listeners.

Identify specific ways podcast creators and listeners engage with each other drawing on theoretical frameworks
Employ podcasting techniques, informed by relevant theory and industry best practice
Develop methods for communicating an assessment of podcasting's utility
Create responses to existing sound works in written or other formats

52608.title: Becoming Australia
52608.description: This subject looks at the ways Australia is understood and imagined both internally and on the world stage, and the forces that have influenced its development. You will engage in hands-on learning with a variety of media to critically analyse and creatively interpret the meanings of Australia, and how the country has arrived at contemporary issues and ideas. Through digitised historical sources, news reports, film, literature, television, music and the visual arts, you will explore recurring tropes and motifs in Australian culture. A variety of concepts are investigated from how Australia deals with the legacies of its colonial past to the way the nation has been shaped by the land's environmental extremes. You will develop skills in the critical evaluation of different types of sources, and learn how to conduct case study research by tracing the histories of specific places, people and issues to explore what these reveal about broader patterns in Australian society and its sense of self across time.
learningOutcomes: Reflect on experiences of ‘Australia’ by different individuals and groups
Critically analyse a variety of texts using theories of race, colonialism and nationalism
Develop arguments and justify with appropriate evidence
Create new understandings of Australia through historical contextualisation and analysis of cultural productions
Communicate in a creative and critical manner

52640.title: Media Law and Ethics
52640.description: This subject delves into the intersection of media law and ethics, focusing on the challenges journalists face in their profession. You will study contemporary legal cases and news stories to understand the legal and ethical frameworks guiding media professionals in Australia and internationally. The subject examines the complexities of producing content in digital and social media environments, the influence of legacy media's commercial, social, and political foundations on current issues, and the evolving ethical standards in digital content production. You will learn to develop a personal ethical compass for news reporting and discuss the latest tools for combating misinformation and miscontextualisation in media stories.
learningOutcomes: Identify and evaluate ethical and legal standards in media professions in Australia and globally.
Engage in self-reflection to improve professional practice.
Construct clear and persuasive arguments.
Demonstrate respect for cultural protocols and professional obligations.

52641.description: This subject equips you with essential news skills and is informed by ethics and diversity principles, providing a strong foundation for a future career in journalism practice. You will learn to identify newsworthy content, practise news judgement, learn verification techniques, and use social media for news creation and distribution, with a focus on truth and digital literacy. As the media landscape evolves, you will adapt to reporting news across various platforms and explore digital media innovations. Assessments involve executing a multiplatform news story from conception to production. The subject also enhances your critical understanding of the pressing issues in contemporary journalism.

Practice ethical journalism based on critical reflection on professional practice.
Communicate clearly in the practice of multiplatform journalism.
Apply different interviewing techniques to appropriate forms of delivery.

learningOutcomes: Apply contemporary journalistic methods and multimedia techniques for effective storytelling.
Demonstrate ethical and critically reflective professional journalistic practices.
Develop comprehensive storytelling skills from conceptualisation to final production.
Integrate theoretical knowledge and concepts into journalism practice.

52643.description: This subject brings together a range of contemporary disciplines within audio journalism to develop your skills in sound communication. Core theories and approaches from sound production are combined with contemporary discourses from podcasting to familiarise you with the genres of audio journalism used in multimedia newsrooms and by audio broadcasters. Exploring a variety of case studies in journalism podcasting, you are introduced to narrative techniques in the audio genre and the principles of sound design as a journalistic tool. With an emphasis on quality communication, this subject explores the modes and practices of sound production, sound design, journalism and reporting and further develops your skills in audio producing, radio presenting, radio interview skills and audio production design.

Develop audio interviewing skills and produce sound to high quality production values
Analyse and apply the characteristics of different sound genres for journalism

Research contemporary issues in journalism practice

52644.description: This subject equips you with visual storytelling skills, combining practical, critical, and theoretical elements, for use in broadcasting, photojournalism, and documentary filmmaking contexts. You will study the history, technical aspects, and visual language of composition and cinematography in news and reporting. You will develop your journalism skills in research, sourcing, interviewing, and storytelling, alongside production competencies in directing, scriptwriting, photography, sound, lighting, editing, and workflows. You will learn advanced narrative techniques and develop technical skills in colour correction, AB cutting, and sound design. Additionally, you will examine how visualisation and editing craft subtext and meaning, and consider ethical responsibilities in journalism.

Demonstrate advanced techniques in photojournalism and filmmaking.
Understand the workflow required to produce broadcast standard newsgathering and documentaries.

52646.description: This subject equips you with digital tools and methods for investigative journalism, focusing on data analysis, verification, and visualisation. You will examine various investigative approaches, their effectiveness, and the significance of journalism serving the public interest. The subject develops your skills in open-source research, information verification, and data investigation techniques. You will study landmark collaborative investigations like The Panama Papers to understand teamwork on large datasets, data leak management, and reporting on transnational issues. By the end of the subject, you will be adept at producing collaborative, multimedia reports that integrate data visualisations with audio, text, and video elements.

Analyse the effectiveness of a range of investigative research techniques
Produce narrative-based investigative journalism
Explain the ethical issues involved in investigative journalism as a form of evidence-based journalism
Apply equity and diversity principles in reportage

52661.description: This subject explores strategic communication within the professional sphere, focusing on its role in public discourse. You'll learn how strategic communication, public relations, and advertising function across not-for-profit, commercial, and government sectors. The curriculum emphasises ethics, persuasion, and understanding diverse audiences and their communication preferences. You'll evaluate the impact of media on public perception and societal outcomes, with a particular focus on responsible engagement with Indigenous Australian communities.

Examine the role of strategic communication in different professional sectors and contexts
Demonstrate knowledge of (or scope and apply?) Australian Indigenous issues for strategic communication
Strategically plan and design a creative communication product
Write professionally and effectively for identified tasks and publics

Analyse the political, cultural and economic contexts within which contemporary branding and reputation management occur
Clearly explain the cultural logic of emerging brand and reputation imperatives
Apply pertinent academic concepts and research skills to analyse brand and reputation phenomena

52665.description:

knowledge and skills required to create multimodal storytelling for strategic communication campaigns.

You will be introduced to introduced to the concept of strategic writing – functional writing undertaken with the intent to persuade important stakeholders. You will experiment with a range of written and visual genres and styles for contemporary practice, including long and short form advertisements, news releases, feature/profile articles, electronic direct mail, advertorials, and digital/social media (creating persuasive, strategic multimodal stories for platforms such as Facebook, Instagram Twitter and Linkedin). You will also explore the theories of rhetoric, narrative, persuasion, semiotics and social media, as applicable to strategic communication.

Identify storytelling styles suited to different communication products and publics
Research background materials for writing and visual design
Apply relevant theoretical concepts to the design of communication products

52667.description: In this subject, you'll work in teams acting as agencies to address real client briefs from various sectors. You'll select a client, collaborate to creatively solve their problems, and develop an integrated communication strategy. Your team will craft a presentation deck and pitch your strategy to industry panels, learning effective pitching techniques such as storytelling, research insights, and campaign mock-ups. This practical experience prepares you with professional skills and knowledge aligned with industry standards.

52670.title: Self and Society
52670.description: How are we shaped by the societies in which we live? This subject introduces students to key ideas in social and political thought which enable us to understand social life. It focuses on concepts such as class, race and gender and explores how these structures shape society and the life-paths of individuals and groups. As a core activity of the subject, students learn how to conduct a life history interview, in order to build their own social analysis of one individual's life story. A close examination of an individual life history enables students to understand how self and society are powerfully intertwined.
learningOutcomes: Explain key concepts of the social sciences
Appreciate different standpoints, viewpoints and frameworks for understanding the social world
Organise and present information from scholarly literature and empirical data
Apply theory and mobilise empirical data for social analysis

52671.title: Histories of the Present
52671.description: This subject introduces students to the histories of contemporary political, economic and social issues confronting the world. Taking a historical perspective enables a deeper understanding of the key challenges of our time, including global inequality, racism, climate change, and immigration. Drawing on historical method, students develop skills in broad contextualisation, long-term thinking, document analysis and archival research. By engaging first-hand with archives and close reading of texts, students emerge with the ability to critically interpret the past and how it continues to shape present social structures.
learningOutcomes: Contextualise contemporary problems and policy issues within broader global historical developments
Formulate arguments and justify them with support from both archival sources and academic scholarship
Reflect critically on different perspectives and experiences across transnational contexts
Communicate effectively and professionally in both oral and written formats

52672.title: Comparing Indigenous Histories and Politics
52672.description: This subject examines Indigenous politics and histories throughout the world. Through comparative case studies, students investigate and compare the agency of Indigenous peoples in contemporary debates, and how different Indigenous peoples are transforming the way society operates in respect to climate change policy, land development and cultural knowledge. Students are introduced to comparative methods and contested ways of seeing the world and they explore how Indigenous peoples have resisted colonialism and fought for rights, recognition and sovereignty.

Demonstrate an understanding of Indigenous perspectives on historical and contemporary issues
Apply comparative methods to analyse global Indigenous experiences
Communicate effectively and professionally in both oral and written formats

52673.title: Political Ideas and Change
52673.description:
This subject investigates the main concepts that define politics, and which influence the everyday political lives of states, economies and civil societies. Drawing on real world contexts, students examine a range of contemporary political ideologies, including liberalism, conservatism, social democracy and nationalism.

Using ethnographic research methods, students conduct participant observation of one organisation, choosing from a range of political parties, non-government organisations, religious institutions, trade unions and political movements. By immersing themselves in their chosen organisation, students learn how the organisation’s goals and activities are shaped by different political ideas.
learningOutcomes: Identify the key features of major contemporary political ideologies
Analyse how contemporary social, political, cultural and religious institutions reflect political ideologies
Undertake qualitative research, in particular, participant observation, and mobilise resulting empirical data for social analysis
Communicate effectively and professionally in both oral and written formats

52674.title: Global Economies
52674.description: Global markets, corporations, and institutions structure the world and shape our everyday lives. A critical understanding of how internationally connected economies work is essential to engage with social and political issues that arise in various industries and policy environments. Students use concepts and case studies to understand economic activity, without any need for a background in economics or mathematics. The subject examines government policy making, corporate power, labour rights, poverty and wealth, resource depletion, and other topics. Students research a world-spanning supply chain of an everyday commodity (such as coffee, fast fashion, bottled water, or coal), exploring the varied international and national contexts impacting on production and distribution. Students develop introductory skills in data analysis by taking part in online data labs, through which they identify high-quality data sources and question the extent to which statistical claims can be trusted.
learningOutcomes: Explain concepts, terms and debates in political economy, and critically analyse their deployment within contemporary processes of social and political change.
Design, manage and complete self-directed research, including the production of a professional research report.
Collate and analyse evidence critically in relation to concepts introduced in the subject.
Develop policy recommendations based on evidence and ethical frameworks, arrived at through reflexive dialogue with others.
Develop and employ introductory skills in data analysis.

52675.title: Investigating Urban Change
52675.description: What makes for sustainable and socially just cities in an era of climate change and growing inequality? In this subject, students learn how to investigate change in urban environments, examining the politics and social implications of development, gentrification and population movements. Students design and conduct a survey to gauge how local urban changes affect the lives of residents. Survey method enables students to understand the uses and limitations of larger-scale research. Students analyse their survey results using statistical analysis software, developing confidence in quantitative research methods.
learningOutcomes: Undertake quantitative research, and mobilise resulting empirical data for social analysis
Synthesise empirical data with scholarly reading
Reflect on the value and ethics of quantitative research methods for investigating social issues
Collaborate with others to organise and present information
Communicate clearly, in written and verbal formats

52676.title: Policy and Advocacy
52676.description: What perspectives shape public policy making? How do citizens and organisations advocate for their interests in the contested process of policy development and implementation? This subject explores the various strategies used by political actors to gain influence over the policy process and its outcomes, and how governments respond. Using contemporary local and international case studies, the subject examines how activists in social movements, NGOs, political parties and other groups advocate for policy change. Students develop skills in policy analysis, policy evaluation, policy development and advocacy strategies.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and evaluate public policies and their impacts on key stakeholders
Apply social and political concepts in policy analysis
Develop policy submissions, campaign strategies and negotiation skills.
Communicate and collaborate effectively.

52677.title: Professional Placement
52677.description: As the capstone subject for the Social and Political Sciences major, this subject provides students with the opportunity to apply in a practical setting the knowledge and skills they have gained throughout their course. Students complete a major research project with an external organisation, such as a government department, local council, non-government organisation or corporation. Research projects are co-designed with these organisations and include tasks such as literature reviews, media analysis, community needs analysis and program evaluations. The placement enables students to consolidate their knowledge and gain skills in project management and workplace communication.
learningOutcomes: Design and manage an applied research project
Develop professional skills, including workplace communications, negotiating with colleagues, and personal resilience
Explain how their degree has prepared them for working life
Critically reflect on their development of professional skills in an area of the social sciences and communication

The subject equips you with a critical understanding of transformation in diverse fields, providing readiness for professional work environments.

Critically examine the impacts of digital media on a range of industries in the service and knowledge economy
Express complex ideas and processes in a cogent and engaging manner accessible to a variety of academic and non-academic audiences and publics.

52683.title: User Experience Research
52683.description: This subject introduces you to the fundamentals of user experience (UX) research and UX design for online and mobile platforms. You will explore contemporary user research methods and design strategies, and examine the interaction of software, devices, and platform affordances in shaping user experiences. Through case studies, user research activities, and project-based learning, you will develop a comprehensive UX research plan for an existing real-world mobile application and conduct research with real users to identify pain points and generate recommendations and solutions. You will build core skills in design thinking, the application of UX principles, collaborative teamwork, and intercultural communication, you will also develop an understanding of ethical research practices and protocols for researching with and for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
learningOutcomes: Apply fundamental theories and practices of user experience research and design
Communicate ideas within a professional and academic context
Communicate understanding of ethics and protocols of researching with Indigenous Australians
Synthesise knowledge through the development of user experience research plans and activities
Collaborate effectively with peers

Employ narrative techniques in original creative writing
Demonstrate how literary traditions can influence contemporary creative practice
Employ theoretical concepts as diagnostic tools to develop their creative work

52710.title: Climate Justice and Climate Policy
52710.description: Climate change transforms society in profound ways. This subject focuses on social and political debates about climate change. It addresses the changing relationships between social justice and ecological sustainability, drawing on international experience. It especially focuses on issues of land justice and climate justice, drawing on Indigenous contexts and perspectives. Students debate the 'big picture', addressing impacts, discussing responses, investigating solutions. They evaluate a specific policy measure, either proposed or implemented, e.g. renewable energy transitions, 'resilient' urban planning, or climate geoengineering. Building on this, they develop 'blue sky' proposals, and test them in real-world contexts, mapping-out scenarios for implementation. In the process, students gain skills in policy evaluation and development, and in scenario-testing and planning.
learningOutcomes: Assess the threats and possibilities that arise out of climate crisis
Explain the impacts of climate change, and implications for political and social change
Critically assess policy proposals designed to address climate change
Describe the implications of indigenous perspectives on climate change
Identify ethical implications of climate change and climate justice, especially for the professions

52715.title: Environmental Communication
52715.description:
This subject explores the strategies through which citizens, corporations, public officials, journalists, artists, environmental groups and Indigenous people strive to influence public debate and shape important decisions that affect the environment. While many environmental controversies hinge on expert knowledge, decisions about what to do turn on how scientific evidence is communicated in the public sphere, on public perceptions of science and technology and the responsibility of individuals, organisations and governments to act. Addressing a range of environmental problems, this subject focuses primarily on planetary heating as a fundamental challenge in environmental communication across a range of media and professional practices.

Students are introduced to key theories, concepts and practices in science communication, risk anticipation, environmental policy and environmental studies. They analyse how knowledge of existing and anticipated environmental hazard is communicated in public forums, the often unexamined cultural and ideological commitments embedded in talk about the environment, and the ways that ignorance and uncertainty (lack of knowledge, secrecy, disinformation) can be manipulated, even manufactured to shape public opinion and set policy agendas. Students research and analyse case studies and/or develop their own environmental communication projects across a range of local and international environmental issues.
learningOutcomes: Analyse the processes whereby environmental issues are communicated in the public sphere and influence public policy
Identify the social, political, economic and cultural interests which shape the communication of climate change
Develop critical literacy in evaluating strategies of environmental communication
Reflect on the ethical dilemmas and responsibilities of citizens and communications professionals in the communication of environmental issues
Comprehend international and intercultural dimensions of environmental communication

52716.title: Design Thinking for Social Innovation
52716.description: This subject empowers you to lead in social entrepreneurship and innovation using design-thinking methodologies and interdisciplinary approaches, while working with an industry client in the social innovation space. You will learn to identify and define wicked social problems, empathise with everyone affected, ideate and prototype solutions, and innovate through experimentation and radical collaboration to drive social change. The course helps you develop essential design-thinking skills such as observation, interviewing, empathy, communication, team building, and analysis of issues, enabling you to devise community-level solutions to social challenges. Working in teams that replicate professional roles, you will collaboratively create a design solution for a real-world scenario, refining an innovative project plan to present to the industry client, and enhance your portfolio.
learningOutcomes: Apply a design thinking methodology to tackle a ‘big picture’ problem or a social justice issue in society through proposing a small but significant change at a local level.
Engage in radical collaboration with students from across disciplines in the School of Communication and other Faculties, and mentors from both university and industry.
Empathise with users/clients in a specific domain, and from this, develop a point of view towards a chosen problem
Actively reflect on the processes and methodologies being used and be able to identify learning needs and seek answers independently.

52717.title: Interactive Documentary
52717.description: This subject explores the use of interactive digital platforms and tools for , journalistic, factual and non-fiction storytelling. You consider interactivity from an audience perspective, and examine a range of interactive projects for online, mobile, transmedia and other emerging platforms that extend content beyond traditional broadcast and publishing formats. You gain an understanding of iterative design and development for interactive content, through analysing existing works and developing your own project ideas. You develop your creative and technical skillset in digital content production through in-class activities using a range of digital tools and software, expanding your capacity to imagine and collaboratively create material for new interactive, immersive and non-linear media. The subject culminates with students working in small interdisciplinary teams to develop interactive prototypes.
learningOutcomes: Critically analyse interactive documentary projects, platforms and approaches
Examine the role of interactivity and audience engagement in a range of contemporary interactive documentary works
Engage with experimental, innovative and creative application of interactive tools
Synthesise theoretical, creative and technical skills through the production of an interactive documentary project
Collaborative effectively in interdisciplinary teams

52718.title: The Social Life of Technology
52718.description: This subject examines the interplay between technology and social change through case studies on media, transport, and domestic technologies. The subject addresses the social resistance to technologies and theories explaining the adoption or rejection of technologies for social reasons. You will analyse how technologies have historically shaped society and consider the future impact of AI and automation. You will gain a solid understanding of the social and ethical implications of technology.
learningOutcomes: Explain important concepts, terms and debates in Science and Technology Studies
Collate and analyse evidence in relation to concepts introduced in the subject.
Communicate complex ideas professionally.

54004.title: The Future of Work
54004.description: This subject provides an internship-like experience for students. Students explore contemporary debates concerning the future of work and employment. Critical insights are developed into changes now taking place in the labour market and students have opportunities to reflect on their own working futures in light of these changes. The subject covers new forms of work, including debates around digital labour, creative labour and affective labour; entrepreneurship and the demand to create your own work; free labour and the changing relations between work and remuneration; flexible work and the erosion of boundaries between work and leisure. Opportunities are provided for students to apply knowledge and insights gained through observational workplace experiences, as well assessing their own transferable workplace skills via skills audits.
learningOutcomes: Debates the future of work and employment
Analyse how work is changing in specific industries using ideas and concepts explored in the subject
Use ideas and concepts explored in the subject to analyse the characteristics of different workplaces
Reflect on the relationship between their university studies and their career aspirations
Reflect critically on their transferable professional skills

54081.title: Global Cinema
54081.school: MAP and Sound and Music Design
54081.description: Global Cinema examines the key themes, production techniques, and cultural contexts that shape contemporary world cinemas. Students become familiar with different national and regional cinematic traditions, develop critical vocabularies for understanding and interpreting cinematic storytelling devices, and consider the role that cinema plays in addressing social inequalities and injustices. The subject also invites students to explore diverse forms of film-making, which may include high-budget national cinemas, films by Indigenous communities and film-makers, independent and experimental film-making, multilingual and diasporic cinemas, cinema as political activism, and documentary cinema (among others). Throughout, students are given opportunities to focus on specific elements within film-making processes, including narrative, genre, and characterization; cinematography, editing, lighting, sound, and production design; and the industrial contexts of production, distribution, and reception.
learningOutcomes: Analyse diverse film-making traditions and production processes, including representations of and by Indigenous people.
Use appropriate critical vocabulary to explain fundamental concepts and debates in screen studies.
Assess cinema's influence on ethical citizenship and transforming societies.
Conduct independent research in film production and reception.

Analyse theories and social/cultural practices relating to gender and identity within a transnational context
Explain theories of gender, culture and power through contemporary issue-centred debates
Examine gender from a critical theoretical, interdisciplinary and cross-cultural framework

54092.title: Popular Culture: Plugged and Unplugged
54092.description: In this subject, you will explore the histories and complexities of popular culture, with a particular focus on the 20th and 21st centuries. You will reflect on your own participation in various forms of popular culture and explore how it is important to the formation of individual and collective identities. You will examine a number of key topics facing individuals and communities, including environmental challenges, race, (dis)ability, and the invasion of digital technologies into everyday life. Your understanding of popular culture will be enriched as you explore deep philosophical problems raised and represented by popular culture, and its ramifications for politics, economics and society more broadly.
learningOutcomes: Identify contextual and historical understandings of popular culture and how individuals embody cultural positionings.
Critically analyse how forms of cultural production create meanings.
Communicate and collaborate effectively.
Critically reflect on their own engagement with, and consumption of, popular culture.

54098.title: Becoming Australia
54098.description: This subject looks at the ways Australia is understood and imagined both internally and on the world stage, and the forces that have influenced its development. Students engage in hands-on learning with a variety of media to critically analyse and creatively interpret the meanings of Australia, and how the country has arrived at contemporary issues and ideas. Through digitised historical sources, news reports, film, literature, television, music and the visual arts, students explore recurring tropes and motifs in Australian culture. A variety of concepts are investigated from how Australia deals with the legacies of its colonial past to the way the nation has been shaped by the land's environmental extremes. Students develop skills in the critical evaluation of different types of sources, and learn how to conduct case study research by tracing the histories of specific places, people and issues to explore what these reveal about broader patterns in Australian society and its sense of self across time.
learningOutcomes: Reflect on experiences of ‘Australia’ by different individuals and groups
Critically analyse a variety of texts using theories of race, colonialism and nationalism
Develop arguments and justify with appropriate evidence
Create new understandings of Australia through historical contextualisation and analysis of cultural productions
Communicate in a creative and critical manner
