70104.title: Civil Practice
70104.description:
This subject explores civil practice in New South Wales and develops your understanding of case management, court processes and practices and the role of lawyers.  You will develop skills in problem-solving, research and drafting. The subject focuses on the Supreme Court of New South Wales, including the Civil Procedure Act 2005 (NSW) and the Uniform Civil Procedure Rules 2005 (NSW). Civil Practice is considered through the lens of access to justice with broad coverage, including Indigenous Peoples and western civil practice and the role of technology in the courts and in access to the law.  
Each week you’ll undertake a range of activities, involving reflective law reform scenarios, advising on hypothetical legal scenarios and drafting documents. You will collaborate in problem solving exercises similar to those encountered by lawyers. You will also learn and interact with different approaches to the resolution of disputes. This subject leads into the Practical Legal Training program at UTS.
learningOutcomes: Analyse legal principles to determine the interests that drive disputes and the ways that Courts manage civil disputes.
Evaluate ethical decision-making processes and develop well-reasoned arguments.
Collaborate and communicate effectively to achieve required outcomes within legal and academic contexts.
Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of technology on civil practice and access to justice technology.
Evaluate and reflect upon the relationship between civil procedure and social justice, particularly in the context of First Nations people.

70106.title: Principles of Public International Law
70106.description:
This subject explores the foundational principles of Public International Law. Public International Law is a well-established yet rapidly developing branch of law that seeks to respond to complex global challenges. It has a wide scope of application and far-reaching implications for States, individuals and other actors including corporations and civil society. Public International Law is increasingly relevant for all areas of legal practice and for understanding Australia’s position in the world.     
 
The topics you will examine in this subject are the key building blocks of Public International Law: the nature and scope of the international legal system, sources of international law and its relationship with national law, legal personality and recognition of states and governments, jurisdiction and immunity from jurisdiction, law of treaties, state responsibility, and settlement of disputes and use of force under the United Nations Charter. 
  
In this advanced-level subject, you will collaborate with classmates to analyse case studies and solve scenario-based problems addressing contemporary issues in Public International Law. You will work on a small-group project to develop your collaborative and communication skills.
learningOutcomes: Understand how the international legal system regulates the behaviour of nation States through the formation of international rights and obligations.
Apply rules and principles of international law to matters of contemporary international concern.
Critically evaluate the rules of international law and formulate legal arguments based in treaty and custom, synthesising judicial decisions, scholarship and soft law.
Effectively collaborate with peers to convey legal ideas, and inform, analyse, and persuade.
Develop logical, reasoned and persuasive oral legal arguments, managing competing time and task demands

70107.title: Principles of Company Law
70107.description: This subject critically examines the role and operation of companies registered under the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) and other business structures involving trusts and associations. You will examine in detail the life cycle of the company from formation to the internal operation including directors’ and officers’ duties, members meetings and rights, through to the termination of companies in distress and external administration. Through the application of statutory interpretation, skills to real-world problem questions, you will develop a detailed of how to advise companies within the legislative and regulatory framework. You will also explore the role of state regulation of corporate activity using a range of social, political and theoretical perspectives. Through collaborative practical exercises such as tutorial discussions, and drafting legal documents, you'll develop the skills required by corporate lawyers. By participating in debates and group work, and independent analysis in your research essay task, you will refine your analytical abilities and learn to critically evaluate policy positions and the role of the modern company in Australia.
learningOutcomes: Locate, analyse and apply the principles, doctrines and structures of Australian company law to solve legal problems involving the rights and liabilities of members, creditors and officers of Australian companies;
Draw on theoretical and practical knowledge and independent research in to order to critically evaluate the adequacy of Australia’s current framework of corporate law and the scope for reforms;
Apply and justify professional ethical judgment to address complex issues relating to the impact of diversity, cultural and gender values in corporate law settings;

Creatively and analytically evaluate facts, problems and issues raised in a range of corporate law disputes and respond with effective arguments that critically appraise the available options for parties involved.

70109.title: Evidence
70109.description:
This subject examines the rules for admissibility and use of evidence in court proceedings. You’ll develop an understanding of the law of evidence and consider the interpretation of the Evidence Act 1995 (NSW and Commonwealth) in judicial decisions. You will also explore the types of evidence and how they can be used to establish facts. Evidence is one of the key topics you’ll study to become a lawyer as it is one of the four topics assessed in the NSW Bar Exam.  

 All tutorials involve collaborative whole-of-class discussions to interpret and analyse legislation and cases. You’ll also work in small groups to identify and apply the standards of admissibility to practice resolving evidentiary problems. You will undertake research to critically evaluate the legal, ethical and policy frameworks that underpin the law to better understand how it is applied in practice.
learningOutcomes: Interpret the fundamental rules of evidence under the Evidence Act 1995 (NSW and Commonwealth).
Identify and apply the relevant standards of admissibility of evidence in problem-based scenarios.
Evaluate evidentiary and policy issues and construct legal and scholarly arguments.
Identify, evaluate and analyse source materials and justify their relevance to evidentiary and policy issues.
Reflect on the impact of Anglo-Australian laws on Indigenous peoples.

70110.title: Introduction to Law
70110.description:
The subject is designed to provide students from a range of disciplines and backgrounds with a fundamental understanding of the Australian legal system, the Common Law traditions underpinning it and its operation within the Australian federal structure and the Westminster system. Its objective is for students to develop an understanding of the Australian legal framework and the role of law and then consider the law in a business context in regulating individual and commercial relationships. This provides a basis for undertaking further studies in law in Australia.

An overall introduction to the subject is provided in the ‘Get Started’ Module. The subject topics are then structured in eleven Modules numbered 1-11. The Modules comprise topics which address learning about the Australian legal system and the civil, criminal and business relationships it regulates, and several topics covering public international law. Modules 1-3 introduce students to the Australian legal system and help them understand the operation of Australian law. These topics aim to equip students with a foundational understanding of the operation of the Australian legal system to enable an effective transition into the more specialised learning involved with Modules 4-9. Modules 10-11 explore international law with some reflection on the relationship of Australian law to international law. Module 12 enables students to revise the main topics for exam preparation.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a knowledge of the law and the Australian legal system including its Common Law traditions along with historical, sociological, jurisprudential, cultural, ethical, philosophical and international contexts;
Critically analyse fact scenarios to identify legal issues and solutions;
Apply legal principles to fact scenarios and discussion questions to evaluate the likely legal outcomes for client advice or legal controversies; and
Succinctly summarise a key case to reflect its core principles, outcomes and implications for future cases of a similar kind and subject matter.

Formulate logical, reasoned, justifiable and persuasive arguments regarding the application of criminal law to factual problems, as well as the theoretical and policy issues surrounding the laws and their application

70121.title: Migration Agent Skills
70121.description:
This online subject is the first subject in the Graduate Diploma of Migration Law and Practice (C06122). You’ll be introduced to migration legislation in the context of Australia's legal system, as well as the ethical obligations applicable to a professional migration advisor.

You will learn to use essential databases of law and policy. You will gain the skills needed to communicate with clients and key stakeholders and research relevant law. You’ll develop an awareness of the role of migration agents in Australia and learn to apply migration law and policy to practical scenarios.

Numerous tasks and activities give you the opportunity to test and develop your knowledge as you progress through the subject.

You’ll participate in case analysis, drafting and interviewing exercises to practise these key skills. Through discussion and collaboration with your peers, you will develop an ethical framework for problem solving and decision making to equip you to competently advise clients.

This subject covers Standards 1, 4, and 6 of the Occupational Competency Standards for Migration Agents. These standards set out the knowledge, skills and professionalism required of an Australian migration agent.

Undertake and synthesise research to underpin migration advice.
Develop an ethical framework for practice in order to recognise and resolve ethical challenges.
Apply effective oral and written communication skills to provide ethical and professional advice to clients
Develop strategies to manage as self-directed, independent and reflective professionals working, at times, in a challenging environment.

70211.title: Contracts
70211.description:
This subject deals with the formation, interpretation and termination of contracts. You will explore the requirements for a contract to be considered legally binding, the terms required for a contract to remain valid, what constitutes a breach of contract, when a party to a contract may end performance of it, and when a party’s consent to contract may be vitiated.

Through video lectures you will develop your initial understanding, which will then be developed in tutorials. By collaboratively working on problem questions, you will practice your problem-solving skills, including critical analysis and evaluation, to apply legal principles to various scenarios. You will use these skills to provide a written advice, thereby developing your written communication skills.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a coherent understanding of the fundamental elements of contract law, using appropriate legal authority and citation;
Building on the matters covered in 70103 Ethics Law & Justice, understand ethical challenges arising in key areas of contract law;
Critically analyse fact scenarios to identify contractual issues;
Identify and apply relevant contract law to fact scenarios and evaluate the likely legal outcomes in order to advise a party of their contractual rights;
Apply legal problem-solving skills to produce a clear, rational, coherent and professional written response to a contract law question using appropriate legal authority and citation.

70311.description: This subject examines the law of torts, which deals with claims for civil wrongs. You’ll explore aspects of torts such as trespass to the person, trespass to land, negligence and nuisance, with a particular focus on the Civil Liability Act 2002 (NSW). Torts is a topic required for admission as a legal practitioner in all Australian jurisdictions and provides you with foundational knowledge required for more advanced subjects in the law degree. Learning takes place in collaborative, discussion-based classes where you’ll focus on the key cases and statutes in detail. Each week you will collaboratively engage in solving set problems that enable you to apply your readings to factual scenarios. By the end of this subject, you’ll be equipped to analyse complex problems, including causes of action and possible defences, and advise each party on their rights and liabilities.

Critically analyse the policy, development and application of the law of torts, making reasoned choices amongst alternatives to develop logical, justifiable and structured arguments, and advice to parties as to the tortious rights and liabilities in specific scenarios.

70317.title: Real Property
70317.description:
This subject introduces you to the law and practice of real property. You’ll examine the underlying principles and interests in land that underpin property transactions in New South Wales. You’ll explore the connections between the doctrines of real property law and the bureaucratic practices associated with transacting property within the Torrens Title system. This subject has a strong practice-oriented focus on solving realistic real property law problems, alongside building your understanding of the relationship between the law of real property and other legal domains; such as contract law, equity and trusts. 

You’ll learn through scaffolded, self-paced learning exercises to develop your knowledge of real property law and your problem-solving skills. You will also improve your critical analysis and communication skills through participating in problem-solving focused tutorials where you’ll collaborate to apply your new knowledge to practice-based scenarios.
learningOutcomes: Analyse the framework of contemporary real property law; its key legal doctrines and the implications of the relationships between them.
Relate the basic doctrines of real property to the ways in which property is identified and transacted in practice.
Reflect, evaluate and improve their core skills in real property case analysis.
Evaluate the relative merits of different legal doctrines and strategies in assessing, advising and responding to simulated ‘real world’ legal scenarios.
Analyse and monitor their own performance and implement strategies for developing their self-management, particularly time-management.

70327.title: Introduction to Property and Commercial Law
70327.description:
In this subject students explore the rights and obligations of persons engaged in commercial transactions involving personal property. The main topics include rights arising from dealing with personal property generally; the sale of personal property; consumer protection and the provision of finance secured by personal property.
You will examine what is meant by personal property and how legal rights arise depending on the nature of property being dealt with as well as the type of transaction.
While the focus is on personal property and legal rights you will also be introduced to concepts of trusts and equitable interests and aspects of real property. This coverage is an introduction to the subsequent core subjects 70517 Equity and Trusts and 70317 Real Property.
You will gain the relevant legal knowledge from readings, podcasts and vodcasts. You will also develop skills in statutory interpretation as much of the subject involves dealing with major legislation.
The application of legal concepts and legislation will be put into practice in weekly seminars. These seminars will enable you to develop skills in critical legal analysis as well as statutory interpretation.
Students are expected to have completed the listed readings and to have engaged with the online materials prior to each class. Further, students within each tutorial group will be assigned set tasks at the commencement of the session in which they will be required to lead class discussion on directed issues. This responsibility is non-assessable but is a useful motivation for a students to immerse themselves in a topic for a week.
Your assessment will include the weekly quizzes, a practice-oriented file note exercise and a final exam.
By engaging with the material and participating in tutorials, you will build a solid foundation in dealing with personal property in the context of commercial law transactions as well as developing an expertise in reading statutes. These skills will prepare you for more specialised subjects and ultimately professional legal practice.
learningOutcomes: Understand and apply the law relating to commercial transactions with a particular focus on personal property transactions and related concepts of finance law.
Apply statutory interpretation skills to navigate, interpret and apply specific legislation to solve legal problems.
Critically analyse how the law may affect common commercial transactions and make reasoned choices amongst alternatives.
Develop a logical and justifiable argument as to how legislation affects common commercial transactions involving personal property.

Accurately assess their capabilities, wellbeing and performance by undertaking and initiating self-directed work and learning, including identifying gaps in their own knowledge and skills and determine how best to eliminate those gaps.

70417.title: Corporate Law
70417.description:
This subject provides you with a comprehensive overview of the key principles of Australian corporate law under the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth). You will examine issues such as the formation of Australian corporations, corporate decision-making processes and corporate governance, and the role of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission in regulating companies, financial markets and financial services. You’ll also develop your appreciation of the involvement of indigenous peoples with Australian corporations. 

You’ll develop your skills in applying the relevant principles of Australian corporate law to hypothetical problems in interactive tutorials. Through collaborative practice-based exercises, you will practice tasks that corporate lawyers are commonly involved in - including simulated meetings and the provision of advice to clients.  You will also reflect on the adequacy of Australia’s current framework of corporate law in balancing the interests of various stakeholders, as well as the scope for reforms.
learningOutcomes: Correctly apply the relevant legal rules to communicate well-reasoned advice to internal and external stakeholders of Australian companies about their rights and liabilities;
Critically evaluate the adequacy of Australia’s current framework of corporate law in balancing the interests of various stakeholders and the scope for reforms;
Appreciate the competing ethical, social responsibility and commercial factors that may impact upon the business of Australian companies, and formulate strategies for managing potential conflicts;

Understand the role of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission in regulating Australian companies, financial markets and financial services to ensure honesty, integrity and accountability;

Demonstrate the capacity to be a reflective and resilient professional who can implement appropriate self-management and self-directed learning strategies to address gaps in their current knowledge and skills.

70517.title: Equity and Trusts
70517.description:
This subject explores the range of remedies developed to overcome the harshness of the common law. In civil litigation, a solid understanding of equitable principles and remedies is essential, especially for litigation lawyers. You will also explore the equitable concept of the 'trust', where an interest in property is legally owned by one party but held for the benefit of another person. You’ll compare Australian equity with other common law jurisdictions to understand how they differ. 

The tutorials scaffold your learning in the skills of analysing legal problems and communicating findings appropriately. You will discuss the principles applicable to giving legal advice on hypothetical legal problems. You’ll also practise providing written advice based on legal research, written in a plain legal English style that is appropriate for professional client communication.
learningOutcomes: Explain the nature and purpose of the equitable doctrines covered in the subject, and the range of remedies which might be available in respect of breaches of these particular doctrines

Evaluate a real-life legal problem and analyse the equitable doctrines and remedies which might be available in the circumstances; and collaborate effectively in small groups to formulate the best approach to a legal problem
Prepare and write legal advice, in a form appropriate for a client, addressing the range of options for equitable relief in the circumstances
Critically analyse unsettled questions in equity and issues in relation to which Australian law differs from the principles applied in other common law jurisdictions
Conduct effective legal research to support an argument for equitable relief on behalf of a client or in relation to an unsettled or developing area of equity

70616.title: Australian Constitutional Law
70616.description: This subject equips you with a solid grasp of Australian Constitutional law, focusing on the Commonwealth Constitution's role in our legal system. You'll gain insights into federalism and the fundamentals of State constitutional law, the power distribution between the Commonwealth and States, and the interplay of Commonwealth legislative, executive, and judicial powers. You'll also examine the express and implied rights and freedoms within the Australian Constitution. Through analysis of constitutional texts, cases and High Court interpretative approaches, you'll develop the ability to research, solve, and forecast constitutional issues. This is essential, as Constitutional law underpins the Australian legal system and is a prerequisite for legal practice. Your learning journey includes practical exercises to enhance your understanding and application of Constitutional law.
learningOutcomes: Explain the philosophies and principles that shape Australian Constitutional law, the content of the Commonwealth Constitution, the fundamentals of state constitutions and the role of the High Court in interpreting the Commonwealth Constitution.

Locate, evaluate and organise information from recognised sources, using their research to generate a written legal argument that synthesises legal and contextual principles and issues, in order to critically evaluate and address Constitutional issues.
Prepare logical, succinct and persuasive responses to constitutional problems that are supported by relevant evidence and appropriate for a professional legal context.
Examine a set of facts, identify relevant Constitutional issues raised and consider Constitutional principles and cases, to determine the likely success of arguments for or against constitutionality.

Critically engage with the relationship between First Nations people, the Australian Constitution and legal institutions, including the Federal Parliament, High Court and Executive branch of Government.

70617.title: Administrative Law
70617.description: In this subject, you will consider the various tools we can use to control government power. You’ll examine mechanisms that exist outside the courts that play a role in controlling government power, such as tribunals, ombudsmen and integrity commissions. You will also explore the critical role of the courts in overseeing government power: judicial review. Judicial review enables the courts to scrutinise government actions to ensure the exercise of public power remains within legal limits. You will engage in tasks that require you to understand the real world of administrative law practice, using research and statutory interpretation skills. Each week you’ll participate in tutorial discussions with opportunities to seek immediate feedback and clarification of your learning.
learningOutcomes: Develop an advanced understanding of how governments lawfully make decisions and an individual’s rights in relation to the exercise of governmental authority.
Evaluate and apply the components of, and procedures for, lawful decision-making by government bodies and the administrative and judicial avenues for the review of those decisions.
Demonstrate advanced skills in statutory interpretation.
Generate reasoned and persuasive arguments appropriate to different forums.
Express themselves in a professional manner through conveying succinct, logical and relevant legal analysis.

71116.title: Remedies
71116.description:
This subject considers the various court-ordered remedies sought for private law wrongs, such as torts, breach of contract and restitution. You’ll also learn about statutory remedies for misleading and deceptive conduct. You will compare and evaluate the causes of action and the remedial choices available. You will discover how a particular interest may be protected by the law in several ways. 

Through weekly videos you will develop your knowledge of the key concepts. You will then work collaboratively in tutorials to advise clients in hypothetical scenarios on the legal remedies available to them. You will learn to identify alternative causes of actions and remedies arising from factual scenarios and critically evaluate which are the most desirable for the client.
learningOutcomes: Identify, evaluate and appropriately describe and apply the various private law remedies available at common law, in equity and under statute.
Critically and comparatively evaluate the historical, practical, strategic and jurisprudential differences between remedies available at common law, in equity and under statute.
Make and justify informed choices about particular remedies, select and apply an appropriate remedy recognising when its application to different wrongs will differ.
Write a professional, logical and properly-argued legal advice on remedies available to a client, based upon a fact scenario.
Apply legal research skills to locate relevant primary and secondary materials to identify and apply the correct legal principles to provide a written advice to a client.

75422.title: Property and Commercial Practice
75422.description:
This subject encourages students to experience and reflect on the targeted graduate attributes developed by the Faculty of Law. The subject covers the skills, practice areas and values required of a law student to be admitted to practise law as prescribed by the 'competency standards' set out in the Second Schedule to the Legal Profession Uniform Admission Rules 2015. The subject assumes an understanding of disciplinary knowledge taught in core law subjects in a relevant degree. Students learn and practise the application of this knowledge through the development of skills and reflection in preparation for professional practice as an entry-level lawyer. The focus is on property and commercial work. Practise in drafting, research and problem-solving will enable you to develop essential skills in a client- focused environment. This subject has three components:

1. Property/Conveyancing - Students follow the steps undertaken in a residential conveyancing transaction, including financing the transaction and revenue aspects. They are encouraged to develop life-long strategies for meeting their ethical obligations, including compliance with due dates, completion times and clients’ instructions.

2. Commercial – Students draft a commercial lease. They also consider the purchase of a business including the contract of sale, the revenue aspects and the choice and establishment of a business structure. This involves collaborative discussion of issues related to the purchase.

3. Electives: either Banking and Finance OR Planning and Environmental Law Practice.
learningOutcomes: apply an understanding of the law, its principles and procedures to conduct a conveyance of real property within a prescribed time period.

advise and competently act for clients in respect of the sale and purchase of a residential property and a business, including the evaluation of relevant business structures and the drafting of clear and concise legal documents in accordance with client instructions

analyse practical legal and non-legal issues arising in property and commercial transactions and to evaluate and communicate options and solutions to clients in a professional and effective manner, including advice on ﬁnancial arrangements and securities.
draft clear and concise legal documents in accordance with client instructions in various property and commercial transactions.
analyse legal issues and evaluate clients’ needs in either a banking and ﬁnance or planning and environmental matter and provide appropriate advice and representation.

75423.title: Litigation Practice
75423.description:
This subject encourages students to experience and reflect on the targeted graduate attributes developed by the Faculty of Law. The subject covers the skills, practice areas and values required of a law student to be admitted to practise law as prescribed by the 'competency standards' set out in the Second Schedule to the Legal Profession Uniform Admission Rules 2015. The subject assumes an understanding of disciplinary knowledge taught in core subjects in your law degree. The focus is on litigation and advocacy with students managing a civil litigation matter followed by a choice of two electives in specialist areas of practice.  Participation in drafting, advocacy and problem-solving will enable you to practise essential skills in a client- focused environment. 

This subject has three components:  

  1. civil litigation
  2. either criminal law practice or family law practice, and either
  3. employment and industrial relations practice or consumer law practice.
learningOutcomes: Critically analyse the theory and key concepts of civil practice and procedure within the court structures in order to provide competent advice and representation to a client.

Apply their understanding of the law, its principles and procedures and ethical considerations to draft documents in accordance with a client’s instructions, conduct effective legal research, identify and resolve problems and provide relevant advice.

Analyse legal issues and evaluate clients’ needs in either a family or criminal Law matter and an employment and industrial relations or consumer law matter and provide appropriate advice and representation.
Communicate clearly and appropriately in documents and with clients and articulate options effectively within a litigation context, including alternative dispute resolution options.
Utilise self-management skills to advance the interests of a client in the conduct of litigation practice.

You will also develop a capacity for building professionalism and resilience as a legal practitioner

Demonstrate an understanding of ethical and professional and personal frameworks to solve challenges and manage risk in legal practice.
Demonstrate an understanding of financial principles in legal practice including cost disclosure, trust and general accounting.
Demonstrate an understanding on how to build resilience in a professional context and strategies to manage such conduct.
Demonstrate the skills required to effectively engage with legal work, including will drafting, client interviews, dispute resolution with a focus on principled based negotiation and advocacy.

75425.description:

Through intensive skills training, simulations and project work, students be well equipped to enter the legal profession.

This subject is delivered in a hybrid format: Intensive on-campus week, online simulations, on-campus advocacy and online legal project.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and apply legal principles and procedures to the management of a client’s matter across a range of legal environments within an ethical and professional framework
Demonstrate advanced skills in drafting, advocacy and problem-solving

Demonstrate advanced knowledge and skills in legal professional work through the integration of their learning in the academic degree and in the PLT program.
Demonstrate autonomy, well-developed judgment, adaptability and responsibility as an entry-level lawyer.
Apply an understanding of the professional and ethical obligations of a legal practitioner.

76003.title: Asian Law and Legal Systems
76003.description:
As Australia seeks to strengthen its political, cultural and economic links with Asia, developing knowledge and cultural understanding of Asian legal systems is increasingly important. This subject introduces you to the legal systems of China, Japan, Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore, with special reference to the reception of European law and Islamic law by these countries. You’ll explore alternative perspectives of law to understand how legal systems develop in the context of particular historical and cultural experiences. 

As well as online discussions, a key element of your learning will be a reflective journal that provides an opportunity to reflect on how your learning has shaped or changed your views of selected Asian countries and their legal systems. You’ll undertake independent research on a topic of interest and critically review other students’ assignments to develop the skill of reviewing other people’s work and providing and responding to feedback.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a basic knowledge and understanding of several different Asian legal systems and the historical, cultural and political contexts within which these legal systems have developed.
Articulate the concept of legal pluralism and its practical application in different Asian countries.
Examine and evaluate the impact of the introduction of western legal systems in selected Asian countries.
Develop critical thinking, especially challenging preconceived notions about Asian law and cultures, and learn to evaluate legal and academic materials from a variety of different sources.
Collaborate with peers by participating in online discussion, sharing research and, giving and receiving feed-back.

76007.title: International Human Rights Law
76007.description:
International human rights law, a body of law designed to oversee the treatment of individuals and groups by the State, formalises the principles of freedom, justice, equality and human dignity. It is relevant not only to societies with oppressive regimes but also to those with more sophisticated, democratic institutions, and has significant implications for international relations and global security. 

This subject introduces you to the fundamental principles of international human rights law, primarily through an analysis of international instruments and their judicial application. In addition, you will examine the philosophical, political and social dimensions of human rights through case studies of current human rights problems. 

Each weekly seminar is designed to include both a topical whole-of-class discussion and a small-group activity. The small-group activity involves engaging with classmates in small groups, focusing on either a discursive theme or a case study of a human rights problem.
learningOutcomes: Interpret and evaluate the principles, institutions and mechanisms of international human rights law.
Analyse human rights problems by identifying and applying legal principles to factual situations and formulating reasoned legal arguments.
Critically evaluate the philosophical, historical, political and social issues relevant to the theoretical and practical aspects of international human rights law.
Construct and communicate rigorous and persuasive written and oral arguments supported by textual readings and contextual analyses.

76008.title: Jurisprudence
76008.description: This subject deals with the theoretical foundations of law. You may consider such questions as the following: • What is law? • What is the purpose of law? • What is the relationship between law and morality, law and power, law and emotion or law and literature? • How should (and do) judges decide cases? • What should judges do in cases in which an applicable legal rule mandates an unjust outcome? • Should law prohibit conduct that does not harm third parties on the ground of its immorality? • Does law discriminate against or disadvantage women, men, racial minorities, LGBTI people or the poor? • Can criminal punishment be justified, and if so what types of punishment ought to be employed? • How can law be used as a resource for the oppressed? You will discuss and critically analyse the implications of particular theories for specific legal issues. The long research essay allows you to develop your research skills by identifying, researching and critically analysing a relevant legal issue.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and evaluate a range of approaches of jurisprudence.
Identify, analyse and synthesise jurisprudential questions and insights about the law and apply these to complex practical issues.
Develop and apply skills to hear and engage with other points of view with respectful attitudes.
Locate and synthesise legal and interdisciplinary research relevant to legal issues in order to creatively and analytically evaluate the factual, legal and theoretical issues.
Construct clear, original and persuasive written and oral arguments that are supported by research and textual readings.

76009.title: Introduction to Chinese Business Law
76009.description:
With China's emergence as an economic superpower this subject is important to understand the interactions between law, business, politics and culture in China today. You’ll explore the major differences between Australian and Chinese legal and business cultures. You will also examine ethical issues and legal problems in a Chinese commercial context, with a view to advising a range of potential clients in a corporate legal practice environment. 

You will learn through in-class and online collaborative practice-based exercises that will involve a range of common tasks that lawyers with a China practice are typically involved in. These include meeting simulations, client advice simulations, drafting exercises and small group debates and discussions.
learningOutcomes: Understand current legal and cultural issues affecting: (i) businesses in China, and (ii) foreign entities trading with or doing business within China;
Locate and analyse information on Chinese business law and apply such information to solve practical legal problems;

Identify and synthesise relevant and reliable primary and secondary sources to creatively and critically evaluate factual and legal issues to support original and persuasive oral and written arguments;
Develop online and in-class discussion skills to hear and engage with other points of views with respectful attitudes and respond to feedback from one's peers;
Develop an awareness of cultural diversity issues, particularly within the Chinese context.

76012.title: Criminology
76012.description:
This subject introduces you to the study of criminology, a multidisciplinary field that focuses on crime, penalty and imprisonment. Drawing from a range of disciplines including sociology, psychology, science, law, philosophy and history, you’ll examine the construction of ‘crime’, the causes of crime, crime prevention, and the impacts of criminalisation on individuals and communities. You will critically interrogate both the criminal justice system and criminology itself, focusing on the impact of various factors such as ethnicity, race, gender, sexuality and colonisation. 

Guest lectures by people with lived experience help you to contextualise criminological theory. You’ll also complete your own research project, applying relevant criminological theory to a crime issue and developing a short oral and visual presentation.
learningOutcomes: Identify, analyse and apply a range of theoretical approaches in order to investigate and critically reflect upon contemporary issues relating to the nature and causes of criminal behaviours and state responses to offending.
Critically evaluate a range of research methods used in criminological research.
Conduct effective research by locating and evaluating multidisciplinary scholarship and apply that research to investigate a crime and/or criminal justice issue.
Construct clear, critical and persuasive written and oral arguments that are substantiated by empirical research.

76013.title: World Trade Law
76013.description:
This subject will focus on the law, policy, and function of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) which underpins the conduct of international trade in some 160 countries. You will also focus on the Australian application of trade rules and domestic and international laws governing international transactions. You’ll develop an understanding of the basic legal principles underpinning the multilateral trading system, key agreements, the dispute settlement mechanism of the WTO, and its institutional structure and decision-making processes. 

Your learning resources will be a combination of readings, lecture materials, film, class discussion, debate and presentations. Classes will be discussion- based and collaborative, you will work with real-life cases and problem scenarios. You’ll also complete your own research project.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate independent thinking, creativity, and critical analysis in dealing with issues in international trade, and; develop a coherent and extensive knowledge of substantive and procedural law relating to international trade issues.
Use high-level research skills and critically analyse issues in international trade law; this will include locating, citing, and distilling relevant primary and secondary sources.
Communicate ideas and argue clearly, with a particular focus on questions relevant to Australia’s engagement in international trade.
Identify and apply international collective obligations relating to equitable trade and the impact of trade on the environment.

76015.title: Labour Law
76015.description:
In this subject you will examine the key aspects of Australian labour law relating to workplace rights, entitlements and obligations of employers and workers. Given the extensive coverage of Commonwealth workplace relations legislation, you’ll focus on analysis of that amended Commonwealth legislation, especially the law determining the pay and conditions of workers. In addition to considering current law, you’ll consider the development of legislation and case law regulating work. You will also examine the reasons for and against reforms to labour law, as well as the position and influence of key stakeholders involved in law reform processes. 

You will learn the skills of applying current labour law to provide advice in a form appropriate for a client. Students also undertake critical analysis and evaluation of debates within labour law which underlie legal reforms. You’ll also develop your analytical and evaluative skills by making oral and written submissions about proposals to reform labour law that mirror the work undertaken by professionals involved in making submissions to governmental inquiries. Importantly, students will learn how to construct arguments persuasively by critically analyzing primary and secondary material and applying that material to answer conceptual and policy-focused questions.
learningOutcomes: Identify and explain the key legal principles and policies underpinning Australian labour law.

Analyse and apply relevant legislation and case law in resolving legal problems involving the rights, entitlements, obligations and liabilities of workers and employers to provide effective legal advice to a client.
Critically evaluate the adequacy of, and the scope for reform in, Australia’s current framework of labour law from the perspective of key stakeholders.
Construct and effectively articulate critical, justifiable, persuasive and well-reasoned legal and scholarly arguments.

76019.title: Media and Digital Platform Regulation
76019.description:
This subject examines the global multi-platform delivery environment in which media operates and the disruption caused by new technologies and business models. Using case studies, you will examine specific aspects of media and digital platform regulation to explore contemporary regulatory challenges. In examining these issues, you’ll consider the variation in methods of regulation and reflect on the rationale for these different approaches. You’ll address such questions as:  

• who can provide these services? 

• what regulatory obligations are imposed on businesses providing these services?  

• how are these sectors regulated to ensure that competition is promoted?  

• how do attempts to regulate digital platforms involve departures from established regulatory practice? 

This is a very topical course with a changing menu of current issues. These include laws to restrict the distribution of disinformation; regulatory schemes to make search and social media platforms pay for news content; and rules to promote Australian content on streaming services. Your learning will be a mix of online content and face-to-face seminar discussions. Class discussions will provide an opportunity to critically explore and reflect on these issues.

This subject will help you become familiar with a range of subordinate regulatory instruments such as licence conditions, standards and ministerial directions. The skills and knowledge you acquire in dealing with these instruments – for example, how a regulator enforces a code of practice – can be applied across different areas of the law. The subject will be of particular value to students who would like to practice in the TMT (telecommunications, media, technology) area or work in a legal or regulatory role for a media or platform company or in government.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the regulatory framework for media and communications in Australian and an in-depth knowledge of selected topics.
Identify and articulate emerging issues and policy considerations in media and digital platform regulation.
Demonstrate comprehensive knowledge of laws governing electronic communications and digital platforms.
Apply regulatory design approaches to the broadcasting and online communications sectors within a digital platforms context.

76023.title: Deceptive Trade Practices and Product Liability
76023.description:
This subject examines the statutory actions in the Australian Consumer Law (ACL). Because the remedies under the ACL are usually easier to establish than remedies available at common law or in equity, legal practitioners often rely on the statutory action of misleading and deceptive conduct as an alternative to traditional claims.

You will examine how loss or damage is assessed, as well as the connection between a contravention of the ACL and any loss or damage suffered. You’ll also explore the remedies available under the ACL. Learning will involve case study analysis, participating in seminar discussions and conducting research for a case note.

You will also develop your presentation and communication skills through presenting a seminar paper in class in group formatt simulating presentations you would give in a work environment. This presentation will be then presented as a written report. Final assessment will focus on topical issues that are affecting consumers and businesses alike in this area of law. The aim is to develop practical skills needed to work with clients, understanding of statute and applicable case law which is changing rapidly.

In the ACL we will focus on misleading and deceptive conduct (S18) but will further explore misleading representations, product recalls, manufacturer’s liability and statutory guarantees, all of which are tools to provide protection for consumers, businesses and society in general. We will focus on the remit of the ACCC and their operations and priorities.

We will further focus on the role of the Courts and its interaction with the ACCC in implementing and enforcing the ACL. This subject is well suited to all consumers. From a career perspective completing this subject will stand you in good stead for working in the area of competition and consumer law in law firms, working with the ACCC, working as in house legal counsel in businesses or even working in a non legal capacity in businesses providing services to consumers.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of Australian Deceptive Trade Practices and Product Liability laws.
Critically evaluate the Australian Consumer Law remedies and how they are applied.
Critically evaluate the concept of ‘norm of conduct’ demanded by the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 in commercial dealings.
Demonstrate advanced research and communication skills and generate accurate and persuasive legal arguments.

76025.description:

You will develop a complex understanding of the law of IOs, including their legal status and powers, membership and internal governance structures, privileges and immunities, and dispute settlement procedures. 76027.title: Competition Law
76027.description:
This subject provides you with a comprehensive and engaging examination of the economic and legal principles of competition law (also known as antitrust law or restrictive trade practices law) in Australia. You will explore key aspects of statute law, particularly Pt IV of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (CCA), and how common law courts interpret the CCA. You will also understand how the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) operates and policy issues.

The course covers the evolution and objectives of Australian competition law and how it is administered and enforced both nationally and internationally. You will gain in-depth knowledge of major anti-competitive statutory conduct in Part IV of the CCA, including civil and criminal cartels, anti-competitive agreements (including concerted practices), secondary boycott, misuse of market power, exclusionary dealings, resale price maintenance and mergers and acquisitions. You will learn about the administration and enforcement of competition law in Australia.This includes authorisation and notification regimes, remedies for private litigants, and other related matters.

76030.description:

76037.title: Advanced Criminal Law
76037.description:
Building on foundational knowledge from the first-year Criminal Law subject, this unit adopts a socio-historical and theoretically informed approach to understanding the criminal justice system, criminal law and penal practices. Drawing on diverse perspectives—including criminology, penology, sociolegal studies, critical Indigenous studies and feminism—this subject encourages a multifaceted understanding of criminal law. It introduces students to the legal scholarship and debates that interrogate the construction, application, and impact of criminal law. This subject focuses on the theoretical underpinning of criminal law and the realities of its practice and impacts.

Students examine the roles of key actors in the criminal justice system, including police, prosecutors, judicial officers, defence lawyers, and lawmakers. The subject explores how and why certain behaviours and omissions are criminalised, how and why certain social identities and social-economic statuses are criminalised more than others, and the broader social and cultural consequences of criminalisation processes. Particular attention is paid to the differential impacts of criminalisation on some populations (such as those who are racialised, women, and those in some locations).

Through sustained engagement with academic literature and case studies, students will interrogate the general principles of criminal law and their application in practice. The subject encourages students to consider normative, historical, and sociolegal critiques of the criminal justice system and to reflect on the values that underpin legal responses to crime. Framed by a commitment to social justice, this unit actively incorporates First People’s perspectives and knowledge systems. It challenges students to consider alternative frameworks for understanding criminal law and its systems, and the often obscured impacts of criminalisation on individuals and communities.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate advanced knowledge of criminal law principles and their application in historical and contemporary contexts.

Synthesise, explain and evaluate different theoretical approaches (including those of critical criminal justice, critical criminology, and sociolegal studies) to criminal law, criminalisation and the role of the State in regulating criminal conduct.
Conduct interdisciplinary legal research using diverse research sources and methods.
Analyse the differential impacts of criminal law on diverse social groups, demonstrating insight into diverse perspectives considered in this subject.
Reflect critically on the roles and responsibilities of and constraints on the practitioner in the criminal justice system.

76038.title: Law and Mental Health
76038.description:

You’ll also increase your skills in accessible communication with, advocating for and working alongside people with psychosocial and cognitive disability.

76039.title: Jessup International Moot
76039.description:
This subject is only for students who have been selected to represent UTS Law in a mooting competition via a competitive process. If selected, it offers you an opportunity to participate in the 'Philip C. Jessup International Law Moot Court Competition' for credit. This is the world's largest moot court competition, organised by the International Law Students Association, Washington, DC. It was established to provide law students with simulated courtroom experience in international law advocacy. This competition simulates a hypothetical dispute between countries and a mock case before the International Court of Justice, the judicial organ of the United Nations. Each year a new hypothetical case, based on complex current issues of public international law, is published. The limited set of facts – concerning a dispute between the two fictional states appearing before the International Court of Justice – requires detailed research into both international and comparative law to prepare complex pleadings for both sides. 

Teams analyse the problem, conduct detailed legal research, develop legal arguments and prepare written and oral pleadings arguing both the applicant and respondent positions of the case. Teams compete against each other, presenting their submissions which are evaluated by judges based upon advocacy skills and knowledge of international law.

The Australian national rounds take place in Canberra in February. The top two or three teams qualify to represent their universities at the international rounds in Washington DC each April.

This subject is demanding and equivalent to a substantial research project. A team of up to five students is selected to represent UTS:Law. For information about the mooting competitions see: www.uts.edu.au/current-students/current-students-information-faculty-law/competitions-and-prizes
learningOutcomes: Plan and analyse wide-ranging, strategic legal research to provide targeted information for effective international legal arguments
Evaluate and apply the principles of public international law to develop original arguments in response to complex international legal issues
Implement multiple forms of feedback to reflect upon and improve individual and team preparation and performance
Develop and communicate coherent, persuasive and balanced written memorials and oral submissions for the International Court of Justice
Engage with extensive preparation and effectively collaborate with a team to successfully prepare and present a competitive moot

76045.description: This subject deals with the aspects of law relevant to healthcare, with a focus on the patient-practitioner relationship. You will consider intersecting legal, ethical and policy issues in the contemporary Australian context, with some international comparisons. Topics include: • legal foundations of the health care system; • health practitioner regulation; • negligence; • consent to treatment; • privacy and confidentiality of health information; •and law, ethical issues and the beginning and end of life. You will also undertake independent research to create logical, justifiable and persuasive written and oral arguments.

Conduct research on health law topics, including locating and critically analysing legal and health sources;
Assess different legal and policy approaches to health law problems.

76048.title: Citizenship and Immigration Law
76048.description:
This subject examines Australian immigration law and policy from a variety of perspectives, including contemporary and historical, substantive and procedural, statutory, regulatory and constitutional. You’ll discuss the criteria for admission to Australia as a permanent resident, temporary migrant or the citizen, as well as the grounds for exclusion or removal and the role of the courts in ensuring the legality of official action. You’ll also focus on laws and policies that relate to those seeking asylum in Australia. The core issues at stake in this subject – the boundaries of political membership and debates about asylum, just treatment of non-citizens and population policies – play a significant role in many areas of the law and present fundamental challenges to Australia.  
 
You will obtain a sophisticated level of knowledge of a specific area of citizenship and immigration law by completing a research paper. Class discussions, including with guest speakers from private practice, and human rights and community lawyers, will enhance your oral communication skills and deepen your understanding of critical tensions and recent issues in this field of law and policy.
learningOutcomes: Research, understand and apply relevant statutes and case law in the area of migration law;
Critically analyse the relevant principles of constitutional, statutory and common law;
Strategically apply legal principles to research questions and problem solving;
Effectively and persuasively communicate in writing issues in citizenship and immigration law.

76052.title: Dispute Resolution Advocacy
76052.description:
This subject deals with the jurisprudence of dispute resolution and the theory, dynamics and essential characteristics of the major dispute resolution processes. Your focus will be the role of lawyers in dispute resolution processes. You will learn to formulate effective strategies for resolving a wide range of disputes. You’ll also learn how to advise clients on, and prepare clients for, suitable dispute resolution processes. Additionally, you will explore the institutionalising of dispute resolution processes; the nature of disputes and the theoretical, ethical and practical issues. 

Through a two-day intensive weekend workshop, you will practice and develop your negotiation and mediation skills through simulated role-plays and exercises. These will help you think critically, strategically, and creatively about the nature, role, and range of dispute resolution processes. You will also meet with practitioners to discuss contemporary professional and advocacy issues. Case study analysis in seminars allows you to explore key concepts, interpret information, practise advocacy and develop creative solutions.
learningOutcomes: Explain and evaluate the nature and purpose of different dispute resolution processes covered in the course and the range of options in each process.

Critically analyse and distinguish dispute resolution processes and systems that are being incorporated into legal practice and the court systems and differentiate the role of the lawyer in adversarial and non-adversarial processes.
Develop and implement a tool to assist legal professionals to select the appropriate dispute resolution process for a client’ s problem.
Construct clear, succinct, reasoned, integrated and insightful analysis and arguments that are supported by research and scholarship

76056.title: Intellectual Property Commercialisation Overview
76056.description:
This subject examines the commercialisation of intellectual property (IP) rights as a business asset. You will explore the legal, business and economic issues that are relevant to the commercialising and licensing of IP rights in both domestic and global contexts. The scope is interdisciplinary and you’ll look at relevant IP laws, competition law, compulsory and voluntary licensing, contract and consumer laws, and selected issues in international practice. You will also explore the business and economic aspects of IP licensing and investment.

Your learning involves practical skills training in drafting and negotiating licenses as well as practice-focused exercises that provide you a better sense of the deal-making process in licensing transactions both in Australia and abroad. You will also give oral presentations and receive feedback from both seminar leaders and peers on your critical legal analysis, policy interpretation, and problem-solving skills.
learningOutcomes: Identify, critically analyse and apply intellectual property (IP) laws in business and commercial contexts and explain the key features of IP negotiation to stakeholders.
Advise clients on the business and economic implications of licensing and other IP commercialisation strategies.
Evaluate a client’s intangible assets and formulate a feasible IP commercialisation strategy aligned with the client’s objectives.
Identify and locate research material relevant to contemporary issues in IP commercialisation and creatively and analytically evaluate the legal and theoretical issues that arise.

76057.title: Judgment and the Rule of Law
76057.description:
This subject critically questions dominant concepts with respect to the rule of law, precedent and the values that underpin legal judgments. You will focus on two essential rule of law principles: that law-making powers are not exercised arbitrarily, and that laws sustain a normative order and thereby stability, security and order in a community. You will critically explore whether there is something particular about legal judgments which differentiates them from judgments in other spheres, such as politics or art. You’ll also examine the philosophical foundations that underpin objectivity and how these relate to legal judgments and the rule of law. 

You will explore these themes through case studies and critical literature, forming a learning community that supports and engages with each other online. You’ll respond to critical journal entries, and actively lead and contribute to online discussions, including regularly posting blogs and responding to other students’ blogs.
learningOutcomes: Explain how judgments are made about legal and moral disputes in law but also more generally in society.
Articulate justifications for adhering to and overturning precedent.

Critically evaluate the role of community values in making judgments, judging in plural societies – with particular reference to First Nations peoples - and the meaning, purpose and potential of the rule of law.
Distinguish neo-liberal values from liberal legal values and critically evaluate the quandaries neo-liberal values pose for common law jurisprudence.
Undertake Research and present an extended written response to a research question related to the subject materials.

76063.title: Media Law
76063.description:
This subject analyses and evaluates certain legal restrictions on free speech affecting the media. You will examine the law of defamation, contempt, vilification, censorship, counter-terrorism measures and privacy. The legal framework consists of a wide range of federal and state/territory laws, both legislation and common law. You’ll explore whether the law strikes an appropriate balance between free speech on the one hand and relevant competing interests on the other. 

You will learn from industry guests who are current practitioners to consider how they apply the law, and what might be involved if you choose to pursue a career as in-house counsel. You’ll also learn through in-depth consideration of some of the leading cases as well as the broader constitutional and policy context. This allows you to develop a coherent understanding of the nature, scope and application of current laws. You will identify emerging issues and challenges of regulating the media and free speech – notably, those posed by online communication – and evaluate proposals for reform.

This is an essential subject for students who would like to work in a legal, regulatory, editorial or executive role in the media, and will benefit those interested in related communications roles across a range of industries.
learningOutcomes: Examine, evaluate and explain key media laws, related principles and concepts and the broader theoretical, constitutional and policy contexts informing the regulation of the media and free speech.
Identify, analyse and apply relevant media laws and generate solutions to contemporary media law problems.
Critically analyse and evaluate a range of perspectives and opinions relating to the issues and challenges of regulating free speech and the media.
Construct clear, succinct, reasoned, justifiable and persuasive legal and scholarly analyses and arguments.

76068.title: Indigenous Peoples and the Law
76068.description:
This subject examines the historical and contemporary relationships between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, their nations, and the Australian nation through the lens of the Australian legal system. You will critically analyse the concept of 'settlement,' its manifestation in legal practice, and its philosophical underpinnings, reflecting on its implications for Indigenous nations today. Furthermore, the course delves into the role of law and the concept of justice during the establishment and assessment of the legitimacy of the Anglo-Australian legal system. This analysis is aimed at deepening your understanding and critique of both existing and potential future approaches to reconciliation and greater inclusion of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in the practice of law as you progress in your legal career.

The course also spotlights cutting-edge areas of legal and policy development, with a focus on the active contributions of Indigenous activism, advocacy, and law reform. Learning will occur through interactive seminars and a selection of audiovisual materials, all designed to foster your critical thinking. In this dynamic educational setting, you will participate in classroom discussions, deliver a presentation, and compose a research essay, thereby enhancing your research and communication skills.
learningOutcomes: Think critically about set readings to identify and articulate legal issues in context
Apply reasoning and research from recommended sources to generate appropriate responses
Demonstrate the ability to construct a logical, reasoned and persuasive argument
Demonstrate active listening skills and respond with appropriate verbal and non verbal interpersonal messages in group discussion

76081.title: Gender and Law
76081.description:
This subject explores how understandings of gender are embedded in the law and legal system. You will consider a range of key feminist legal theories to examine how law constructs and regulates society by reference to gender. You will examine key concepts including the public/private divide, the sexual division of labour and equality/inequality. You will also focus on the way law shapes areas of human experience including work and the economy, family and relationships, sexuality and reproduction, and violence and bodies. 

The subject provides you with skills to understand and critically apply feminist legal theories to contemporary gender issues. A critical lens allows law to be reimagined and developed in new directions to address gender inequalities in society. You will engage in a rigorous process of reading and discussion as well as completing a research essay and a critical media journal to analyse media coverage on issues relevant to the subject of gender and law. Seminars will include several guest speakers involved in various parts of the legal profession.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and evaluate a range of feminist legal theories.
Identify, analyse and synthesise theoretical questions and insights about the gender of law and consider these in relation to current social issues.
Develop and apply skills to hear and engage with other points of view with respectful attitudes.

Locate and synthesise primary and secondary legal and interdisciplinary research relevant to the topic of gender and law in order to creatively and analytically evaluate the factual, legal and theoretical issues.
Construct clear, original and persuasive written and oral arguments that are supported by research and textual readings.

76088.title: Discrimination and the Law
76088.description:
This subject provides a comprehensive practical and theoretical overview of Australian discrimination law. You will explore relevant federal and state anti-discrimination laws, with a focus on sex, disability and race discrimination, and sexual harassment. Along with a grounding in discrimination law practice, you’ll consider anti-discrimination laws in their vibrant and constantly changing legal, political and social contexts. People's lived experiences of discrimination are incorporated through guest lectures and multimedia first-person narratives.  
 
There is a focus throughout on emerging issues and areas of law reform. You will analyse legislation and key cases, developing crucial legal skills such as statutory interpretation and legal problem-solving. You’ll also learn about key procedures of discrimination law in practice, including complaints processes, conciliation and state tribunals.  You will conduct an in-class law reform exercise, practicing how to impact discrimination law reform, and trace the original political, social or legal impetus for change to a draft bill and final legal change.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a comprehensive knowledge of Australian Discrimination Law as a body of law and in relation to key overlapping areas of law such as human rights, constitutional and labour law;
Engage in critical analysis of discrimination laws in their social and political context, including identifying gaps in legal coverage and potential areas for law reform;
Apply research skills to identify and integrate a diverse range of legal and policy materials in addressing identified legal problems;
Demonstrate critical and creative skills in generating appropriate theoretical and practical responses to complex legal issues;
Apply cognitive and strategic skills in developing viable recommendations for new regulatory approaches and legislative reforms.

In seminars you will learn through group-based discussion around allocated questions to develop coherent and reasoned arguments in response to questions of privacy and surveillance law and its operation and to present recommendations for legal reform. You’ll also engage in two Assignment Readiness Workshops designed to assist in successful completion of the subject assessments.

76090.description:
This subject is compulsory if you wish to be awarded a Bachelor Degree with Honours and you’re enrolled in an LLB Honours Course. Through a combination of interactive and self-directed learning activities, you gain a thorough grounding in what it means to undertake legal research and to produce an effective research strategy and high quality legal writing. 76093.title: Elder Law
76093.description:
In this subject you will learn about the legal needs and rights of older people, with a focus on health, justice and inclusion in society. You’ll explore topics including planning for future incapacity, elder abuse, medical decision-making and age discrimination. Elder law is a rapidly growing area of legal practice as Australia's population ages and more people are living longer with chronic illnesses, including dementia and other cognitive impairments. 

Through practical workshops involving  discussions, debates and problem scenarios, you’ll reflect on the role of lawyers in advocating and working collaboratively with older people and other professionals in the area of elder law reform. You will also explore ethical and professional responsibility issues with guest experts.
learningOutcomes: Understand and explain key areas of Australian law relevant to the needs and rights of older people;
Critically consider the impacts of laws and practices on the autonomy, dignity and right to self-determination of older people;
Analyse and justify options for law reform to respond to problems in an ageing society;
Identify and respond appropriately to ethical and professional responsibility issues that may arise in interactions with older people who experience impaired decision-making ability.

76094.title: Oxford International Intellectual Property Moot
76094.description:
This subject offers you the opportunity to participate in the Oxford International Intellectual Property Moot for credit. The moot is held annually in Oxford, UK, over three days and is hosted by the Oxford Intellectual Property Research Centre. The competition invites teams from universities around the world to prepare written submissions and present oral argument on a hypothetical problem question in the field of intellectual property law. 

In a team, you will analyse a problem relating to copyright, trade marks, patents, confidential information, passing off or any combination thereof. You will conduct detailed and in-depth legal research on various national, regional and international laws and treaties and prepare written and oral pleadings arguing both appellant and respondent positions of the case. The subject is demanding and equates to a substantial research project. 

A team of two or three students is chosen following a competitive selection process. The team develops written submissions, under the close supervision of UTS academics. Participation in the oral rounds is by invitation only, on the basis of the written submissions. The written submissions are usually due in December, while the announcement of teams making it through to the oral rounds is in January. You will therefore only enrol in the subject if you are selected to compete in the oral rounds.
learningOutcomes: Plan and analyse a wide-ranging, strategic selection of legal research to provide targeted information for advocating a position on issues of intellectual property law
Evaluate and apply the principles of intellectual property law to develop original arguments in response to complex international legal issues
Implement multiple forms of feedback to reflect upon and improve individual and team preparation and performance
Develop and communicate coherent, persuasive and balanced written memorials and oral submissions in intellectual property law to reflect professional practice
Engage with extensive preparation and effectively collaborate with a team to successfully prepare and present a competitive moot

76095.description:
During this subject, students will obtain knowledge on Strategic Lawyering theory generally and the use of legal action as part of a strategic campaign for change. Students will gain real-life experience working within a legal clinic to develop their practical skills learnt in the first semester (78290 Strategic Litigation Practice), supervised jointly by solicitors from the National Justice Project and researchers from the Legal Strategies Hub at Jumbunna Institute for Indigenous Education and Research.

You will have opportunities to to gain practical experience in strategic litigation for First Nations clients and nations through the development of Strategic Litigation plans addressing First Nations justice issues. The concurrent placement and education nature of this unit will provide you with the opportunity to deep dive into a reflection and analysis of the transformative possibilities of legal (and non-legal) actions. You will interact with practitioners and other students to identify how strategic litigation can advance the rights of First Nations peoples and nations.

High-achieving students may be eligible to complete their volunteer PLT over the summer session with the National Justice Project.
learningOutcomes: Critically reflect on the multiple axis of discrimination faced by First Nations peope and within Australia's colonial systems, including within the legal system.

Apply their knowledge of the law, legal systems, legal practice and legal issues to develop creative and considered legal strategies, which promote and strengthen the rights of First Nations peoples and other marginalised communities within Australia .
Think critically, creatively and reflexively to connect learnings to the broader systemic issues discussed in seminars and develop a capacity to self-reflect on their practice.
Well-developed cognitive and practical skills necessary to identify, research, evaluate and synthesise relevant factual, legal and policy issues.
Critical understanding of the possibilities and limitations of the colonial legal system to achieve appropriate change sought by communities.

76097.description:
This subject provides you with the opportunity to obtain practical legal experience and develop professional skills through work on a placement. 76098.title: International Legal Internship
76098.description: This subject provides you with the opportunity to gain international and practical legal experience to develop professional skills through 'real-world' legal work. An internship is an invaluable workplace supplement to your academic program and can help to enrich and enliven the classroom experience. The international experience promotes cross cultural awareness, adaptability and resourcefulness and encourages you to think of yourself as a future global professional. This subject is taught at master's level and requires a four week (minimum) placement with an international host organisation that can be arranged in three ways: 1) Apply for a Faculty provided placement; 2) Apply to UTS Global Short Programs via their list of approved internship providers for Law students; 3) Apply to have a placement you have organised independently approved by the Faculty. The subject is offered in the July and Summer sessions but placements at other times of the year may also be accommodated. You will also participate in a pre-departure preparatory workshop, complete four reflective journals and give a post-internship presentation.
