76099.title: International and Comparative Study in Law (UG)
76099.description:
This subject enables you to undertake a specialised short course within the discipline of law overseas, and to obtain credit for this study.  You will develop legal skills taught in another legal tradition and gain intercultural awareness, adaptability and resourcefulness to become a future global professional.  There are two components to this subject. The first is the successful completion of all the requirements of the short course overseas, and the second is the successful completion of all of the assessment requirements of this subject.  
You may choose from a range of faculty recommendations or identify your own subject for study. However, before enrolling in this subject you must:  
• consult and seek approval in writing from this subject’s coordinator that the short course will be appropriate for credit, and  
• conclude enrolment in the short course overseas.  
 Possible features of a short course that is acceptable for recognition include:  
• A course presented by an overseas university;  
• a structured learning experience (this may include field trips or on-location visits and lectures);  
• the course’s content is within the discipline of law  
• while typically taught intensively, the length of the subject will be an equivalent of 24 full time hours (for postgraduate students) and 36 full time hours (for undergraduate students).  
A short course may also be a UTS Law Faculty led overseas study tour. Such a course would contain most of the above features but will be convened and taught by Faculty. Assessment for these courses may also vary.  

All financial, travel and visa requirements are dependent upon the host country and are to be negotiated by the student. The short course upon which this subject is based is not a Faculty or University arranged course.
learningOutcomes: Gain specialised , international and comparative legal knowledge in an overseas academic environment. Targeting Graduate Attributes: 3, 4, 5
Critically reflect on their experience and evaluate the implications for their current studies and future professional pathways. Targeting Graduate Attributes: 3
Research, analysis and critical skills. Targeting Graduate Attributes: 3, 4, 5
Cultural competence and an international consciousness. Targeting Graduate Attributes: 4, 5
Written communication skills Targeting Graduate Attributes: 3, 4, 5

76105.title: Disruptive Technologies and the Law
76105.description:
This subject covers how the legal system responds to disruptive technologies. More than ever before, lawyers need to be problem solvers. They also need to be adaptive and technically capable.

You will explore three main themes:

• Modern technology is changing the way that people relate to each other and how laws are broken.

• Regulators and legal professionals are struggling to keep pace with innovation.

• Disruptive technology is having a significant impact on the type of work that lawyers do and the way that they do it.

You will engage in weekly discussions and oral presentations on various aspects of legal issues arising from disruptive technologies, with immediate feedback. You’ll also collaborate in problem solving exercises in the legal technology context, often considering problems from different points of view, including regulators, legal practitioners and disruptors developing new technologies.
learningOutcomes: Identify how new technologies are changing, challenging and enabling the way that lawyers work.

Evaluate new risks, obligations and liabilities arising from the social and commercial use of new technologies, applying existing legal principles, ethical issues and reasoning to disruptive technology case studies.
Collaborate in groups and online to generate ideas and possible solutions to the challenges arising from new technologies.
Prepare and present lightning talks and case studies to the rest of the seminar, based on each of the 12 topics in the subject.
Explore and reflect on the way that disruptive technologies challenge regulators across global jurisdictions, in particular the requirements to know your client and anti-money laundering policies.

76106.title: Technology Law, Policy and Ethics (Capstone 1)
76106.description: This subject explores the policy and ethical issues that technology presents for legal practitioners. You’ll examine the role of lawyers in regulation of technology, shaping policy and supporting vulnerable populations using technology. You will also explore ethical and policy issues arising from innovative technology that poses new threats at the same time as providing new opportunities to find solutions to some of the world's wicked problems. This subject is taught by academics and guest lecturers who specialise in legal technology. You’ll engage in weekly discussions on various aspects of legal issues arising from disruptive technologies and present lightning talks that engage with these issues. Classes examine the key role that lawyers can play in ethical policy-making and draw on professional conduct obligations, international human rights law and humanitarian law. You will also become familiar with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and consider which of them may be supported by the use of technology.
learningOutcomes: Identify policy and ethical considerations arising from recent technological advances and the policy response of governments and international organisations to these developments.

Evaluate new risk, obligations and ethical issues for the courts and practitioners arising from the use of technology in the delivery of justice and legal services and collaborate in groups and online to generate ideas and possible solutions to the challenges arising from new technologies.
Prepare and present lightning talks to the rest of the seminar.

Explore and reflect on the way that disruptive technologies challenge regulators across global jurisdictions, in particular the UN Declaration of Human Rights and the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals.
Investigate how existing statutory instruments can regulate policy issues raised by disruptive technologies.

76107.title: Applied Project in Law, Innovation and Technology (Capstone 2)
76107.description: This subject is the final subject in the Legal Futures and Tech Major and will draw together  the threads of all the different law and tech subjects you have studied so far. It focuses on the practical skills you will need to tackle ‘law and tech’ problems in your future careers as lawyers, policy advisers, regulators etc. These issues are tackled through class activities, individual research and a group project intended to solve a real world problem pitched by a ‘client’. Your class work will enable you to develop further your area of ‘law and tech’ interest. Your group work will require you to provide a solution that requires high-order collaborative legal research, innovative and creative thinking and the capacity to manage a project and communicate a sustained and persuasive solution to the 'client'. You will be supported through face-to-face workshops and feedback from your peers and academic supervisor.
learningOutcomes: Develop the capacity to solve a real world law and tech problems pitched by 'clients' in creative and innovative ways.

Develop skills in self-management and working collaboratively to locate and synthesise legal and interdisciplinary research in order to creatively and analytically evaluate and resolve a law and tech problem.
Construct clear, original and persuasive written and oral arguments that are supported by research and consistent with professional needs and standards.
Develop the capacity to apply legal knowledge and skills to law and tech problems and to work independently and in an interdiscplinary team.

76108.title: International Law and Cultural Heritage
76108.description:
This subject examines the international legal protection of cultural heritage. Rapid developments in recent decades are leading to the emergent field of international cultural heritage law. You will focus on Australia's role in the development of key aspects of the international protection of cultural heritage, the impact of these international instruments on Australia's protection of cultural heritage and cultural rights, and the protection of the heritage and cultural rights of Indigenous Australians and Torres Strait Islanders. 

Your learning is based on small group seminars that are active, discussion-based and collaborative. Through case studies you will consider how the law has developed and identify the central debates that inform the field today.
learningOutcomes: Understand, reflect upon and interrogate the principles and rules relating to the international legal protection of cultural heritage.
Distil, interpret and apply these principles and rules to contemporary cultural heritage disputes.
Critically evaluate and synthesise the key theories used to explain and analyse the complex nature and scope of international cultural heritage law.

Identify, analyse and critically evaluate primary and secondary source materials on the international legal protection of cultural heritage and assess their significance and relevance for advance research in this field.
Construct clear, informed, critical, persuasive oral and written arguments distilling advance legal knowledge and independent research.

76109.title: History and Theory of International Law
76109.description:
This subject covers selected topics in the history and theory of public international law. You’ll gain an introduction to current key theoretical debates in international law through topics including empire and colonialism; human rights and citizenship; international economic law and climate displacement; use of force and national liberation struggles; and self-determination and minority rights.  

Through analysing international law with reference to historical debates, you’ll explore questions such as: 

• Is international law 'international'? 

• Who belongs and who is excluded in international legal regimes?  

• How is justice defined and determined?  

• What values does international law promote? 

You’ll use cases studies to practice the application of theory upon the real-world operation of international law. Case studies may include legal instruments and artefacts created as a result of legal conflicts or historical struggles. You will read and discuss these scenarios to formulate arguments and develop creative solutions.
learningOutcomes: Critically analyse the evolution and complexity of contemporary international law.
Apply theoretical frameworks and relevant laws to contemporary international law issues to generate advanced insights into international law.
Demonstrate advanced research skills through locating and critically evaluating primary and secondary sources of law.
Construct clear, informed, critical, and persuasive written and oral arguments distilling advanced legal knowledge and independent research.

76112.title: Australian Private International Law
76112.description:
In this subject you will focus on the principles of law that govern interaction of Australian and overseas legal systems. You’ll examine the international jurisdiction of the Australian courts, the recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments and decrees, and the problem of choice of law as it arises with respect to areas of contract, torts and inter vivos property transactions. As issues of private international law often arise in the context of litigation, this subject also introduces you to advocacy skills in a private international law context with a strong emphasis on mirroring real-world application of private international law in oral advocacy and mooting.  

You will have the opportunity to present oral arguments for the principles of a case in class, or by presenting arguments as to when, how or why the case should be distinguished. Feedback from this oral advocacy will then help you prepare for a final moot involving written submissions and oral submissions in court. In the final moot you will receive further feedback in three ways: opposing counsel challenging your arguments, questioning from the bench, and final assessment of your written and oral submissions to the moot court by the judge.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of how a foreign element in a legal problem or dispute is dealt with through application of legal principles relating to jurisdiction, recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments and choice of law;

Demonstrate critical thinking with respect to foreign elements in a legal problem or dispute, and evaluate legal and academic materials relating to foreign law elements from a variety of different perspectives;
Demonstrate skills in oral advocacy and argument sufficient to present a case relating to private international law as advocate before a moot court;

76113.title: Regulating Technologies
76113.description:
This subject provides you with the knowledge and skills needed to examine the question of how to best regulate new and rapidly changing technologies. This is one of the most important and difficult problems confronting governments, regulators and policymakers in Australia and worldwide today. You’ll examine the ‘fundamentals’ of regulation including rationales for market intervention. You will consider matters relating to enforcement and compliance and how a regulatory system can be designed to overcome the limits of rules. 

You’ll learn through critically assessing key concepts, theories, tools and strategies and applying them to case studies drawn from the communications and technology sectors. Legal and regulatory practitioners working in these sectors may also give guest presentations. 

The subject is useful if you are enrolled in the Legal Futures and Technology major, but also if you are interested in public law or intend to work for a regulatory body following graduation. No prior knowledge of technology or regulation is required.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of, and a capacity to apply, key concepts, ideas, theories, tools and strategies that inform regulatory policy and design.
Critically analyse and evaluate the strengths and limitations of the theories, tools and strategies that inform regulatory policy and design.
Be able to assess proposals to address current and emerging regulatory issues in the technology sector.
Identify, reflect on and apply ideas from relevant research materials that inform contemporary regulatory debates in the technology sector.

76114.title: Just Tech
76114.description:
This subject provides you with a robust legal story about technological developments and the significance of justice to tech developments. Rapid changes in technology are of urgent significance to law, and legal thinking is uniquely relevant to the future direction of technology. You will analyse law’s roles in producing justice when thinking through technology including protecting rights, protecting people from harm, and in establishing frameworks of responsibility. You’ll also explore the purpose of law in relation to technology with justice as the central value of your enquiries. 

You’ll discuss the implications of particular theories in response to specific technological issues and engage in critical analysis of theoretical approaches in small groups and as a class. You’ll gain depth of understanding by applying these theories to specific technological issues.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and evaluate a range of theoretical concepts of law, justice, ethics and technology of relevance to contemporary law and technology questions.
An integrated reflection upon and application of theories of law, justice and ethics to challenges raised by technological developments.
Identify, analyse, evaluate and synthesise research materials, scholarly arguments and primary and secondary sources of law.
Construct clear, justifiable, original and persuasive written and oral arguments that are supported by research and textual readings.

76115.title: Insolvency
76115.description:
This subject provides an introduction to the administration and regulation of insolvent individuals and corporations. You will examine insolvency within the social context as well as the impact of insolvency law. You’ll also explore the legal procedures involved in insolvency law, as well as the impact of insolvency on stakeholders such as employees, creditors and debtors. Both individual and corporate insolvency are examined. 

You will learn through weekly readings and podcasts that provide a framework for understanding foundational concepts. You will then class join small and large group discussions to further explore the main issues. Each week you will also analyse a hypothetical problem scenario that will simulate a legal advice session where you’ll advise the client of their legal position and offer advice that is legally sound and commercially appropriate for the client’s situation.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate the ability to correctly apply relevant insolvency laws to a range of common commercial situations involving all forms of business structures by providing written and verbal advice;
Critically assess and synthesise the range of commercial and legal issues that arise during times of financial difficulty;
Efficiently and effectively identify and apply electronic and paper-based research strategies to inform and facilitate the formulation of sound oral and written legal arguments for clients;
Effectively balance and synthesise the competing interests of different stakeholders involved in an insolvent estate.

76116.title: Personal Injury Law in Practice
76116.description:
This subject examines the key principles of Australian law governing the compensation of personal injuries. You’ll focus on the relevant aspects of civil liability legislation relating to public liability, medical negligence and product liability claims. You will also look at the statutory schemes governing workers compensation, military veterans’ compensation, motor vehicle accidents and dust diseases. Personal injury compensation is a very significant area of practice for the Australian legal profession as employers, insurers, governments and businesses frequently seek expert guidance to manage their legal liabilities. 

Your classes will be interactive and include guest presentations by current legal practitioners. Through collaborative in-class activities, case discussions and legal advices, you’ll develop practical skills in researching and applying the relevant rules of law to advise hypothetical clients of their rights and options. You will also evaluate the effectiveness of Australia's current laws and the scope for law and policy reform
learningOutcomes: Explain and critically analyse the development of the key legislation and general law principles governing the compensation for personal injuries in Australia

Apply relevant legislative rules and general law principles to solve legal problems involving the rights and liabilities of injured persons and other stakeholders, and provide written advices to hypothetical clients
Critically evaluate the adequacy of Australia’s current legal framework relating to the compensation of personal injuries, and where relevant the scope for the reform
Identify and evaluate appropriate electronic and paper-based information resources to assist in resolving practical legal problems involving the compensation for personal injuries in Australia

76516.title: Family Law
76516.description:
In this subject you will develop an understanding of the Family Law system including the dispute resolution procedures in the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia. You will learn about the laws that govern the rights and obligations of parties in parenting and/ or interpersonal relationship disputes by examining fundamental provisions of the Family Law Act 1975 and the Child Support legislation. You’ll develop your knowledge base and analytical skills through problem-solving exercises that mirror the legal and factual issues that arise in legal practice when advising on, or adjudicating family law matters. 

You will engage in weekly class and group discussions and oral presentations on various issues and problems raised in the readings. Role-playing allows you to develop empathy for those involved in the Family law system. You’ll also take part in a compulsory negotiation exercise, acting for parties in a financial dispute to add authenticity to the way that you resolve disputes and prepare for litigation.
learningOutcomes: Identify and apply the legislation, case law and policy that inform the operation of the family law system in Australia in resolving problem-based scenarios.
Critically analyse the legal framework pertaining to the regulation of different types of domestic relationships and families in Australia.
Construct logical, reasoned, persuasive and justifiable legal and scholarly arguments.
Creatively and analytically evaluate factual, legal and policy issues and justify their relevance to contemporary family law debates.

76517.title: Succession
76517.description:
Succession law, sometimes called the law of wills, concerns the legal transfer of rights and obligations upon death. 
 
This subject takes a theoretical and practical approach to the study of succession law in New South Wales. You will investigate the legal requirements of a valid will, including the common law requirement of testamentary capacity, and the circumstances in which the courts may recognise a less formal document, such as a homemade will. While the subject has a focus on the Succession Act 2006 (NSW), other relevant statutes and case law are considered.
 
You will also the examine how the history and development of succession law impacts on the current law, as well as consideration of related concepts of families and death, what happens when a person dies without a will, challenges to wills and how a deceased estate is administered.
 
The subject includes a strong practical element in which you will apply your succession law learning in exercises which develop valid will drafting skills. 
 
Written and oral communication is an important component of the work of lawyers and other professionals, particularly in succession cases involving people's emotions. Tasks are undertaken that require critical analysis of a client’s succession wishes and develop ability to analyse, draft wills and advise succinctly and clearly.
learningOutcomes: Apply key concepts of succession law and legislation and identify the requirement of a valid will;
Identify analyse and evaluate a client's instruction to draft a valid will that complies with legal requirements;
Critically analyse and evaluate fact scenarios concerning construction and validity of wills, intestacy and and administration of estates;
Recognise current and future trends in succession law and effectively communicate in writing their impact of property and relationships.

76521.title: Intellectual Property and Traditional Knowledge
76521.description:
This subject considers the nature of traditional knowledge, how intellectual property in this area is protected under the Australian legal framework, and the development of strategies for its protection. You’ll gain an overview of the international treaty framework, relevant Australian legislation and concerns for Australian Indigenous peoples such as appropriation of Indigenous arts and culture, language, spirituality, medicinal knowledge, film and music. You’ll also examine comparisons with protection regimes in other nations, such as China and India. 

Through the major research project, you’ll have the opportunity to explore specific aspects of the protection of traditional knowledge and culture in greater depth. The learning modules enable you to consolidate your understanding of the law and issues in the field. You will engage in a range of collaborative activities to develop and test your understanding.
learningOutcomes: Reflect on and interrogate the nature and scope of national and international laws, policies and organisations relating to Traditional Knowledge (TK) and Intellectual Property (IP).
Critically and creatively analyse the theoretical bases for TK protection and the commercial and cultural implications of that protection.
Conduct effective research by locating and evaluating legal and other disciplinary sources and apply that research to investigate a legal or policy issue related to IP and TK and/or culture.

76900.title: Moot
76900.description:
This subject offers you the opportunity to participate in a variety of national mooting competitions for credit towards your degree. Mooting is a mock-court experience where students argue questions of law and develop their ability to persuasively argue a case in court and become intimately familiar with relevant law through research. It is an exciting way for you to gain high-level courtroom skills and research experience, and participation in a mooting team is coveted by high-achieving law students and future employers. 

Several months of preparation is required to participate in a mooting competition and you work in a team to develop your understanding of the area(s) of law relevant to the particular moot. You will prepare written memorials that consist of submissions for the applicant and the respondent. You’ll also participate in intensive advocacy training prior to the oral rounds of the competition.  

Selection for a mooting team is competitive and calls for expressions of interest from students are made each year. You will need an above-average academic record and demonstrate strong research and writing skills. You are encouraged to sharpen your mooting technique through junior level competitions run by the UTS Law Students' Society. 

The moots available for completion of this subject vary each year but have included the QUT Torts Moot, Gibbs Constitutional Moot and AAT Moot.  

For current opportunities and further information on mooting competitions, see the UTS:Law Mooting pages at: https://www.uts.edu.au/future-students/law/beyond-classroom/mooting-competition-program.
learningOutcomes: Identify, analyse and apply relevant principles of law to complex legal issues to construct clear, original, persuasive and balanced written and oral arguments
Advocate on legal issues in legal submissions
Successfully work in a team to achieve an effective collaborative outcome under pressure
Reflect upon and critically evaluate individual and team preparation and performance in the competitive advocacy arena

76902.title: Law and Literature
76902.description:
This subject examines literary and legal responses to violence and trauma. You’ll read and discuss some of the most thought-provoking literary works of the present, and of the 20th century, as well as judgments and other legal documents.  You will apply advanced critical analysis to these texts, learning to evaluate and synthesise information as well as critique legal and academic arguments. 

Classes are interactive and you will be encouraged to offer your opinions and ask questions to develop your understanding of the relationship between literature and the law and the responses to violence and trauma. You’ll develop a conceptual and analytical understanding of legal and humanities scholarship.
learningOutcomes: Analyse, and evaluate law and humanities scholarship and engage with legal and literary texts to respond to questions of injustice.
Identify, analyse and synthesise research materials and sources of law.

Identify and explain examples of complex problems of violence and trauma, including concepts in the interdisciplinary area of law and the humanities and the role that law has played in responding to collective violence.
Construct clear, original and persuasive written and oral arguments that are supported by research and textual readings.

76903.description:
In this subject you’ll develop an understanding of international commercial transactions. You will examine the major legal frameworks for the international regulation of commercial transactions, as well as major international trade organisations such as the World Trade Organisation and the European Union. You’ll also explore dispute resolution issues in the context of international transactions, along with the legal rights involved in these transactions. 

You will develop skills in drafting, statutory interpretation and legal analysis through real-time transaction workshops. This will include providing written advice to clients as well as practice problems involving navigating, explaining and applying complex provisions in the international regulatory context.

Locate and synthesise legal research relevant to International Commercial transactions in order to critically evaluate factual and legal issues.
Construct clear and persuasive legal arguments in writing that are supported by research and textual readings.

Construct logical and justifiable analysis as to how international regulation affects international transactions.

76904.title: Price International Media Law Moot
76904.description:
This subject offers you an opportunity to participate in the Price Media Law Moot Court Competition for credit towards your degree. Established in 2008, this international moot focuses on freedom of expression issues and the role of the media and information and communication technologies. It enables you to develop your expertise in arguing a case before an international bench of judges from different legal systems and backgrounds. The teams invited to participate in the international rounds uphold the rights enshrined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights at Oxford University while competing against teams from law schools from Europe, Asia, the Middle East and the US. 

You’ll analyse a problem of international human rights and be challenged to engage in comparative research of legal standards at the national, regional and international levels, and to develop original arguments on cutting-edge questions in media law. 

 Teams prepare written and oral pleadings arguing both the applicant and respondent positions of the case. Submissions are evaluated by judges based upon advocacy skills and knowledge of international law. Australian teams are invited to participate internationally based on their written submission scores. This subject is demanding and equates to a substantial research project.  

Selection for the UTS Law team is competitive and is limited to a maximum of five students annually. Calls for expressions of interest are made in July. For information about mooting competitions see: www.uts.edu.au/current-students/current-students-information-faculty-law/competitions-and-prizes
learningOutcomes: Plan and analyse a wide-ranging, strategic selection of legal research to provide targeted information for advocating a position on regulation of the media and international human rights law
Evaluate and apply the principles of international human rights and media law to develop original arguments in response to complex international legal issues
Implement multiple forms of feedback to reflect upon and improve individual and team preparation and performance
Develop and communicate coherent, persuasive and balanced written memorials and oral submissions in international human rights and media law
Engage with extensive preparation and effectively collaborate with a team to successfully prepare and present a competitive moot

77697.title: Higher Degree Research Seminar
77697.description: This subject prepares you for higher degree research in law, specifically for undertaking and writing a research thesis. Through a series of seminars and workshops (exploring positioning your work within the literature, methodology, ethics, research questions, and academic writing and presentations) you’ll be provided with a thorough grounding in the components of an effective research strategy and positioned to produce either a written research proposal to prepare for your Candidature Assessment at the end of stage one, or a literature review assignment on an area of relevance to your research topic. The substantive content of this subject will be taught in spring semester in the first year of your candidature. You will attend 8 x 3-hour small group sessions using a combination of seminar-style discussions and workshops, in the final class you will present your research proposal to the class. The final assessment task provides students with a choice to either submit a written revised proposal or a literature review on an area of relevance to their research topic. Students should discuss with their supervisor the most appropriate task at their stage in their candidature.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the broad contexts of legal research, the different constituencies of that research and various research methodologies

Demonstrate ability to critically analyse and evaluate literature in order to prepare a comprehensive and critical review of the field, articulate complex issues, situate the research project in the field and frame research questions
Demonstrate sophisticated creative and cognitive skills in designing a thesis project, developing an appropriate research methodology and formulating a research proposal
Demonstrate ability to execute a written research proposal or literature review that demonstrates advanced critical thinking, academic writing and research skills
Demonstrate ability to present a research proposal to an audience of scholars

77716.description:

You’ll develop the key skills of legal research and writing, presentation skills and the ability to analyse problems and apply the law to resolve issues from a legal and global perspective.

77745.title: Negotiation
77745.description:
This subject brings together current theories and practice in negotiation skills and analysis, with an emphasis on identifying effective negotiation strategies. Negotiation is an essential subject for you as a law student given that lawyers negotiate with clients and for clients, with their employers, employees and colleagues, with lawyers for the other side, with the court system, with the judicial officer and with their families. Understanding how to negotiate fairly and effectively is likely to be more important to your future career than any other skill. 

You will practise and develop your negotiation skills and understanding through simulated role-plays and exercises focused around various aspects of negotiation. You’ll also use a student-developed scenario and evaluation checklist to measure the effectiveness of a simulated negotiation process and its outcomes. Through the role-plays and debriefs, you’ll have continuous opportunities to receive feedback from peers and teaching staff.
learningOutcomes: Investigate, analyse, evaluate and apply negotiation processes and bargaining styles, including integrative and distributive bargaining;

Differentiate Principled Negotiation from other techniques and negotiation approaches and apply the cognitive, technical and creative skills of Principled Negotiation at practical and theoretical levels;
Prepare, manage, design and execute a formal negotiation by applying Principled Negotiation techniques and evaluate and review a completed negotiation;

Critically analyse, distinguish and communicate the major theoretical propositions, methodologies, and professional issues in negotiation literature including power, coalition building, persuasion, trust and ethical issues;

Implement self-directed work and development including preparing for and applying feedback on negotiation tasks, managing individual contribution to group work and employing reflective practices to evaluate their personal contribution when working with others.

77889.title: Trade Marks Law
77889.description:
This subject provides a critical and analytical understanding of the principles of trade marks law in Australia and New Zealand. You’ll examine the registration, protection and licensing of registered trade marks. You will also examine the legal protection of unregistered trade marks, brands and other indicia of commercial reputation in Australia and New Zealand, through the actions for statutory misleading or deceptive conduct and passing off. You will also explore the parallel systems of registration for business names, domain names and indications of geographical origin in Australia and  New Zealand. 

You’ll learn through detailed expert feedback, guided activities and discussion topics to develop skills in legal analysis, evaluation and reflection, which are essential for successful practice in trade marks law whether as a lawyer, patent attorney, Australian trade mark attorney or a brand development professional. This subject is accredited by the Trans-Tasman IP Attorneys Board as fulfilling part of the knowledge requirements for registration as a trade mark attorney in Australia or as a trans-Tasman patent attorney in Australia and New Zealand.
learningOutcomes: Identify, understand and apply specialised knowledge of trade marks law, the law of passing off and of statutory misleading or deceptive conduct in Australia and New Zealand and of the parallel systems of registration for business names, domain names and indications of geographical origin in Australia and New Zealand.

Critically analyse, evaluate and compare the legal framework and the legal process of trade marks law, the law of passing off and of statutory misleading or deceptive conduct in Australia and New Zealand and of the parallel systems of registration for business names, domain names and indications of geographical origin in Australia and New Zealand.

Think critically, ethically and strategically in advising on and obtaining appropriate protection for brands and signs under the law of trade marks, the law of passing off and of statutory misleading or deceptive conduct in Australia and New Zealand and of the parallel systems of registration for business names, domain names and indications of geographical origin in Australia and New Zealand.

Construct and articulate logical, reasoned, persuasive and justifiable legal and scholarly arguments, supported by accurate and authentic references to authority, to resolve practical problems and issues in the process of registration and enforcement of rights in registered trade marks, brands and unregistered trade marks under trade marks law and the law of passing off and statutory misleading or deceptive conduct in Australia and New Zealand.

77890.title: Trade Marks Practice
77890.description:
This subject provides a critical, ethical and practical understanding of trade marks practice in Australia and New Zealand. You will learn how to advise and handle the interests of a client in the prosecution and maintenance of trade mark applications and the management of trade mark portfolios. This includes giving advice on the desirability of seeking trade mark protection and provision of alternative protection for unregistered trade marks in Australia and New Zealand and and in other countries. You’ll examine classification systems, types of application and registration, trade mark office procedures, international practice in trade marks applications and issues in enforcement of trade mark registrations including border controls, infringement, misuse and criminal sanctions.
You’ll learn through a guided approach to legal analysis and problem-solving, with activities based on sample problems and scenarios in trade marks practice with opportunities to discuss and reflect on the trade marks practice issues they present. You’ll receive individual feedback on your legal problem-solving skills followed by expert presentations on the problems and scenarios concerned. This subject is accredited by the Trans-Tasman IP Attorneys Board as fulfilling part of the knowledge requirements for registration as a trade mark attorney in Australia or as a trans-Tasman patent attorney in Australia and New Zealand.

77894.title: Drafting of Patent Specifications
77894.description:
This subject develops your ability to draft competent independent and dependent patent claims with an accompanying patent description. This is the most important set of skills that a patent attorney can have. You’ll learn how to draft:

  • Independent claims that are valid, clear and succinct and whose scopes are not too broad and not too narrow so as to be difficult for competitors to avoid.
  • A set of dependent claims that provide adequate fallback positions if the independent claim on which they depend are found invalid.
  • A patent description that supports the claims and is sufficiently clear and complete.

You will develop practical patent drafting and analytical skills through online group assessments, individual assessments and case studies that mirror the legal and factual drafting issues that arise in practice. This subject is accredited by the Trans-Tasman IP Attorneys Board as fulfilling part of the knowledge requirements for registration as a trans-Tasman patent attorney in Australia and New Zealand.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and conceptualise the essence of an invention.
Draft, review and refine comprehensive patent claims based on the inventive concept.
Think critically and strategically regarding a complex professional conduct problem in a patent drafting scenario.
Draft, review and refine an effective patent specification.

77903.title: Copyright Law
77903.description:
This subject explores the principles of copyright law in Australia. You will develop an understanding of the doctrinal law of copyright in Australia in terms of the relevant statutory frameworks and their application in the case law. You’ll examine where copyright law fits within the broader field of intellectual property law in Australia, as well as the international environment and international treaties in which Australian copyright law operates.

This subject also sets Australian copyright law in context by comparing it with the copyright law of the European Union, the United States of America, the United Kingdom and New Zealand. You will explore subsistence of copyright and what copyright protects, the nature of copyright infringement and how the defences and exceptions to infringement operate. You will also consider the neighbouring rights to copyright including moral rights and performers' rights. You’ll learn about ownership of copyright, and the commercialisation of copyright including collective management of copyright. You will also gain insight into the enforcement of copyright and anti-piracy measures, as well as remedies for copyright infringement and aspects of litigation processes in the Federal jurisdictions in Australia.

You are encouraged to explore current issues in Australian and international copyright law, such as copyright in Indigenous traditional cultural expressions and the challenges to copyright doctrines posed by rapidly changing technologies, including artificial intelligence. You will develop skills in critical analysis, evaluation, problem-solving and research in copyright law. Together, these skills and knowledge enable you to critique theoretical, jurisprudential and policy issues as well as the laws, cases, practices and policies in this area.
learningOutcomes: Understand, critically analyse and evaluate the factual, legal and theoretical issues relevant to contemporary policy debates and law reform in copyright law and practice in Australia and internationally, including the impact of new technology (including artificial intelligence) on copyright law and practice and the recognition, proper attribution and protection of Indigenous works and traditional cultural expressions;
Think critically, ethically and strategically in relation to commercial disputes in copyright law and practice and adopt an ethical and solution-focused approach to legal problems in copyright;

Research, construct and articulate ethical, logical, reasoned, persuasive and justifiable legal and scholarly arguments, supported by accurate and authentic references to authority, to comment on and resolve practical problems and issues in copyright law and policy, including the impact of new technology (including artificial intelligence) on copyright law and practice and the recognition, proper attribution and protection of Indigenous works and traditional cultural expressions;

Undertake independent research and analysis to construct and articulate logical, reasoned, persuasive and justifiable legal and scholarly arguments, supported by accurate and authentic references to authority on emerging issues in copyright law in Australia and internationally on copyright law and practice (including the impact of new technology (including artificial intelligence) and the recognition, proper attribution and protection of Indigenous works and traditional cultural expressions.

77938.description:
This subject examines Australian taxation law in a practical business environment. You will focus on the application of tax law concepts to both individuals and entities. This process may involve determining assessable income, and understanding how this is determined, as well as specific and general deductions.

Communicate knowledge of taxation law both in writing and orally clearly and be open to critical analysis and reflection of own ideas and others;
Interpret and synthesise relevant taxation legislation and rules accurately and apply to problem scenarios.

77942.description:

You’ll learn to identify the legal issues of contract formation, the contents of a contract, how a contract can be discharged and the remedies available when one of the parties to the contract has breached the contract. Through hypothetical problems, you will develop an understanding of legal and ethical issues relating to the relationship between contracting parties. Learning also involves active engagement with media reports, video presentations, tutorials and a range of online exercises.

Formulate a legal argument by the correct interpretation and application of relevant cases and statutory materials and manage competing arguments using the IRAC (Issues, Rules, Application and Conclusion) format for answering legal problems.

78008.title: Law of the Sea
78008.description:
This subject examines the status of the Law of the Sea today, as well as its history and development. You will examine the Law of the Sea as it is now codified in the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), and its associated implementing agreements. You will analyse how UNCLOS and other sources of international law define and delineate nation states jurisdiction in the oceans as well as maritime boundaries. You will explore how this area of international law regulates navigation; exploitation of valuable mineral and fishery resources; protection of the marine environment and marine pollution. The subject exposes you to how the law balances the interests of coastal, landlocked, developed and developing states across all its provisions. You will consider how activities such as marine scientific research, the military uses of the ocean, terrorism and piracy are regulated under UNCLOS and other sources of international law. New and emerging challenges posed by climate change and commercial activities such as bioprospecting are also considered. One of the significant innovations of UNCLOS was the introduction of clear international dispute resolution mechanisms which have facilitated resolution of disputes in relation to all the issues covered in this subject. As such the subject also integrates consideration of how these international dispute resolution mechanisms have helped in the progressive development of international law in and for the oceans and their contributions to international peace and security.

Working in small teams on a range of activities, you’ll develop and practise strategies and skills for collaborative work. Your group will then present a topic of Law of the Sea to your peers. You will also have the opportunity to conduct in depth research on an issue relating to the Law Sea through preparation of a research paper on a selected topic of interest.
learningOutcomes: demonstrate knowledge of the international legal system and how it regulates the relationships between nation States, including regulating all human uses of the seas;
apply fundamental rules and principles of international law to select areas of the Law of the Sea;
appreciate how the international Law of the Sea affects domestic legal systems, in particular the Australian legal system;
research, read and synthesise legal information, including primary materials (treaties, UN resolutions, domestic legislation, case law) and secondary materials.
effectively and persuasively communicate orally and in written legal arguments.

78013.title: Refugee Law and Practice
78013.description:
This subject introduces you to the legal principles and procedures of international refugee law and their application within a domestic context. You’ll learn about the historical development of refugee law and evaluate the key features and limitations of the current refugee determination system in Australia. You will explore the practical realities of refugee law and practice through a clinical experience, working on 'real-life' refugee law cases and current legal issues. This practical work is supervised by UTS Law staff in conjunction with a local refugee legal organisation.  
 You will apply your academic learning to a professional context by undertaking research and drafting submissions informing real-life refugee casework. This will deepen your understanding of refugee law and policy and provide a critical understanding of refugee status determination processes. By working on real-life refugee cases, you’ll gain practice-based, cross-cultural skills and insights necessary for work as a refugee lawyer.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of the key concepts, principles and procedures of international and national legal frameworks for the protection of refugees and asylum seekers with a particular focus on the United Nations Convention Relating the Status of Refugees and the 1967 Protocol and the applicability of these instruments in Australian law.
Apply legal knowledge and research skills to practical refugee legal projects in a professional context.
Demonstrate practical legal skills required to draft legal documents and make written submissions in the context of refugee status determination processes.
Exercise ethical judgment and responsibility in relation to the practice of refugee lawyering.

Reflect on learning experiences gained from working on refugee legal casework in a clinical setting, including critically evaluating the effects of legal frameworks on the lived experiences of refugees in Australia including issues of access to justice and statutory recognition of refugee rights.

78015.title: Global Aspects of Intellectual Property Law
78015.description:
This subject considers the international framework of intellectual property law.  You’ll examine topics such as the international institutions dealing with intellectual property, particularly considering their treaties and dispute mechanisms. You’ll also focus on bilateralism and the future of multilateralism in international intellectual property. Emerging issues likely to affect international intellectual property over the coming years will also be explored, such as health and access to pharmaceuticals, genetic resources and biodiversity, protection of traditional knowledge and the digital agenda. 

Your online participation in this subject will be active, discussion-based and collaborative. You will share your reflections on topics, answering and asking questions, and responding to and debating with your peers’ views and interpretations. You’ll also work in small teams on a range of collaborative activities to help you develop and test your understanding.
learningOutcomes: Describe, evaluate and critically and creatively analyse the nature and scope of international IP laws and policies;
Demonstrate a coherent and extensive knowledge of the latest developments in IP laws and policies at international and regional level;
Critically and creatively analyse the nature, role and scope of the major IP-related International Organisations;
Demonstrate a coherent and extensive knowledge of the implications of IP laws and policies in the real world;
Critically apply legal research skills and independent thought.

78039.title: Wickedness and Vice
78039.description:
This subject analyses the various ways that the legal system communicates conceptions of wickedness and vice. You will apply various jurisprudential and general philosophical accounts to specific issues, including questions about our duty to obey, the regulation of morality and the characterisation of terrorism. You’ll also examine representations of evil in literature and film to analyse legal representations of wickedness. 

The subject will provide you with skills to understand and critically apply theory. Theory provides you with a way of thinking about issues and imagining the world differently, particularly when a legal problem appears to be insurmountable.

You will learn through a rigorous process of reading and discussion that includes thought-provoking philosophy and jurisprudence, as well as judgments and other legal documents and events. You’ll also develop your ability to critique  by presenting your ideas in seminars and through written assessment.
learningOutcomes: Identify and evaluate the various philosophical accounts of wickedness.
Apply theoretical insights about wickedness and vice and apply these to practical issues.
Identify and explain examples of complex practical issues, and critically evaluate the role that law has played in constructing and responding to wickedness and vice.
Locate and synthesise legal and interdisciplinary research relevant to legal issues in order to creatively and analytically evaluate the factual, legal and theoretical issues which arise.
Construct clear, original and persuasive written and oral arguments that are supported by research and textual readings.

78105.title: Genetics and the Law
78105.description:
This subject examines the scope and limitations of the regulation of genetic technologies with respect to humans. You will also emerging technological innovations in the area of human genetics and the effectiveness of law in managing these new developments. There is a specific focus on current issues including:
 
• genetic screening, including of adults, children and newborns;
• prenatal genetic testing and preimplantation genetic testing
• individual decision-making versus State responsibility for genetic risk,  
• individual versus group rights,  
• genetic privacy,   
• genetic discrimination,  
• reproductive autonomy, and  
• ownership, storage and control of genetic information
 
You’ll learn through a seminar style format, with delivery of content via mini lectures providing the frameworks and guidance for understanding key principles and cases. You will also engage in interactive learning using case studies, hypotheticals, group presentations and general discussion.
learningOutcomes: Critically evaluate the ethical and social justice implications for legal frameworks in response to recent advances in genetics.
Critically reflect on the social, economic and political foundations of legal regulation in the context of emerging technologies.
Critically reflect on the impact of new technologies on identity and legal categorisation.

Demonstrate advanced research and communication skills by locating and critically evaluating primary legal sources and complex interdisciplinary materials to construct original and effective legal arguments.

78107.title: Climate Law and Carbon Markets
78107.description:
This subject examines the potential role of the international and policy communities as well as the legal and business communities in confronting climate law. You will analyse the existing and emerging legal rules and frameworks, both internationally and in Australia, and the impact of these on business. You’ll critically evaluate the incentives for firms to comply with environmental laws and participate in voluntary programs, as well as the role of business in adaptation measures and climate justice issues.  

You will prepare for classes by examining international law and developments, policy materials, and other multimedia resources. In seminars you’ll actively contribute and respond to others’ views and interpretations as part of wider class discussions. You will also lead a class discussion on one of the prescribed seminar questions and facilitate class discussion on that question.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and reflect upon international climate law frameworks and emerging policy or legal issues involved in international climate law negotiations
Critically and creatively analyse the nature and scope of market-based instruments available to deal with climate change and the implications of business incentives
Evaluate the impacts of Australia’s response to climate change and the response from industry

Conduct effective research by locating, evaluating and synthesising legal and other disciplinary sources and apply that research in order to investigate the operation of climate law and policy in a global context

Present clear, critical and persuasive written and oral arguments that are substantiated by research and demonstrate the ability to critically evaluate contemporary issues in the development of climate law in a global context.

78122.description: This subject will give you a practical understanding of the various insolvency and restructuring options that are available to companies in financial distress. You will also discuss the range of formal and informal debt restructuring techniques that may be used to assist a company in financial distress. We will also consider alternatives to bankruptcy. Both individual and corporate insolvency are examined. You’ll engage with legal problems that simulate professional practice as a corporate insolvency lawyer. This means you will apply the law in a professional context, incorporating stakeholder interests, client pressures, and regulatory context.

appreciate the commercial and legal issues that arise during times of financial difficulty;
identify and use electronic and paper-based information resources to locate relevant and up-to-date legal materials to assist in resolving insolvency law problems critically and creatively;
balance the competing interests of different stakeholders involved in an insolvent estate.

78126.title: Corporate Governance
78126.description:
Corporate governance is the framework of rules, relationships, systems and processes by which authority is exercised and controlled in corporations. Corporate governance provides a framework that shapes the dealings and relationships between directors, managers, shareholders and other parties with a stake in the corporation's success.

This subject looks at the governance of large business corporations, especially those that are publicly held. You’ll explore the various theoretical perspectives on corporate governance, such as director primacy theory, enlightened shareholder value theory and stakeholder theory. Using these theories, you will investigate how authority within business corporations is allocated, exercised and controlled. 

You’ll apply principles of corporate governance in problem based scenarios and consider the ethical and social implications of corporate law. Learning will also involve participation in group and class discussions, oral presentations and undertaking critical research on selected governance topics
learningOutcomes: Apply their advanced understanding of the policy, practices, theory and doctrines that govern business corporations, especially in large publicly-held companies;
Evaluate and compare approaches to corporate governance and ‘best practice’ in the design and application of policies of corporate governance;
Actively apply the theories and doctrines of corporate governance to the resolution of everyday legal problems and issues that arise in the management of business corporations;
Generate persuasive, coherent and logical legal analysis and arguments on corporate governance issues, both in writing and orally; and
Conduct effective legal research by identifying and synthesising primary and secondary legal and interdisciplinary texts in order to investigate selected aspects of corporate governance.

78150.title: Law and Mental Health
78150.description:
This subject explores legal frameworks for coercive mental health interventions encountered by people with psychosocial and cognitive disability. You will critically reflect on these interventions in the context of broader consideration of law’s role in enabling and responding to violence and inequality. You’ll also examine the application of current legal practices as well as alternatives offered by international human rights norms and domestic law reform proposals. The subject takes an interdisciplinary approach that centres the narratives and perspectives of the disability community.  

You will learn directly from members of the disability community, including through guest lectures to gain a deepened appreciation for the importance in law and policy work of directly engaging with the disability community. You’ll also increase your skills in advocating for and working alongside people with psychosocial and cognitive disability.
learningOutcomes: Critically engage with a range of primary and secondary sources in relation to law and mental health, including narratives and perspectives of the disability community;
Explain and critically reflect upon contemporary legal approaches to mental health, particularly in relation to coercive mental health interventions;
Critically assess and evaluate law’s role in enabling and responding to violence and inequality, in relation to people with psychosocial and cognitive disability;
Evaluate contemporary debates on domestic law reform and international human rights developments in relation to law and mental health;
Formulate well-researched and persuasive law reform proposals related to contentious issues in law and mental health.

78181.title: Deceptive Trade Practices
78181.description:
This subject examines the statutory actions in the Australian Consumer Law (ACL). Because the remedies under the ACL are usually easier to establish than remedies available at common law or in equity, legal practitioners often rely on the statutory action of misleading and deceptive conduct as an alternative to traditional claims.

You will examine how loss or damage is assessed, as well as the connection between a contravention of the ACL and any loss or damage suffered. You’ll also explore the remedies available under the ACL. Learning will involve case study analysis, participating in seminar discussions and conducting research for a case note.

You will also develop your presentation and communication skills through presenting a seminar paper in class in group formatt simulating presentations you would give in a work environment. This presentation will be then presented as a written report. Final assessment will focus on topical issues that are affecting consumers and businesses alike in this area of law. The aim is to develop practical skills needed to work with clients, understanding of statute and applicable case law which is changing rapidly.

In the ACL we will focus on misleading and deceptive conduct (S18) but will further explore misleading representations, product recalls, manufacturer’s liability and statutory guarantees, all of which are tools to provide protection for consumers, businesses and society in general. We will focus on the remit of the ACCC and their operations and priorities.

We will further focus on the role of the Courts and its interaction with the ACCC in implementing and enforcing the ACL. This subject is well suited to all consumers. From a career perspective completing this subject will stand you in good stead for working in the area of competition and consumer law in law firms, working with the ACCC, working as in house legal counsel in businesses or even working in a non legal capacity in businesses providing services to consumers.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a coherent knowledge of Deceptive Trade Practices and Product Liability law in Australia;
Identify and examine the nature and scope of the remedies available under the ACL and how the Court applies these remedies;
Identify and evaluate the concept of ‘norm of conduct’ demanded by the Trade Practices Act in commercial dealings;
Analyse, evaluate and apply the principles of key cases to given factual situations;
Communicate orally and in writing in a logical, reasoned and persuasive manner utilising appropriate communication strategies;
Conduct effective legal research and apply critical analysis in order to critically evaluate a Deceptive Trade Practices issue.

78186.title: Intellectual Property and Traditional Knowledge
78186.description:
This subject considers the nature of traditional knowledge, how intellectual property in this area is protected under the Australian legal framework, and the development of strategies for its protection. You’ll gain an overview of the international treaty framework, relevant Australian legislation and concerns for Australian Indigenous peoples such as appropriation of Indigenous arts and culture, language, spirituality, medicinal knowledge, film and music. You’ll also examine comparisons with protection regimes in other nations, such as China and India. 

Through the major research project, you’ll have the opportunity to explore specific aspects of the protection of traditional knowledge and culture in greater depth. The learning modules enable you to consolidate your understanding of the law and issues in the field. You will engage in a range of collaborative activities to develop and test your understanding.
learningOutcomes: Critically and creatively analyse and evaluate the complex nature and scope of international laws, policies and organisations relating to Traditional Knowledge (TK) and Intellectual Property (IP);
Critically and creatively analyse the theoretical bases for TK protection and the practical commercial and cultural implications of that protection;
Apply advanced knowledge of current developments in IP & TK laws and policies at international, national and regional level;

Take responsibility for complex research, identifying and evaluating significant technical information, legal judgments and issues; to interpret, justify, or critique propositions, methodologies, conclusions and professional decisions;

Communicate accurately and persuasively arguments in relation to how intellectual property in this area is protected under the Australian legal framework, and the development of strategies for its protection using appropriate structure, spelling, grammar and punctuation and in accordance with the Faculty’s preferred style (AGLC3).

78188.description: This subject covers much of the law and some of the business and economics of buying, selling and licensing intellectual property (IP). 78206.title: International Organisations
78206.description:
This subject explores the place of international organisations (IOs) in the contemporary international legal order. You will develop a complex understanding of the law of IOs, including their legal status and powers, membership and internal governance structures, privileges and immunities, and dispute settlement procedures. You’ll also analyse the creation and evolution of IOs in their historical, legal and political contexts, applying your understanding to complex contemporary problems and controversies.   

You will investigate and critically evaluate IOs as key actors and sites of law making and engage with current issues and legal developments concerning IOs. You’ll have an opportunity to test and apply your understanding through seminar discussions and group-based activities.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a sophisticated understanding of the key concepts, principles and procedures of the law of IOs.
Critically analyse and reflect upon the legal structures, powers and responsibilities of IOs and their effect on the development of international and municipal laws.
Apply their advanced understanding of the law of IOs to complex contemporary problems, with reference to historical examples and theoretical debates concerning the function and practice of IOs.
Demonstrate greater confidence and effectiveness in oral communication skills in a formal legal context.
Construct clear, coherent, original and persuasive legal and scholarly arguments concerning the place of IOs in the contemporary international legal order.

78210.title: Law and Literature
78210.description:
This subject examines literary and legal responses to violence and trauma. You’ll read and discuss some of the most thought-provoking literary works of the present, and of the 20th century, as well as judgments and other legal documents.  You will apply advanced critical analysis to these texts, learning to evaluate and synthesise information as well as critique legal and academic arguments. 

Classes are interactive and you will be encouraged to offer your opinions and ask questions to develop your understanding of the relationship between literature and the law and the responses to violence and trauma. You’ll develop a conceptual and analytical understanding of legal and humanities scholarship.
learningOutcomes: Analyse, synthesise and evaluate law and humanities scholarship and engage with legal and literary texts to generate complex arguments responding to the role of law in adjudicating suffering and violence.
Identify, analyse, evaluate and synthesise research materials, complex scholarly arguments and primary and secondary sources of law.

Identify and explain examples of complex problems of violence and trauma including concepts in the interdisciplinary area of law and the humanities and the role that law has played in responding to collective violence.
Construct clear, justifiable, original and persuasive written and oral arguments that are supported by research and textual readings.

78216.title: Competition Law and Policy
78216.description:
This subject provides you with a comprehensive and engaging examination of the economic and legal principles of competition law (also known as antitrust law or restrictive trade practices law) in Australia. You will explore key aspects of statute law, particularly Pt IV of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (CCA), and how common law courts interpret the CCA. You will also understand how the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) operates and policy issues.

The course covers the evolution and objectives of Australian competition law and how it is administered and enforced both nationally and internationally. You will gain in-depth knowledge of major anti-competitive statutory conduct in Part IV of the CCA, including civil and criminal cartels, anti-competitive agreements (including concerted practices), secondary boycott, misuse of market power, exclusionary dealings, resale price maintenance and mergers and acquisitions. You will learn about the administration and enforcement of competition law in Australia.This includes authorisation and notification regimes, remedies for private litigants, and other related matters.
learningOutcomes: Identify and analyse the rationale for, and implementation of, competition policy and law in enhancing market efficiency in both a static and ongoing sense, and to adjust quickly to the needs of law firms with competition practices
Effectively and persuasively communicate critical analysis of a variety of major issues on competition law and policy;
Interpret and explain the practical operation and enforcement of competition law in business and commerce;
Analyse and evaluate selected business scenarios in relation to international enforcement of competition law, in which Australia is involved.

78218.title: Animal Law and Policy in Australia
78218.description:
This subject examines the effectiveness of animal welfare regulation in Australia. You will evaluate Australia's regulatory regime, focusing on the legal status of animals and the law’s role in preventing cruelty. This provides the foundation for assessing whether regimes in Australia, or internationally, foster accountability and ethical standards. A consistent theme you will examine is the debate surrounding the animal welfare paradigm versus animal rights. This debate is contrasted with more recent developments, such as animal dignity and the capabilities approach. The material is presented against the historical influences of philosophy, morality and science.  

You will take a practice-oriented approach to learning, including interactions with expert speakers. Working collaboratively in groups, you will draw on your developing understanding of theoretical frameworks, law and policy to consider hypothetical scenarios and lead class discussion on issues that are typical of those that lawyers and policy-makers will encounter in the practice of animal law.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and evaluate animal law principles and policies to respond to deficiencies in animal protection.
Synthesise and critique historical and theoretical animal welfare approaches and their impact on animal laws.
Identify and analyse the implications of ethics in decision-making involving animal law and policy.
Formulate research questions and use effective research and communication skills to justify and interpret theoretical propositions and conclusions.
Reflect critically on personal communication and collaboration skills and apply strategies to facilitate teamwork, synthesise discussions and improve group and class outcomes.
Engage with Artificial Intelligence in an ethical and appropriate manner

78220.title: Commercial Equity
78220.description: This subject examines the role that equitable doctrines, particularly fiduciary obligations, and equitable remedies, play in commerce. You will consider their relationship with contractual, tortious and statutory duties within a series of complex commercial scenarios. You’ll also examine the important role of trusts as vehicles for trading and investment in Australia as an alternative to the corporation, and the issues that arise with insolvent trusts. You will collaborate with other students in discussion and problem-solving activities.
learningOutcomes: Identify and explain the complexities of case law, legislation and scholarly literature dealing with equity in commercial law, at an advanced and integrated level that is informed by professional practice;
Distinguish and evaluate the legal and commercial factors that influence the resolution of disputes in different jurisdictions;
Articulate professionally and persuasively legal arguments that reflect the unsettled nature of equitable principles and their relationship with statute.

Critically, strategically, and creatively analyse how equitable doctrine relates to other areas of legal study and practice, including use of trusts and recognition of commercial fiduciary obligations
Critically, strategically, and creatively analyse issues that emerge from the relationship of equitable doctrine and the use of smart contracts in financial transactions and digital currencies.

78222.title: Law of Slavery and Human Trafficking
78222.description: This subject examines the evolution of international and domestic legal responses to human trafficking and modern slavery. While the subject addresses international law, you’ll also examine the practical application of the law of slavery and human trafficking in the Australian context. Key areas of focus include: • the international legal framework; • analysis of key legal definitions and concepts, including ‘modern slavery’; • the intersection between migrant worker exploitation and modern slavery; • the intersectional dimensions of vulnerability to modern slavery; and • human trafficking and international refugee law. You will conduct independent legal research about critical issues in the evolution of legal responses to human trafficking and slavery. You’ll also critically examine key aspects of Australia’s response to modern slavery, including the operation and implementation of the Modern Slavery Act and efforts to prevent and remedy modern slavery. Drawing on recent cases, news reports and research, you will critically evaluate the law of slavery and human trafficking in practice to contribute to current law and policy reform debates.
learningOutcomes: Identify and analyse the social and legal contexts underpinning slavery and human trafficking and evaluate international obligations and the role of international agreements in the development of effective responses internationally and in the domestic sphere, including criminal justice responses.

Critique and evaluate international and domestic legal definitions, legal frameworks, and propose improvements to state responses to slavery and human trafficking including through legislative reform and criminal justice processes.

Apply research and evidence related to slavery and human trafficking to formulate and refine workable responses to prevent trafficking, protect those trafficked and improve monitoring mechanisms and responses.

78229.title: Disability and the Law
78229.description:
This subject explores disability and impairment as a legal category. To do so you will examine the practical implications of the social and medical models of disability, among others. You will also evaluate how law can best achieve the goals of social justice and equality for individuals with disabilities. Specific issues examined include:   
•                The concepts of normal and disabled, healthy and diseased and able-bodied and impaired
•                The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disability
•                State and Federal anti-discrimination legislation.   
•                The National Disability Insurance Scheme
•                Constraints on reproductive decision making;  
•                End of life decision making;   
Seminars in this subject emphasise an interactive approach driven by group discussion of topics pertinent to disability and the law. You are encouraged to pose questions, propose interpretations of relevant legal theories and concepts. You will also work in a group to present on a chosen topic to improve your oral communication skills and defend your understanding of the relevant law.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an advanced critical, analytical and cross disciplinary approach to legal categories.
Critically analyse key aspects of disability discrimination law and core concepts of disability studies theory, and critical legal theory.
Synthesise complex theoretical, legal, inter-disciplinary materials to apply and communicate sophisticated knowledge and analysis of disability discrimination law and theory.
Evaluate complex legal issues surrounding genetic testing, and reproductive decision-making.
Critically analyse the law relating to treatment decisions.
