78235.title: Justice
78235.description: This subject introduces you to the concept of 'justice' and its relationship to our legal system, and to the theory and practice of law. It asks the questions: 'what is justice?', 'what does law have to do with justice?', and 'what is a just decision?'. You’ll explore these questions through traditional and contemporary theoretical approaches to justice. For example you may consider the following approaches: natural law, legal realism, critical legal studies, feminist theories, critical race theory, environmental and indigenous perspectives. You will develop your critical understanding of justice by applying distinct theoretical approaches to specific legal case studies and legal issues. You’ll learn how to take an active and applied approach to resolving questions of justice, and develop your capacity to make informed legal and ethical judgments. The aim of this approach is to rapidly immerse you in global, practice-orientated, research-inspired accounts of theories of justice and their relationship to contemporary law and legal regulation.
learningOutcomes: Investigate, synthesise and evaluate a range of legal and political theories of justice and articulate their relevance to the analysis of law, jurisprudence and legal authority.
Critically evaluate literature relating to law and theories of justice and be able to apply this literature to contemporary legal problems.
Present a clear and persuasive written argument that demonstrates the ability to critically evaluate at least one theory of justice and apply it to a legal context.
Express, debate and justify each student’s own interpretation of the relationship between law and justice, based on theoretical approaches and scholarship covered in this subject.

Conduct effective legal research by identifying and synthesising primary and secondary legal and interdisciplinary texts in order to investigate the relationship between law and justice and historical and contemporary theories of justice.

78239.title: Feminist Perspectives on Law and Justice

Critically evaluate areas of law that have been subject to feminist critique and be able to identify feminist contributions to law reform.
Express, debate and justify interpretations of feminist theories of law and justice through contribution to class discussion and debates.

Conduct effective legal research by identifying and synthesising primary and secondary legal and interdisciplinary texts and resources in order to investigate feminist insights in theories of law and justice.
Present a clear and persuasive written argument that demonstrates detailed understanding and knowledge of feminist approaches to law and justice and apply them to legal contexts.

78244.title: Mergers and Acquisitions Law
78244.description:
This subject examines the law relating to takeovers of public companies and publicly listed trusts. You’ll consider key issues relating to regulated acquisitions, acquiring a relevant interest prior to a takeover, disclosure of substantial shareholdings and defensive tactics. You will explore regulated industries such as telecommunications, broadcasting and financial services, as well as foreign investment rules relating to mergers and acquisitions.   

Your classes will be taught weekly through a combination of recorded lectures, seminars and discussions and small class group assignments.  The assessment will culminate in an analysis of a current merger/acquisition from a number of facets.  Mergers and acquisitions are inherently multi faceted and it is important to understand the processes and input by lawyers and non lawyer parties who take part in the process. 

Each class will involve both small and large group discussions analysing a range of hypothetical problem scenarios. You’ll present one case study to the class involving either a decided case or a practical case study based on a recent M&A transaction. 

The focus of this subject is to be as practical and real world focused as possible. Mergers and acquisitions are taking place regularly, providing us with many real life case studies to learn from.
learningOutcomes: demonstrate an appreciation of the range of legal and commercial issues that shape the form and outcomes in mergers and acquisitions;
demonstrate the ability to apply the appropriate legal rules to a range of issues that commonly arise in mergers and acquisitions transactions;
demonstrate a sound understanding of the legal position of key participants in common mergers and acquisitions transactions;
apply appropriate research techniques to identify relevant legal and equitable rules to assist with advising on undertaking mergers and acquisitions.

78245.title: Public Health Law
78245.description:
This subject examines public health law as a framework for understanding and addressing population-level health risks. Focusing on contemporary public health problems, students explore how legal and regulatory systems shape exposure to harm and support the protection and promotion of health. Students examine law as a determinant of health, explore how legal authority, evidence and policymaking interact, and analyse tensions between public health objectives, individual rights and industry interests.

Learning is structured around collaborative inquiry, with students working in groups to investigate specific public health challenges and develop law reform responses. Through this process, students build skills in critical analysis, evidence synthesis and policy-focused legal writing.
learningOutcomes: demonstrate competency in analysing the legal and ethical arguments that are applied to public health problems;

appreciate the sources of Federal, State, and local regulatory authority over public health and health care and the major ways in which it has historically been exercised. Understand the implications of the federal system for lawmaking in public health. Develop an awareness of the controversies and policy questions that surround these areas and reflect on them;

explain the respective roles of legislatures, courts, administrative agencies, and the market in regulating public health and health care, and the strengths and weaknesses of each. Recognise how public health law is approached in jurisdictions in Australia;

understand the tensions between promotion of public good and the protection of private rights. Analyse the implications of those rights for government authorities to regulate in the interest of public health;
understand the use of law as a mechanism to protect population health and ways in which it can be applied.

78246.title: Employment Law
78246.description:
Employment law is an important component of the legal regulation of business. In this subject, students examine the key aspects of Australian employment law currently pertaining to workplace rights, entitlements, liabilities and obligations of work providers and workers pursuant to the legislation and case law regulating work, especially the law determining the pay and conditions of workers. Given the extensive coverage of Commonwealth workplace relations legislation, there is a focus on analysis of that Commonwealth legislation as amended.

Employment law is a rapidly changing field. There have been frequent system-wide changes to the legislative framework over the last few decades. In addition to considering current law, this subject considers the development of legislation and case law regulating work. Students examine the reasons for and against reforms to employment law, the position and influence of key stakeholders involved in law reform processes and changes that are likely to be made to employment law in the future and on what basis those changes will be made.

In the seminar activities in this subject, students have the opportunity to learn the skills of applying current employment law to provide advice. Students will develop advanced legal problem-solving skills through a focus on these skill in-class and in the final assessment. Students also undertake critical analysis and evaluation of debates within employment law which underlie legal reforms. One option for students is to set their own research topic for the first written assessment in this subject.

Given that most students go on to be involved in paid work regulated by the law studied in this subject, employment law forms an important part of the knowledge required for professional life.
learningOutcomes: Identify and explain the key legal principles and policies underpinning Australian employment law.

Analyse and apply relevant legislation and case law in resolving legal problems involving the rights, entitlements, obligations and liabilities of workers and employers to provide effective legal advice to a client.
Develop and apply advanced legal problem-solving skills.
Critically evaluate the adequacy of, and the scope for reform in, Australia’s current framework of employment law from the perspective of key stakeholders.
Construct and effectively articulate critical, justifiable, persuasive and well-reasoned legal and scholarly arguments.

78248.title: Privacy and Surveillance: Law and Policy
78248.description:
This subject explores key legal questions relating to the invasion of personal privacy, data protection and surveillance. You will tackle emerging issues and challenges prompted by new technologies, including online privacy protection and the right to be forgotten. You will navigate a complex mix of common law and statute, federal as well as state/territory laws. You will also engage with a range of perspectives, ideas and interests, and deepen your understanding of key privacy and surveillance law issues by interrogating the wider theoretical, constitutional, policy and international contexts.  

In seminars you will learn through group-based discussion around allocated questions to develop coherent and reasoned arguments in response to questions of privacy and surveillance law and its operation and to present recommendations for legal reform. You’ll also engage in two Assignment Readiness Workshops designed to assist in successful completion of the subject assessments.
learningOutcomes: Examine, evaluate and explain complex privacy and surveillance laws, advanced principles and concepts and the broader theoretical, constitutional, policy and international contexts informing the regulation of privacy and surveillance.
Identify, critically analyse, apply and reflect on advanced privacy and surveillance laws and generate sophisticated solutions to complex privacy and surveillance regulatory problems.
Critically analyse and evaluate a range of complex perspectives and opinions relating to the issues and challenges of regulating privacy and surveillance prompted in particular by new technologies.

Construct and convey professionally, clear, succinct, reasoned, justifiable and persuasive legal and scholarly analyses and arguments, referencing where appropriate using the Faculty’s preferred style (AGLC3).

78257.title: Australian Discrimination Law
78257.description:
This subject provides a comprehensive practical and theoretical overview of Australian discrimination law. You will explore relevant federal and state anti-discrimination laws, with a focus on sex, disability and race discrimination, and sexual harassment. Along with a grounding in discrimination law practice, you’ll consider anti-discrimination laws in their vibrant and constantly changing legal, political and social contexts. People's lived experiences of discrimination are incorporated through guest lectures and multimedia first-person narratives.

There is a focus throughout on emerging issues and areas of law reform. You will analyse legislation and key cases, developing crucial legal skills such as statutory interpretation and legal problem-solving. You’ll also learn about key procedures of discrimination law in practice, including complaints processes, conciliation and state tribunals.  You will conduct an in-class law reform exercise, practicing how to impact discrimination law reform, and trace the original political, social or legal impetus for change to a draft bill and final legal change.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of Australian Discrimination Law as a body of law and in relation to key overlapping areas of law such as human rights, constitutional and labour law;
Engage in critical analysis of discrimination laws in their social and political context, including identifying gaps in legal coverage and potential areas for law reform;
Apply high-level research skills to identify and integrate a diverse range of legal and policy materials in addressing identified legal problems;
Demonstrate critical and creative skills in generating appropriate theoretical and practical responses to complex legal issues;
Apply sophisticated cognitive and strategic skills in developing viable recommendations for new regulatory approaches and legislative reforms.

78258.title: Intellectual Property and Human Rights
78258.description:
This subject considers interactions between two areas of international law: intellectual property law and human rights law. These areas intersect increasingly but fragmentation between them presents challenges for states to integrate international obligations for both fields of law into domestic law. In class you will examine why these interactions are important and consider how scholars have proposed harmonising interactions between the fields. You will use Australian, international and theoretical perspectives to understand how protection of copyright, trade marks, patents and confidential information can impact on realisation of rights to health, freedom of expression, a clean, healthy and sustainable environment and education. 
 
You will learn through online participation: collaboratively examining potential conflicts and solutions for ensuring that domestic intellectual property law is consistent with States’ obligations in both international intellectual property law and human rights law, and individually presenting your insights on discussion boards. Your individual research project gives you the opportunity to identify and reflect upon the relationship between the two fields in a specific area of interest. You’ll present your research project to your peers online and engage with each others’ research to examine important contemporary issues relating to intellectual property and human rights.
learningOutcomes: Reflect on and interrogate the nature and scope of national and international laws, policies and organisations relevant to intellectual property and human rights;
Critically and creatively analyse the theoretical bases for intellectual property protection and human rights protection;
Apply advanced and complex knowledge of relevant theory to intersections between intellectual property laws and human rights laws;

Conduct effective research by locating and evaluating legal and other disciplinary sources and apply that research to investigate a legal or policy issue related to human rights and intellectual property;
Construct and present clear, critical and persuasive written and oral arguments that are substantiated by research

78259.title: International Intellectual Property Moot (Oxford)
78259.description:
This subject offers you the opportunity to participate in the Oxford International Intellectual Property Moot for credit. The moot is held annually in Oxford, UK, over three days and is hosted by the Oxford Intellectual Property Research Centre. The competition invites teams from universities around the world to prepare written submissions and present oral argument on a hypothetical problem question in the field of intellectual property law.  
 
In a team, you will analyse a problem relating to copyright, trade marks, patents, confidential information, passing off or any combination thereof. You will conduct detailed and in-depth legal research on various national, regional and international laws and treaties and prepare written and oral pleadings arguing both appellant and respondent positions of the case. The subject is demanding and equates to a substantial research project.  
 
A team of two or three students is chosen following a competitive selection process. The team develops written submissions, under the close supervision of UTS academics. Participation in the oral rounds is by invitation only, on the basis of the written submissions. The written submissions are usually due in December, while the announcement of teams making it through to the oral rounds is in January. You will therefore only enrol in the subject if you are selected to compete in the oral rounds.
learningOutcomes: Plan and analyse a wide-ranging, strategic selection of legal research to provide targeted information for advocating a position on issues of intellectual property law
Evaluate and apply the principles of intellectual property law to develop original arguments in response to complex international legal issues
Implement multiple forms of feedback to reflect upon and improve individual and team preparation and performance
Develop and communicate coherent, persuasive and balanced written memorials and oral submissions in intellectual property law to reflect professional practice
Engage with extensive preparation and effectively collaborate with a team to successfully prepare and present a competitive moot

78261.title: Special Topics in International Law and Cultural Heritage
78261.description:
This subject examines the international legal protection of cultural heritage. Rapid developments in recent decades are leading to the emergent field of international cultural heritage law. You will focus on Australia's role in the development of key aspects of the international protection of cultural heritage, the impact of these international instruments on Australia's protection of cultural heritage and cultural rights, and the protection of the heritage and cultural rights of Indigenous Australians and Torres Strait Islanders. 

You will engage in reading and discussion of foundational legal instruments, case law, and theoretical texts that define the field of international cultural heritage law. Through analysing case studies, you’ll consider how the law has developed as well as the central debates which inform the field today.
learningOutcomes: Understand, reflect upon and interrogate the principles and rules relating to the international legal protection of cultural heritage.
Distil, interpret and apply these principles and rules to contemporary cultural heritage disputes.
Critically evaluate and synthesise the key theories used to explain and analyse the complex nature and scope of international cultural heritage law.

Identify, analyse and critically evaluate primary and secondary source materials on the international legal protection of cultural heritage and assess their significance and relevance for advance research in this field.
Construct clear, informed, critical, persuasive oral and written arguments distilling advance legal knowledge and independent research.

78262.title: Jessup International Moot
78262.description:
This subject is only for students who have been selected to represent UTS Law in a mooting competition via a competitive process. If selected, it offers you an opportunity to participate in the 'Philip C. Jessup International Law Moot Court Competition' for credit. This is the world's largest moot court competition, organised by the International Law Students Association, Washington, DC. It was established to provide law students with simulated courtroom experience in international law advocacy. 

This competition simulates a hypothetical dispute between countries and a mock case before the International Court of Justice, the judicial organ of the United Nations. Each year a new hypothetical case, based on complex current issues of public international law, is published. The limited set of facts – concerning a dispute between the two fictional states appearing before the International Court of Justice – requires detailed research into both international and comparative law to prepare complex pleadings for both sides. 

Teams analyse the problem, conduct detailed legal research, develop legal arguments and prepare written and oral pleadings arguing both the applicant and respondent positions of the case. Teams compete against each other, presenting their submissions which are evaluated by judges based upon advocacy skills and knowledge of international law.

The Australian national rounds take place in Canberra in February. The top two or three teams qualify to represent their universities at the international rounds in Washington DC each April.

This subject is demanding and equivalent to a substantial research project. A team of up to five students is selected to represent UTS:Law. For information about the mooting competitions see: www.uts.edu.au/current-students/current-students-information-faculty-law/competitions-and-prizes
learningOutcomes: Plan and analyse wide-ranging, strategic legal research to provide targeted information for effective international legal arguments.
Evaluate and apply the principles of public international law to develop original arguments in response to complex international legal issues.

Engage with extensive preparation and effectively collaborate with a team to successfully prepare and present a competitive moot and implement multiple forms of feedback to reflect upon and improve individual and team preparation and performance.
Develop and communicate coherent, persuasive and balanced written memorials and oral submissions for the International Court of Justice.

78263.description:
This subject, for students who have been selected to represent UTS Law in a mooting competition, offers you the opportunity to participate in a variety of national mooting competitions for credit towards your degree. Mooting is a mock-court experience where students argue questions of law and develop their ability to persuasively argue a case in court. It is an exciting way to gain high-level courtroom skills and research experience, and participation in a mooting team is coveted by high-achieving law students and future employers scoping talent. 

Several months of preparation is required to participate in a mooting competition. Students work in teams to develop their understanding of the area(s) of law to which the moot in question relates and prepare written memorials that consist of submissions for the applicant and the respondent. You will also participate in intensive advocacy training prior to the oral rounds of the competition. Selection for a mooting team is competitive, and calls for expressions of interest from students are made each year. You will need an above-average academic record and demonstration of strong research and writing skills. 

For current opportunities and further information on mooting competitions see UTS Law Mooting Competition Program. 

Students interested in mooting are encouraged to get involved with the program run by the Law Students' Society. More information on the LSS website.

Well-developed cognitive and practical skills necessary to identify, research, evaluate and synthesise relevant factual, legal and policy issues.
Well-developed ability to clearly and succinctly develop legal arguments in written submissions cooperatively with others and develop advanced advocacy skills.

78266.title: Special Topics in Disruptive Technologies and the Law
78266.description:
This subject covers how the legal system responds to disruptive technologies.  are having on the type of work that lawyers do and the way that they do it. More than ever before, lawyers need to be problem solvers. They also need to be adaptive and technically capable.  

You will explore three main themes: 

• Modern technology is changing the way that people relate to each other and how laws are broken. 
• Regulators and legal professionals are struggling to keep pace with innovation. 
• Disruptive technology is having a significant impact on the type of work that lawyers do and the way that they do it.

You will engage in weekly discussions and oral presentations on various aspects of legal issues arising from disruptive technologies, with immediate feedback. You’ll also collaborate in problem solving exercises in the legal technology context, often considering problems from different points of view, including regulators, legal practitioners and disruptors developing new technologies.
learningOutcomes: Identify how new technologies are changing, challenging and enabling the way that lawyers work.

Evaluate new risks, obligations and liabilities arising from the social and commercial use of new technologies, applying existing legal principles, ethical issues and reasoning to disruptive technology case studies.
Collaborate in groups and online to generate ideas and possible solutions to the challenges arising from new technologies.
Prepare and present synopses to peers that evaluate emerging issues.
Explore and reflect on the way that disruptive technologies challenge regulators across global jurisdictions, in particular the requirements to know your client and anti-money laundering policies.
Investigate how anonymity, cryptocurrencies and smart contracts might enable democratic processes and financial support in developing and politically unstable nation states.

78271.description:

You will also explore ethical and professional responsibility issues with guest experts.

78275.title: Private International Law
78275.description: This subject is an advanced study of private international law as it operates within the Commonwealth of Australia and in relation to overseas countries, with emphasis on issues of current relevance, and with reference to American and European law. In this context, governing doctrinal principles and leading cases on conflicting issues from private law, including torts, contracts, agency, marriage, divorce, inheritance and real property are discussed. Important rules laid down in international treaties, which have priority over national conflict of laws are addressed. In particular, current developments at the Hague Conference on Private International Law and in the European Union are examined. The foundation of private international law is also explored.

78284.title: Courts and Judges
78284.description: This subject will deepen your understanding of courts as a system of dispute resolution in civil and criminal matters by examining their structures, personnel, and core values. You will focus primarily on the Australian judicial system but use comparative examples to identify alternative organising principles and models of regulation. You will gain an appreciation of the interplay of values that underpin courts in liberal democracies, including judicial independence, impartiality, efficiency, accountability, and access to justice. Your learning in this subject will be informed by extensive sampling of the literature from different academic disciplines (eg law, political science, and history), case studies, group work, student-lead discussion and, when possible, guest lectures from past or present judicial officers. Assessment is focussed on continuous learning through regular quizzes, short answer questions, and class participation, supplemented by a research essay.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an advanced and integrated understanding of the structure and operation of the Australian judicial system in its legal, political, social and historical context.
Understand a range of methodological approaches to studying judicial systems in order to critically evaluate their legal, political, social and historical dimensions.

Conduct effective research by locating and synthesising multidisciplinary scholarship in order to analyse and critically evaluate institutions, policies, processes and laws that affect the operation of the judicial system.
Construct and present clear, succinct, creative and persuasive written arguments relevant to the judicial system, which are substantiated by scholarship and research.

78285.title: Refugee Law and Practice
78285.description:
This subject introduces you to the legal principles and procedures of international refugee law and their application within a domestic context. You’ll learn about the historical development of refugee law and evaluate the key features and limitations of the current refugee determination system in Australia. You will explore the practical realities of refugee law and practice through a clinical experience, working on 'real-life' refugee law cases and current legal issues. This practical work is supervised by UTS Law staff in conjunction with a local refugee legal organisation.  
 You will apply your academic learning to a professional context by undertaking research and drafting submissions informing real-life refugee casework. This will deepen your understanding of refugee law and policy and provide a critical understanding of refugee status determination processes. By working on real-life refugee cases, you’ll gain practice-based, cross-cultural skills and insights necessary for work as a refugee lawyer.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of the key concepts, principles and procedures of international and national legal frameworks for the protection of refugees and asylum seekers with a particular focus on the United Nations Convention Relating the Status of Refugees and the 1967 Protocol and the applicability of these instruments in Australian law.
Apply legal knowledge and research skills to practical refugee legal projects in a professional context.
Demonstrate practical legal skills required to draft legal documents and make written submissions in the context of refugee status determination processes.
Exercise ethical judgment and responsibility in relation to the practice of refugee lawyering.

Reflect on learning experiences gained from working on refugee legal casework in a clinical setting, including critically evaluating the effects of legal frameworks on the lived experiences of refugees in Australia including issues of access to justice and statutory recognition of refugee rights.

78290.title: Strategic Litigation Practice
78290.description:
Strategic litigation uses law to pursue systemic and social change. It sits within a broader context of Strategic Lawyering and deploys litigation as part of a cohesive campaign to achieve a social change. This subject is a unique subject in Australia. This subject is taken prior to completing 76095 Strategic Litigation and is limited to 12 students.

This subject gives you skills to work in strategic litigation generally, as well as particularly as it applies to advancing First Nations justice and systemic change. In recognising First Nations sovereignty, knowledge and activism, you will be encouraged to centre a decolonial approach in your strategic practice. 

Seminars will explore the nature, history, theory and examples of processes of strategic litigation, as well as the importance of trauma informed and culturally safe lawyering. You will develop your drafting and communication skills as well as evidence gathering, research and case preparation skills. Assigned reading and assessments will advance your advocacy skills which will be complemented by insights from legal professionals regarding how to be an ethical and responsive practitioner.
learningOutcomes: Develop a broad understanding of social justice lawyering and strategic litigation and its position in the Australian legal framework.

Demonstrate competency in practical legal skills, such as conducting legal research, preparing file notes and court documents, drafting legal correspondence and other forms of legal and non-legal writing.
Demonstrate highly effective written and oral advocacy skills that furthers social justice objectives in court settings and broader community forums.

Demonstrate effective and appropriate communication skills regarding obtaining instructions and acting competently for First Nations clients, including the ethics of acting for collectives and culturally aware communication with First Nations clients and organisations.
Reflect on their professional skills and knowledge and develop and implement plans for continuous learning, including on ethical issues and trauma-informed practices.

78293.title: International and Comparative Study in Law (PG)
78293.description:
This subject enables you to undertake a specialised short course within the discipline of law overseas, and to obtain credit for this study.  You will develop legal skills taught in another legal tradition and gain intercultural awareness, adaptability and resourcefulness to become a future global professional. 

You may choose from a range of university recommendations or identify your own subject for study. However, before enrolling in this subject you must: 

- consult and seek approval in writing from this subject’s coordinator that the short course will be appropriate for credit, and 

- conclude enrolment in the short course overseas. 


Possible features of a short course that is acceptable for recognition include: 

- A course presented by an overseas university;  a structured learning experience (this may include field trips or on-location visits and lectures); 

- the course’s content is within the discipline of law (doctrinal and theoretical and interdisciplinary);

While typically taught intensively, the length of the subject will be an equivalent of 24 full time hours (for postgraduate students) and 36 full time hours (for undergraduate students). 

 Other important information about this subject
- All financial, travel and visa requirements are dependent upon the host country and are to be negotiated by you. 
- Some Faculty or University arranged courses are sometimes available as this subject
- This subject requires completion of assessment outlined in the subject outline. This assessment is additional to any assessment completed in the overseas subject.

78300.description:
This online subject is the second subject in the Graduate Diploma of Migration Law and Practice (C06155). 78301.title: Australia's Visa System
78301.description: In this online subject you will explore Australia's visa system, including an overview of all visa classes and subclasses. You’ll also consider the Code of Procedure set out in the Migration Act 1958 for dealing with visa applications. This will familiarise you with core requirements such as communication between the Minister and visa applicants, and when adverse information must be disclosed to a visa applicant. You’ll also cover what is required to make a valid application for a visa, the criteria visa applicants must meet to be granted a visa and the conditions that must or may be imposed when a visa is granted. In the final module you’ll cover Compliance visas - the non-substantive visas that keep non-citizens lawful (C06155 students) or learn the requirements for Australian citizenship (C06122 students). Low stakes tasks give you the opportunity to test and develop your knowledge as you progress through the subject. You will learn through problem-solving activities that mirror the legal and factual issues that arise in migration practice. You’ll practise and receive feedback on applying the relevant validity and eligibility criteria to identify and advise on a client’s appropriate visa pathways. This subject covers Standards 1, 2, and 3 of the Occupational Competency Standards for Migration Agents. These standards set out the knowledge, skills and professionalism required for practice as a Migration Agent.

78304.title: Compliance and Cancellation
78304.description:
This online subject introduces you to the role of the Department of Home Affairs (DHA) in enforcing compliance with Australia's migration laws. You’ll examine offences under the Migration Act 1958, and DHA's compliance powers including: visa refusal and cancellation, search and seizure, detention, removal and deportation, exclusion periods, and employer monitoring and sanctions. You’ll also learn how to respond to Notices of intention to consider cancellation and how to apply for revocation of a mandatory character cancellation.

C06122 students also cover the options following visa refusals or cancellations, including merits review, judicial review and the Minister for Immigration's personal intervention powers.

Low stakes tasks give you the opportunity to test and develop your knowledge as you progress through the subject. You will practise providing oral and written advice and writing submissions in relation to client matters. This subject covers standards 1,2,3, 4 and 5 of the Occupational Competency Standards for Migration Agents. These standards set out the knowledge, skills and professionalism required for practice as a migration agent.

78727.title: Australian Family Law
78727.description:
In this subject you will develop an understanding of the family law system. You will examine dispute resolution procedures, court practice and procedure, and the social research that underpins parenting and the legal division of property post separation. You’ll also learn about the laws that govern the rights and obligations of married and de facto parties in property and interpersonal relationship disputes. 

You will use social, political and theoretical perspectives to consider suggestions for reform of the Australian system. Through problem-solving exercises and discussions, you’ll explore social policy issues, including the impact of family violence. You’ll also undertake research and lead class discussion to critically evaluate relevant laws, practices and policies.

78728.title: Tech Law, Policy and Ethics (Law Tech Capstone 1)
78728.description: This subject explores the policy and ethical issues that technology presents for legal practitioners. You’ll examine the role of lawyers in regulation of technology, shaping policy and supporting vulnerable populations using technology. You will also explore ethical and policy issues arising from innovative technology that poses new threats at the same time as providing new opportunities to find solutions to some of the world's wicked problems. This subject is taught by academics and guest lecturers who specialise in legal technology. You’ll engage in weekly discussions on various aspects of legal issues arising from disruptive technologies and present lightning talks that engage with these issues. Classes examine the key role that lawyers can play in ethical policy-making and draw on professional conduct obligations, international human rights law and humanitarian law. You will also become familiar with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and consider which of them may be supported by the use of technology.
learningOutcomes: Identify and analyse policy and ethical considerations arising from recent technological advances and the policy response of governments and international organisations to these developments

79032.title: Competition and Consumer Law
79032.description:
This subject offers you a comprehensive and engaging exploration of competition law (antitrust law) and consumer law (deceptive trade practices law) in Australia. You’ll understand why these laws are crucial, what they entail, and how they are enforced. You’ll learn the importance of competition and consumer laws in ensuring fair markets and protecting consumers. By understanding these principles, you can critically assess current legal frameworks and their impact on the economy and society.
You’ll delve into the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (CCA), its evolution from the Trade Practices Act 1974 (TPA), and its interpretation by common law courts. You’ll also explore major international treaties on antitrust and consumer law enforcement involving Australia. Current issues and recent cases will provide you with real-world context.
The subject is structured into three parts for better clarity and focus. First, you will trace the evolution of competition law in Australia, understand key legislative features of the CCA, examine major anti-competitive conduct (including monopolistic agreements, misuse of market power, and mergers/acquisitions), and learn about enforcement mechanisms such as authorization and notification regimes and available remedies.
Next, you will grasp the policy objectives of consumer law, study general prohibitions under Schedule 2 of the CCA - the Australian Consumer Law (ACL) (such as misleading or deceptive conduct, unconscionable conduct, and unfair contract terms), and explore enforcement issues to understand how consumer rights are protected. Finally, you will analyse major international treaties on consumer protection and competition enforcement, and review significant international cases involving Australia to understand global implications.
By the end of this subject, you will have a strong understanding of the economic and legal principles that underpin competition and consumer laws in Australia. You’ll be equipped to critically analyse and engage with these laws, both in a national and international context, preparing you for a career in law, policy-making, or business.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the rationale for, and implementation of, competition and consumer policy and laws in enhancing market efficiency and promoting competition and consumer welfare.
Analyse and apply competition and consumer law principles to legal problems in a commercial context to achieve legitimate business objectives for clients.
Demonstrate critical analysis and written communication skills to generate accurate and persuasive legal arguments.

79771.title: Dispute Resolution
79771.description:
This subject deals with the jurisprudence of dispute resolution and the theory, dynamics and essential characteristics of the major dispute resolution processes. Your focus will be the role of lawyers in dispute resolution processes. You will learn to formulate effective strategies for resolving a wide range of disputes. You’ll also learn how to advise clients on, and prepare clients for, suitable dispute resolution processes. Additionally, you will explore the institutionalising of dispute resolution processes; the nature of disputes and the theoretical, ethical and practical issues. 

Through a two-day intensive weekend workshop, you will practice and develop your negotiation and mediation skills through simulated role-plays and exercises. These will help you think critically, strategically, and creatively about the nature, role, and range of dispute resolution processes. You will also meet with practitioners to discuss contemporary professional and advocacy issues. Case study analysis in seminars allows you to explore key concepts, interpret information, practise advocacy and develop creative solutions.
learningOutcomes: Explain and evaluate the nature and purpose of different dispute resolution processes covered in the course and the range of options in each process.

Construct clear, succinct, reasoned, integrated and insightful analysis and arguments that are supported by research and scholarship

80035.title: Photography and the Body
80035.description: You will explore the representation of the body in photography and its social, political, cultural, and ethical impacts. You'll create works that challenge perceptions of the body in imagery, using experimental methods to address body diversity across media. Suitable for all disciplines, you'll engage in practical projects to enhance your image-making skills in photography and video, contemplating the experience of being a visible body in the 21st century.
learningOutcomes: Develop an advanced understanding of the issues surrounding body representations in visual culture.
Demonstrate the ability to visualise the body in a way that is informed by research and an understanding of historical and contemporary body-centred practices.
Capacity to initiate and execute self-critique, critical thinking and iterative processes in the making of ethically engaged body-centred work.
Develop and apply technical skills using image based technologies appropriate to representing the body ethically and creatively.
Demonstrate skills in experimenting with image based technologies in interdisciplinary ways using performative methods.

80082.title: Photography and the Object
80082.description: This subject covers the basic principles of still life photography. It explores documentary photography, studio photography and the space in between. You will learn the fundamentals of digital photography, available and artificial studio lighting, and creative and innovative approaches to conceiving photographs. The objects photographed are those that already exist and those that you create to make a photograph.
learningOutcomes: Develop the ability to maintain a consistent and reflective practice
Present processes and outcomes effectively in a variety of ways including oral, written and visual
Develop the ability to engage in, and contribute to, studio discussion
Develop inventive and explorative approaches to photography
Demonstrate appropriate levels of skills in crafting fabricated objects

80083.title: Memory and the Image
80083.description: You will explore how visual culture influences memory through image-based practices. This subject examines the complex yet contributory role of images in shaping personal and political narratives, storytelling, and autobiography. You'll delve into photographic theory, memory philosophies, and historiography, analysing diverse sources from family albums to public archives and manipulated photographs. The course also reveals techniques used by creatives to manipulate the interplay between image and memory, including photographic montage, archive remixing, the interplay of image and text, synthetic media, and interviews.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between photography and memory in current image based practice and photographic history and theory
Communicate ideas effectively in a variety of ways, including visual, written and oral.
Initiate and execute self-critique, critical thinking and design responses to memory related photographic work.
Demonstrate a practical and conceptual strategies for working with photography in the field of memory studies.

80084.title: Photography and Fashion
80084.description: You will engage with the language of fashion photography, blending theoretical understanding with practical skills. The course introduces a spectrum of contemporary and historical fashion photography, linking these to significant technical advancements. You'll develop your own vision by researching and assembling reference materials with aesthetic and conceptual depth, translating these into industry-relevant applications. The subject also covers industry practices like client pitches and team communication for executing professional results. You'll work both independently and collaboratively to create a fashion shoot, supported by research and technical instruction.
learningOutcomes: Innovatively approach and utilise photographic and media technologies and techniques in fashion-based photography projects
Communicate ideas effectively in a variety of ways including oral, written and visual, and to engage in discussion in studio contexts
Initiate and execute self-critique, critical thinking and self-directed iterative processes, taking responsibility for actions and decisions in academic and fashion industry contexts
Develop and demonstrate a knowledge of photography and fashion history and theory, sourcing and utilising references from photography, fashion and broader disciplinary and fields
Work cooperatively and professionally as part of a team in order to contribute to peer learning, and work in ways relevant to fashion and photography industries

80113.title: Advanced Virtual Reality for Architectural Design
80113.description:
Students learn how to view, present, and interact with architectural designs in virtual reality (VR) via contemporary visualisation software Unreal Engine 4 and the HTC Vive head-mounted display. This course follows on from the Real-time visualisation for architectural design short course.  

This course is focused on the creation of immersive experiences through VR. Increasingly used by major architectural firms such as COX, BVN, Woods Baggot and Bates Smart, VR is a critical tool in the design and development process as it provides 1:1 scale representation of architectural designs. Valuable for both designers and clients as it provides insight into how the architecture would appear at completion, well before construction begins. 

Students of this course, produce, view, and interrogate design using industry-standard VR tools and hardware. They prepare an Unreal Engine 4 model for use in VR and learn how to provide interaction with the model for immersion into, and interrogation of, the architectural design.

80114.title: Architectural Lighting Design
80114.description:
Stundets learn fundamental principles and project applications of architectural lighting design.


They explore the art and science of lighting as an essential part of architecture with this uniquely hands-on course. They also learn the fundamental principles and gain an understanding of project applications of current lighting design within the built environment, preparing them to work in a niche, in-demand and growing global sector.

80116.title: Open-source GIS for Landscape and Architecture Offices
80116.description:
This practical, design-office-oriented course prepares students to work with a range of GIS-based NSW government data sources that can support architectural, engineering and construction projects. 

While GIS sources, environmental data, proprietary local government and industry data are used widely in the public service, their potential remains largely under-utilised in architecture, engineering and construction projects.  

This course provides a practical demonstration of the data types and GIS resources available in NSW, as well as the open source and proprietary software's that can be used to visualise, analyse, and manipulate the data contained within them. This data can then be integrated into various aspects of architectural and landscape architecture office practice. 

The course content is relevant for architecture, landscape, engineering and planning projects at all scales and stages, from site appraisal and selection through to feasibility and environmental impact assessments.

80117.title: Real-time Visualisation for Architectural Design
80117.description:
Stundets explore and represent architectural and spatial design from both cinematic and human perspectives via contemporary visualisation software, Unreal Engine 4. 

Real-time visualisation is an emerging tool in architectural practice. Through the use of software like Unreal Engine 4, architects can produce project flythroughs, rendering, interactive apps and VR experiences to support design and its communication. Real-time visualisation affords minimal setup, reducing the time and cost associated with the use of dedicated 3D visualisers. Importantly, it enables architectural experimentation throughout the design process, from concept development through to construction.  

Student of this course learn the fundamentals of Unreal Engine 4, using the software to leverage existing digital models to produce visualisations alongside design changes. 

They also create their own 3D model and use it to study the effects of lighting and materials, cinematic cameras and movement through space, and interaction as they relate to architectural real time visualisation. 

By completing this course, participants  are eligible to participate in the course ‘Advanced Virtual Reality for Architectural Design'.

80118.title: Robotic 3D Printing for Architectural and Structural Performance
80118.description:
This course investigates the use of 3d printing to structurally reinforce architectural elements, in which the applications of digital modelling, structural analysis and robotic fabrication are utilised for the exploration of complex geometries.

The geometries of load distribution paths are often far more complex, non-uniform and compelling than the structural elements themselves.  This course focusses on the use of analysis software to determine the stress lines for a given load-case or combination of load cases and the possible design responses to this information.   

As a student of this course, students design reinforcement patterns that are robotically 3D-printed onto planar elements in order to test the structural performance of the composite element.  This process is repeated throughout the course to generate a field of design outcomes and a first principles understanding of the concepts explored.

81511.title: Problems to Possibilities
81511.description: This introductory subject in the Bachelor of Creative Intelligence and Innovation introduces a broad understanding of the role of creative intelligence, transdisciplinary practice and complex problem solving. Through practical and creative learning you’ll experience firsthand the nature of today's open, complex, dynamic and networked problems. Working in inter-disciplinary teams you’ll be challenged to analyse problem situations from multiple perspectives and integrate these findings and insights to create new possibilities in a place-based challenge. Through this process you’ll develop and hone your skills in collaboration, problem-solving, visualisation and presentation.

81512.title: Creative Practice and Methods
81512.description: Creativity is consistently listed as a key 21st-century capability in that it allows us to view, understand and respond to challenges in new and more open ways. In this subject you'll explore the role creativity plays in the innovation process and discover your potential as a creative, transdisciplinary change-maker. You will examine what creativity is, and explore creative practice, process and methods from a variety of perspectives. You will learn how to remix and reimagine existing practice, applying new approaches to design your own creative method. You will apply these skills by collaboratively devising and leading your own innovation process in response to a complex challenge set by an external partner.

Develop and lead innovation processes that draw on and justify the application of diverse methods.

You'll learn to critically examine past, present and emerging paradigms of innovation, the conditions that enable it, the values that shape it, and the social and environmental impacts it creates. Responding to a real-world challenge set by an industry partner, you will learn and use transdisciplinary theories and creative intelligence methods to redirect innovation towards ecologically sustainable and socially responsible futures.

You’ll then engage in a complex system challenge and be tasked with proposing creative insights and perspectives that account for the dynamic, interconnected nature of the issues we tackle.

The journey includes creating and identifying opportunities, shaping initiatives, experimenting, communicating potential value to different stakeholders to gain feedback, and making decisions about whether to pivot, persevere or abandon entrepreneurial ideas. In this subject, students reflect on the role of entrepreneurial initiatives within broader social and economic systems, including considerations about ethics and impact.

81529.description: In this subject, you will think beyond the world as it stands today and consider the different futures that may impact your personal innovation practice towards sustainability. 81538.title: Frame Innovation
81538.description: This subject centres on frame creation, a design-based approach to networked problem solving, developed and used in the UTS Design Innovation Research Centre. Working with the multidisciplinary staff from the centre, participants in this subject engage with the question of how to 'solve the unsolvable' – the open, complex, dynamic and networked problems facing society today. Participants learn the theory behind the nine-step frame creation methodology, putting into practice and testing its associated methods and tools. Through first-hand experience of the power of frame creation, participants create new approaches to problems that have confounded conventional problem-solving practices. They then shift towards the broader practices of frame innovation – the skills, knowledge and mentality required to drive frame creation in an organisation and society.

81548.title: Research Methods and Proposal
81548.description: This is the first of two subjects in the Bachelor of Creative Intelligence and Innovation (Honours) program. In this subject, qualifying final year BCII students are equipped with skills and theoretical foundations needed to develop a transdisciplinary research proposal. Students explore the distinct characteristics of transdisciplinary research, its pragmatic and scholarly opportunities and challenges, as well as experiment with diverse methods, skills, and strategies that enable transdisciplinary practitioners to creatively and rigorously navigate their research. 83122.title: Machine-knitted Textiles
83122.description: This subject introduces students to the creative and technical potential of machine-knitted textiles. Through practice-based studio learning, students develop skills in domestic machine knitting (Single needle bed), Dubied industrial hand knitting (Double needle bed) and Shima Seiki digital fabric simulation. Students begin with structured technical sampling and then extend these skills into experimental knitted fabrics through yarn, colour, surface, structure and material exploration. The subject supports students to develop original knitted textile outcomes for fashion and textile design, with a focus on technical control, creative experimentation and professional presentation.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate technical skills and safe practice in using domestic knitting machines and Dubied industrial hand knitting machines.
Develop an original knitted textile aesthetic through experimentation with materials, yarns, knitting techniques and fabric structures.
Apply digital fabric simulation skills to translate original knitted textile ideas.
Develop effective presentation skills relevant to fashion and/or textile design.
Demonstrate professional ability in creating and presenting a comprehensive portfolio that showcases the knitted fabric designs and technical skills.

83231.title: Fashion Cultures
83231.description: This subject deepens your exploration of fashion design by integrating research into studio work. Lectures discuss the interplay between cultural innovation and fashion, with a focus on sustainability. You'll examine the significance of everyday dress, sustainable practices, and the future of fashion. Weekly activities offer hands-on experience with alternative garment-making methods, creative processes, documentation, reflection, and image creation. The course concludes with an original fashion design project, positioning your work as forward-looking cultural research.
learningOutcomes: Understand how the design process is applied and practiced in fashion
Carry out independent research to inform the design process
Conceptualise and articulate knowledge of the significance of fashion in culture and society during the 20th century, through both visual and theoretical research

You'll study contemporary fashion illustrators and experiment with various mediums and techniques to produce detailed range drawings. Illustration, as a vital tool in fashion, requires precision to convey design concepts effectively. You'll also learn to digitise hand-rendered illustrations and technical drawings using industry-standard software like Photoshop and Adobe, opening up new ways to present your work and broaden your fashion and textile practice.

83234.title: Fashion's Regulatory Landscape
83234.description: This subject prepares you for working within a rapidly evolving regulatory landscape in fashion in Australia and internationally. You will develop your risk management skills in relation to regulation such as the Modern Slavery Act, ESG risks, animal welfare risks, and other risks that impact the fashion industry. Through case studies you learn how fashion businesses are negotiating the increasingly complex regulation that governs their operations from supply chains to reporting requirements to distribution.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate broad and coherent knowledge of national and international regulatory frameworks impacting the fashion industry, including modern slavery legislation, ESG requirements, and animal welfare standards.

Critically evaluate the role of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) principles in shaping fashion business strategies, compliance practices, and stakeholder engagement.
Analyse case studies to assess how fashion businesses navigate regulatory challenges across supply chains, reporting obligations, and market distribution.
Apply risk management frameworks to identify, assess, and propose mitigation strategies for regulatory, social, and environmental risks within the fashion industry.
Examine the fashion industry's participation in regulatory development, considering the roles of key industry bodies and the influence of advocacy on policy-making and compliance.

83235.title: The Economics of Fashion
83235.description: In this subject you build your understanding of economics through a lens of the fashion industry.  You learn about different economic theories, worldviews and value systems, and how these shape business thinking and operations within fashion. Emergent economic models, such as doughnut economics, are presented alongside dominant economic theories. You are introduced to consumer psychology and citizen behaviour and how these intersect with fashion and economics.
learningOutcomes: Identify and explain dominant economic theories and their influence on the fashion industry and its business practices.
Critically evaluate emergent economic models and their potential in transitions to sustainability in the fashion industry.
Analyse how different economic worldviews and value systems shape decision-making within fashion businesses.
Examine the relationship between consumer psychology, citizen behaviour, and economic systems in the context of fashion.
Apply economic thinking to assess challenges and opportunities within the fashion industry, from both business and societal perspectives.

83236.title: Fashion Industry Futures
83236.description: In this subject the fashion industry is presented as a set of interconnected systems and you learn how change occurs in these systems, including in fashion businesses and the industry. You are introduced to concepts of leadership and organisational theory in the context of transitions and change. You will learn about the significant economic and cultural contribution that First Nations fashion, including how Indigenous knowledge informs circular practices in Australian fashion. Pluriversal theory is presented in relation to design, and you will have the opportunity to try tools like speculative design and design fiction to explore preferable futures for the fashion industry.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and interpret the fashion industry as an interconnected system and its economic, social, cultural, and environmental dimensions, and their implications for transitions.
Demonstrate broad knowledge of First Nations fashion and Indigenous knowledge systems, including Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property Rights (ICIP) in Australian fashion.
Apply concepts of leadership, systems change, and organisational theory to examine how transitions toward more sustainable and inclusive fashion business practices can be initiated and sustained.
Investigate and communicate pluriversal theory in the context of fashion, demonstrating awareness of how multiple worldviews can influence the fashion industry.
Select and apply futuring methods such as transition design, speculative design and design fiction to critically explore and propose preferable futures for the fashion industry.

83237.title: Business Models in Fashion
83237.description:
In this subject you will learn about business models, the frameworks that outline how a company creates, delivers, and captures financial, cultural or social value. You are introduced to the diversity of for-profit and not-for-profit business models in the fashion industry, ranging from conventional retail to service models to social enterprises.  

Guided by industry insights, the subject covers the end-to-end retail process, including product ideation and design, data-driven trend forecasting, buying and planning, and store operations. You'll investigate onshore and offshore supply chains, with a focus on circularity, and the ethical and empathetic dimensions of supply chain management. 

Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and their impact on fashion business models are also explored, preparing you to design innovative, responsible, and future-focused fashion enterprises.
learningOutcomes: Identify, analyse and compare a range of business models in fashion, including for-profit, not-for-profit, and circular models.
Apply knowledge of business models to develop a business plan for sustainable and responsible fashion enterprises.
Understand the end-to-end retail process, from product ideation and design to store operations.
Understand the role of data and AI in forecasting, planning, and decision-making in the fashion industry.
Assess supply chain structures and understand the role of ethics and empathetic principles in their management.

83238.title: Fashion Industry Internship
83238.description: You will develop a structured industry experience project within the fashion industry in a self-sourced internship. This involves the negotiation of a learning contract to identify the outcomes of the experience and designing a program of activities to achieve these outcomes. Supervision is provided to assist you in identifying the capabilities you need to develop in completing the placement and to provide support and advice during your industry involvement. You will reflect on your learning experience in the workplace in the context of the fashion industry. You will undertake a paid or non-paid internship of 40 hours (minimum) in the teaching session that you are enrolled in to be eligible to study this subject.
learningOutcomes: Identify goals, strategies and resources for workplace learning and transferable skill development
Analyse incidents in the workplace from an ethical perspective
Advance the development of their professional skills within the fashion industry and in communication
Reflect on their internship experiences and observations to identify lessons and strategies to improve their future professional practices
Demonstrate appropriate professional performance, conduct and attitudes in a working environment

83239.title: Fashion Industry Capstone
83239.description: This subject integrates the knowledge from your fashion business studies. It is an opportunity to undertake a project built around your interests and career goals. The capstone will involve working with an industry partner to enhance the quality of the learning experience. You will apply negotiation skills, as well as analytical and problem-solving skills, to address challenges presented by the client brief. The subject involves regular supervisor meetings, culminating in a project report for the client.
learningOutcomes: Integrate and apply broad and coherent knowledge from fashion business studies to develop a professional project that addresses an industry-defined problem or opportunity.
Demonstrate effective negotiation skills, including active listening, ethical reasoning, and creative problem-solving, in collaborative engagement with an industry partner.
Apply project management principles—such as leadership, time and risk management, and conflict resolution—to plan, execute, and deliver a project aligned with professional standards.
Communicate project outcomes effectively using appropriate storytelling, visual and verbal communication strategies tailored to specific audiences.
Reflect critically on personal and professional learning throughout the capstone project to identify strengths, challenges, and future development opportunities in fashion industry practice.

83341.title: Fashion Intersections
83341.description:
Fashion transcends mere commodities, embodying identity, culture, and sometimes self-critique. It thrives in virtual spaces and curated environments, intersecting with art and media. As the world faces challenges like climate change and social inequality, critical fashion theories provide insight and advocacy for the industry's practices and products. Learning about fashion involves appreciating both Western and non-Western traditions, valuing tacit knowledge, and developing skills in critical thinking, research, and academic writing.

In the core second-year subject, Fashion Intersections, of the Bachelor of Design in Fashion and Textiles, you'll explore how contemporary fashion theory intersects with various scholarly fields. With expert guidance, you'll understand how fashion practice merges with other creative forms and articulate your ideas in a proposal for a self-devised exhibition project.
learningOutcomes: Research, source and debate ideas as the basis for informed design development.
Analyse and interpret information to inform new avenues of personal research.
Explore creative interpretation of ideas into design solutions.
Explore a wide range of references to inform individual design practice.
Present appropriate visual and written representation of ideas and designs.

83621.title: Studio: Foundations in Patternmaking and Construction 1
83621.description: This subject teaches you the fundamentals of pattern making and garment construction, turning fashion design concepts into tangible garments. You'll learn to convert fashion drawings into flat patterns and then into three-dimensional forms. You'll explore material qualities crucial for crafting precise and professional clothing, mastering industry techniques for production patterns. You'll become familiar with garment block patterns, essential garment forms, and their details. Additionally, you'll complete accreditation and health and safety training for working in the industrial sewing workshop.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate self-directed learning and decision-making in pattern making and construction
Demonstrate appropriate levels of technical skills for patternmaking and garment construction
Develop accuracy, rigour and care for patternmaking and construction documentation
Develop an understanding of methods to enable accuracy, rigour and care when constructing finished patterns and garments
Utilise a variety of research methods for patternmaking and construction including visual research

You'll delve into additional hand illustration methods and digital techniques using Adobe software, including Photoshop, Illustrator, and InDesign, to craft professional illustrations and booklet layouts. Effective visual communication is vital in the fashion and textile industries, and this course aims to enhance these professional skills. 83722.title: Studio: Body Mapping
83722.description: This subject introduces you to sustainable fashion practices, specifically working with sustainably sourced knit and jersey fabrics. You'll create a fashion collection that prioritises extended garment use, reflecting sustainability. Supported by lectures to deepen your industry knowledge, the course focuses on contemporary and future practices, blending design with technical skills. You'll learn sustainable design approaches, patternmaking, garment toile construction, and critical reflection. The challenge is to craft original designs and translate them into tangible outcomes, including lookbooks and media presentations suitable for the fashion industry.
learningOutcomes: Develop effective presentation and communication skills appropriate for design within fashion and textiles
Develop self-directed learning techniques and the ability to reflect upon, and critique finished outcomes
Learn how to develop an original design aesthetic through experimenting with fashion and textile design
Learn to apply a variety of research methods including visual research to document and generate creative outcomes
Develop technical design and construction skills through innovative sampling and garment construction

83723.title: Constructed Textiles
83723.description: This subject provides a foundation in machine knitting and weaving, covering hand and domestic knitting techniques. You'll learn basic knit structures and machine operation, producing hand-knitted samples to test various fibres and dyes. The course emphasises professional presentation and the creation of a technical file analysing knit structures and dye outcomes. You'll also explore material innovation and cultural narratives through techniques like weaving, with a focus on sustainable material sourcing and circularity theories. Guest lectures will keep you abreast of industry trends and contemporary design. By the end, you'll have a technical grasp of knitting, dyeing, and sustainable practices, and an understanding of textiles as a medium for social and cultural expression.
learningOutcomes: Develop and learn the ability to respond to verbal feedback and constructive criticism through active participation in the textile tutorial sessions.
Develop and engage with projects that enhance their ability to challenge boundaries and take risks within each textile design project.
Engage with relevant textile skills that will enhance creative approaches to thinking and problem solving relevant to fashion and textile practices.
Develop an original aesthetic sensibility in textile design project throughout each textile design brief.
Apply creative approaches to technology based activities throughout each textile brief.

83724.title: Studio: Body Form
83724.description: This subject takes your speculative design concepts from the first year and transforms them into tangible garments through draping. You'll delve into the subtle yet constant interactions between clothing and the body in motion, termed emergent dynamics. These dynamics, often overlooked unless causing discomfort, reveal the intricate relationship between garment and wearer. By focusing on these interactions, you'll shift from traditional visual-centric fashion design to a more holistic approach that fosters originality and creativity. With a commitment to sustainability, you'll employ upcycling and recycled materials to craft a collection that includes two distinct looks and a design research proposal, embodying this innovative perspective on fashion.
learningOutcomes: Respond to feedback and constructive criticism and work collaboratively within studio.
Develop an original design aesthetic through experimenting with design on the mannequin.
Understand the importance of taking risks and challenging boundaries.
Apply skills in self directed learning and time management within and outside of studio.
Demonstrate new appropriate levels of technical skills aimed at the high-end fashion market.

83821.title: Fashion and Textiles Major Studio 1
83821.description: This subject immerses you in the international sphere of fashion, with a focus on original menswear design, creation, and presentation. You'll engage with a lecture series that delves into the contemporary and historical aspects of male culture and its influence on men's style and masculine identity. Challenging your aesthetic preferences, you'll work with an established design signature to develop a substantial portfolio of creative work, employing research, technical, and conceptual skills. The course emphasises industry relevance, centring on range development and contemporary menswear presentation. You'll explore alternative presentation methods, including 2D imagery, publications, and spatial or performative displays.
learningOutcomes: Effectively analyse research data and assimilate findings into innovative and effective design outcomes
Demonstrate an understanding of the complexity of designing for menswear at an international level
Apply, analyse and evaluate the relationship of clothing structures to the male body
Effectively demonstrate the ability to design concepts to professional and industry specifications
Demonstrate a high level of competency in communicating both visually and verbally.

83822.title: Fashion and Textiles Major Studio 2
83822.description: In this subject, you will engage in experimental fashion practice, focusing on designing a fashion range that pushes the boundaries of archival research, experimental textiles, brand identity, and sustainability. Your work will be deeply rooted in archival research, exploring how historical materials, garments, textile remnants, and objects can inform contemporary design practice. Through this process, you will create a collection that embodies a tangible and meaningful expression of design values, research, creative vision, and contemporary craftsmanship. By engaging with archival materials through a design-oriented lens, you will reinterpret these artefacts, unlocking new aesthetic and conceptual possibilities for design.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of contemporary fashion and textile design practices.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of an experimental design process, through approach to materiality, textiles and design
Demonstrate a high level of competency in communicating concepts through practice and outcomes.
Demonstrate a professional understanding of appropriate technical details for fashion outcomes
Demonstrate how to develop a rigorous individual project with an independent point of view and outcomes.

83823.title: Fashion and Textiles Professional Practice
83823.description: This subject enhances your grasp of professional practice in the fashion and textile design industries, concentrating on contemporary practices within local and global markets. You'll deepen your understanding of various roles and industry practices that you'll adopt as a professional. The role of the designer within these systems is examined. The course prepares you for the transition from study to industry, taking into account imminent industry developments.
learningOutcomes: Cultivate a critical understanding of contemporary issues and innovative thinking in the fashion and textiles industry.
Advance professional development by integrating prior knowledge in personal fashion and textile design practice.
Employ appropriate research methods and reflect on research outcomes to inform and enhance fashion and textile practice.
Collaborate professionally and develop effective communication strategies within the fashion and textile industry.
Develop professional project outcomes while challenging boundaries and taking risks.
83823.recommended: This subject is recommended as the final subject in the 3rd Year Fashion and Textiles Design degree, to be taken alongside 83886 Fashion & Textiles Major Studio 2. It is recommended that all subjects, including most electives, are completed before undertaking this subject.
