96139.title: Prescribing Skills 2
96139.description: In this subject you will extend your prescribing skills to manage complex patients and scenarios, applying advanced clinical reasoning to initiate, adjust and monitor pharmacotherapy. You will learn to document prescribing decisions in line with professional standards and critically reflect on your practice. You will also enhance your ability to collaborate effectively with other health professionals by documenting patient care plans and referrals and apply culturally responsive prescribing principles for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Learning is conducted online through a blend of self-directed modules, interactive workshops, peer review, and practice-based tasks that focus on advanced prescribing decision-making. You will also complete a period of work-integrated learning (WIL) with a designated prescriber and submit work-based assignments (WBA) and a case logbook to be assessed for prescribing competence.
learningOutcomes: Apply advanced clinical reasoning and professional judgement to manage, monitor and review prescribing decisions safely, including those involving complex or unapproved therapies.
Use digital prescribing systems and clinical decision-support technologies to enhance accuracy, safety and accountability in prescribing practice.
Communicate and document prescribing decisions clearly and professionally, maintaining collaboration, cultural safety, integrity and compliance with governance and ethical standards.
Reflect critically on prescribing practice and feedback to identify areas for improvement and demonstrate ongoing professional learning and development.
Demonstrate leadership and accountability in prescribing practice through evidence-based decision-making, peer engagement and adherence to professional standards.

96301.description:

It emphasises equipping students with the knowledge, decision-making abilities, and applied research skills necessary to design programs and implement interventions that supports athlete health and performance.

Your learning will focus on the development of theoretical and practical skills essential for high-performance sports professionals. You will learn to apply advanced concepts in professional settings using critical thinking, self-directed learning, and effective communication.

It offers a comprehensive understanding of how the fundamentals of resistance training and aerobic/anaerobic conditioning can be integrated with modern techniques to enhance athletic performance.

You will learn to critically assess new strength and conditioning methods and gain expertise in exercise prescription applicable across various sports and individual circumstances. 96630.description: This subject introduces you to the core concepts of psychological science and focuses on building your skills in critical thinking and academic writing. You will explore the history and philosophy of psychology and learn about key theories across major subfields. 96647.description: This subject equips you with advanced interpersonal and professional skills crucial for psychological practice and research, such as effective communication, cultural responsiveness, micro-counselling, and self-regulation. You will further develop skills in reflective practice and ethical decision-making, applying your knowledge to case studies and enhancing your learning through feedback.
learningOutcomes: Critique and apply ethical principles and guidelines for the provision of psychological services.
Craft communications that show respect for communication styles from different groups and peoples.
Apply advanced knowledge of culture difference and biases to reduce misunderstandings in communication.
Develop self-awareness and self-care strategies for professional performance.
Practice advanced interpersonal communication skills.

96648.title: Advanced Topics in Psychology
96648.description: In this subject you will deepen your understanding of selected psychology subfields through team-based collaboration. Your team will develop a research proposal addressing a global issue (e.g., poverty, health, migration, human rights, international conflict, sustainability), integrating psychological principles and justifying ethical considerations, while showcasing your advanced knowledge of replicability, open science, and research transparency.
learningOutcomes: Appraise ethical principles in research and ethical research practices in various contexts.
Collaborate effectively on team-based projects.
Critically evaluate key theories and empirical evidence in a psychology subfield.
Use advanced technology to create professional presentations.
Craft a research proposal that applies psychological principles to an issue of global concern.

96649.title: Foundations of Business and Management in Community Pharmacy
96649.description: Prepare for success in community pharmacy practice with this elective subject. Tailored for students transitioning into the profession, this subject will equip you with foundational business and management skills necessary for thriving in the dynamic environment of community pharmacy during the initial years post-graduation. You will delve into key aspects of community pharmacy operations, gaining practical knowledge and skills that are directly applicable to your roles within pharmacy practice. The curriculum is designed to bridge the gap between academic learning and real-world application, providing you with the tools and competencies needed to excel in your intern year.
learningOutcomes: Critically analyse business data, interpret financial reports, and make informed decisions to assess the financial health of a community pharmacy and make informed business decisions.

Demonstrate proficiency in key operational aspects of community pharmacy practice including workflow, stock management, supply chain logistics, automation technologies, and quality assurance to enhance operational efficiency and patient safety.

Acquire foundational practical skills in business management, such as business planning, financial management, budgeting, reimbursement models, franchising/banner group options, and strategies for sustainable growth and profitability
Develop effective leadership and communication skills within teams in pharmacy practice settings, fostering collaboration, innovation, and optimal patient care outcomes.
Demonstrate a commitment to continuous learning, employing a reflective approach to maintain professional competence.

96801.title: Communicating and Collaborating for Optimal Person Centred Care
96801.description:
This subject is designed for healthcare professionals seeking to enhance communication and collaboration in palliative care, with an emphasis on cultural safety and psychological wellbeing for patients and their support networks. It stands out for its commitment to inclusivity, particularly for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, and those from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds.

You will learn to empower these groups and communicate the benefits of palliative care effectively to health professionals and families. The subject fosters self-awareness and interaction skills for delivering optimal care. Learning activities include practical exercises and reflective learning to apply these skills in real-world settings.
learningOutcomes: Examine psychological, social, and spiritual issues in death, dying, and grief and discuss ways in which these impact on patients, carers, and families.
Critically self-appraise and improve their knowledge, attitudes, beliefs, practice, and communication style in relation to delivering culturally respectful palliative care.
Explain and integrate the role of culture and context in a person’s palliative care needs.
Prioritise cultural considerations for delivering culturally respectful care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Justify the role of inter-disciplinary collaborative teams in optimising care for patients and families.

96802.title: Delivering Best Palliative Care Any Place Every Time
96802.description:
This subject is designed for health professionals seeking to enhance palliative care accessibility and equity in their communities. It offers a unique public health perspective, equipping you with the knowledge to assess and address palliative care needs on a population level. You will learn about harnessing community support for palliative care through a health-promoting approach. Key topics include public health principles applied to palliative care, understanding social determinants, epidemiology, and health promotion strategies.

You will also explore tools for evaluating health determinants, identifying access barriers, and planning service improvements. The subject will enable you to understand the influence of policy, social, and economic factors on palliative care outcomes in various healthcare settings. Learning occurs through a blend of theoretical study and practical application, preparing you to become a catalyst for change in palliative care services.
learningOutcomes: Examine needs at a population level, recognising core functions of public health as it applies to palliative care;
Devise a population-based approach to the planning of palliative care services to improve access for populations who currently have inadequate access;
Analyse and integrate models of care to enhance delivery of best palliative care practice any place every time;
Recommend and justify a persuasive written business case to reimagine service solutions.

96803.title: Complex Symptom Management
96803.description:
This subject is designed for health professionals who are seeking to enhance their complex symptom management capabilities in the context of person-centered palliative care.

You will learn new ways of thinking using the latest evidence and critical decision making to screen, assess, and manage common, yet complex palliative care symptoms. You will learn how to optimise patient-practitioner encounters to collect the most relevant assessment data, integrate and apply different types of knowledge, and critically reflect on differential diagnoses to arrive at an individualised management plan.

Teaching methods include interactive, practice-oriented sessions, case analysis, and reflective exercises.
learningOutcomes: Critically appraise clinical diagnosis, reasoning and decision making skills to manage complex palliative care symptoms.
Examine the microsystem of a person, their psychosocial, physical and multi morbidity characteristics and symptom to deliver best palliative care outcomes.
Combine, appraise and integrate the comprehensive assessment (microsystem) with a management plan underpinned by quality evidence to address complex symptoms.
Prioritise delivering person centered complex symptom management inclusive of transitional care to optimise time spent in preferred place of care.
Identify opportunities to integrate the existing complex symptom management evidence into routine clinical practice across different health care settings.

96804.title: Immersive Palliative Care Futures
96804.description:
This subject is designed for aspiring clinical leaders seeking to shape the future of palliative care. It offers a strategic approach to embracing challenges and opportunities in the field, fostering innovation and creativity.

You will learn to critically assess the role of technology in clinical decision-making and care delivery, and strategise interdisciplinary care across various levels to ensure equitable, top-tier, and secure services for diverse patient groups.

Teaching methods include interactive sessions, case studies, and reflective exercises, promoting practical understanding and application of concepts.
learningOutcomes: Debate differing perspectives on the opportunities and limitations of technology for supporting care of people with life-limiting illness
Analyze shortcomings of palliative care for meeting future need to identify foci for improvement
Appraise health service responses to changing needs for palliative care, including solutions for optimising access and equity and better integrating care
Create technological solutions through applying new knowledge, facts and techniques to improve care for people with life-limiting illness and their families

96806.title: Translating Evidence into Change
96806.description:
This subject targets health professionals seeking to enhance their understanding of evidence-based practice in palliative care. It provides a comprehensive grasp of healthcare research methodologies pertinent to palliative care and fosters critical appraisal skills for research evidence. You will learn to integrate and synthesise evidence and consider approaches to using evidence to affect change.

As an integral part of the Master of Palliative Care, this subject serves as the initial step in a two-part capstone experience. Learning occurs through practical application and critical analysis, ensuring skills are directly transferable to professional settings.
learningOutcomes: Examine the role of evidence-based practice and factors influencing its implementation in improving palliative care.
Design an effective, reproducible, and transparent search strategy to access relevant evidence.
Critically appraise available research evidence for rigour, importance, and applicability in palliative care decision-making.
Analyze, synthesize, and apply research evidence to support recommendations for future practice and research.

96808.title: Generating Evidence to Improve Palliative Care Outcomes
96808.description:
This subject is designed for health professionals seeking to enhance their research and practical skills in quality improvement and translational research within healthcare settings. It offers a unique blend of theoretical knowledge and practical application, focusing on improving person-centred palliative care.

You will learn to critically analyse service-level data, utilise quality improvement tools, and develop solutions for identified care delivery issues. The subject equips you with understanding of securing project approvals, applying for funding, navigating ethical considerations, and managing data effectively.

Through this subject, you will gain proficiency in creating compelling written and oral presentations to garner workplace support for quality improvement and research initiatives. Instruction is delivered through a combination of interactive sessions and hands-on project work, ensuring a comprehensive learning experience.
learningOutcomes: Map approval processes for quality improvement and research projects within a local service setting.
Analyse service-level data and use quality improvement tools to identify and appraise a gap or problem in care.
Develop a rationale for a quality improvement or research project to further enhance the delivery of person-centred palliative care based on local data and evidence from research.
Devise an aim and methods for a proposed plan for palliative care quality improvement.
Present their project in written and oral formats in readiness for undertaking the project.

96824.title: Clinical Assessment in Palliative Care
96824.description:
This subject is designed for healthcare professionals seeking to enhance their clinical assessment capabilities for providing person-centred palliative care. It equips you to understand aspects of the physical assessment most valuable when providing tailored comfort-focused palliative care.

You will learn to identify and manage common symptoms effectively, ensuring tailored care for patients with advanced disease or nearing the end of life.

Teaching methods are interactive and practice-oriented. You will refine your physical assessment techniques through practical exercises, including structured clinical examinations and simulations.
learningOutcomes: Examine and interpret the main components of, and prioritise, patient health data including patient history, focused palliative care physical assessment and diagnostic data.
Justify and demonstrate skills in differential diagnosis supported by a comprehensive physical assessment of common symptoms in people living with life-limiting illnesses.
Appraise and respond to multidimensional symptoms and abnormal physical changes correlated with assessment findings, including clinical signs of deterioration and imminence of death.

96825.title: Pharmacology in Palliative Care
96825.description:
This subject is designed for healthcare professionals seeking to enhance their expertise in palliative care medication management. It supports understanding of pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics for drugs commonly used in end-of-life care, to enable delivery of tailored,person-centred treatments. Particularly, it emphasises the application of net clinical benefit principles in medication decisions for patients with life-limiting illnesses and co-morbidities.

You will acquire skills in assessing and managing palliative care needs effectively, focusing on comfort and individual patient requirements.

Learning occurs through practical application of theoretical knowledge to real-world scenarios, fostering critical thinking and decision-making in complex care situations.
learningOutcomes: Examine and interpret the key principles of pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics applied to common symptom control medicines for people living with life-limiting illness.
Justify and apply the principles of net clinical benefit to medicine decisions for people with life-limiting illness including those with co morbidities.
Integrate the delivery of person-centred palliative care in medication management and prescribing applying detailed knowledge of pharmacology and individual goals of patient and/or their carers.

96826.title: Optimising End-of-Life Communication
96826.description:
This subject prepares you to master communication and decision-making skills crucial for end-of-life care, ensuring you can support patients and their families effectively. You'll learn to integrate contemporary communication theories and digital health practices to enhance interactions. Through practical scenarios, you'll refine these skills, making them relevant to your current and future professional settings.

Your learning involves collaborative problem-solving and role-play in small groups, fostering a safe space for skill development with peer and academic support. Interactive online tasks will help you evaluate various communication strategies, complemented by feedback on group discussions, assessments, and written assignments.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate optimal communication tailored to people with differing palliative care needs, social and life circumstances, and their families, within varied healthcare settings
Evaluate creative ways of working to optimise communication and shared decision making that support person-centred palliative care in a digital age
Compose and implement effective communication strategies to manage patients or families expressing high levels of distress and/or anger

96827.title: Optimising End-of-life Communication within Complex and Diverse Situations
96827.description:
This subject is designed for health professionals seeking to enhance their communication skills in end-of-life care in complex and diverse situations or populations across various settings, including hospitals, aged care, and community services. It offers a unique focus on culturally sensitive practices, particularly for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

You will learn to foster effective partnerships and advocate for quality palliative care through creative and innovative approaches grounded in evidence-based methods. The subject employs interactive learning methods to ensure practical skill development in delivering optimal end-of-life care.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate effective communication and advocacy for patients with complex palliative care needs, and their families/carers irrespective of care setting or diversity of needs
Justify optimal considerations for delivering culturally safe care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people with palliative care needs and services engaged in such care provision

Argue the importance of inter-disciplinary collaborative teamwork, partnerships and service development based on principles of collaboration, openness, respect and empowerment to optimise palliative care provision across the health system

96828.title: Ethical Dimensions of Palliative Care
96828.description:
This subject is designed for healthcare professionals seeking to enhance their ethical decision-making in person-centred palliative care. It supports you to become creative, enquiring and responsive health professionals with the ability to critically evaluate and adapt your role in response to ethical and policy challenges. You will learn to navigate complex ethical principles, address care goals, and fulfil responsibilities to various stakeholders, while reflecting on personal beliefs and values.

The subject stands out by addressing ethical dilemmas specific to palliative care, including cultural sensitivity and the nuances of working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Through this training, you will gain the skills to uphold ethical conduct and apply core practice principles effectively in diverse settings.

Interactive learning methods, including case studies and reflective exercises, will facilitate your understanding and application of the course material in real-world scenarios.
learningOutcomes: Appraise ethical principles in the context of palliative and end of life decision-making and patient capacity and preference.

Evaluate ethical situations, including cultural beliefs and attitudes to death, dying, meaning of life, existential suffering and moral distress that health professionals may encounter when caring for people with palliative and end of life care needs.
Justify a well-considered course of action and script potential responses to situations of ethical conflict for people with palliative care needs and/or their families.

Examine the personal and professional dimensions of practice as they interact with and uphold ethical imperatives to facilitate optimal palliative and end of life care, including applying ethical principles for care of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients, families and communities.

96829.title: Legal Dimensions of Palliative Care
96829.description:
This subject is designed for healthcare professionals aiming to deepen their legal understanding of person-centred palliative care. It emphasises legal principles in palliative and end-of-life care, preparing you to source jurisdiction-specific legal information and services.

You will learn to critically analyse and reflect on your role, enhancing adaptability in your practice. Interactive learning, through case studies and discussions, ensures practical application of legal knowledge in healthcare.
learningOutcomes: Describe legal principles relevant to decision-making and provision of care in palliative and end of life contexts.
Appraise legal principles relevant to palliative and end of life decision-making within the context of patient capacity and preference.
Examine the personal and professional dimensions of practice as they interact with and uphold legal imperatives to facilitate optimal palliative and end of life care.

96831.title: Medical Devices: Regulatory and Quality Systems Requirements
96831.description: This subject equips you with an industry focused foundation in the growing Medical Device industry to broaden your skill base. Regulatory pathways and quality management systems for medical devices in the major global markets including US, EU and Australia will be studied using ISO 13485:2016 Medical Devices - Quality Management Systems, FDA 21 CFR Part 820 - Quality System Regulation and ISO 14971 Medical Devices - Application of Risk Management as the basis for the development of practical skills. You will test your developing skills by engaging in challenging assessments based on industry scenarios.
learningOutcomes: Evaluate international and local regulatory frameworks and quality management systems for medical devices.
Apply regulatory and risk management standards in medical device development and manufacturing.
Evaluate compliance with regulatory requirements and recommend improvements.
Devise a comprehensive risk assessment for a medical device.
Generate ideas and contributions within a group dynamic, demonstrating effective communication, feedback and collaboration.

96832.title: Introduction to Psychology Foundations
96832.description: This subject introduces you to psychology's fundamental concepts and the scientific method, laying the groundwork for critical thinking and academic writing. You will explore key theories across psychology's subfields and examine how mental and physical health affect individuals and society. You'll also investigate how social, personality, developmental, and perceptual factors shape experiences, enhancing your understanding of human behaviour, individual differences, and promoting values of diversity, equity, and inclusion.
learningOutcomes: Explain the foundational elements, concepts and theories of psychology.
Describe key psychological research concepts.
Describe the cultural, historic, and contemporary contexts that influence the lives of Indigenous Australians.
Communicate psychological concepts accurately and effectively, adhering to APA standards where appropriate.
Examine psychological methods and interventions via research participation.

96833.title: Introduction to Psychological Science
96833.description: This subject introduces you to the core concepts of psychological science and focuses on building your skills in critical thinking and academic writing. You will explore psychology's history, philosophy, and scientific principles, learning about leading theories from major subfields. By examining the influence of biology, learning, cognition, motivation, and emotion on experience, you'll gain a deeper understanding of human behaviour, individual differences, and the importance of diversity, equity, and inclusion.
learningOutcomes: Understand foundational concepts and theories in psychology and their application to everyday life.
Examine psychological methods and interventions via research participation.
Explain psychological research concepts and procedures.
Describe the roles of whiteness, power and dominance and the manner in which these influence and shape understandings, realities and experiences.
Communicate key psychological ideas from research.

Apply principles of learning to solving behavioural problems.

96835.title: Psychological Disorders and Interventions
96835.description: This subject delves into the study of psychological disorders and interventions, where you'll critically assess the evolution of their development, as well as contemporary models of classification, diagnosis, and treatment. You will explore how socio-cultural influences and scientific advancements inform current professional practices. Through case examples, you'll apply your knowledge and critical thinking to assess various theoretical models and scrutinize the evidence supporting psychological interventions.

Critically reflect on ethical and/or social issues relevant to theoretical models of psychology.
Critically evaluate evidence-based treatments and/or reflect on professional practice issues in psychology.

96836.title: Development Across the Lifespan
96836.description: This subject examines how psychological, biological, social, and cultural elements shape developmental changes, from babies and children to adolescence, adulthood and into older age. You will gain insight into how the brain and mind continue to grow, as well as neurodevelopmental and neurocognitive disorders, providing a comprehensive view of psychological development across the lifespan.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate developmental psychology knowledge based on evaluation of key theories and relevant literature.
Collaborate effectively in team-based projects.
Evaluate and critique information for credibility and objectivity.
Advocate for sensitive interaction with people of diverse abilities and backgrounds.

96837.title: Research Methods and Theory in Psychology
96837.description: This subject focuses on the research methods and theory foundational to psychological research. You will investigate the scientific method integral to the scientist-practitioner model, differentiating scientific approaches from pseudoscience by comparing and contrasting various research designs. Additionally, you'll engage with the ethical considerations and principles essential to being a responsible psychological researcher and practitioner.
learningOutcomes: Evaluate the scientific development of psychology and biases that appear in various media.
Compare and contrast diverse research methodologies in psychology.
Apply knowledge of the importance of reproducibility.
Critically assess credibility and objectivity of information.
Produce research reports adhering to APA standards.

96838.title: Research Design and Analysis in Psychology
96838.description: This subject equips you with practical skills in research design, data analysis, and data visualisation, utilising contemporary and accessible software. You will develop professional teamwork abilities and learn to critically interpret and communicate research findings, reflecting the empirical and adaptive nature of psychological science.
learningOutcomes: Evaluate research designs, procedures, and statistical methods used in psychological research.
Apply and interpret statistical methods in psychology.
Develop teamwork and collaboration skills.
Use technologies that help to prepare for job entry.
Evaluate the appropriate scales of measurement used for different research purposes.

96839.title: Psychological Assessment, Ethics, and Professional Skills
96839.description: This subject provides hands-on experience in administering, scoring, and interpreting psychological assessments, emphasising the use of valid and reliable tools in practice and research. You will learn about the Code of Ethics governing psychological work and how to manage ethical dilemmas. The skills acquired lay a solid foundation for a career in applied psychology, blending assessment proficiency with ethical competence.
learningOutcomes: Analyse ethical principles in psychology research and practice.
Apply cultural and linguistic considerations in psychological testing and communication.
Evaluate the cultural limitations of normative tests and assessments.
Administer valid psychological assessments and interpret, critique, and communicate the results.
Participate in relevant activities to gain experience in the application of psychological methods, interventions, and online interactions appropriate to professional contexts.

96840.title: Society, Psychological Health and Wellbeing
96840.description: In this subject, you'll understand how a mix of biological, psychological, social, and cultural factors impact health, wellbeing, and behaviour. You will explore the significant role of social connections and contexts in shaping life, and how psychological insights help to drive positive change in individuals and communities. Critical reflection on social influences and health inequalities will enable you to address interpersonal and intercultural conflicts, enhance wellbeing, and respond to community health disparities.
learningOutcomes: Analyse the influence of psychological and social factors on health and behaviour.
Apply advanced knowledge and skills that are responsive to cultural diversity, including Indigenous Australians and Indigenous Australian contexts.
Evaluate and address issues of prejudice and discrimination.
Analyse problems that develop when working with teams and implement possible solutions.
Justify how psychological intervention strategies can be adapted for use across various contexts.

96841.title: Cognitive Psychology
96841.description: This subject examines how perceptions and biases filter our view of the world through an imperfect lens. You will explore classic theories and empirical studies in psychology to understand why we make irrational decisions, why our memory is malleable, and how unconscious mental processes impact on our experiences.
learningOutcomes: Employ principles of cognitive psychology to interpret and predict behaviour.
Apply critical thinking to enhance research outcomes and analyse key ideas from psychology sources.
Design or replicate a research study to confirm or disconfirm a testable hypothesis.
Critically evaluate how the resilience, strengths and capacity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander (and other Indigenous) peoples may contribute to professional practice in psychology.

96842.title: Psychological Science Career Readiness
96842.description: This subject enhances your psychology workforce literacy, preparing you for a career that will contribute positively to lives, organisations, and communities. You'll apply lifelong learning, social impact, research, and innovation skills to furthering your career plans. You will create a resume that showcases qualifications in psychological science including capability required for working with and for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Practical exercises in self-reflection, interpersonal skills, and interviewing will boost your competitiveness in the job market or for further postgraduate training.
learningOutcomes: Analyse psychology academic and career pathways in relation to required attributes.
Critique a service or government policy intended to improve the health and wellbeing of Indigenous Australians.

96843.description: This subject delivers advanced interpersonal and professional skills such as effective communication, cultural responsiveness, micro-counselling, and self-regulation, crucial for psychological practice. You will gain insights into reflective practice and ethical decision-making, applying this knowledge to case examples and enhancing learning through feedback and self-reflection.
learningOutcomes: Analyse ethical principles and apply the Psychology Board of Australia’s Code of Conduct for the provision of psychological services for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

96844.title: Advanced Psychological Assessment and Intervention
96844.description: This subject allows you to step into the roles of both psychologist and patient, providing advanced insights into psychological assessment and evidence-based interventions for behavioural change and symptom reduction. You will learn about the scientist-practitioner model, mental health, and applied psychology, while developing key professional skills for a career in psychological science or clinical practice through interactive and collaborative learning experiences.
learningOutcomes: Collaborate effectively and offer constructive feedback on team projects.
Enhance professional performance through self-awareness and adaptation to changing technologies.
Evaluate psychological intervention strategies for research and practice and argue the importance of the scientist-practitioner approach.
Assess the validity, reliability, and suitability of assessment tools and measures in psychology.
Select appropriate assessment measures and methods for a given case and communicate the results in an appropriate format.

96845.title: Advanced Research Methods
96845.description: This subject advances your research skills, focusing on culturally responsive and ethical research methods. You will use modern, accessible software to enhance your data analysis and visualisation capabilities. Practical experience will enable you to critically assess and articulate the published findings that inform both research and clinical practice, and address real-world issues.
learningOutcomes: Apply advanced knowledge and work within the current ethical guidelines (APS, NHMRC, AIATSIS) for the conduct of psychological research with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Evaluate qualitative approaches to psychological research.
Use technologies that help to prepare for job entry.
Apply advanced research methods and statistical techniques in data analysis.
Communicate research findings effectively through various presentation formats.

96846.description: In this subject, you'll work with a research supervisor within a collaborative lab group to identify an individual research question in psychology. You will submit a literature review, present your thesis background, receive feedback on your study design, and gain ethical approval for your research project.
learningOutcomes: Construct clear arguments based on evaluation of evidence-based psychological concepts and theories.
Design a research methodology to confirm or disconfirm a testable hypothesis.
Evaluate psychological research for adherence to relevant ethics codes.
Apply knowledge and skills in advanced research methods and statistical analysis techniques.

learningOutcomes: Construct clear arguments based on evaluation of evidence-based psychological concepts and theories.
Produce effective communications to fulfil a purpose and address specific audiences.

96861.title: Advanced Primary Health Care
96861.description: This subject enhances your primary health care knowledge, preparing you for expanded roles in community pharmacy. You'll develop advanced skills in clinical decision-making, patient assessment, and service delivery, focusing on pharmacist prescribing. You'll cover the entire prescribing process, including patient assessment, clinical reasoning, therapy selection, monitoring, and follow-up, along with de-prescribing principles. You'll also learn to deliver advanced services such as travel health consultations and minor wound management. Through case-based learning and practical application, you'll refine your ability to provide timely, evidence-based care, positioning you to deliver high-quality, accessible health services in a pharmacy setting.
learningOutcomes: Apply an evidence-based approach to prescribing within the pharmacist’s scope, integrating patient assessment, clinical reasoning, and shared decision-making.
Formulate individualised, patient-centred prescribing plans, integrating initiation, monitoring, follow-up, and de-prescribing, to achieve optimal medication outcomes.
Implement pharmacist-led primary care services, such as travel health and minor wound management, within professional and regulatory frameworks.
Communicate prescribing decisions and care plans clearly to patients and healthcare professionals to support adherence and shared care.
Reflect on and refine prescribing and service delivery, ensuring alignment with professional responsibilities and the evolving pharmacist role.

97101.title: Chinese Language and Culture 1
97101.description:
This subject is designed to provide students who have no prior knowledge of the Chinese language with basic reading, listening, speaking and writing skills. You'll learn Pinyin for pronunciation and acquire your vocabulary by around 200 words. Through active participation in collaborative activities, you'll develop intercultural competence, learning to navigate between cultures.

Your learning will involve a communicative approach, engaging in interactive tasks and activities to enhance language proficiency. You will be expected to prepare for classes through various exercises and utilise online and peer resources. The language learning approach will focus on linguistic and cultural practices across the Chinese world.

You'll be expected to commit to approximately 12 hours of weekly study, including class time, and immerse yourself in Chinese both inside and outside the classroom to build confidence and fluency.
learningOutcomes: Comprehend and respond to basic texts in oral and written Chinese.
Produce basic texts in oral and written Chinese.
Demonstrate intercultural awareness across two or more cultural contexts.

97109.title: Communicating About Chinese Media
97109.description: This subject equips you with advanced Chinese linguistic skills, preparing you for careers in Chinese-language media and critical reflection on media practices. You'll master crafting nuanced texts, employing specialised vocabulary and rhetoric, and analysing contemporary China through diverse media sources. Learning combines online and in-person methods, including interactive practice and group work, with a focus on personalised and collaborative learning. Prior to classes, you'll engage with preparatory exercises and materials to enhance in-class discussions and presentations. You'll also tailor your studies to your interests, exploring Chinese media, culture, and society through independent research and creative analysis, fostering a deep intercultural understanding.
learningOutcomes: Develop awareness of register, rhetoric, genre, concept and specialist vocabulary through exposure to a wide variety of media and academic readings
Communicate professionally and academically in writing and speech in Chinese through competent use of specific linguistic skills and devices
Reflect on and analyse critically the impact of social issues as seen from media sources on the Chinese society and its people.

97111.title: Chinese Festivals and Ceremonies
97111.description:
This subject is designed to provide students who are proficient in reading, listening, speaking and writing in Chinese with opportunities to engage with Chinese culture. It corresponds to Level 3/4 of the Chinese Proficiency Test (HSK). You’ll examine and engage with the sociocultural contexts in which the language is used, specifically with regard to festivals and ceremonies in the Chinese world.

Via written and oral assessments that demonstrate continuing mastery of the Chinese language, your learning will involve a communicative approach, engaging in interactive tasks and resources to enhance language proficiency. You'll be expected to prepare for classes through various exercises and analyse a variety of authentic sources in a manner that considers their cultural provenance and role. You’ll explore subject materials and concepts through independent research, creative outputs and/or close textual analysis. The language learning approach will focus on linguistic and cultural practices across the Chinese world.

You’ll be expected to commit to approximately 12 hours of weekly study, including class time, and immerse yourself in Chinese both inside and outside the classroom to build confidence and fluency.
learningOutcomes: Comprehend and respond to complex texts in oral and written Chinese.
Produce complex texts in oral and written Chinese.
Demonstrate intercultural awareness across two or more cultural contexts.

97112.title: Language in Chinese Screen Studies
97112.description: This subject equips you with advanced Modern Standard Chinese skills, focusing on specialised vocabulary and linguistic nuances relevant to film analysis. You'll gain proficiency in evaluating Chinese cinema within its socio-economic milieu, mastering technical language in both Chinese and English to critique films and script your mini screenplays. Learning is interactive, blending online and in-person sessions for practice and discussion, while independent study and resource utilisation enhance your grasp of professional practices and theoretical concepts. You'll tailor your experience by exploring the Chinese film industry's cultural context, fostering a deeper appreciation of China's heritage and societal norms through independent research and creative engagement.
learningOutcomes: Develop awareness of register, rhetoric, genre, concept and specialist vocabulary through exposure to contemporary Chinese movies and a wide variety of academic and professional readings
Communicate professionally and academically in writing and speech in Chinese through competent use of specific linguistic skills and devices
Analyse cinematic representation of Chinese social, cultural and political themes;
Develop basic writing skills to prepare a movie synopsis, storyboard, screen play and film reviews

97900.title: International Internship
97900.description: This subject consists of an international internship program with a UTS and coursework (two online seminars) at UTS. This subject provides you with the opportunity to develop your intercultural awareness, and professional competencies through the completion of an intensive internship, virtual placement, practicum, or entrepreneurship placement with an international organisation. It is offered in July and Summer sessions with some varying programs. You will also attend two online seminars at UTS before the start of your international program, as well as after returning from your international internship program to support your learning experience. This intensive internship includes in-person or virtual placement. The international internship program in a company, organisation, or institution focuses on collaboration in interdisciplinary teams on tasks and projects, tackling the real world, as well as gaining insights into diverse work practices and functions. The subject also focuses on improving your intercultural communication skills and developing a cultural awareness of the multi-dimensional nuanced nature of culture teams, as well as professional competences. The collaborative and reflective learning activities during the coursework will allow you to develop your intercultural capabilities via critical thinking through the understanding of your own culture and others. The assessments will require your critical and reflection skills through theoretical and methodological approaches. With the knowledge, values, and skills that you have gained through this course, you will be able to apply them in your professional life. To enrol, firstly, you must be accepted into an approved international internship program such us UTS Global Short Programs and other pre-approved Faculty led international activities. Secondly, you need to provide the confirmation of your acceptance when you submit your eRequest.
learningOutcomes: Communicate effectively and appropriately in written and oral academic and professional English
Critically analyse the behaviours, norms, and values of host and home cultures, paying particular attention to work and work-place related practices and interactions

97901.title: International Internship
97901.description: This subject consists of an international internship program with a UTS and coursework (two online seminars) at UTS. This subject provides you with the opportunity to develop your intercultural awareness, and professional competencies through the completion of an intensive internship, virtual placement, practicum, or entrepreneurship placement with an international organisation. It is offered in July and Summer sessions with some varying programs. You will also attend two online seminars at UTS before the start of your international program, as well as after returning from your international internship program to support your learning experience. This intensive internship includes in-person or virtual placement. The international internship program in a company, organisation, or institution focuses on collaboration in interdisciplinary teams on tasks and projects, tackling the real world, as well as gaining insights into diverse work practices and functions. The subject also focuses on improving your intercultural communication skills and developing a cultural awareness of the multi-dimensional nuanced nature of culture teams, as well as professional competences. The collaborative and reflective learning activities during the coursework will allow you to develop your intercultural capabilities via critical thinking through the understanding of your own culture and others. The assessments will require your critical and reflection skills through theoretical and methodological approaches. With the knowledge, values, and skills that you have gained through this course, you will be able to apply them in your professional life. To enrol, firstly, you must be accepted into an approved international internship program such us UTS Global Short Programs and other pre-approved Faculty led international activities. Secondly, you need to provide the confirmation of your acceptance when you submit your eRequest.
learningOutcomes: Communicate effectively and appropriately in written and oral academic and professional English
Critically analyse the behaviours, norms, and values of host and home cultures, paying particular attention to work and work-place related practices and interactions
Evaluate own culture-based assumptions and how they are informed
Reflect on how learning has occurred through the overseas program

97903.title: Intercultural and International Communication
97903.description: This subject equips you with essential intercultural communication skills for the global workplace, covering key theories and practical strategies for effective interaction across cultures. You'll learn to analyse and navigate diverse organisational contexts, applying your knowledge to real-world scenarios. Through active engagement, you'll refine your ability to operate competently in varied intercultural settings.
learningOutcomes: Use and apply knowledge of intercultural communication theories, concepts and frameworks
Understand perceptions and the role of discourses and representations in the Australian context, including Indigenous people related aspects
Reflect critically on one’s own perceptions and behaviours in intercultural communication and apply to professional contexts
Design and conduct independent, ethical, small scale research in and about aspects of intercultural communication
Present assignments in an appropriate professional and intercultural register

98000.title: Introduction to Criminology
98000.description: This subject provides an introduction to key concepts, significant theme, and theoretical underpinnings in criminology. It covers crime definitions, causation theories, societal responses, and the roles of policing, prisons, and community corrections. You'll also explore the evolution of crime across times and contexts. Case studies will equip you with foundational skills and knowledge for a career in the field of criminology.
learningOutcomes: Explain key criminological concepts, theories, and the evolution of the discipline.
Describe the criminal justice system's structure, functions, and key participants.
Analyse the institutional frameworks of criminal justice and their societal impacts.
Examine the effects of crime and criminal justice responses on marginalised communities.
Develop professional skills and apply theoretical knowledge to criminological practice.

You'll analyse these complex relationships from multiple viewpoints and enhance your professional skills in Indigenous cultural safety.

Critique contemporary issues about the experiences of Indigenous Australians and their interaction with the criminal justice system.
Critically evaluate criminal justice policies and practices that focus on Indigenous Australians.

98006.title: Criminology Industry Project
98006.description: How can research and/or policy analysis be used to influence and change professional practice? In this capstone subject, students undertake a criminology project that focuses on an issue faced by at least one industry partner e.g., the police; community corrections; cyber analysts; intelligence services. Building on the knowledge and skills acquired throughout the Bachelor of Criminology program; students develop and undertake a project with an applied focus led by a Studio Leader. There is a selection of projects offered each year and students work under the supervision of their Studio Leader to prepare a literature review, conduct empirical research and/or policy analysis, and write a report embodying the results of the project. To support the development of the industry project, students must participate in a weekly face to face 3-hour studio session. This subject has a 90% attendance requirement in order for students to qualify for a pass. As this is a capstone subject, only Bachelor of Criminology students in their final session of study will be permitted into the subject.
learningOutcomes: Students will apply a range of research and/or policy analysis skills acquired throughout their Bachelor of Criminology degree to deliver an empirical study and/or policy analysis addressing a specific issue within the criminology field.

Students will collaborate with/on behalf of a partner agency to plan and implement the criminology project, developing skills in stakeholder engagement, teamwork, and project management within a professional setting.

Students will prepare a comprehensive literature review, gather relevant data, analyse findings using appropriate methods, and draw evidence-based conclusions to inform their research/policy analysis report.

Students will demonstrate the ability to translate theoretical knowledge into practical solutions by addressing real-world challenges in the criminology industry through their project work, emphasising applied and translational aspects in their research outcomes.

Students will communicate their research/policy analysis findings and recommendations effectively through written reports and oral presentations, showcasing their ability to convey complex information clearly and persuasively to diverse audiences, including stakeholders and industry professionals.

98007.title: Criminal Justice in Action
98007.description: This subject provides a comprehensive and critical examination of the criminal justice system, focusing on its foundational principles, key actors, and processes. Students will explore criminal law alongside the operations of the criminal justice system and a range of professions and their professional practices. The subject examines punishment, rehabilitation, and public protection strategies, as well as comparative perspectives on criminal justice systems worldwide. Through an evidence-based and scientific lens, students will critically analyse contemporary challenges and innovations shaping criminal justice in the 21st century. This subject encourages informed and constructive engagement with the system, promoting balanced perspectives that support effective and just responses to crime, disorder and threats to public safety & security.
learningOutcomes: Explain the foundational concepts and structures of the criminal justice system and how they interact to address crime and maintain public safety.
Critically assess the role of law and justice in relation to Indigenous Australians and other marginalized groups within the criminal justice system.
Analyse key categories of crime and the legal frameworks governing their prosecution, including violent, sexual, acquisitive, and drug-related offenses.
Describe and compare international criminal justice systems, and explain emerging trends using a balanced, evidence-informed perspective on reform and policy.
Evaluate the processes and authority of law enforcement, courts, and sentencing practices, applying evidence-based approaches to their effectiveness and fairness.

98008.title: Safeguarding Society in the 21st Century
98008.description: This subject introduces students to the principles and applications of crime science as an evidence-based approach to safeguarding communities in the 21st century. Drawing on criminology, psychology, technology, and environmental design, students will examine how evidence-based methods are used to prevent and reduce crime, harm, and insecurity. The subject explores contemporary threats from cybercrime and terrorism to urban disorder and antisocial behaviour along with the tools and techniques used to counter them. Students will engage with case studies, spatial data, and policy frameworks to develop a holistic understanding of prevention, detection, and resilience building. Emphasis is placed on translating theory into practice through applied learning tasks, simulations, and problem-solving activities that reflect real-world public-safety challenges.
learningOutcomes: Explain the core principles of crime science and its relationship to criminology, crime prevention, and public safety.
Analyse contemporary threats and risks to community safety through an evidence-based, problem-solving lens.
Apply key techniques in situational and social crime prevention to real or simulated cases.
Evaluate the effectiveness and ethical implications of crime prevention technologies and interventions.
Design innovative, multi-disciplinary responses to safeguard individuals, organisations, and communities from emerging harms.

98009.description: This subject teaches you to find, interpret, and create new information using quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods research approaches. You'll learn to employ technologies and techniques for data collection, organisation, and analysis, gaining insights into social phenomena. The focus of learning is on research design, methodology, ethical practices, and analytical choices, alongside developing practical skills in presenting social research findings.

Compare and contrast research designs, sampling, data collection and data analysis methods used by researchers in the social sciences
Evaluate the appropriateness of methodological choices in relation to research question/s
Appraise the reliability and validity of published research, considering the reported methods and results to support the formulation of a study
Critically engage with the role of ethics, appropriate communication and referencing in the research process

99026.title: Coastal Protection and Restoration
99026.description: This subject addresses the environmental challenges facing coastlines, such as erosion, overfishing, species loss, and climate change effects. With over 40% of the global population living near coasts, understanding these areas is crucial for environmental scientists. You'll study the human impact on coasts and seas, and examine solutions spanning technology, society, economy, and policy. Topics include habitat restoration, species conservation, artificial reefs, and sustainable fishing, with a focus on collaborative research with industry, government, NGOs, and citizen science. You'll gain valuable scientific skills through a blend of online learning and hands-on training, connecting with leading experts to enhance your industry readiness.
learningOutcomes: Understand and explain the current effects of anthropogenic forces on environmentally sensitive coastlines and efforts to reverse these effects.
Reflect on and discuss current, real-world challenges in this field, as identified by industry experts during hands-on workshops and in online forums.
Explore innovative solutions to these challenges, including technological, social, economic, and political responses.
Communicate the nature of selected challenges and pitch creative solutions in a suitable manner and format for the target audience.
Identify and reflect on the professional capabilities required to work effectively with Indigenous peoples engaged in conservation efforts in the Sydney Basin.

99027.title: Vegetation Surveys and Plant Identification
99027.description: Mastering plant identification and vegetation survey techniques is vital for careers in environmental sciences. Application of these skills in field assessments of biodiversity is required by a diverse range of stakeholders including government bodies, consultancies, conservationists, scientists, and land managers. In this subject, you learn online at your own pace and attend a field-based training day to sharpen your skills in plant identification and vegetation survey methods. This hands-on experience ensures you're well-equipped to contribute to environmental assessments and management.
learningOutcomes: Understand and apply the fundamental botanical principles of plant identification with particular reference to the plant families and species of the Sydney region
Describe the range of methods available for vegetation surveys and apply plot-based survey skills to perform field assessments of biodiversity
Communicate the key summary findings of field assessments of biodiversity to inform end-users of biodiversity values

99028.title: Water Quality: Issues, Indicators and Safety Guidelines
99028.description: Water is essential - supporting life for all species on Earth. The importance of ensuring water is safe and healthy is paramount, particularly if that water is intended for human use. Best practice water quality testing provides critical data on the condition of a particular body of water and whether it may require intervention and management.       In this subject, you will learn field skills and scientific knowledge focused on water quality guidelines and monitoring, cyanobacteria and pollution risks, ecotoxicology and bioindicators, as well as complexities related to water reservoir management and human developments. The field-focused learning is completed a block-mode complemented with flexible online learning. Your training will enable you to ensure water safety and sustainability for communities and environments in the future.
learningOutcomes: Understand the risks associated with water quality and the guidelines for protecting human and ecosystem health
Identify and perform correct water quality sampling techniques and analyse samples collected
Interpret water quality data based on guidelines used to evaluate the ecological condition of aquatic environments
Effectively communicate water quality information and make recommendations

99029.title: Ground Rules for Contaminated Sites
99029.description: This subject delves into the application of Australian regulations for managing contaminated sites. You'll gain advanced understanding of national guidelines, site assessment trends, contaminant overviews, and learn how to conduct site assessments responsibly and avoid legal pitfalls. The course also covers current remediation methods and technologies. You'll learn about the roles and career trajectories of professionals in this field, such as site auditors, consultants, and government officers, equipping you with the expertise to operate effectively within this regulatory landscape.
learningOutcomes: Describe the process of contaminated land management in Australia and be familiar with the key legislation and Government guidance that regulates it
Understand the history and environmental, ecological and social significance of contaminated land
Design simple site assessment strategies
Recognise the priority and emerging land contaminants in Australia, and describe their essential properties in terms of origin, mobility and toxicity in the environment.

99031.description: This subject equips you with essential skills and knowledge in environmental risk assessment, focusing on the critical differences and links between human health and ecological risks, as well as the methodologies used to create guidelines for various environmental media (i.e. soils, waters, sediments). You will learn to assess evidence in evaluation of potential risk of harm, apply environmental risk assessments to actual contaminated sites, and appreciate the importance of these assessments in safeguarding workers, the environment, and global communities. Through practical learning and real-life examples, you will become proficient in using risk assessment as a tool for environmental protection.
learningOutcomes: Apply a weight-of-evidence approach in assessing contaminant risk
Calculate the likely risk of harm for human health in scenarios
Understand, apply, and synthesize methodologies for human health and ecological risk assessments
Use risk assessment and media quality guidelines in contaminated land management

99040.title: Wildlife Field Techniques: Animal Handling and Survey Methods
99040.description: This subject offers you practical skills in identifying, handling, and conserving Australia's wildlife, combining online learning with a hands-on field trip. You'll study the ethical treatment of wildlife, safety protocols, first aid, and survey design. During the three-day field trip, you will conduct wildlife surveys and will learn how to safely and effectively handle various native species of mammals, birds and reptiles. Your wildlife survey skills will be assessed by leading Australian wildlife experts. You'll also collaborate in teams to evaluate, coordinate, and implement an effective response to a range of wildlife emergencies. This experience prepares you for real-world encounters with wildlife in professional environments.
learningOutcomes: Conduct a risk assessment by applying relevant guidelines, legislation, work, health and safety requirements, and regulations governing working with wildlife
Describe the key concepts for managing and conserving wildlife, including Indigenous fire management
Use scientific keys and guides to accurately identify Australian mammals, reptiles, frogs, and birds
Identify and apply the appropriate first aid in a wildlife emergency while demonstrating competency in wildlife handling skills for a range of species
Identify and apply the six steps involved with planning and performing fauna surveys, including threatened species

99200.title: Intercultural Communication
99200.description: This subject introduces you the core concepts and debates in the interdisciplinary field of intercultural communication. You'll be prepared for the interpersonal and dynamic nature of working in increasingly globalised workplaces and intercultural environments. You'll use a problem-based approach to critically examine numerous frameworks and theories that allow you to interpret intercultural encounters in praxis-based scenarios. You'll apply specific intercultural communication strategies and approaches for their relevance to industry, communities, workplaces and society more broadly.
learningOutcomes: Critically engage with intercultural communication theories and frameworks and apply these theories to analyse diverse cultural situations and spaces
Reflect on own perceptions of intercultural spaces and encounters and intercultural skills development for professional and everyday contexts
Design and conduct independent, ethical, small scale research about aspects of interculturality
Recognise the ongoing impact of colonialism on and positive contributions of Indigenous cultures in intercultural spaces
Communicate effectively and appropriately in written and oral academic English

99211.title: Cultures of Globalisation
99211.description: The domain of culture remains an overlooked resource that can contribute to sustainable futures. This subject invites you to critically examine the cultural dynamics and consequences of globalisation and its relation the concept of sustainability. You begin by exploring how cultures are shaped, contested, and affirmed in globalised contexts. Through case studies such as language, food, music, digital technology, and other mediums, you will investigate how cultural forms and creative practices are linked to complex issues such as cultural homogenisation and preservation, cultural flows and power dynamics, cultural resistance and innovation, with particular attention to how these pertain to the experience of Indigenous and marginalised groups. The subject also considers the role of global institutions and transnational networks in shaping cultural sustainability, and encourages reflection on how cultural practices and expressions can contribute to more sustainable and equitable futures.
learningOutcomes: Identify various processes of globalisation relative to culture and assess their relationship to the concept of sustainability
Analyse globalised cultural phenomena from a variety of theoretical perspectives, including those issuing from outside the recognised centres of global cultural authority
Reflect on one’s own position as a product of and participant in cultural globalisation and how cultural practice can contribute to more sustainable and equitable futures
Communicate complex ideas in a coherent, professional and accessible form, both orally and in writing.

99212.title: Global Governance
99212.description: This subject examines the transformation of governance due to globalisation since the late twentieth century. You'll explore how increased information flows have created new policy networks across various scales, reshaping relationships among nation-states, multilateral institutions, and international organisations. You'll study the role of cities as hubs of policy innovation and how communities address global challenges. Through interdisciplinary methods, you'll analyse how governing bodies across countries tackle critical issues like climate change, water scarcity, migration, and economic inequality, with a focus on the interplay between state, private, and citizen initiatives at the city level.
learningOutcomes: Identify and analyse interrelations between multiple levels of governance and their connections to global issues and events.

Understand and evaluate the history, capacity and limitations of multilateral institutions in governing global problems and identify new and alternative approaches including intersections between regional organisations, non-governmental organisations, private governance, and citizen-led social movements.
Research, analyse, and evaluate selected global issues from theoretical approaches and interdisciplinary perspectives.
Work reflectively on independent and group activities requiring research and analysis of qualitative and quantitative information.
Present complex ideas in oral, written, and visual forms and in a manner suited to the audience.

99218.title: Intercultural Communication
99218.description: This subject provides an introduction to the core concepts and debates in the interdisciplinary field of intercultural communication. It is designed to help prepare students for the interpersonal and dynamic nature of working in increasingly globalised workplaces and intercultural environments. Using a problem-based approach, students learn to critically examine numerous frameworks and theories to interpret intercultural encounters in praxis-based scenarios. The applicability of specific strategies and approaches in intercultural communication are also examined for their relevance to industry, communities and in society more broadly.
learningOutcomes: Critically engage with intercultural communication theories and frameworks and apply these theories to analyse diverse cultural situations and spaces
Reflect on own perceptions of intercultural spaces and encounters and intercultural skills development for professional and everyday contexts
Design and conduct independent, ethical, small scale research about aspects of interculturality
Recognise the ongoing impact of colonialism on and positive contributions of Indigenous cultures in intercultural spaces
Communicate effectively and appropriately in written and oral academic English
