99221.title: Understanding Sustainability
99221.description: This subject introduces you to the foundational concepts and practices of sustainability, focusing on the interconnected pillars of economy, environment, and society. Through an exploration of key theories and contemporary local and global case studies, you will build foundational knowledge needed for a critical understanding of sustainability and environmental studies and develop skills to communicate sustainability concepts. You will be introduced to a range of topics that focus on the elements of social, environmental and economic sustainability and diverse worldviews including Indigenous perspectives to sustainability. Individual and group assignments will develop your critical reading skills and clear written communication and introduce you to mixed methods including data analysis and representation. The subject will also enable you to identify professional pathways in sustainability by engaging with industry guests who will share their career journeys and insights.
learningOutcomes: Identify and explain the key concepts, theories and practices of sustainability along the social, economic and environmental pillars
Develop skills to critique dominant interpretations of sustainability to analyse different standpoints, priorities and frameworks for approaching sustainability
Recognise decolonial approaches to understanding sustainability by engaging with diverse worldviews relating to Indigenous perspectives
Demonstrate skills in identifying appropriate academic sources social science approaches to planning, writing and presenting assignments, individually and in groups

99222.title: Internships in Sustainability and Environment
99222.description: This final Sustainability and Environment core subject supports students to self-source a short placement of 100 hours with an external organisation, in a role that draws on their skills sets from the Bachelor of Sustainability and Environment. The organisation in which students intern also form the basis of a major course-work project. The major project that students undertake, enables them to closely study how a real-world organisation seeks to address issues related to sustainability (environmental, social, and/or economic[KY1] ). Through face to face workshops and online interactive learning modules, students are guided to draw on transdisciplinary knowledge and skills gained from preceding subjects in their substantive discipline stream and the suite of their core Sustainability and Environment subjects. The major project sharpens their capabilities to scope, research and analyse a sustainability and environment problem, and appraise policy and practice strategies to address it. Prior to the session starting, students receive academic guidance and administrative support in sourcing their work placements. The task of securing a placement helps students not only gain insights about sustainability and environment organisations and strengthen their professional networking skills, but also develop professional language and practice capabilities including: being interviewed, workplace communication, and task management.
learningOutcomes: Use ethnographic methods to examine how industries and organisations are addressing environmental, social and/or economic sustainability challenges

Synthesize understandings from studies in Sustainability and Environment, studies in the Professional degree, and workplace experience, to generate arguments about the complexity of tackling sustainability from institutional/organisational contexts
Draw connections between everyday work phenomena, global and local processes, and theories related to environmental, social and/or economic sustainability to develop arguments and rationales
Critically reflect upon industry and workplace standards as to respecting protocols to work with and for Indigenous Australians in relation to sustainable development
Prepare and deliver oral, visual and written communications that are clear, coherent and suitable for the particular professional environment

99223.title: Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning
99223.description: This subject equips you with skills to evaluate and learn from sustainability initiatives, asking how to determine their success and glean lessons, regardless of the outcome. You'll integrate knowledge from various disciplines to identify effective indicators for assessing progress towards sustainability goals, which can be as diverse as water quality and social equity. You'll explore suitable data and methods for evaluation and how these insights can inform the policy/project cycle for enhanced organisational learning.
learningOutcomes: Identify and analyse sustainability indicators and evaluation frameworks.
Reflect on the social implications of monitoring and evaluation practices.
Assess various monitoring and evaluation methods for their effectiveness.
Apply monitoring and evaluation skills in professional settings.
Develop and demonstrate assignment planning, writing, and presentation skills.

99224.title: The Carbonisation of Society
99224.description: This subject will build your understanding of human-environment relations and the social, political, and economic origins of environmental crises such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution. You will explore different theorisations and evidence of how humans have impacted the natural environment and the ‘carbonisation’ of our global societies and economies through processes such as colonisation, marginalisation, industrialisation, and globalisation. You will learn about how social, political, and economic relations have combined and interacted over time to create the current social and environmental challenges we face and consider how we can support a future where humans live in harmony with their environment. The subject assessments develop your research and critical analysis skills for building and communicating an argument in written form and through verbal presentation.
learningOutcomes: Analyse the relationship between socio-environmental crises and the historical development of global society.
Explain the social, political, and economic causes of climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution by using historical and contemporary case studies.
Critically analyse and synthesise academic literature and relate findings to subject themes and key theories of environmental and sustainability studies.
Develop skills in independent research, drawing from academic and grey literature to demonstrate links between socio-political dynamics and environmental sustainability.
Develop skills in written, oral, and visual presentation.

99225.title: Sustainability and Social Justice in the City
99225.description: This subject delves into the connections between the three pillars of sustainability – social, economic and environmental - and how they intersect and compete in issues of inequality that unfold in contemporary cities in the Asia-Pacific. In particular, it deepens your study of the relationship between sustainability and social justice through an intersectional lens, examining how disparities are structured by race, class, gender and other categories of difference.  It focuses on developing your skills in qualitative methods of enquiry and analysis to understand how global sustainability challenges manifest in localised contexts and enhance your professional capacities for meaningful community engagement. Taking the city as the site of analysis, you will ground your learning on a range of pertinent issues such as (but not limited to) Indigeneity and cultural preservation in the context of urban development; geographies of racism and racialised built and natural environments; inclusive citizenship in cities of immigrant diversity; and creating equitable infrastructures across urban, peri-urban, and regional areas.
learningOutcomes: Understand the relationship between sustainability and social justice.
Undertake qualitative research into the experience of social, economic and environmental inequalities in urban life shaped by race, gender and class, and other categories of difference.
Critically discuss issues of inequality and approaches to 'just sustainability' in urban planning and policy
Critically discuss issues of sustainability and social justice relating to Indigenous peoples in cities.
Develop skills in written, visual and oral presentation of arguments based on evidence

99226.title: Planetary Decarbonisation
99226.description: This subject focuses on international social sciences and humanities approaches to the emerging idea of decarbonisation, applying systems and futures thinking to analyse opportunities for remediation of the climate crisis. You will learn to debate key questions about the global carbon budget and the ethics of shared responsibility for decarbonisation through comparative international case studies across urban, industrial, and rural environments. This will inform your learning about the current and emerging strategies for achieving carbon-neutrality across major economic sectors. The major assessment involves developing your own research project to investigate how post-carbon societies might be achieved, and the challenges of implementing these solutions in the context of a global and complex system. You will work with your peers to conduct a comparative international analysis to explore how your collective ideas, strategies, and solutions can work together to address the challenges of the climate crisis. The subject will also support you to develop skills in the professional communication of ideas and innovations to prepare you and your peers to present to a panel of industry practitioners who will engage with and give feedback on your work.

99227.title: Monitoring and Evaluating for Sustainability
99227.description: Monitoring and evaluation is a key part of project and policy design / implementation in government, civil society organisations and businesses. From a sustainability perspective, monitoring and evaluation can show us whether a sustainability initiative has achieved its objectives and what can you learn and improve on from the experience? This subject equips you with skills to evaluate and learn from sustainability initiatives by working with a real-world project with external industry partners. These projects can involve a range of intersecting issues related to sustainability, such as  conservation, gender equity, health, and social inclusion. You will integrate knowledge from various disciplines to learn how to design an effective monitoring and evaluation framework to assess progress towards sustainability goals. You will explore suitable data and methods for evaluation relevant to the project and how these insights can inform the project cycle for enhanced learning about how to achieve sustainability. Group-based work will build on your skills in project management.

221789.title: Financial Analytics
221789.description:
In this subject, you will learn to utilise data to solve real-world financial challenges and drive business decisions. Through hands-on experience with industry-standard tools and techniques, you will develop the essential skills needed in today's data-driven financial world.

You will learn to ask the right questions when approaching financial problems and identify which data can help answer them. Central to your learning will be mastering the IMPACT analytics framework, giving you a structured approach to tackle any financial analytics project. This framework will guide you in developing practical skills in cleaning and preparing both financial and non-financial datasets for analysis.

Throughout the subject, you will create data visualisations that tell clear stories about financial trends and patterns, while applying statistical techniques to uncover meaningful relationships in financial data. You will build your ability to translate complex analytical findings into clear recommendations for business stakeholders, ensuring your insights drive real business value.

By the end of the subject, you will be able to approach financial problems systematically, choose appropriate analytical techniques, and communicate your insights effectively. These skills will position you to make meaningful contributions to financial decision-making in any organisation.
learningOutcomes: Apply the IMPACT analytics framework to systematically solve complex financial business problems
Communicate complex data-informed decisions clearly to a range of business stakeholders
Critically evaluate data practices to improve analytical processes to drive positive and equitable outcomes
Design and implement analytical approaches using appropriate software tools to extract insights from financial data for decision-making

221801.title: Financial Analysis for Decision Making
221801.description:
This subject focuses on the application of financial analysis and data visualisation techniques to support effective decision-making in organisations. Students gain a solid foundation in accounting and finance concepts, including financial statements, ratio analysis, budgeting, forecasting, cost analysis, and investment analysis. They learn to leverage industry-standard tools like Tableau to analyse, visualise, and communicate financial data effectively.

Throughout the subject, students develop practical skills in using data visualisation and analytics techniques to uncover insights, identify trends, and make data-driven financial decisions. They explore the role of financial analysis in strategic decision-making and learn to create visualisations that communicate complex financial information to diverse stakeholders.

By the end of the subject, students are equipped with the knowledge and skills to apply financial analysis techniques, use data visualisation tools, and make informed, data-driven decisions in various business contexts. The subject prepares students to become proficient in leveraging financial data to drive organisational performance and create value.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and interpret financial statements to assess an organisation's financial position and performance, using appropriate financial ratios and analytical techniques
Apply financial analysis and management accounting methods to support decision-making processes in various business contexts
Develop forecasts using industry-standard tools to project future financial performance and evaluate business scenarios
Create effective data visualisations to communicate financial information and insights to diverse stakeholders, facilitating informed decision-making

319265.title: Communication for IT Professionals
319265.description: This core subject will highlight new ways of working and provide insights into the scope of technology. You will learn to make decisions that impact people, community, and the environment. Through an authentic challenge, you will develop skills and knowledge, providing a solid base for your continuous professional development as an IT professional. In the subject, you will complete a set real-world challenge, working in a team to develop solutions. You will form a team with peers, working in and outside class throughout the session on the project that you select. Your team will research the project background, refine scope and identify technological considerations. You will then ideate and prototype potential solutions that work in a community context. Finally, you will propose a fully developed design idea that benefits the identified community. In completing the challenge, you will develop multidisciplinary and professional skills including research skills to inform the development of design solutions; applying the design process to solve genuine humanitarian challenges; considering socio-technical issues; developing professional communication skills; and participating and leading team processes.
learningOutcomes: Identify stakeholder needs and ethical considerations through the empathise design stage. (B.1)
Apply a design thinking approach to meet stakeholder needs. (C.1)
Communicate an evidence-based design solution for an IT or engineering project. (E.1)
Explain how different experiences of a diverse team work together to achieve a design (E.1)

319272.title: Project Management and the Professional
319272.description: This subject equips you with project management skills, focusing on information systems and professional project management. You will learn about ethical standards and the organisational context of projects. You will also learn about the roles of project team members, managing time, risk, cost and communications and the value of quality. These skills are vital for university success and for success in your future career. Learning involves being part of a small project team. You will collaborate to create project documents, receiving constructive feedback to foster improvement. These activities culminate in a significant group assessment followed by a reflection on what you have learnt. You will also write a report stating the possible ethical dilemmas in a given case study and describing how industry codes may be used to suggest solutions to these dilemmas. Academic and professional language and communication skills are measured through a milestone assessment task that gauges both your subject knowledge and communication proficiency.
learningOutcomes: Explain the social impact of information technology and responsibility of IT professionals and importance of ethical codes of conduct within projects. (B.1)

320513.title: Machine Learning
320513.description:
This subject will introduce you to the essential elements of machine learning - a technique that enables a machine to learn from data and automatically derive or enhance its strategy to perform its tasks. Taking a practical and technical approach, you will be guided by hands-on experience to an understanding of the important principles that underlie highly successful machine learning techniques.

You will be presented with core concepts in machine learning as well as exposed to a generic framework for machine learning projects. Different learning models, including Decision Trees, Random-Forest, and Neural Networks will be discussed and practised with real-world applications dealing with structured (tabular), semi-structured (text) and unstructured data (image).
learningOutcomes: Describe the scope, limitations and application of several machine learning methods. (D.1)
Use or program a machine learning method. (D.1)
Design an approach to machine learning problems in specialised domains. (C.1)
Demonstrate an understanding of the issues underlying machine learning to successfully outline an approach to solving a machine learning problem. (D.1)

431008.title: Reinforcement Learning
431008.description: This subject introduces you to reinforcement learning, the study of how machines learn from interactions with their environment. A subset of machine learning, it's essential for automated decision-making and AI, teaching programs to predict and act optimally through experience. You'll explore its applications in control systems, gaming, and inventory management. The subject covers both theory and practice, including Markov Decision Processes, classic and modern algorithms, and hands-on agent training using cutting-edge software tools. By the end, you'll understand value functions, explore exploration versus exploitation, and be able to deploy an AI system to solve real-world problems in your final project.

431025.title: Introduction to Quantum Computing
431025.description:
This subject introduces quantum computation, a model of computation based on the physical laws of quantum mechanics. Quantum computers outperform traditional computers for a range of practical problems, and in many cases offer drastic advantages. In this subject, you will learn about the basic tools for understanding quantum information processing. You will apply this knowledge to study the key quantum protocols: teleportation, superdense coding, and simple quantum algorithms.

The subject covers key features of quantum theory which differentiate it from classical theory, including quantum entanglement and coherence.
learningOutcomes: Analyse quantum information protocols using the basic mathematical structure of quantum mechanics, including states, operations and measurements to validate performance claims. (D.1)
Design and create quantum circuits for quantum algorithms to run on quantum computers. (D.1)
Critically reflect and contrast the historical development of quantum and classical computation to differentiate computational capabilities. (D.1)
Effectively communicate quantum concepts to broad audiences. (E.1)

971102.title: In-country Study and Fieldwork Project 1: France
971102.description:
The In-country Study and Fieldwork Project 1 is the first part of the Bachelor of International Studies Honours Stream. This subject is designed to enable you to live and study in another country and is guided by the principles of cultural immersion and reflection, inquiry-based learning and self-directed learning. It fosters in you a sophisticated capacity for critical reflection – in particular, the ability to identify and question your cultural assumptions, values and beliefs within broader contexts, and thus to acknowledge and empathise with the different perspectives of people from diverse cultures. Furthermore, it equips you with the tools to develop advanced research skills, by scaffolding learning processes towards a major research project (to be completed in the second semester capstone) that investigates an issue of contemporary relevance for the host society.

During In-Country Study (ICS) at a UTS partner institution, you complete host university classes. In addition to this you design and complete reflective research assessments about the host society. During the period abroad, you are guided by an academic supervisor to devise an appropriate topic for a reflection and a project. To do this you draw on your host country experience, engage with relevant secondary sources to deepen your understanding and conduct a small-scale investigation employing social science or humanities research methods.
learningOutcomes: Critically analyse and synthesise knowledge of the historical, political, cultural, social and/or economic situations of the host society.
Articulate coherent, well-structured and appropriate spoken and written academic texts including oral skills in both English and the language(s) of the host society.
Develop intercultural understanding in a sophisticated manner by critically reflecting upon the behaviours and values in host and home cultures.
Design and execute an independent small-scale research project in an international setting by engaging in an advanced way with theory appropriate to the research topic and discipline.

971112.title: Thesis (Criminology)
971112.description: The MRes thesis in Criminology provides students with the advanced research expertise and skills necessary to undertake and critically evaluate criminological and criminal justice research. Combining core research skills with specialist criminology teaching from research-active staff, students critically examine the theoretical foundations that underpin applied criminological research. They not only gain a rigorous and advanced understanding of research design, methodologies and analytical techniques, but also study advanced theory and policy within the discipline of criminology and engage in learning that supports professional practice. The course provides formal, comprehensive, multi-disciplinary training in research methodologies and transferable employment related skills, for those interested in applying for a PhD and/or planning or extending a professional career in field. Students engage in the design and delivery of a thesis that has application to the field as well as explore professional practice knowledge and skills. This cutting-edge program aims to equip students with the necessary ability to contribute to the field of criminology through innovative research, critical analysis, and evidence-based solutions to complex criminological and social issues.

requisite.text: Admission into C03067 Master of Arts (Research)

971113.title: Thesis (Global Asian Studies)
971113.description: The thesis in Global Asian Studies allows students to focus on dynamic dimensions of people and places in Asia. Through the thesis they conduct interdisciplinary research addressing the economic, political, social, and transcultural influence of Asian states and societies. Thesis supervision and research seminars centre on contemporary research design, including multi-sited frameworks, everyday multilingualism, digital humanities, and theory-building. Students are encouraged to develop approaches beyond Eurocentrism and descriptive area studies, to conduct original research for instance focused on Asia in the world, Asian contexts of globalising issues, comparative urbanisms and ways of life, connectivity among Asian societies, regional environmental change, and pathways to political futures. Topics may include cinema, cities, education, the environment, gender, geography, governance and international affairs, labour and social movements, sociolinguistics, media studies, and politics and political economy, and with particular emphasis on China, Japan, Korea, and Indonesia. Advancing a critically insightful understanding of contemporary Asia, based on an intellectual foundation for connectedness in an uneven world, the thesis prepares students for postgraduate research and professional careers in the arts, business, education, government and non-government sectors, international affairs, media, politics, and public policy.

requisite.text: Admission into C03067 Master of Arts (Research)

971114.title: Thesis (International Studies)
971114.description: The MRes thesis in International Studies allows students to develop projects with an international focus, either in Australia or abroad, emphasising local and global connections that drive transcultural, translingual, and transnational processes. The goal is to explore the uneven interactions and movements of cultures, languages, people, ideas and desires that shape the international landscape. Through seminars, students interact with researchers and international guest speakers from various disciplines, including history, cultural studies, language learning and linguistics, geography, ethnography and literary studies. These sessions provide insights into the responsibilities, approaches, and practices essential for impactful research. Students engage deeply with international research methods and receive support in research design and theory-building. This thesis research subject prepares students for postgraduate research and professional careers in their chosen field, equipping them to navigate and influence the complex world of global connections.

requisite.text: Admission into C03067 Master of Arts (Research)

971116.title: Method and Discovery
971116.school: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
971116.description: Research is an active process with a defined method. In this research training subject you plan-out the research method and program for your thesis. You explore a range of research methods relevant to your topic. You draw on peer insights and expertise, across disciplines and genres, to allow cross-fertilisation and re-conceptualisation. Research questions, aims and objectives direct the researcher to specific 'approaches' to research discovery, and entail associated ethical assumptions, including for Indigenous research, normative aims, collaborative possibilities and social and creative impact. The research process may centre on collecting and analysing information, or involve a creative intervention or initiative, or be focused on designing or producing new 'ways of doing'. Engagement with specific methods in the subject is shaped by your priorities and interests and is led by specialist academics in 'masterclass' format.
learningOutcomes: Identify and address methodological challenges
Demonstrate relevant research skills necessary for developing a research plan
Design a feasible research plan
Evaluate and incorporate ethical dimensions of research practice into the research plan

976002.title: Contemporary China
976002.description: This subject provides an overview of contemporary China and its history, culture, politics, society and economy. You will learn to identify and analyse current issues from multiple perspectives using theory and methods for intercultural research. The subject combines lectures with tutorials and independent work to develop your analytical and problem-solving abilities in China studies, with a focus on cultural diversity, social and economic change, and political transformation. Topics include cities, gender, home and work, identity, governance, media, the economy and China's international relationships.

976007.title: Contemporary Spain
976007.description: This subject introduces you to contemporary Spain through its historical, political, cultural, social, and economic dimensions from a local, national, continental, and global context. You will be provided with the critical skills to identify, reflect, and analyse major current socio-cultural challenges that shape contemporary Spain through the learning of theoretical and methodological approaches for engaging you in intercultural research. In weeks 2 and 12, you will follow an umbrella program shared by all contemporary European society subjects that introduces general issues relating to contemporary Europe: definitions, geographical space, addressing its identity, unification, internal divisions, colonialism, and the impact of migration, among others. In the other weeks, the subject focuses on divergent and historical ways of conceptualising Spain. You will learn about important moments in Spain’s history, such as the unification, the Second Republic, the Civil War, the Franco dictatorship, the restoration of democracy, and the sociopolitical developments of recent decades. You will delve into the diversity of national and cultural identities (regionalisms), plurilingualism, gender, film, music, art, migration, economics, and the evolving socio-cultural aspects of contemporary Spain. This subject will also provide you with an understanding of some of the current challenges that the country faces and how a Spanish citizen thinks and feels in the twenty-first century. The collaborative and reflective learning activities will allow you to develop your intercultural capabilities via critical thinking on Spain's diverse and dynamic culture(s), as well as an international perspective. In the assessments, you will apply your critical and reflection skills to identify and analyse contemporary Spain, through theoretical and methodological approaches.

977000.title: In-country Language and Culture Study 2
977000.description: This subject consists of an international study program with a UTS and coursework (two online seminars) at UTS. This subject is for students who have previously participated in an international short-term language program as part of their degree and want to attend a second program of a similar kind. This subject provides you with the opportunity to develop your communication skills in another language and enhance your intercultural awareness, and cultural knowledge of another society through an international study program with an international UTS partner organisation. It is offered in July and Summer sessions with some varying programs. The programs have a range of levels of language proficiency from beginner to advanced. However, the specific program, languages, and levels available may vary. You will also attend two online seminars at UTS before the start of your international program, as well as after returning from your international program to support your learning experience. The international program includes classroom-based or virtual seminars. The subject focuses on linguistic proficiency, improving your intercultural communication skills, and developing a cultural awareness of the multi-dimensional nuanced nature of culture. The collaborative and reflective learning activities during the coursework will allow you to develop your intercultural capabilities via critical thinking through the understanding of your own culture and others. The assessments will require your critical and reflection skills through theoretical and methodological approaches. With the knowledge, values, and skills that you have gained through this course, you will be able to apply them in your professional life. To enrol, firstly, you must be accepted into an approved international program such us UTS Global Short Programs and other pre-approved Faculty led international activities. Secondly, you need to provide the confirmation of your acceptance when you submit your eRequest.

977912.title: In-country Contemporary Society Study
977912.description: This subject consists of an international study program with a UTS and coursework (two online seminars) at UTS. This subject provides you with the opportunity to develop your intercultural awareness, and sociocultural knowledge through an international study program with an international UTS partner organisation. It is offered in July and Summer sessions with some varying programs. You will also attend two online seminars at UTS before the start of your international program, as well as after returning from your international program to support your learning experience. The international program includes classroom-based or virtual seminars. The subject focuses on improving your intercultural communication skills and developing a cultural awareness of the multi-dimensional nuanced nature of culture. The collaborative and reflective learning activities during the coursework will allow you to develop your intercultural capabilities via critical thinking through the understanding of your own culture and others. The assessments will require your critical and reflection skills through theoretical and methodological approaches. With the knowledge, values, and skills that you have gained through this course, you will be able to apply them in your professional life. To enrol, firstly, you must be accepted into an approved international program such us UTS Global Short Programs and other pre-approved Faculty led international activities. Secondly, you need to provide the confirmation of your acceptance when you submit your eRequest.

978110.title: In-country Study and Fieldwork Project 2: China
978110.description:
The In-country Study and Fieldwork Project 2 is the second part of the Bachelor of Arts in International Studies Honours Stream, which involves two sessions of In-Country Study (ICS) at a UTS partner institution. This subject is designed to enable you to live and study in another country and is guided by the principles of cultural immersion and reflection, inquiry-based learning and self-directed learning. It fosters in you a sophisticated capacity for critical reflection, including consideration of Indigenous Australian contexts, the ability to identify and question your cultural assumptions, values and beliefs within broader contexts, and thus to acknowledge and empathise with the perspectives of people from diverse cultures. It also provides you with the opportunity to develop advanced research skills, by scaffolding learning and work toward a major research project investigating an aspect of contemporary relevance for the host society.

You complete host university classes and in addition to this, build upon the work during In-country Study and Fieldwork Project 1 and your continued exposure to and interaction with the host society to recognise the processual nature of intercultural learning. You also continue your work with an academic supervisor to design and research a major mixed-methods project investigating an aspect of contemporary relevance for the host society. To do this you draw on your host country experience, engage with relevant secondary sources to deepen your understanding and conduct an academic innovative project that can include a mixed-media component using social science or humanities research methods.
learningOutcomes: Critically analyse and synthesise an understanding of the historical, political, cultural, social and/or economic situations of the host society.
Articulate coherent, well-structured and appropriate spoken and written academic texts including oral skills in both English and the language(s) of the host society.

Develop intercultural understanding in a sophisticated manner by critically reflecting upon the behaviours and values in host and home cultures, including knowledges of Indigenous Australian contexts.

Design and execute an independent small-scale research project in an international setting by engaging in an advanced way with theory appropriate to the research topic and discipline, including consideration of Indigenous Australian research principles.

992221.title: The Global Professional: Industry Engagement Project
992221.description: This capstone subject offers you the chance to apply and develop your intercultural and global citizenship skills within a professional setting. You will be supported to self-source an internship with an organisation in your field of interest and in a role that strengthens your intercultural competencies. With the global workplace serving as a backdrop for exploring cultural complexities, you will undertake a major project to observe and critically evaluate organisational and industry cultural practices, systems, and policies related to diversity, equity and inclusion, including attention to protocols working with and for Indigenous Australians. Through this workplace learning, you will develop your capacity to enact positive social change in your future places of work and industries of practice. On-campus workshops and online learning will support your preparation and progression through the internship.
learningOutcomes: Identify and explain key sustainability concepts and practices.
Analyse diverse perspectives, frameworks and scales of sustainability and their possible impacts on marginalised social groups.
Develop self-awareness and critically reflect on personal and professional sustainability pathways.
Recognise specific issues of sustainability relating to Indigenous peoples.

992222.title: The Asia Pacific in the 21st Century
992222.description: In this subject, you will study contemporary challenges and politics of the Asia-Pacific, a region with diverse and interconnected political, economic, social, and environmental landscapes. The subject helps you to analyse the region's key trends, challenges, and opportunities within the Asia-Pacific, as well as external dynamics that affect the region. The subject invites you to assess conflicts and regional cooperation among key actors from East Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific. Additionally, this subject enables you to explore nuclear politics, peacebuilding, and climate justice in the region from Pacific, Indigenous, and feminist perspectives. The subject offers case studies and theories for a critical engagement with the Asia-Pacific region and its place in the 21st century as a vibrant, contested, and dynamic region in global politics.
learningOutcomes: Identify domestic, regional, and international policies of actors in the Asia-Pacific.
Evaluate regional stability and security in the Asia-Pacific using concepts and theories introduced in the subject.
Analyse how historical and contemporary challenges shape current political, social, and economic landscapes in the Asia-Pacific.
Communicate complex ideas and arguments related to geopolitical analysis of the Asia-Pacific region consistent with professional and academic standards.

992223.title: The Future of the International Order
992223.description: This subject equips you with an understanding of the factors influencing the international order, vital for forecasting global trends and informing policy decisions. You will dissect the complexities of the international system and the array of actors that shape it, including states, international organisations, and NGOs. In this subject you will learn how to use core theories of International Relations, such as Realism, Liberalism, Constructivism, and Postcolonialism, to deepen your analysis. You will reflect on both the historical evolution of the international order and its possible futures, reflecting on the interplay of power and norms. Through theoretical analysis and case studies you will gain a nuanced understanding of the international order and its significance for global politics.
learningOutcomes: Analyse contemporary and historical case studies using International Relations theories.
Create self-reflexive, analytical, and persuasive arguments about worldviews and the international order.
Communicate effectively about complexities within the international order with consideration of political sensitivities.

992224.title: Geopolitics and Australian Foreign Policy
992224.description: This subject equips you with a nuanced understanding of Australia's foreign policy, blending theory with real-world case studies to enhance your analytical skills in geopolitics and international relations. In today's complex global landscape, foreign policy extends well beyond security concerns. Effective foreign policy requires understanding not only of the intricacies of geography, geopolitics, alliances and security, but also the importance of multilateralism, international law, and reciprocity. You will learn how to navigate questions of state power, territorial issues, and national security. Your learning will be interactive, with a strong emphasis on applying theoretical frameworks to topical geopolitical scenarios.
learningOutcomes: Analyse Australian foreign policy in relation to geopolitics, multilateralism, alliances, and international law.
Apply theories of International Relations to contemporary challenges facing Australia in crafting its foreign policy.
Evaluate how geopolitical considerations shape the foreign policies of states and the international system.
Communicate complex ideas and arguments related to geopolitical analysis, state power, sovereignty, and security.

992225.title: Global Crime, Justice and Security
992225.description: In this subject, you will study global crime, justice and security within the international system, addressing harms including genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and human rights violations. You will study the interconnected nature of harms, justice, and security in a globalised world, attentive to the transnational, national and local justice efforts to address systematic abuses. The subject helps you to analyse these issues through traditional and critical International Relations theories, and encourages you to develop practical insights for pursuing justice through legal, policymaking and activist channels. Additionally, this subject enables you to explore topics such as international criminal justice, human security, inequality and transitional justice, with a focus on gendered, racial and environmental harms. Through case studies, you will have the opportunity to critically engage with the complexities of global crime, justice and security, and its implications for the study and practice of International Relations.
learningOutcomes: Apply theories of International Relations to contemporary challenges and debates concerning crime, justice and security in a global context.
Apply research skills and analytical skills to crime, justice and security in a global context.
Evaluate international, transnational and local policies and responses to crime, justice and security using concepts and theories introduced in the subject.
Communicate complex ideas and arguments related to global crime, justice and security consistent with professional and academic standards.

992226.title: International Relations Applied Research Project
992226.description: This subject enables you to design and execute an applied research project in International Relations, refining your critical thinking and mastering research methodologies. You will be supported to develop a research question, building on theoretical and methodological knowledge from previous coursework subjects, and gain practical research experience. In consultation with teaching staff and peers, you will have the opportunity to choose suitable methods, source data, and conduct analysis. Your assessment will be to develop and conduct your own research project, which you will be encouraged to designed to suit your next career stage and goals.
learningOutcomes: Apply international relations theories and concepts to real-world contexts to explore complex global issues
Formulate clear research questions to guide selection of appropriate data sources and analysis techniques
Demonstrate effective project management skills that ensure professional execution of projects
Demonstrate knowledge of the role of social responsibility in research.
Communicate research findings effectively for a range of audiences and formats as required

992227.title: Reframing International Political Economy
992227.description: This subject offers an interdisciplinary view of International Political Economy, valuable for careers across business, government, diplomacy, and the NGO sphere. You will focus on the interplay between politics and economics rather than economic technicalities or maths. You'll examine the influence of states, international organisations, and transnational corporations, applying both traditional and critical theories to understand power dynamics. Through case studies like economic crises, international development, and climate finance, you will analyse and propose solutions to transnational challenges. The subject integrates diverse theories and empirical data, equipping you with a comprehensive understanding of the global economy and possible directions for the future of global governance.
learningOutcomes: Critically analyse historical and contemporary challenges faced by the global economy.
Apply core theories to interpret the actors that shape the global political economy.
Analyse real-world case studies and complex global issues using key theories within International Political Economy.
Effectively communicate evidence-based solutions to complex issues within the global political economy.

992228.title: Research Design and Methods in International Relations
992228.description: This subject introduces you to research design, methods, and methodologies in International Relations. You will learn about the foundations of International Relations research, and the skills and techniques required to conduct ethical and independent research for careers in global politics. The subject covers topics such as decolonising methodologies and Indigenous research, qualitative and quantitative methods, developing research questions, choosing data sources, and analysis techniques. You will also learn how to navigate the ethical and practical challenges of international research, and how to apply research methods in the international arena.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of key concepts and research design in International Relations, including Indigenous ways of knowing, being, and doing.
Evaluate research methods and their relevance within particular contexts in International Relations.

Critically reflect on and apply Indigenous ethical principles and practices in International Relations research, to inform capabilities to work with and for Indigenous Australians and other Indigenous peoples in domestic and international settings.
Communicate the impact of research and the importance of ethical research practices within professional contexts in International Relations.

992229.title: Sustainability and Global Governance
992229.description: As the climate changes, so too does our capacity to mitigate and adapt to these changes. Global environmental challenges, including climate change, biodiversity loss, and environmental degradation, require you to focus on actors and institutions operating in international contexts. This subject equips you with the knowledge and skills to attempt to effectively tackle these challenges, make informed decisions, and contribute to dialogues on sustainable social, political, economic, and environmental development. You will gain an overview of the development and implementation of multi-scalar environmental policy and international law, and consider the role of key actors including states, international organisations, civil society, and the private sector. You will critically evaluate approaches to international cooperation and assess their effectiveness in addressing specific environmental issues.
learningOutcomes: Analyse key environmental challenges facing international communities and the impacts of these issues on different actors, places and scales
Apply critical perspectives on international cooperation efforts and assess their effectiveness in socially responsible governance in both Australian and international contexts

Examine power relations and decision making across multiple scales and actors to understand and demonstrate knowledge of how they influence global governance on mitigating and adapting to contemporary environmental challenges
Analyse the importance of recognising Indigenous perspectives and rights for sustainable development policies
Effectively communicate complex ideas and arguments related to international cooperation in environmental governance and sustainable development

992230.title: Intercultural and International Communication
992230.description: This subject provides you with theoretical insights and practical skills for intercultural and international communication by equipping you to explore links between culture and identities, and between language and society. This subject prepares you for diverse and complex multicultural workplaces and societies, covering skills in research, policy, and ethical engagement. You will analyse connections between personal experience and professional practice to reflect on how your cultural identity shapes the way you engage with the world, and thus how your identities inform your practices in professional, institutional, and social contexts. By engaging in critical debates on intersections between cultures, languages, and identities, you will have the opportunity to apply your learning to contemporary, real-world instances of intercultural and international communication.
learningOutcomes: Articulate awareness of their own cultural identity (beyond national cultural typologies) and how it shapes their intercultural and international communication.
Recognise and demonstrate awareness of others’ perspectives in intercultural interactions, by critically analysing intercultural communication concepts, theories and frameworks.
Critically analyse and apply professional experiences to interact effectively in intercultural situations in professional settings in Australia and internationally.

999781.title: International Research Methods
999781.description: This subject teaches you research methods for critical social and cultural analysis, focusing on global-local dynamics. You'll distinguish between quantitative and qualitative approaches, with an emphasis on qualitative techniques like interviews, discourse analysis, archival research, ethnography, and observation. You'll learn the research process, from literature reviews to designing questions and data collection strategies, understanding that data types dictate analysis methods. Additionally, you'll become aware of ethical considerations in research planning and execution.

013403.title: Learning Futures: Teaching for Complexity and Diversity
013403.description: This subject equips you with an understanding of the multifaceted influences on Australian secondary education, including social, political, and economic factors. You'll develop critical-reflective skills to examine educational beliefs and practices, focusing on social theories, socialisation, inequality, globalisation, gender, and multiculturalism. Learning involves research-based analysis, fostering culturally responsive teaching methods to navigate and shape educational policies and outcomes effectively.
learningOutcomes: Analyse how schools operate and recognise that they are an integral part of contemporary society (GTS 7.1, 7.2).
Critically reflect on how schooling is influenced by social, cultural, economic and political factors (GTS 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 2.4, 7.1, 7.2) (PA 1.1, 1.2, 6.1, 6.2).

Evaluate the responsiveness of teaching resources and strategies to the learning strengths and needs of students from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socioeconomic backgrounds. (GTS 1.3).
Communicate the contested nature of key aspects of education (GTS 7.4).
Communicate effectively including using academic conventions for writing.

013404.title: Inclusive Education
013404.description: This subject focuses on inclusive education, offering secondary teachers strategies to cater to diverse learners. It covers identifying students with additional needs and tailoring instructional methods for accessible learning. Key areas include legal rights, Universal Design for Learning, classroom management, resource adaptation, assessment, explicit teaching methods, and the use of assistive technologies. Emphasis is also placed on effective communication and collaboration.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate broad knowledge and understanding of legislative requirements and teaching strategies that support participation and learning of students with disability (GTS 1.1, 1.6, 4.4, 7.1, 7.2) (PA2.9, PA5.2, 5.3)

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of strategies for differentiating teaching to meet the specific learning needs of students across the full range of abilities; demonstrate knowledge of practical approaches to manage challenging behavior; apply principles of Universal Design for Learning and make adjustments to curriculum and classroom activities to support diverse student abilities and manage behaviour (GTS 1.5, 3.2, 3.3, 4.1, 4.3) (PA2.1, 2.5, PA 5.7)

Include a range of teaching strategies in teaching; identify strategies to support inclusive student participation and engagement in classroom activities; design and deliver instruction using explicit teaching techniques and critique the effectiveness of various strategies to maximize student outcomes (particularly in relation to literacy) and manage behaviour (GTS 2.2, 2.5, 4.1, 3.3, 4.3, 6.3) (PA2.1, 2.5, PA4.9, 4.11, PA5.7)

Demonstrate knowledge of a range of resources, including ICT, that engage students in their learning; demonstrate a range of verbal and non-verbal communication strategies to support student engagement; demonstrate technical competence and evaluate assistive technologies and mobile devices to support learning (GTS 2.6, 3.4, 4.5) (PA3.1, 3.4, 3.11, PA5.8)

013407.title: Resetting the Future: Indigenous Australian Education
013407.description: This subject recognises the crucial impact secondary school teachers have on the educational experiences of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students. It celebrates the rich diversity of these communities and their connection to Country. You will be prepared to effectively teach Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students (AITSL 1.4) and educate all students on Indigenous languages, histories, and cultures to foster reconciliation (AITSL 2.4). The subject introduces you to key policies and practices affecting Indigenous educational outcomes and equips you with the foundational knowledge to integrate Indigenous perspectives into the curriculum. You will also reflect on your professional identity and its influence on your teaching practices.
learningOutcomes: respect and value the diversity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures and promote reconciliation between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians (GTS 2.4);
identify and reflect on their own life stories to make meaning of the relationship between Aboriginal and non- Aboriginal Australians;
identify how historical, social, cultural, economic and linguistic backgrounds impact on the education of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students (GTS 1.4);

produce accurate and cohesive academic texts.

013408.title: Teaching and Learning with Digital Technologies
013408.description: This subject explores the use of learning technologies to foster design, critical thinking, creativity, and learning in a digital world. You will examine how different technologies can facilitate authentic, active, and collaborative learning within your discipline. The subject encourages you to engage with relevant e-learning theories and pedagogies for diverse environments, including face-to-face, online, and mobile settings. 013409.title: Professional Learning
013409.description: This foundational subject in the professional experience sequence offers an overview of teaching, the profession and ongoing teacher development. You'll prepare for classroom engagement by examining school settings, lesson planning, and effective teaching strategies. The focus is on planning for impactful learning and teaching, linking theory with practice, and reflecting on quality teaching's influence on student outcomes. Workshops and online resources delve into professional teacher learning, highlighting context, collaboration, evidence-based decisions, and educational research through immersive in-school experiences. You will learn to reflect on these professional learning opportunities to develop your teaching practice. All tasks are aligned with the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers: Graduate.

013985.title: Understanding and Engaging Adolescent Learners
013985.description: This subject prepares pre-service teachers to connect with and teach adolescents in modern Australian schools effectively. It merges psychological insights on learning and motivation with sociological views on youth, equipping you to navigate and analyse the complex learning environments affecting secondary students. Through diverse theoretical applications, you'll craft engaging, adaptive teaching practices, considering these theories in real-life school, family, and community scenarios. You'll also integrate insights from professional placements and your educational philosophy, fostering a comprehensive and respectful approach to aiding high school students' success.
learningOutcomes: Analyse how students learn and change, and how student motivation develops
Analyse complex teaching and learning scenarios that affect adolescents
Develop theoretically sound strategies for creating supportive teaching and learning environments for adolescents in diverse and complex contexts
Describe and scrutinise challenging issues facing young Australians and their teachers in schools, drawing on relevant theoretical concepts, research and policy

You'll become aware of how literacy and numeracy are uniquely embedded within each subject area and learn to design lessons that improve students' English and maths skills relevant to the subject content. By building your ability to teach these core skills across the curriculum, you contribute to students' academic growth, functional literacy and numeracy, and their societal engagement.

013252.title: Professional Experience Teaching Practice 2
013252.description: During a six-week placement, you will gain practical experience as a pre-service teacher, receiving feedback on your teaching from both your university supervisor and the classroom teacher. The coursework is designed to consolidate your knowledge and teaching practices, enabling you to complete the Teacher Performance Assessment (TPA). In the TPA, you will evaluate your planning, teaching and assessment whilst on placement and consider their alignment with the Assessment for Graduate Teaching (AfGT) standards. The subject concludes with you curating and annotating a portfolio reflecting demonstration of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers (APSTs). The subject and placement allow you to apply your learning in a real-world educational setting, with continuous feedback on your teaching practice and progress towards teaching domain standards.

013105.title: The Multilingual Learner
013105.description: Learner’s needs, goals and success in developing an additional language interact with a range of linguistic, psychological and socio-cultural factors. In this subject, you will examine key findings from research to understand how these factors mediate learning in a range of different contexts including: an educational context where the language of instruction is an additional language or dialect for the learners; adult migrants learning the dominant language of their new community; and students studying a foreign language in a formal educational setting. You will learn how to build a profile of multilingual learners by conducting an interview with a language learner.
learningOutcomes: Review, explain and synthesise theoretical ideas about linguistic, psychological and sociological factors that interact with a learner’s language development.
Examine factors that may impact on the learning of language learners, including Australian Indigenous learners.

013096.title: Teaching Language for Meaning
013096.description:
This subject provides language and literacy teachers with knowledge about English grammar and vocabulary, and how to teach it. The presentation of this knowledge aligns with contemporary curriculum and syllabus documents.

Knowledge about English grammar and vocabulary is expressed in a metalanguage teachers can share with their students. This knowledge enables students to:

  • reflect on how English works
  • recognise the main features of the English language
  • understand, appreciate and compose spoken and written texts in ways that align with their language learning needs and goals, and curriculum outcomes

Knowledge about how to teach English grammar and vocabulary enables teachers to design sequences of teaching and learning that support language and literacy development across the stages of school and post-school education
learningOutcomes: Analyse texts to understand how grammar and vocabulary choices have been used to make different kinds of meaning and to achieve specific social purposes.
Examine texts to identify and select patterns of grammar and vocabulary use of most relevance to the English language learning needs of one or more specified student profiles.
Evaluate critically approaches to the teaching and learning of English grammar and vocabulary for students learning English as an additional language or dialect.
Design effective sequences of grammar and vocabulary teaching and learning that incorporate modelled, guided, collaborative and independent practice, as well as assessment for and of learning.

013991.title: Research Literacies
013991.description: Research literacies entail understanding of different research approaches, critical reading of research, and ability to develop ideas about potential research problems. In this subject you will develop the skills and knowledge to be research literate in in the language studies field. You will explore how research is designed around assumptions about knowledge, values and the nature of reality, and through research approaches to data collection and analysis. You will engage with a variety of quantitative and qualitative research approaches to develop skills in understanding research and how it is used and adapted into new contexts. You will be encouraged to explore and critically reflect on your own perspectives on knowledge building and how you might act as an ethical researcher.
learningOutcomes: Identify, summarise and analyse published research from the language studies field
Argue the merits of different research methodologies and approaches available to language studies researchers
Reflect on the relevance of selected research studies for particular contexts and purposes

Identify researchable problems, locate and critique existing research on the topic, and articulate possible approaches, demonstrating an understanding of the advantages and limitations of different approaches

013987.title: Oral Language Development
013987.description: In this subject you will explore spoken language and how it is used in language classrooms, as a learning goal and as a teaching tool. It investigates how people learn their first and subsequent languages and the strategies that expand learners’ language repertoires, including use of their first language to support their English skills. You will develop the knowledge and skills to analyse classroom discourse to inform your understanding of how learning is mediated by the teacher through carefully considered language use. Classroom Talk will provide you with a balance between theoretical grounding, evidence-based research and practical strategies for you to enhance the quality and quantity of learner talk so as to maximise student learning.
learningOutcomes: Critique the history of how oral language has been used in TESOL teaching and classroom practice, reflecting on changes in understanding of how language is learnt
Critically reflect on various approaches and methodologies to oral language teaching and learning in TESOL, linking to particular learner needs
Identify how languages are used in the classroom within linguistically and culturally diverse teaching contexts
Analyse classroom discourse to understand the impact on learning

013988.title: Multiliteracies and Multimodalities
013988.description:
In this subject, you will develop advanced knowledge and skills in the analysis of texts and the teaching of multiliteracies in a variety of contexts. Multiliteracies in this subject refers to the range of experiential reading, viewing, designing and writing practices that are relevant for diverse linguistic and sociocultural communities, contexts, texts and purposes in the 21st century. You will explore theoretical understandings of, and practical approaches to, a rich variety of verbal, visual, artifactual, spatial, embodied and digital texts in schools and adult contexts.

In practical terms, you will engage with different perspectives and pedagogies in the design of multimodal materials and activities. You will gain the skills and knowledge to engage in an informed way in current debates and discussions around literacies in scholarly and educational settings and in the public domain.
learningOutcomes: Explain and compare different theoretical perspectives and approaches in literacy education
Describe and evaluate different pedagogic practices in literacy education for specific communities with reference to theory
Design and justify resources and activities for teaching literacy to a defined group of learners
Produce written accounts with coherent structure, clarity of expression, and integrated reference to key literature

028289.title: Numeracy for Lifelong and Lifewide Learning
028289.description: Numeracy is sometimes understood as basic mathematical skills, however, in this subject, you will develop a broader sociocultural perspective that views numeracy as what people do with mathematical ideas, methods and skills in a wide range of activities in which people engage. Through such a perspective, you will see how there are multiple numeracies - not a single numeracy, because numeracy in practice is influenced by its particular social, cultural, political and historical context. You will also see the influence of globalisation and colonisation on numeracy practices and how mathematics education is an aspect of the politics of numeracy. You will examine the practical implications of a socio-cultural theorization of numeracy for your own teaching context.
learningOutcomes: Explain and compare different theoretical perspectives and approaches in numeracy education.
Describe and evaluate different pedagogic practices in numeracy education.
Design and justify a program and resources for teaching numeracy.
Produce written academic texts which are accurate, cohesive and coherent, and which demonstrate correct citation and referencing.

013095.title: Global Englishes and Local Language Practices
013095.description: The global spread and use of English is a central issue in TESOL and applied linguistics. In this subject, you examine how English has spread across diverse contexts, from its colonial histories to its contemporary roles in globalisation, mobility, media, and everyday communication. You explore key issues such as linguistic imperialism, language rights, linguistic inequality, and the complex relationships between English and local languages. You will investigate how English is used, adapted, and reshaped in different parts of the world, as people of diverse cultural and linguistic backgrounds take ownership of the language. Additionally, you will explore the pedagogical implications of Global Englishes, including issues surrounding native and non‑native speaker norms, the representation of English in teaching materials, and the challenges and opportunities for curriculum, pedagogy, and assessment in diverse linguistic contexts.
learningOutcomes: Explain key theories and ideas in the field of Global Englishes.
Analyse and integrate research literature on Global Englishes and local language practices in specific contexts.
Critically evaluate English language teaching (ELT) practices and resources in relation to Global Englishes and local language practices.
Reflect critically on the use and practice of Global Englishes and local language practices in real-life, everyday contexts.
Produce academic texts which are accurate, cohesive and coherent, and which demonstrate correct citation and referencing.

013990.title: Texts in Society
013990.description: This subject focuses on how language is used to shape meaning, identities, relationships, and the world around us. ‘Discourse’ refers to language in use and language that is beyond the level of sentences and grammar. ‘Genres’ are relatively stable and recognisable ways of organising texts and doing things with language. In this subject, you will look at different ways of doing discourse analysis (such as critical discourse analysis, conversation analysis, and multimodal discourse analysis) and at different ways in which discourse and genre may be socially organised in institutional terms (e.g. education, health, law, religion) and in social terms (e.g. class, gender, race, ethnicity, disability). You will focus on the analysis of real texts (written, spoken, visual, media) and what this tells us about broader social relations and ideology in society. You will be encouraged to develop analysis of discourses and genres in your own workplace or other domains of social life and to apply these skills to pedagogical contexts.
learningOutcomes: Explain how texts in society reflect and shape social and cultural contexts
Explain relationships between language, power and ideology across diverse social and cultural contexts
Analyse and interpret spoken, written and multimodal texts using relevant discourse analytic approaches
Analyse and interpret genres in social and institutional contexts
Produce written academic texts which are accurate, cohesive and coherent, and which demonstrate correct citation and referencing

013459.title: Mathematics for Numeracy Teachers
013459.description: This subject introduces the concept that numeracy skills are needed in various aspects of people's lives, including their educational experiences in primary, secondary, and adult education. Your learning in this subject will focus on selected topics in the areas of whole number, geometry and space; measurements and estimation, rational number, patterns and algebra; and data handling and probability. A multimodal pedagogy including digital, visual and artifactual resources is used to facilitate your meaning-making of mathematical ideas in multiple ways. In your assessment tasks, you will be able to focus on an area that is most relevant to your own needs and professional practices. You will design and carry out mathematical investigations to extend your understanding of the selected topics.

013992.title: Aboriginal Sydney Now
013992.description: This subject focuses on contemporary Aboriginal Sydney as a means for exploring current and historical ideas about First Nations culture, Country, and community. It uses a broadly transformative, social justice framework to challenge your assumptions and nurture your curiosity about First Nations ways of knowing and being, while exploring an urban context such as Sydney today. Through incorporating a range of First Nations voices, it provides opportunities to identify how Indigenous Knowledges and perspectives intersect with your particular area of study and potential profession. Delivered completely online, each week you will draw from pre-recorded lectures, television drama, online tutorials and scholarship by leading First Nations authors to critically analyse concepts such as identity, place and First Nations self-determination. You will be introduced to important protocols essential to your professional practice, and the subject’s two written assessments offer opportunities to reframe your thinking using a strength-based lens that recognises First Nations agency and the ongoing need for truth-telling and healing. Through our criterion-focussed assessment, we will also provide you with rich feedback to encourage greater criticality and analysis in your essay writing and professional reflection.
learningOutcomes: Inquire about contemporary Indigenous notions of culture, country and community
Discuss the implications of colonisation for contemporary Indigenous Australia
Investigate methods that professionals from your discipline use to collaborate respectfully with Indigenous peoples
Reflect on the relationship between culture and worldviews, including your own
Analyse and effectively communicate information gleaned from primary and secondary sources relevant to Indigenous knowledges and perspectives.

010301.title: Think: Learning Theories and Implications for Learning Design
010301.description:
How do you know when you’ve learned something? What does learning look like to you?

Understanding the foundations of learning theories is crucial for developing effective learning experiences. By exploring these concepts, you’ll gain insights into how to design learning environments that truly engage and benefit students.

This subject introduces you to a range of learning theories, including behaviourism, cognitivism, constructivism, and connectivism. You’ll explore the implications of these theories on historical, contemporary, and emerging learning design, with a special focus on technology-enhanced learning.

Throughout the course, you’ll engage with these theories in a practical sense. You’ll apply them in various settings and contexts to develop tailored learning experiences. Additionally, you’ll critique the effect that technology has had on the development of learning theories, enabling you to leverage these insights in your own practice as a learning designer.
learningOutcomes: Identify, compare and contrast contesting features of historical, contemporary and emerging learning theories.
Analyse the application of learning theories to learning designs in context-specific ways.
Critique the effect that technology has had and continues to have upon learning theories.
Reflect and evaluate own and others’ learning and practice.
Present arguments for preferred theoretical perspectives that are appropriate to the audience, context and purpose

Understanding different theories, models, and processes of learning design is essential for creating effective educational experiences. This knowledge equips you with the tools to design learning environments that meet diverse needs and enhance student engagement.

010303.title: Critique: Issues in Learning Design
010303.description:
Have you heard about how big data is revolutionising education and training? And how learners’ data are being protected – or not – when different learning platforms are used?

Understanding the ethical considerations, privacy concerns, and appropriate use of learner data is crucial in today’s digital learning environment. This knowledge helps you navigate the complexities of Learning Design with sensitivity to context, culture, and legal issues.

This subject delves into current, historical, and emerging issues in Learning Design. You'll explore topics such as ethical considerations, privacy concerns, appropriate data collection and usage, context and cultural sensitivity, and copyright. Additionally, you’ll examine both unethical and appropriate examples of Learning Design.

By investigating these issues and reflecting on real-world examples, you'll gain a comprehensive understanding of best practices in Learning Design. You’ll then apply this knowledge to design suitable learning experiences tailored to your specific context.
learningOutcomes: Examine the ethical challenges and issues that learning designers must navigate within the learning design field.
Critique and evaluate learning materials from an ethical and culturally appropriate perspective
Construct learning designs and elements that are ethical and appropriate to their context.
Reflect and evaluate own and others’ learning and practice.

How do you effectively assess learning in your course?

Assessment of learning is a crucial part of effective learning design. Understanding the best ways to evaluate learning ensures that the educational experiences you create are impactful and meaningful.

This subject introduces you to various forms of assessment, along with different methods and tools used for evaluating learning. You'll explore the significance of feedback and how various technologies can enhance its delivery. Additionally, you'll delve into different models of evaluating learning designs, examining their development and contextual appropriateness.

Through this course, you'll gain practical knowledge on how to deploy assessments constructively. You'll learn to use feedback effectively, leveraging technology to improve its impact. You'll also have the opportunity to apply different evaluation models in various contexts, ensuring your learning designs are both effective and relevant. This hands-on approach will equip you with the skills to create robust and insightful assessment strategies.

Design effective assessments tasks for learning activities.
Evaluate learning designs using different models to gauge their effectiveness.
