Educators have never had access to as much data as they do now – but how can they make sure that this data is used efficiently to improve student learning?

Understanding how to leverage data effectively is essential for improving student learning and driving educational, organisational, and social change more broadly. This knowledge helps you harness the power of data to inform and enhance your learning designs.

This subject delves into the burgeoning field of learning and data analytics, examining its influence on education, training, and broader social change. You'll explore various approaches and techniques used in learning analytics, including the use of AcaWriter, a tool that provides rapid formative feedback.

You will analyse and apply different learning analytics techniques, learning how to use tools to gather and interpret data. You'll reflect on how this data can inform and enhance your learning designs, while also considering the epistemological and ethical implications of learning analytics. This hands-on approach ensures you can effectively utilise data to improve educational outcomes and create more impactful learning experiences.

010307.title: Create: Creating Interactive Multimedia Objects
010307.description:
Are you curious about how to create engaging learning activities and environments?

Understanding the theories of educational communication and instructional media is essential for designing effective learning activities and environments. This knowledge empowers you to create engaging and impactful educational experiences.

This subject introduces you to the theories of educational communication and instructional media, exploring how these influence the design of learning activities and environments. You'll examine and critique examples of print, online, visual, and audio multimedia to understand their educational impact.

You’ll design and develop your own interactive media object, such as an interactive learning activity, a screencast, an infographic, or something similar. You'll analyse, critique, and evaluate your design based on your understanding of learning theories. Additionally, you'll prepare and communicate a rationale for your interactive media object's design, ensuring it aligns with educational best practices and effectively engages learners.
learningOutcomes: Explain how instructional media and educational communication theories influence the design of learning activities and environments.
Analyse and critique interactive media elements and evaluate their effectiveness for learning.
Design and develop basic interactive media objects, taking into consideration accessible and contextual factors.
Reflect and evaluate own and others’ learning and practice.
Prepare and communicate a compelling rationale for the design of an interactive media object.

010306.title: Predict: Current and Future Trends in Learning and Technology
010306.description:
What does the future of education look like? Are educators going to be replaced by robots? Is STEM going to take over?

Understanding the future of education and the role of emerging technologies is crucial for educators and learning designers. This knowledge equips you to navigate and leverage new developments to enhance learning experiences and outcomes.

This subject critically evaluates current and emerging trends within e-learning and educational technology. You'll engage with developments such as machine learning, artificial intelligence, virtual reality, augmented reality, gamification, robotics, STEM education, and more. Additionally, you’ll examine past educational trends to assess their success or failure and apply various learning and instructional theories to evaluate the educative potential of these trends.

Through practical engagement with these technologies, you'll design and develop prototype learning objects using emerging technologies. You will also gain experience justifying your design choices in a professional context.
learningOutcomes: Critically evaluate the trends and innovations that influence current and future directions in learning design.
Design and develop suitable learning objects by selecting and using emerging tools to meet learning outcomes within personal or professional contexts.
Reflect and evaluate own and others’ learning and practice.
Communicate and justify chosen design of learning objects in ways that are appropriate to the audience, context and purpose.

013464.title: Inclusive Education in Primary Schools
013464.description: This subject explores issues of inclusive education and how you, as an educator, can meet the needs of diverse learners within their classrooms. The subject provides strategies for identifying school students with additional needs and developing instructional approaches that ensure all school students can access relevant learning experiences. Subject content includes: legal and human rights obligations; Universal Design for Learning and adjustments; behaviour and the learning environment; accessing texts; assessment and error analysis; explicit instructional techniques; explicit strategy instruction; resources and assistive technologies; communication and collaboration.
learningOutcomes: Accurately explain legislative requirements and inclusive teaching strategies that support the participation and learning of students with disabilities, while incorporating principles of Universal Design for Learning and making adjustments to curriculum and classroom activities.

Use assessment strategies effectively, including informal and formal, diagnostic, formative, and summative approaches, to assess student learning, design learning sequences and lesson plans, and set achievable learning goals for students of varying abilities; analyze assessment results to develop specific learning objectives and monitoring techniques.

Apply strategies for differentiating teaching to meet the diverse learning needs of students, including managing challenging behavior and employing practical approaches to engage students of all abilities in classroom activities through explicit teaching techniques.

Compare and contrast a range of resources and technologies, including ICT and assistive technologies, to enhance student engagement and learning outcomes, while using a variety of verbal and non-verbal communication strategies to support student participation.

Collaborate effectively with parents, carers, and external professionals by applying strategies for sensitive and confidential communication, and understand the sources of professional learning to continuously improve teaching practices.

013454.title: Professional Experience: The Primary School Child
013454.description: In this subject, pre-service teachers focus on developing a learner-centred approach to teaching, which considers the unique needs and characteristics of developing children and pre-adolescents. Through a multidisciplinary approach, exploring key theories, empirical research, and practical applications, the subject develops theoretical perspectives on human development and applies them to the primary school context to inform the development of practice in diverse educational settings and learner needs, with a focus on inclusive, effective, and developmentally appropriate learning environments. A key part of this subject is a four-week placement where pre-service teachers work in a school with support and mentoring from their UTS tertiary supervisor and supervising classroom teacher. During their placement, pre-service teachers are closely supervised and begin learning practice capabilities in lesson planning, teaching, assessment, Indigenous truth telling and knowledge, equity and inclusion, classroom management, digital supported learning, and school-community building.
learningOutcomes: Analyse how primary children learn and change, and how student motivation develops
Analyse complex teaching and learning scenarios that affect the primary child
Develop theoretically sound strategies for creating supportive teaching and learning environments for primary school children in diverse and complex contexts
Articulate and scrutinise challenging issues facing young Australians and their teachers in schools drawing on relevant theoretical concepts, research and policy
Identify how teachers can draw on their understanding of primary school children’s development to support the students they teach in schools

013455.title: Professional Experience: Classroom Management
013455.description: This subject develops your capacity to support the wellbeing of primary-aged students. You will learn how to develop and refine your classroom management skills to equip you with the essential tools for creating a conducive learning environment by investigating instructional planning, delivery techniques and relationship development. Emphasising the significance of classroom management policies, legislation, and guidelines related to school student well-being, the subject aims to empower you to maximize school student engagement and foster an optimal learning experience in primary education settings. A key part of this subject is a four-week professional experience placement, during which you will receive support and mentoring from your UTS tertiary supervisor and supervising classroom teacher. This the second of three 20-day placements you will undertake for your Masters program. You will develop your capabilities in lesson planning, teaching, assessment, ensuring equity and inclusion, classroom management, ICT- supported learning, and school-community building and receive feedback from your classroom supervisor and UTS Tertiary Supervisor. Please note that you are required to meet the expectations of the English/Literacy national specialisation with which all UTS Masters students will graduate. The supervisor will, therefore, include in their assessment report, feedback about evidence of your capacity to implement classroom practices in the teaching of English/literacy to a level than can be expected of a pre-service teacher who is mid-way through their Masters of Teaching in Primary Education. Satisfactory completion of the placement is a minimum requirement for this subject so you must pass your placement in order to pass the subject overall. The placement is pass/fail. The coursework component of the subject is graded and designed to help you designed to help you develop strong communication skills, including positive reinforcement and conflict resolution, to effectively manage student behaviour and foster a respectful classroom culture.
learningOutcomes: Organise classroom activities and provide clear directions.
Apply practical approaches to manage challenging behaviour in the classroom and the whole-school context.

Devise and implement strategies that support students’ wellbeing and safety, and promote compliance with curriculum and legislative requirements in codes of ethics and conduct for the teaching profession.
Appraise theoretical approaches to manage wellbeing and challenging behaviour in the classroom and the whole-school context.
Produce accurate and coherent academic text.

013456.description: In this subject, you will be introduced to the study of language as you work towards becoming English language teachers. Your focus will be on understanding how language works to make meaning for users, and specifically, how the English language works. You will gain fundamental knowledge of English structures, including text organisation, grammatical resources and word and sound structures. You will develop the knowledge you need in order to teach learners who are learning English as an additional language or to enhance learners’ first language.
learningOutcomes: Identify language forms, using recognised terminology
Use a range of language resources to analyse particular meanings being made through language use.
Apply academic theory and research to justify approaches taken in the analysis of English language use
Produce professional and academic writing about the field that is cohesive and accurate.

013457.title: Professional Experience: Teacher Performance Assessment
013457.description:
This is your final professional experience subject and includes a 20-day internship where you will take responsibility for lesson planning and teaching a class-cohort in a primary school. You will be supervised by an experienced in-service teacher who prepares an assessment report about your achievement of selected Australian Professional Standards for Teachers. Please note that you are required to meet the expectations of the English/Literacy national specialisation with which all UTS Masters students will graduate. The supervisor will, therefore, include in their assessment report, feedback about evidence of your capacity to implement highly effective classroom practices in the teaching of English/literacy. The external supervisor does not recommend grades or marks; instead, either an ungraded Pass or Fail. In the coursework component, you will be required to prepare a Teaching Performance Assessment (TPA) portfolio, which is developed and implemented by a consortium of Australian higher education providers that have Initial Teacher Education (ITE) faculties or schools. Four elements have been designed, trialled and consequently refined, to generate an assessment instrument that represents a robust, comprehensive and authentic series of tasks that reflect teaching. The four elements are: 

Element 1: Planning for learning and teaching 

Element 2: Analysing teaching practice 

Element 3: Assessing for impact on student learning 

Element 4: Expanding practice. 

Please note that you are required to orient your TPA assessment tasks to the English/Literacy national specialisation with which all UTS Masters students will graduate.
learningOutcomes: Analyse the evidence of teaching practice according to the NESA Graduate Teacher Standards (GTS) through the TPA during school placements, incorporating the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers (APST).
Implement effective teaching and learning experiences based on diverse student needs and school contexts.
Assess student learning to support individual growth and achievement.
Establish a supportive and safe learning environment that encourages student engagement and well-being.
Develop collaborate practices to promot positive student interactions and professional growth.

013447.title: Mathematics Education for Primary School 1
013447.description: In this subject you will study the major components of the NSW Mathematics K-10 Syllabus. This will include syllabus content such as whole number, measurement, data and chance. You will be introduced to planning mathematics activities and lessons for primary school students at different stages of their learning. You will also be expected to apply learning theories about primary aged students’ development of mathematical concepts and proficiencies to create powerful learning experiences in primary mathematics. This subject includes assessment tasks that require you to practise your teaching and explanation skills while on professional experience placement. The subject guides you in developing understanding of how to work mathematically and how to teach the Mathematics K-10 Syllabus. You will develop your teaching practice through modelling using hands-on collaborative tasks so you can learn and use mathematical knowledge confidently in your teaching. You will develop critical insights about the teaching of mathematics in primary school and develop your capacity to reflect on your knowledge and practice.
learningOutcomes: Identify and apply the foundational skills and knowledge of the NSW Mathematics K-10 Syllabus.
Plan, implement and evaluate mathematical lessons appropriate for primary-aged students.
Understand and apply mathematics teaching and learning theories and pedagogies.
Communicate mathematical ideas using appropriate mathematical terms, clear and explicit classroom instructions.

requisite.text: Admission into C04326 Master of Teaching in Primary Education

013449.title: Mathematics Education for Primary School 2
013449.description: This is the second of two core Mathematics Education subjects. In this subject you will develop understanding of how to work mathematically in the teaching and learning of aspects of the NSW K-6 Mathematics syllabus. As a pre-service teacher, you will examine the construction of, and build, your own understandings of sound methodological principles for the development of concepts of rational numbers, percentage, geometry, patterns and algebra. Indigenous Australian mathematics knowledge is examined both to appreciate different mathematical knowledges that have developed in different cultures and to consider how Indigenous knowledges can be integrated into the teaching and learning of mathematics. You will learn to communicate mathematical ideas using appropriate mathematical terms and clear and explicit language for explanation and questioning and use language, images, symbols, resources including ICT as tools to design learning sequences and lesson activities to support school students’ mathematical learning. You will be guided to undertake unit planning for primary school students at different stages. Good teaching practice is modelled using hands-on collaborative tasks.
learningOutcomes: Deploy foundational skills and knowledge of the NSW Mathematics syllabus K-6, including rational number, percentage, geometry, patterns and algebra.
Plan and design a variety of assessments that are suitable for different mathematics topics.
Plan and design units of work appropriately for students at varying stages of mathematical development.
Plan and implement effective use of learning activities, teaching approaches and resources including ICT, to enable students to learn mathematics appropriate to their diverse needs.

013448.title: Science and Technology Education for Primary Schools
013448.description: This subject engages pre-service teachers with the teaching and learning of science and technology in the primary school. In this subject, pre-service teachers reflect on their reading of the literature and experiences in the classroom to develop their philosophy of learning and teaching in science and technology. The pre-service teachers also develop their understanding of the nature of science and technology, an important component of scientific knowledge and its development as a human endeavour. A focus of this subject is on clarifying and developing primary school students' conceptions in science and technology, primarily through inquiry-based, constructivist, pedagogical practices. Pre-service teachers learn how to access information in a variety of forms from a range of sources, and how to critically evaluate information and ideas. This is fundamental to lifelong learning and for developing scientific, technological, information and language literacies. The pre-service teachers are guided to use the NESA Science and Technology K–6 syllabus to organise content into effective learning and teaching sequences and to employ a range of teaching strategies and resources, including ICT, that engage school students in their learning. The subject locates learning and teaching in intellectual, practical, creative, social, gender-inclusive and culturally sensitive contexts.
learningOutcomes: Develop personal understandings of, and professional skills in applying, science and technology concepts and processes
Explain, devise and deploy concepts, substance and structure of the content and teaching area
Organise content into an effective learning and teaching sequence using knowledge of student learning, content and effective teaching strategies
Deploy a range of teaching strategies and use a range of resources, including ICT, that engage students in their learning
Communicate professionally and academically, showing accuracy and cohesion of text

013445.title: English Education: The Early Years
013445.description: This subject introduces you to the NSW English K–10 curriculum with a focus on Early Stage 1 and Stage 1, utilising current research and methodologies for the explicit and systematic instruction of early reading and writing. It aligns with the Australian Curriculum (English), focusing on Foundation to Year 2. The subject also introduces the Early Years Learning Framework for Australia V2.0, addressing the important transitions from the early years and the critical role of oral communication in literacy classrooms. Culturally responsive pedagogies and strategies are introduced, also addressing Indigenous Australian ways of learning. The subject will enable you to become capable and competent in planning to teach early reading and writing instruction in super diverse classrooms for the early years of primary schooling, including for students with various abilities and disabilities and/or students from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socio-economic backgrounds.
learningOutcomes: Describe how vocabulary, oral language and communication are developed prior to formal schooling
Explain the nature and level of phonological awareness and phonic knowledge that is suitable for K–2

028215.title: English Education: Language in Use
028215.description: In this subject, you will learn how to enable English Language Learners to develop literacy across the disciplines in the formal schooling sector. You will look at how both English as an Additional Language or Dialect [EAL/D] and Literacy are framed in curriculum documents, and subsequently translated into teaching and assessment activities in school settings. Taking an approach of “high challenge, high support” you will explore how teachers provide explicit and targeted language and literacy support to help students achieve learning goals. The Australian context is the primary focus for the content, but you will also find the subject relevant if you are working within settings where English is not the dominant or official language.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of EAL/D teachers and the scope the role in a school
Know and use the policy and curriculum documents that orient the provision of EAL/D support in Australian schools, K - 12
Identify learners’ language needs as the basis for planning and implementing teaching and learning strategies to enhance language development

Communicate clearly and competently in an academic setting, theory and research as well as application of ideas

013446.title: Creative Arts Education for Primary Schools
013446.description: This subject develops pre-service teachers' understanding of visual arts, music, movement, and dance in a primary school context. The subject provides a comprehensive foundation of theory and practice in creative arts education in primary school. Pre-service teachers have the opportunity to develop skills in creating 2D, 3D and digital art forms in a variety of media. They also learn what equipment and materials are suitable to teach visual arts in the primary school classroom, and how to manage them safely. Pre-service teachers develop, also perform, create, listen and respond to sound and silence through various music genres. The movement and dance components of the subject develop knowledge, skills and understanding about the elements of dance, and composing, performing and appreciating dance.
learningOutcomes: Acquire the generalised artmaking skills across a range of visual art mediums needed to deliver art sessions in a safe, constructive and inclusive environment at the primary level

Demonstrate the capacity to deliver and manage learning in K-6 visual arts education through the development of effective programming (inclusive of age-appropriate learning experiences, assessment, resources) in accordance with the NSW K-6 Visual Art syllabus and support documents

Embed and make explicit the teaching of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and cultures through visual arts, music and dance.
Create and maintain a learning environment that encourages artistic excellence but also is inclusive and safe.

013444.title: Personal Development, Health and Physical Education for Primary School
013444.description: The aim of this subject is to develop your knowledge and understanding of the Key Learning Area of personal development, health and physical education (PDHPE) in primary schools. It introduces relevant theories and processes for safe, and inclusive teaching of PDHPE. This encompasses you gaining knowledge and understanding of strategies for differentiating teaching PDHPE to meet specific needs all students, including those from across the full range of abilities; and those from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socio-economic backgrounds. A unique feature of this subject is that you will gain knowledge about, and be encouraged to introduce to primary school students to a variety of pre-colonial Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander sports and games.  You will be taught and get to practice interpersonal and practical skills in the areas of human movement, fundamental movement skills, dance, games and sports, active lifestyles in addition to healthy growth and development. It will require you to participate in active movement, dance and games experiences. The subject has an applied focus inasmuch as you, as a pre-service teacher, will also be guided to help primary school children develop PDHPE literacies and numeracies to address hot topics such as the climate crisis, mis- and dis-information. This will include making interdisciplinary connections with HSIE, English, Mathematics, Science and Technology, and Creative Arts.
learningOutcomes: Explain the concepts, substance and structure of, and teaching strategies suitable for the NSW K-6 PDHPE syllabus
Plan PDHPE lesson sequences using knowledge of student learning, content and effective teaching strategies to suit primary school classrooms
Describe strategies for sport activities that support students’ wellbeing and safety working within school and/or system, curriculum and legislative requirements.
Apply age-appropriate, literacy- and numeracy-related vocabulary and teaching strategies to K-6 PDHPE and hot topics such as the climate crisis and mis-and dis-information

013443.title: Human Society and its Environment in Primary Education
013443.description: This subject develops your understanding of the NSW K-6 Key Learning Area of Human Society and its Environment (HSIE). This includes the two primary curriculum areas of History and Geography (as well as the learning across the curriculum areas of Civics and Citizenship and Work and Enterprise). As a pre-service teacher, you are to acquire proficiency in designing and implementing learning experiences and assessing and evaluating the learning of primary school students in K–6. You are encouraged to critically reflect on the wider challenges of preparing Australian school children to become active and informed members of their communities, or in other words, active citizens. Through studying this subject, as a prospective teacher you will do more than inform yourself about the humanities and social sciences: you will hone your skills as a social scientist, formulating and expressing the views and questions that social scientists (and all of us) do. You are supported to broaden your teaching to beyond the classroom by facilitating action-oriented learning experiences that apply History and Geography to researching and addressing real-world hot topics. Examples include the climate crisis; the rising tide of mis- and dis-information; how to explain and reflect on ways to celebrate Australia Day; humanitarian support for refugees; the impact of ever-expanding use of single-use plastics or rising meat consumption on the environment; and government roles in deciding what religion people can pursue. Experts and campaigners from external organisations support the teaching of this subject. The subject has an applied focus inasmuch as you, as a pre-service teacher, will also be guided to help primary school children develop HSIE discipline-specific literacies and numeracies to address hot topics. This will include making interdisciplinary connections with Science and Technology, English, PDHPE, Mathematics and Creative Arts.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the concepts, substance and structure of the content and teaching strategies to manage learning in K-6 HSIE
Plan HSIE lesson sequences using knowledge of student learning, content and effective teaching strategies to suit primary school classrooms
Plan and implement various strategies for involving community and industry stakeholders in the educative process
Demonstrate literacy and numeracy teaching strategies and their application to K-6 HSIE
Develop inter-disciplinary and age-appropriate understandings of ways to apply History and Geography concepts and processes to hot topics such as the climate crisis and mis-and dis-information

096340.title: Managing for Value-Based Care
096340.description:
This subject is essential grounding for clinicians, managers and planners of health and social care services, who seek to improve the value of care, within the context of expectations of clinical and corporate governance, organisational performance and workplace change.

The subject examines each of the components of quality, risk, health outcomes and cost as they relate to high value health and social care. The subject aims to build core skills in new thinking in care delivery by focusing on the way care is planned, organised, managed and delivered in relation to quality, risk, health outcomes and cost. Utilising the Institute for Healthcare Improvement’s Triple Aim framework and Porter’s Value-based Health Care Framework as a starting point, students will develop a critical view on the organisation of health care, measurement and delivery of outcomes, from the patient and population perspective, as well as organisational accountability for cost and quality.

The subject focuses on current approaches to quality and safety, identifying and maximising value in healthcare, patient/client satisfaction, and commonly recognised issues with healthcare delivery systems, as well as different ways of organising and managing health care.
learningOutcomes:
Consider the key imperatives for meeting health service objectives of safety, quality, and cost-effectiveness within a management context, and how they relate to achieving value;

Critically appraise contemporary strategies and frameworks designed to manage value within the healthcare environment;

Propose improvements in value at a local healthcare organisation level by identifying issues, considering ethical implications, offering policy direction and formulation and recommending priorities for action;

Create a variety of ways in which complex issues can be effectively communicated for a variety of target audiences.

096335.title: Contemporary Approaches to Digital Health
096335.description:
This subject is designed for health professionals, particularly those in management and leadership, seeking to enhance their understanding of digital health interventions and their integration into health and social care services.

Students will learn about the principles of digital health technology, differentiate between data and knowledge, and understand the role of digital solutions in patient safety and service improvement. Additionally, students will develop an appreciation of the complex socio-technical benefits, challenges and risks associated with the adoption and use of digital health interventions and develop an understanding of how to successfully implement these technologies into practice.

Teaching and learning will be interactive, utilising real-world examples to illustrate the complexities of digital health technology implementation and to foster a deeper understanding of its potential impact on health and social care services.
learningOutcomes:
Analyse the development and implementation of digital health interventions.





Apply evaluation frameworks relevant to digital health interventions and reflect on future directions for digital health interventions.





Recognise and describe the challenges and opportunities of digital health interventions.





Identify and appraise digital health interventions for various stakeholders.

090046.title: Ageing: Health, Illness and Decline
090046.description:
This subject focuses on enhancing your ability to provide evidence-based care for older people across various settings, emphasising person-centred approaches to address common geriatric syndromes. In response to a rapidly ageing population, you'll learn to navigate the complexities and seize the opportunities in providing person-centred care to ensure optimal health outcomes for older people.

Orientation activities will introduce you to the subject and peers, setting you up for success in assessments. Weekly online materials, including readings and videos, will deepen your understanding and support your progress. Engage in Zoom meetings for collaborative learning, discussions, and feedback, which are vital for assessment preparation. You'll receive diverse feedback, including self and peer assessments, to improve your performance. Based on positive feedback, only minor updates to resources and readings have been made to ensure the subject's continued relevance and quality. Access all materials and the subject outline on Canvas.
learningOutcomes: Apply knowledge of the aging process and principles of person-centred care to plan safe and effective care for older people across a range of care settings.
Evaluate strategies aimed to promote healthy and productive ageing.
Implement appropriate assessment tools and care approaches for geriatric syndromes.
Demonstrate effective communication and support for older people, including their family and caregivers.
Apply evidence-based strategies for developing resilience and wellbeing for older people and those responsible for their care.

Students emerge with the ability to apply health data analysis to their leadership and management roles. Learning is facilitated through guest lectures and real-world scenarios, linking theory to practice and other subjects within the Master of Health Services Management framework.

Apply data management principles to ensure data quality and integrity.
Use data analytics to identify patterns and inform decision-making.
Assess methods for effective data reporting and communication.
Reflect on the ethical collection, analysis and interpretation of Indigenous health data and its influence on decision- making

096337.title: Foundations of Healthcare Systems
096337.description:
In this subject, students will explore the key components and workings of healthcare systems, focusing on the Australian healthcare system. The course will cover how health systems are built, how they change over time, and how they operate. Students will gain the skills needed to lead and make a difference in the healthcare sector.

Key areas of study include:

1. Structure and Function: Understanding the organization and roles within the Australian health and social care systems.

2. Service Delivery: Learning how health and social services are provided and the challenges faced.

3. Policy and Governance: Examining how policies and governance impact healthcare delivery and outcomes.

4. Health Inequities: Investigating how the structure, policies, and delivery of health services contribute to unequal health outcomes for different groups, especially Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

5. Equity and Access: Reflecting on the barriers to and enablers of equitable access to health and social care.

6. Intersectionality: Understanding how various social categories like age, disability, mental health, location, socioeconomic status, refugee status, and migrant status intersect to influence health outcomes.

By the end of the subject, students will be able to critically assess healthcare systems and suggest meaningful ways to address health inequities.
learningOutcomes:
Appraise the structural and functional components of the Australian healthcare system and the roles and responsibilities of the differing levels of government.





Explain trends and structure and functional challenges in service provision models, health system performance and health service outcomes and outputs within the Australian healthcare system.





Reflect on the impact of ongoing colonisation and its pervasive discourse on Indigenous Australians and their health and wellbeing for the design, delivery and management of the Australian healthcare system.





Examine the role of person-centred care in the Australian health care system.

Building on prerequisite knowledge and principles of normal anatomy and physiology of the human body, you'll critically evaluate the presentation and management of patients within your clinical context.  

You'll engage in independent learning through curated readings, videos, and activities available online, fostering your progression and assessment readiness. Interactive Zoom meetings offer collaborative learning and feedback opportunities, vital for your preparation. Continuous feedback from various sources, including peers and instructors, will guide your improvement. Updates to resources ensure the subject's ongoing relevance and accuracy.

Opportunities to promote development will incorporate simulation, virtual reality and individual clinical settings. Justify differential diagnoses using advanced diagnostic reasoning.
Create comprehensive management plans in collaboration with the patient, family and interdisciplinary team.
Identify and prioritise the focus of assessment and management to prevent life threatening situations.
Integrate social, cultural, and person-centered considerations into patient care.

You will take a strategic approach to designing learning systems and practices for teams and organisations, examining contemporary organisational learning approaches and their applicability to different professional contexts, particularly your own practice. You will also analyse contextual factors, like power and culture, that may affect organisational learning. Using insights from the subject, you will create strategic plans to enhance learning in your workplace.
learningOutcomes: Identify and articulate a strategic learning scenario relevant to own professional context.
Analyse organisational context to establish strategic requirements.
Engage with theory to develop evidence-informed learning strategy for a team or organisation.
Develop strategies to addresses identified current and future organisational learning needs.
Communicate appropriately using a range of genres and technologies.

096341.description:
This subject is designed for clinicians, health service managers, planners, and aspiring health sector professionals. It offers a deep understanding of the political and policy contexts influencing the funding and delivery of health service and social care services.

Students learn to navigate the complexities of policy-making, from conception to implementation, and manage the impact of media and stakeholder power and influence. They consider how policy problems are defined, and by whom, and the evidence needed to support and persuade decision-makers. Students also reflect on the ethical dimensions of policy-making.
learningOutcomes: Analyse the development of government policy and the impact of stakeholder power on policy decision-making
Understand the political and ethical frameworks that influence health care policy.
Evaluate the evidence necessary for effective health policy decision.
Develop communication strategies for complex issues to influence senior decision-makers.

090019.title: Planetary Health
090019.description:
Human activity significantly impacts Earth’s natural systems, posing risks to human health. Ecosystem disruptions due to biodiversity loss, climate change, water depletion, deforestation, and urbanisation exacerbate health challenges. The public health community is ill-prepared for these changes, which lead to heat-related deaths, infectious diseases, malnutrition, psychological distress, and pollution-related illnesses. Disadvantaged communities suffer more. Planetary health expands the health definition to include human civilisation’s dependence on a healthy environment.

This subject introduces students to planetary health concepts, research, and policy. It explores global and local challenges, emphasising innovative approaches to address environmental and health issues. Interactive learning activities enhance understanding, fostering independent work and online engagement with peers.
learningOutcomes: Describe and discuss the concept of planetary health, the direct and indirect pathways that connect human health and ecosystems, and how they relate to the Sustainable Development Goals.

Critically assess the impacts of environmental change on intergenerational health equity, vulnerability and resilience, and how these relate to environmental justice and ecological sustainability with consideration of Australian Indigenous ways of knowing, being and doing.
Critically appraise the role of public health practitioners and the broader health care system in addressing planetary health challenges and opportunities.
Identify the complex systems involved in environmental change and human health outcomes and priority areas for intervention.
Develop practical interventions that provide co-benefits for human and environmental health with consideration of interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary approaches.

090017.title: Indigenous Public Health
090017.description:
This subject equips you with an understanding of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health and wellbeing, focusing on contemporary perspectives, historical influences, and responses to colonisation. You'll gain insights into social determinants of health, important cultural dimensions, and comparative health indicators, shaping public health strategies for Indigenous communities. Emphasising equity in healthcare, you'll assess the availability and suitability of services under current health policies.

Your learning involves active participation in online modules and Yarning Circles, supported by the REM Framework to ensure cultural safety. You'll engage with case studies, webcasts, and expert discussions, fostering skills pertinent to Indigenous health. Independent work and collaborative online interactions, including preparatory Zoom workshops, are integral to your development.

Real-world case studies and practitioner insights deepen your practical understanding, with assessments designed to track and apply your knowledge, complemented by ongoing feedback.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the demography and epidemiology of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people’s health
Describe Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health in historical context and assess the impact of colonisation on health outcomes
Identify and describe the impact of critical social issues on the health of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and communities
Engage as a professional with knowledge and skills in public health research, ethical practices, stakeholder analysis, information synthesis, effective communication and cultural safety

090011.description: This subject explores the conceptual foundations and historical development of public health. Students examine diverse health definitions, including personal, lay, non-Western, gender-diverse, Indigenous, and organisational perspectives. They delve into the question of ‘What is public health?’ and explore key approaches, processes, and models. The course also traces the evolution of public health from historical events to contemporary practices. Students engage in online activities, including readings, webinars, and discussions, while focusing on academic integrity and referencing.
learningOutcomes: Analyse the historical roots and current scholarship of public health.
Differentiate between biomedical and public health approaches to health.
Identify the contributions of various health disciplines to public health.
Recognise the significance of diverse health perceptions in different communities.
Apply new public health insights to address key health challenges.

096331.title: Planning for Health and Social Services
096331.description:
Planning is the systematic process of setting goals, developing strategies, and detailing the resources and tasks to achieve the desired outcomes in healthcare delivery. It involves anticipating future healthcare needs, allocating resources, and coordinating activities to ensure efficient, effective, and equitable health services.

This subject explores the principles and methods that guide planning in the health and social care system. In the first half of the subject, students will learn about the overarching goals of planning, examine different approaches to systems-level health planning, and review the evidence necessary for effective planning. In the second half of the subject, the focus shifts from the systems level to the organisational level. Students will learn about the relationship between organisational strategy and planning and learn tools for effective planning, including budgets and business cases. The subject concludes with planning strategies for uncertain future scenarios.
learningOutcomes:
Apply evidence-based health planning principles, frameworks and processes within a
range of contexts.
Differentiate between systems and population health approaches to planning.
Undertake basic operational planning and develop a business plan.
Effectively communicate complex health service planning issues.

090014.title: Fundamentals of Qualitative Research
090014.description:
This subject offers a practical introduction to qualitative research in health. Students explore the role and application of qualitative research, including theoretical perspectives, methodological approaches, data collection, and analysis. They engage in qualitative data collection, analysis, and reporting, reflecting on the challenges and opportunities encountered during fieldwork.
The subject spans six weeks, with weekly online activities. Students are expected to complete all activities, deepening their understanding of qualitative research concepts and their relevance to health care and public health. Through case studies and discussions, students apply their knowledge to real-world public health issues. Interaction with peers and teachers occurs via discussion forums and Zoom meetings, fostering collaborative analysis and idea development.
learningOutcomes: Justify the selection of theoretical positions and qualitative research tools in alignment with research questions.
Discuss practical and ethical considerations in participant recruitment, especially for vulnerable populations.
Demonstrate data analysis skills using selected qualitative approaches.
Ensure rigor, trustworthiness, and critical reflexivity in qualitative research.

090020.title: Social Perspectives in Public Health
090020.description:
This subject equips you with an understanding of social science concepts to tackle health issues, focusing on the human experience of illness and the societal structuring of health. You'll learn how social processes affect health and contribute to inequity, and how to address health challenges amid technological and social changes.

You'll develop skills in qualitative research, critical analysis, and applying theoretical perspectives to public health problems. Learning is interactive and online, comprising weekly activities, discussions, and case studies over six weeks. You're expected to work independently, engage with peers and instructors, and attend weekly Zoom sessions for collaborative problem-solving.

Assessments are practical, allowing you to apply your knowledge and receive feedback to enhance your understanding of qualitative research in health care.
learningOutcomes: Define key concepts in health inequalities
Critically appraise research findings relevant to social determinants and health inequalities
Evaluate explanations for socially determined health inequalities in relation to selected public health issues

Examine the impact of social norms and behaviour on access to health services, care and information and health policy and practice examples in health care in a range of Australian Indigenous, national and global settings
Apply theoretical perspectives on health inequalities to policy options for public health

Topics include epidemiological methods, understanding evidence limitations, using population health data, and applying findings to inform public health and health services decisions. Students also gain practical skills in calculating and interpreting disease frequency, association, and impact. The subject emphasises the connection between epidemiological theory and real-world applications in public health and health services decision-making. 

Learning is interactive and online, involving discussions, polls, and collaborative exploration of real-world cases. You'll engage with peers and experts, preparing for and participating in virtual sessions
learningOutcomes: Evaluate and explain the major epidemiological research techniques and designs.
Recommend strategies for data management in population health.
Identify and address biases in epidemiological studies.
Communicate complex epidemiological data effectively to diverse audiences.

You'll learn to present data, manage datasets, and understand confidence intervals, descriptive statistics, and bivariate analyses. Rather than computing, the focus is on interpreting research and selecting appropriate analysis methods, including power and sample size calculations for study design.

Learning unfolds over six weeks through interactive online activities, requiring your active participation for maximum benefit. You'll engage with statistical software, analyse data, and critique research findings, supported by peer and instructor discussions and weekly live sessions.

Assessments are practical, allowing you to apply biostatistical concepts and receive feedback, ensuring a comprehensive grasp of the subject's applications in healthcare and public health.

Compare and contrast different methods of data collection and statistical analysis
Generate (using a statistical package) and interpret descriptive statistics and bivariate statistical analyses
Determine the appropriate sample size and statistical power for a study design

Historical and contemporary examples, including the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, inform public health responses and challenges.

The subject covers principles of communicable disease control, such as surveillance, outbreak investigation, and prevention, using case studies. Additionally, it emphasises integrated, collaborative approaches, consumer engagement, and advocacy. Demonstrate the epidemiological principles underpinning communicable disease prevention and control

Critically appraise the use of public health approaches to communicable disease control

Adopting type 2 diabetes mellitus, as an exemplar, emphasis is placed on appraising the contributory factors and addressing the challenges in the prevention, management and minimisation of complications of chronic conditions.  The subject emphasises health promotion and health literacy to support self-management and prevention of chronic conditions.

You'll engage in orientation activities to prepare for assessments and connect with peers. Independent learning is facilitated through weekly online resources, enhancing your knowledge and application in practice. Participation in Zoom meetings is crucial for collaborative learning and receiving feedback, which is integral to your development. The subject content is regularly updated to ensure its quality and relevance, with positive feedback from previous offerings.

Explain the aetiology of type two diabetes and its role as a determinant in other chronic conditions.
Appraise strategies to optimise self-management and health promotion in populations with chronic and complex illnesses.
Identify the health inequalities and specific needs of Indigenous Australians at risk of, or living with, chronic conditions.

090043.description:
This subject introduces students to economic principles relevant to healthcare. It covers market behaviours, welfare economics, and market failure in the health care sector. Students learn to apply economic concepts to optimise health and wellbeing despite resource constraints. Additionally, the subject emphasises the role of government interventions in health care markets.

Engage with independent learning activities, including quizzes and exercises, to progress effectively through the subject. Online collaborative Zoom sessions offer practical case studies and discussions, facilitating shared learning and the opportunity to ask questions. You'll receive both formative and summative feedback throughout the course to guide your learning journey.

Analyse the implications of common sources of market failure in health and health care
Appraise the economic reasons for policy intervention in health and health care and the consequences of such interventions

090041.title: Legal and Ethical Issues in Women's Health
090041.description:
Women’s health issues across the lifespan can generate challenging ethical and legal considerations. This subject explores these issues and provides students with the opportunity to critically analyse how women’s health issues can also be a result of legal and ethical infringement upon women’s bodies. In particular, matters pertaining to reproduction and birth disproportionately affect women, and engender controversial ethical debate and legal disputes. By focusing on health issues and the use of case studies, students consider some of these issues as they have developed in Australia, but also understanding broader concerns from an international perspective.

This subject also allows students to explore the ethics of being a health care practitioner for women and children in relation to codes and principles affecting women’s health and well-being, as well as individual perceptions of integrity and morals.
learningOutcomes: Critically analyse how women’s health issues across the lifespan can generate challenging ethical and legal concerns.
Connect debates and legal disputes of reproduction and birth to female autonomy and reframe these within a woman-centred philosophy.
Critique reporting of legal and ethical trespass upon the female body in order to interpret the impact on female autonomy.
Critically reflect on the components of self (physical, psychological, social, cultural, environmental & spiritual) as an element to self-perceptions of women’s legal and ethical status.

013458.title: Mathematics for Numeracy Teachers
013458.description: This subject introduces the concept that numeracy skills are needed in various aspects of people's lives, including their educational experiences in primary, secondary, and adult education. Your learning in this subject will focus on selected topics in the areas of whole number, geometry and space; measurements and estimation, rational number, patterns and algebra; and data handling and probability. A multimodal pedagogy including digital, visual and artifactual resources is used to facilitate your meaning-making of mathematical ideas in multiple ways. In your assessment tasks, you will be able to focus on an area that is most relevant to your own needs and professional practices. You will design and carry out mathematical investigations to extend your understanding of the selected topics.

Use multimodal resources to make meaning of mathematical concepts
Identify, analyse and resolve mathematical misconceptions
Design and carry out mathematical investigations to extend understanding of mathematical topics and apply mathematical methods to solve problems
Communicate clearly and accurately using academic conventions appropriate to the field of numeracy

013450.title: Professional Experience: The Primary School Child
013450.description: In this subject, you will focus on developing a learner-centred approach to teaching, which considers the unique needs and characteristics of developing children and pre-adolescents. Through a multidisciplinary approach, exploring key theories, empirical research, and practical applications, the subject develops theoretical perspectives on human development and applies them to the primary school context to inform the development of practice in diverse educational settings and learner needs, with a focus on inclusive, effective, and developmentally appropriate learning environments. A key part of this subject is a four-week placement where you will work in a school with support and mentoring from your UTS tertiary supervisor and supervising classroom teacher. During your placement, you are closely supervised and begin learning practice capabilities in lesson planning, teaching, assessment, Indigenous truth telling and knowledge, equity and inclusion, classroom management, digital supported learning, and school-community building.
learningOutcomes: Analyse how primary children learn and change, and how student motivation develops
Analyse complex teaching and learning scenarios that affect the primary child
Develop theoretically sound strategies for creating supportive teaching and learning environments for primary school children in diverse and complex contexts
Articulate and scrutinise challenging issues facing young Australians and their teachers in schools drawing on relevant theoretical concepts, research and policy

013451.title: Professional Experience: Classroom Management
013451.description: This subject develops your capacity to support the wellbeing of primary-aged students. You will learn how to develop and refine your classroom management skills to equip you with the essential tools for creating a conducive learning environment by investigating instructional planning, delivery techniques and relationship development. Emphasising the significance of classroom management policies, legislation, and guidelines related to school student well-being, the subject aims to empower you to maximize school student engagement and foster an optimal learning experience in primary education settings. A key part of this subject is a four-week professional experience placement, during which you will receive support and mentoring from your UTS tertiary supervisor and supervising classroom teacher. You will develop your capabilities in lesson planning, teaching, assessment, ensuring equity and inclusion, classroom management, ICT- supported learning, and school-community building, communication skills, including positive reinforcement and conflict resolution, to effectively manage student behaviour and foster a respectful classroom culture. Please note that you are required to meet the expectations of your chosen specialisation in the four-year, vertical stack BEdFut/MTeach Primary. The supervisor will, therefore, include in their assessment report, feedback about evidence of your capacity to implement classroom practices in the teaching of your chosen specialisation, plus a breadth of other KLAs and cross-curriculum priority areas, to a level than can be expected of a pre-service teacher who is one year through their four-year, vertical stack BEdFut/MTeach Primary. Satisfactory completion of the placement is a minimum requirement for this subject so you must pass your placement in order to pass the subject overall. The placement is pass/fail. The coursework component of the subject is graded and is designed to help you learn to establish clear expectations and consistent routines to create a structured, supportive learning environment. This subject will also help you to develop strong communication skills, including positive reinforcement and conflict resolution, to effectively manage student behaviour and foster a respectful classroom culture.
learningOutcomes: Organise classroom activities and provide clear directions
Apply practical approaches to manage challenging behaviour in the classroom and the whole-school context.
Devise and implement strategies that support students’ wellbeing and safety aligned to current local and centralised policy directives.
Appraise theories that inform approaches to manage student wellbeing and challenging behaviour in the classroom and the whole-school context.
Produce accurate and coherent academic text.

013452.title: Professional Experience: Teaching EAL/D and Literacy in Primary Schools
013452.description: In this subject, pre-service teachers build knowledge about the language and learning environment for students in schools learning English as an Additional Language or Dialect (EAL/D). The subject looks at how EAL/D and literacy are framed in curriculum documents, and subsequently translated into teaching and assessment activities in school settings. The subject takes an approach of “high challenge, high support” to explore how teachers provide explicit and targeted language and literacy support to help school students achieve learning goals. A key part of this subject is a four-week placement as a pre-service teacher, receiving support and mentoring during this period from their UTS tertiary supervisor and supervising classroom teacher. During their placement, pre-service teachers are closely supervised and begin learning practice capabilities in lesson planning, teaching, assessment, Indigenous truth telling and knowledge, equity and inclusion, classroom management and school-community building. Pre-service teachers receive feedback and the opportunity to reflect on their experience and learning after lesson observations with their classroom supervisor and UTS Tertiary Supervisor. Feedback is supported by appropriate strategies and lesson modelling. Satisfactory completion of the placement is a minimum requirement for this subject so pre-service teachers must pass their placement in order to pass the subject overall. The placement is pass/fail. The coursework component of the subject is graded and is designed to help pre-service teachers develop a better understanding of themselves as educators, gaining insight into the principles that underpin effective teaching practices.

013453.title: Professional Experience: Teacher Performance Assessment
013453.description:
This is the final professional experience subject and includes a 20-day internship where pre-service teachers take responsibility for lesson planning and teaching a class-cohort in a primary school. Pre-service teachers are supervised by an experienced in-service teacher who prepares an assessment report about the students’ achievement of AITSL/NESA graduate teaching standards. The external supervisor does not recommend grades or marks; instead, either an ungraded Pass or Fail. In the coursework component, pre-service teachers are required to prepare a Teaching Performance Assessment portfolio, which is developed and implemented by a consortium of Australian higher education providers that have Initial Teacher Education (ITE) faculties or schools. Four elements have been designed, trialled and consequently refined, to generate an assessment instrument that represents a robust, comprehensive and authentic series of tasks that reflect teaching. The four elements are:

Element 1: Planning for learning and teaching

Element 2: Analysing teaching practice

Element 3: Assessing for impact on student learning

Element 4: Expanding practice.

012241.title: Mathematics Education for Primary School 1
012241.description: In this subject you will study the major components of the NSW Mathematics K-10 Syllabus. This will include syllabus content such as whole number, measurement, data and chance. You will be introduced to planning mathematics activities and lessons for primary school students at different stages of their learning. You will also be expected to apply learning theories about primary aged students’ development of mathematical concepts and proficiencies to create powerful learning experiences in primary mathematics. This subject includes assessment tasks that require you to practise your teaching and explanation skills while on professional experience placement. The subject guides you in developing understanding of how to work mathematically and how to teach the Mathematics K-10 Syllabus. You will develop your teaching practice through modelling using hands-on collaborative tasks so you can learn and use mathematical knowledge confidently in your teaching. You will develop critical insights about the teaching of mathematics in primary school and develop your capacity to reflect on your knowledge and practice.

Plan and implement mathematical lessons appropriate for primary-aged students.

010046.title: Learning Futures: Teaching for Complexity and Diversity
010046.description: This subject analyses how social, political, economic, and cultural factors converge to shape Australian secondary schools, educational policies, and outcomes. You will engage with theories and debates to critically reflect on and understand the social and historical constructs of educational beliefs and practices. Key topics include socialisation in schools, capital and inequality, globalisation, gender, and multicultural education. Through a research-based approach, you will learn to apply culturally responsive practices in classrooms, preparing you to navigate and influence the complex educational landscape.

028003.title: Children's Literature and Drama for Primary School
028003.description: This subject develops pre-service teachers' understanding of literature and drama in a primary school context. Students examine a wide range of literature in growing complexity with specific reference to texts that evoke personal, social, cultural, and aesthetic values for K-6 students across genres including contemporary, historical and classical texts. Texts include conceptualisations of childhood and adolescence, subjectivity and gender, hope and sustainability, ethnicity, culture and Indigenous stories by Australian Aboriginal authors. Pre-service teachers critically analyse key aspects of literary theory including narrative theory, metafiction, and intertextuality to examine and respond to the literature. They explore acting techniques and skills required to perform for children at different stages of development – developing imagination, audibility, voice production, concentration and an awareness of the skills involved in interpreting a role and developing a character through drama, resulting in producing reader’s theatres and digitised story improvisations.

010308.title: Work: Learning Design Project
010308.description:
Ready to put all your skills and knowledge into practice?

This capstone subject is essential for synthesising and applying the skills and knowledge you have developed throughout the Graduate Certificate in Learning Design. It provides you with a real-world context to demonstrate your capabilities and create impactful learning solutions.

In this subject, you will engage in a comprehensive learning design project. You'll collaborate closely with an organisation or subject matter expert from industry or UTS to propose and develop a learning design solution for a specific scenario. This practical project allows you to integrate and apply what you've learned in previous subjects.

You'll identify a learning need and create a tailored solution. This involves conducting a needs analysis, designing and developing the learning intervention, and ensuring it meets the specified requirements. You will also present your solution to your fellow students and panel of industry experts.

It is recommended that this subject be completed last in the Graduate Certificate, as it builds on all the knowledge and skills acquired in prior subjects, culminating in a real-world application that showcases your proficiency as a learning designer.

This subject examines the sociocultural and environmental influences on the health and wellbeing of children. Students gain an understanding of the unique challenges experienced by children and young people, exploring the role that the modern world has on the social, developmental, physical, intellectual, emotional, environmental and spiritual dimensions of a child’s health and wellbeing. 090002.title: Family and Community Health in Practice
090002.description: Children and families live within communities and are an integral part of the wider socio-ecological model of society. This subject investigates the broader perspective of community health and wellness. The shared community responsibility of family support is explored together with processes that promote family and community health and wellness. Students develop their understanding of family function, assessment, and stress factors, especially related to transitional periods. Using a strengths-based, anticipatory guidance model, students develop advanced skills to interact appropriately with families building on families' strengths and determining appropriate interventions. Students gain an increased appreciation of the significant role the family plays in relation to the mental and physical health and wellbeing of its members and to the health of the whole community.

013126.title: Human Society and its Environment Teaching Methods 2
013126.description:
This subject builds upon the foundations established in HSIE Teaching Methods 1 and prepares pre-service teachers for more advanced curriculum interpretation, pedagogical decision-making, assessment design, and disciplinary teaching within senior secondary HSIE contexts. The subject supports pre-service teachers to deepen their understanding of curriculum, pedagogy, inquiry, and assessment within one of four disciplinary pathways: Business Studies, Economics, Legal Studies, or Society and Culture.

The subject combines a shared pedagogical core with discipline-specific pathways. Across the shared components, pre-service teachers critically examine contemporary approaches to explicit teaching, formative assessment, differentiation, disciplinary literacy, retrieval practice, scaffolded instruction, feedback, inquiry learning, ICT integration, and evidence-informed teaching practice within senior secondary HSIE classrooms. 

Within the disciplinary pathways, pre-service teachers develop increasingly specialised understandings of the distinctive epistemologies, inquiry traditions, literacy practices, curriculum structures, assessment approaches, and pedagogical orientations associated with Business Studies, Economics, Legal Studies, or Society and Culture education. This includes engagement with forms of disciplinary reasoning such as economic analysis, legal reasoning, civic and ethical dialogue, social inquiry, policy critique, stakeholder analysis, evidence evaluation, interpretation of competing perspectives, and analysis of contemporary social, economic, legal, political, and cultural issues.

The subject foregrounds the role of HSIE education in supporting democratic participation, civic engagement, ethical reasoning, consumer and financial literacy, social justice, intercultural understanding, and informed participation in contemporary society. Pre-service teachers engage critically with contemporary debates and controversies relevant to their disciplinary teaching area and examine approaches to teaching sensitive, contested, and complex issues in secondary classrooms.

Pre-service teachers participate in curriculum interpretation activities, collaborative planning workshops, micro-teaching, assessment design, lesson sequencing, disciplinary inquiry activities, and structured reflection tasks designed to strengthen classroom readiness and professional judgement. The subject also strengthens preparation for Professional Experience through sustained engagement with syllabus interpretation, assessment practices, classroom management, differentiation, and professional reflection within senior secondary HSIE contexts.

The subject maintains a strong emphasis on disciplinary competence within individual HSIE teaching pathways while simultaneously preparing pre-service teachers to work collaboratively across the broader HSIE learning area and within contemporary whole-school educational contexts.
learningOutcomes: Analyse and interpret Stage 6 HSIE syllabus documents to identify the distinctive curriculum structures, disciplinary inquiry traditions, conceptual frameworks, and pedagogical expectations associated with Business Studies, Economics, Legal Studies, or Society and Culture teaching.

Design, sequence, and justify lesson plans, learning activities, and assessment strategies that incorporate explicit teaching, scaffolded instruction, disciplinary literacy, retrieval practice, formative assessment, and evidence-informed pedagogy within senior secondary HSIE classrooms.

Apply discipline-specific pedagogical approaches appropriate to Business Studies, Economics, Legal Studies, or Society and Culture, including economic reasoning, legal reasoning, social inquiry, policy critique, stakeholder analysis, evidence evaluation, interpretation of competing perspectives, and inquiry-based learning.

Critically evaluate contemporary social, economic, legal, political, business, and cultural issues and examine approaches to teaching controversial, sensitive, and contested topics within secondary HSIE classrooms.

Develop and apply strategies that support democratic participation, civic engagement, ethical reasoning, consumer and financial literacy, intercultural understanding, and informed participation in contemporary society through HSIE education.

Select, evaluate, and apply a range of resources, including ICT, digital technologies, multimodal texts, case studies, policy documents, legal sources, economic data, media texts, and inquiry materials that support student engagement and disciplinary understanding in senior secondary HSIE.

Demonstrate professional judgement through reflective practice, collaborative planning, peer feedback, curriculum evaluation, and micro-teaching activities designed to strengthen classroom readiness and professional learning within senior secondary HSIE contexts.

Compose scholarly written and oral responses, based on sound academic conventions, including accurate referencing, and communicate disciplinary ideas, pedagogical reasoning, curriculum interpretations, and professional reflections clearly and effectively in written, oral, and multimodal forms.

013204.description:
HSIE Teaching Methods 3: Business Studies, Economics, Legal Studies and Society and Culture focuses on advanced pedagogical practices for teaching Stage 6 Human Society and Its Environment (HSIE) subjects within the disciplinary pathways of Business Studies, Economics, Legal Studies, and Society and Culture. The subject develops your capacity to design coherent learning sequences, implement standards-referenced assessment practices, interpret and apply HSC marking criteria, support disciplinary literacy, and exercise professional judgement within complex senior secondary teaching contexts. The subject foregrounds advanced curriculum planning, explicit teaching, inquiry-based learning, disciplinary reasoning, formative assessment, metacognition, and evaluation of teaching programs within Stage 6 classrooms. You will engage critically with the distinctive epistemologies, inquiry traditions, literacy practices, and assessment cultures of their specialist discipline while also examining the shared pedagogical core underpinning senior secondary HSIE teaching. Particular emphasis is placed on:

  • HSC-oriented pedagogy;
  • standards-referenced assessment;
  • stimulus-based assessment design;
  • marking and moderation practices;
  • disciplinary literacy;
  • quantitative, legal, sociological, and commercial reasoning;
  • formative feedback;
  • differentiation;
  • and reflective professional practice.

You will analyse and design assessment tasks, marking guidelines, learning sequences, and disciplinary inquiry activities aligned to NESA Stage 6 syllabus outcomes and contemporary evidence-informed pedagogical approaches. The subject also develops your capacity to evaluate teaching programs, interpret evidence of student learning, and adapt curriculum and assessment practices to improve student engagement and achievement. The subject builds upon concepts introduced in Professional Learning, Literacy and Numeracy Across the Curriculum, Teaching Practice 2: Teaching Practice Portfolio by extending them into advanced Stage 6 disciplinary contexts requiring autonomous curriculum judgement, sophisticated assessment literacy, and advanced pedagogical reasoning. The subject prepares you for autonomous professional practice within senior secondary HSIE classrooms through engagement with authentic teacher work including:

  • curriculum programming;
  • assessment design;
  • HSC marking and moderation;
  • feedback practices;
  • inquiry pedagogy;
  • and reflective evaluation of teaching and learning programs.
learningOutcomes: Analyse syllabus documents to ascertain assessment policies, procedures and practice in Stage 6 HSIE subjects within the disciplinary pathways of Business Studies, Economics, Legal Studies, and Society and Culture, including standards-referenced assessment requirements and curriculum structures.

Explain the disciplinary concepts, inquiry traditions, disciplinary literacy practices, and curriculum requirements accurately, including catering to the needs of Indigenous Australian (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander) students and other students with identified needs.
Evaluate and reflect on student assessment evidence, feedback practices, and teaching programs as a means of modifying and improving professional HSIE teaching practice and student learning.

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of research into how students learn and the implications for teaching, including explicit teaching, disciplinary inquiry, formative assessment, metacognition, differentiation, and evidence-informed pedagogical practice.
